The contact of sense-organ and object is to be mentioned, not the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>. For sometimes a person, having set a time for waking, sleeps and wakes due to that prior resolution. But when intense sounds and touches become the cause of waking, the waking-knowledge of the sleeping person arises due to the contact of sense-organ (with object). In that case, the contact of the knower and <s>manas</s> does not have primacy. Rather, the contact of sense-organ and object (has primacy). For the <s>ātman</s>, desiring to know, does not then impel <s>manas</s> by effort.
Sometimes a person, whose mind is absorbed in another object, desiring to know another object due to volition, connects the sense-organ through effort-impelled <s>manas</s> and knows that other object. But when knowledge arises for one who is without volition, without desire to know, and whose mind is absorbed, due to the impingement of an external object — then the contact of sense-organ and object has primacy.

children.text:
% -sannikarṣasya prādhānyam/] p.458
na hy atrāsau jijñāsamānaḥ prayatnena manaḥ prerayatīti/ prādhānyāc cendriyārthasannikarṣasya grahaṇaṃ kāryaṃ guṇatvād nātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasyeti//27//
children.translated_text:
[Note: -sannikarṣasya prādhānyam/] p.458
For in that case, he does not, desiring to know, impel <s>manas</s> by effort. And because of the primacy of the contact of sense-organ and object, its mention should be made; because of the subsidiary role of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, theirs should not. // 27 //
[Section: NySBh_2,1.28]
And another reason for the primacy —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.28: And the designation of specific cognitions is by those (sense-organs and objects).

children.text: tair indriyair arthaiś ca vyapadiśyante jñānaviśeṣāḥ/ katham? ghrāṇena jighrati, cakṣuṣā paśyati, rasanayā rasayatīti, ghrāṇavijñānaṃ cakṣurvijñānaṃ rasanāvijñānaṃ gandhavijñānaṃ rūpavijñānaṃ rasavijñānam iti ca/ indriyaviṣayaviśeṣāc ca pañcadhā buddhir bhavati/ ataḥ prādhānyam indriyārthasannikarṣasyeti//28//
children.translated_text: Specific cognitions are designated by those sense-organs and objects. How? 'One smells with the nose, one sees with the eye, one tastes with the tongue' — and '<s>ghrāṇa-vijñāna</s> (nose-consciousness), <s>cakṣur-vijñāna</s> (eye-consciousness), <s>rasanā-vijñāna</s> (tongue-consciousness), <s>gandha-vijñāna</s> (smell-consciousness), <s>rūpa-vijñāna</s> (form-consciousness), <s>rasa-vijñāna</s> (taste-consciousness).' And because of the specific difference of sense-organs and sense-objects, cognition is fivefold. Therefore the contact of sense-organ and object has primacy. // 28 //
[Section: NySBh_2,1.29]

children.text:
% p.451
yad uktam indriyārthasannikarṣagrahaṇaṃ kāryam, nātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasyeti, kasmāt? suptavyāsaktamanasām indriyārthayoḥ sannikarṣasya jñānanimittatvād iti/ so 'yam ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.451]
It was stated that the mention of the contact of sense-organ and object should be made, not of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>. Why? Because for those who are asleep or whose minds are absorbed, the contact of sense-organ and object is the cause of knowledge. This —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.29: (This reason) is not valid because it is self-contradictory.

children.text: yadi tāvat kvacid ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasya jñānakāraṇatvaṃ neṣyate, tadā ``yugapajjñānānutpattir manaso liṅgam'' iti vyāhanyeta/ nedānīṃ manasaḥ sannikarṣam indriyārthasannikarṣo 'pekṣate/
children.translated_text: If the causal status of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> for knowledge is denied in some cases, then the statement 'the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is the mark of <s>manas</s>' would be contradicted. In that case, the contact of sense-organ and object would not depend on the contact of <s>manas</s>.

children.text:
% p.460 -yārthasannikarṣo .pekṣate/] p.460
manaḥsaṃyogānapekṣāyāṃ ca yugapajjñānotpattiprasaṅgaḥ/ atha mā bhūd vyāghāta iti sarvavijñānānām ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣaḥ kāraṇam iṣyate, tadavastham evedaṃ bhavati; jñānakāraṇatvād ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣasya grahaṇaṃ kāryam iti//29//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.460 -yārthasannikarṣo .pekṣate/] p.460
And when the dependence on the contact of <s>manas</s> is denied, the consequence of simultaneous arising of cognitions follows. If, to avoid this contradiction, the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is accepted as a cause of all cognitions, then the situation remains the same — because of the causal status of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, its mention should be made. // 29 //
[Section: NySBh_2,1.30]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.30: No, because of the strength of the particular object.

children.text: nāsti vyāghātaḥ, na hy ātmamanaḥsannikarṣasya jñānakāraṇatvaṃ vyabhicarati/ indriyārthasannikarṣasya prādhānyam upādīyate/ arthaviśeṣaprābalyād dhi suptavyāsaktamanasāṃ jñānotpattir ekadā bhavati/ arthaviśeṣaḥ kaścid evendriyārthaḥ, tasya prābalyaṃ tīvratāpaṭute/ tac cārthaviśeṣaprābalyam indriyārthasannikarṣaviṣayaṃ nātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣaviṣayam, tasmād indriyārthasannikarṣaḥ pradhānam iti/
children.translated_text: There is no contradiction. For the causal status of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> for knowledge does not deviate. The primacy of the contact of sense-organ and object is maintained. For it is because of the strength of the particular object that the arising of knowledge sometimes occurs for those who are asleep or whose minds are absorbed. The 'particular object' is a certain sense-object; its 'strength' is its intensity and sharpness. And that strength of the particular object pertains to the domain of the contact of sense-organ and object, not to the domain of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>; therefore the contact of sense-organ and object is primary.

children.text:
% p.461
asati praṇidhāne saṅkalpe cāsati suptavyāsaktamanasāṃ yad indriyārthasannikarṣād utpadyate jñānam, tatra manaḥsaṃyogo 'pi kāraṇam iti manasi kriyākāraṇaṃ vācyam iti/
yathaiva jñātuḥ khalv ayam icchājanitaḥ prayatno manasaḥ preraka ātmaguṇaḥ, evam ātmani guṇāntaraṃ sarvasya sādhakaṃ pravṛttidoṣajanitam asti, yena preritaṃ mana indriyeṇa sambadhyate/ tena hy apreryamāṇe manasi saṃyogābhāvāj jñānānutpattau sarvārthatāsya nivarttate/ eṣitavyaṃ cāsya guṇāntarasya dravyaguṇakarmakāraṇatvam, anyathā hi caturvidhānām aṇūnāṃ bhūtasūkṣmāṇāṃ manasāṃ ca tato 'nyasya kriyāhetor asambhavāt śarīrendriyaviṣayāṇām anutpattiprasaṅgaḥ//30//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.461]
In the absence of prior resolution and in the absence of volition, when knowledge arises for those who are asleep or whose minds are absorbed from the contact of sense-organ and object, even then the contact of <s>manas</s> is a cause — and so an operative cause for <s>manas</s> must be stated.
Just as this effort born of desire of the knower is a quality of <s>ātman</s> that impels <s>manas</s>, so too there exists in <s>ātman</s> another quality, born of the defect of activity (<s>pravṛttidoṣa</s>), that accomplishes everything, by which <s>manas</s>, being impelled, connects with the sense-organ. For when <s>manas</s> is not impelled, due to the absence of conjunction, knowledge does not arise, and its omnipresence is negated. And the status of this other quality as a cause of substance, quality, and action must be investigated; for otherwise, since there is no possibility of another cause of activity for the four kinds of atoms, subtle elements, and minds, the consequence of non-origination of body, sense-organs, and sense-objects would follow. // 30 //
[Section: NySBh_2,1.31]
[Note: p.462]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.31: <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is (really) <s>anumāna</s> (inference), because apprehension arises from grasping only a part.

children.text: yad idam indriyārthasannikarṣād utpadyate jñānaṃ vṛkṣa iti, etat kila pratyakṣam, tat khalv anumānam eva/ kasmāt? ekadeśagrahaṇād vṛkṣasyopalabdheḥ/ arvāgbhāgam ayaṃ gṛhītvā vṛkṣam upalabhate/ na caikadeśo vṛkṣaḥ/ tatra yathā dhūmaṃ gṛhītvā vahnim anuminoti tādṛg eva tad bhavati/
children.translated_text: The knowledge that arises from the contact of sense-organ and object as 'this is a tree' — that, it is claimed, is perception; but it is really just inference. Why? Because the apprehension of a tree arises from grasping only a part. One grasps the near side and apprehends the tree. But a single part is not the tree. In that case, just as one grasps smoke and infers fire, so too is this.

children.text:
% p.463
kiṃ punar gṛhyamāṇād ekadeśād arthāntaram anumeyaṃ manyase? avayavasamūhapakṣe avayavāntarāṇi dravyāntarotpattipakṣe tāni cāvavavī ceti/ avayavasamūhapakṣe tāvad ekadeśagrahaṇād vṛkṣabuddher abhāvaḥ, nāgṛhyamāṇam ekadeśāntaraṃ vṛkṣo gṛhyamāṇaikadeśavad iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.463]
But what other thing do you consider to be inferred from the part that is being grasped? On the view that the whole is a collection of parts, (what is inferred are) the other parts; on the view that a distinct substance arises (from parts), those (other parts) and the whole (<s>avayavin</s>). On the view that the whole is a collection of parts, the cognition of a tree would be absent from grasping a single part, for the other part that is not grasped is not (identical with) the tree in the way the grasped part is.

children.text:
% p.464
athaikadeśagrahaṇād ekadeśāntarānumāne samudāyapratisandhānāt tatra vṛkṣabuddhiḥ? na tarhi vṛkṣabuddhir anumānam evaṃ sati bhavitum arhatīti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.464]
If, from grasping a single part, by inferring the other parts and synthesizing the collection, there arises the cognition of a tree? Then the tree-cognition, in that case, would not deserve to be (called) inference.

children.text:
% vṛkṣabuddhir anumānam evaṃ sati bhavitum arhatīti/] p.467
dravyāntarotpattipakṣe nāvayavyanumeyaḥ, asyaikadeśasambaddhasyāgrahaṇāt grahaṇe cāviśeṣād anumeyatvābhāvaḥ/ tasmād vṛkṣabuddhir anumānaṃ na bhavati//31//
children.translated_text:
[Note: vṛkṣabuddhir anumānam evaṃ sati bhavitum arhatīti/] p.467
On the view that a distinct substance arises, the whole is not to be inferred, because this (whole), which is connected to the part, is not grasped; and if it were grasped, there would be no difference (from perception), and hence no status as something to be inferred. Therefore the tree-cognition is not inference. // 31 //
[Section: NySBh_2,1.32]

children.text:
% p.468
ekadeśagrahaṇam āśritya pratyakṣasyānumānatvam upapādyate/ tac ca ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.468]
Relying on the grasping of a part, the status of perception as inference is argued. And that —

children.text: NyS_2,1.32: na, pratyakṣeṇa yāvat tāvad apy upalambhāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 2.1.32: No, because apprehension extends to as much as is (presented) by perception.

children.text:
na pratyakṣam anumānam, kasmāt? pratyakṣeṇaivopalambhāt/ yat tadekadeśagrahaṇam āśrīyate pratyakṣeṇāsāv upalambhaḥ/ na copalambho nirviṣayo 'sti/ yāvac cārthajātaṃ tasya viṣayas tāvad abhyupajñāyamānaṃ pratyakṣavyavasthāpakaṃ bhavati/
kiṃ punas tato 'nyad arthajātam, avayavī samudāyo vā? na caikadeśagrahaṇam anumānaṃ bhāvayituṃ śakyaṃ hetvabhāvād iti/
children.translated_text:
Perception is not inference. Why? Because it is apprehended by perception alone. That grasping of a part which is relied upon — that apprehension is by perception. And there is no apprehension without an object. And to the extent that there is a class of objects serving as its object, to that extent what is acknowledged is that which establishes the perceptual [nature of the cognition].
What then is the other class of objects — the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) or the aggregate (<s>samudāya</s>)? And the grasping of a part cannot be made into inference, because there is no inferential mark (<s>hetu</s>).

children.text:
% p.469
anyathāpi ca pratyakṣasya nānumānatvaprasaṅgas tatpūrvakatvāt --- pratyakṣapūrvakam anumānam, sambaddhāv agnidhūmau pratyakṣato dṛṣṭavato dhūmapratyakṣadarśanād agnāv anumānaṃ bhavati/ yac ca sambaddhayor liṅgaliṅginoḥ pratyakṣam, yac ca liṅgamātrapratyakṣagrahaṇam, naitad antareṇa anumānasya pravṛttir asti; na tv etad anumānam indriyārthasannikarṣajatvāt/ na cānumeyasyendriyeṇa sannikarṣād anumānaṃ bhavati/ so 'ya. pratyakṣānumānayor lakṣaṇabhedo mahān āśrayitavya iti/
children.translated_text:
[p.469]
Moreover, there is no possibility that perception becomes inference for another reason as well — because [inference] is preceded by it. Inference is preceded by perception: one who has perceived the connection (<s>sambandha</s>) between fire and smoke through perception, from the perceptual observation of smoke, makes an inference regarding fire. Both the perception of the connected sign (<s>liṅga</s>) and the signified (<s>liṅgin</s>), and the perceptual grasping of the sign alone — without these, inference does not proceed. But this [perception] is not inference, because it arises from the contact of a sense organ with an object. And inference does not arise from the contact of a sense organ with what is to be inferred. This great difference in the definitions of perception and inference must be maintained.

children.text:
% p.470
na caikadeśopalabdhir avayavisadbhāvāt/ na caikadeśopalabdhimātram/ kiṃ tarhi? ekadeśopalabdhiḥ tatsahacaritāvayavyupalabdhiś ca/ kasmāt? avayavisadbhāvāt/ asti hy ayam ekadeśavyatirikto 'vayavī tasyāvayavasthānasyopalabdhikāraṇaprāptasyaikadeśopalabdhāv anupalabdhir anupapanneti/
akṛtsnagrahaṇād iti cet, na kāraṇato 'nyasyaikadeśasyābhāvāt --- na cāvayavāḥ kṛtsnā gṛhyante avayavair evāvayavāntaravyavadhānāt,
children.translated_text:
[p.470]
And the apprehension of a part is not [merely that] because of the existence of the whole (<s>avayavin</s>). [The cognition] is not merely the apprehension of a part. What then? It is the apprehension of a part together with the apprehension of the whole that accompanies it. Why? Because of the existence of the whole. For this whole, being distinct from the parts, when the part — which is the locus [of the whole] and which is expected to be a cause of apprehension — is apprehended, it is untenable that [the whole] is not apprehended.
If [one objects] 'because the whole is not grasped' — no, because there is no part other than its cause. And the parts are not grasped in their entirety, because other parts are obstructed by [intervening] parts,

children.text:
% kṛtsnā gṛhyante avayavair evāvayavāntaravyavadhānāt, ] p.471
nāvayavī kṛtsno gṛhyata iti, nāyaṃ gṛhyamnāṇeṣv avayaveṣu parisamāpta iti, seyam ekaddeśopalabdhir anivṛttaiveti/
kṛtsnam iti vai khalv aśeṣatāyāṃ satyāṃ bhavati, akṛtsnam iti śeṣe sati, tac caitad avayaveṣu bahuṣv asti avyavadhāne grahaṇād vyavadhāne cāgrahaṇād iti/ aṅga tu bhavān pṛṣṭo vyācaṣṭāṃ gṛhyamāṇasyāvayavinaḥ kim agṛhītaṃ manyate?
children.translated_text:
[cont.] parts are not grasped in their entirety because other parts are obstructed by parts themselves; [p.471]
nor is the whole grasped in its entirety — thus [the whole] is not completed in the parts that are being grasped — and so this is merely the apprehension of a part and nothing more.
'Entire' (<s>kṛtsna</s>) indeed applies when there is completeness; 'not entire' (<s>akṛtsna</s>) when there is a remainder. And this applies to the parts — many [parts] are grasped when there is no obstruction, and not grasped when there is obstruction. But let the questioner, when asked, explain: of the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) that is being grasped, what does he consider to be ungrasped,

children.text:
% bhavān pṛṣṭo ... agṛhītaṃ manyate?] p.472
yenaikadeśopalabdhiḥ syād iti/ na hy asya kāraṇebhyo 'nye ekadeśā bhavantīti tatrāvayavavṛttaṃ nopapadyata iti/
children.translated_text:
[p.472]
such that there would be [merely] the apprehension of a part? For there are no parts of [the whole] other than its causes; therefore the account in terms of parts is untenable.

children.text:
% nopapadyata iti/] p.473
idaṃ tasya vṛttam --- yeṣām indriyasannikarṣād grahaṇam avayavānāṃ taiḥ saha gṛhyate, yeṣām avayavānāṃ vyavadhānād agrahaṇaṃ taiḥ saha na gṛhyate/ na caitatkṛto 'sti bheda iti/
children.translated_text:
[p.473]
This is its [correct] account: together with those parts whose grasping occurs through sense-contact, [the whole] is grasped; together with those parts whose grasping does not occur because of obstruction, [the whole] is not grasped. And there is no real difference produced by this.

children.text:
% p.477
samudāyaśeṣatā vā samudāyo vṛkṣaḥ syāt tatprāptir vā, ubhayathā grahaṇābhāvaḥ/ mūlaskandhaśākhāpalāśādīnām aśeṣatā vā samudāyo vṛkṣa iti syāt prāptir vā samudāyinām iti, ubhayathā samudāyabhūtasya vṛkṣasya grahaṇaṃ nopapadyata iti/ avayavais tāvad avayavāntarasya vyavadhānād aśeṣagrahaṇaṃ nopapadyate/ prāptigrahaṇam api nopapadyate prāptimatām agrahaṇāt/ seyam ekadeśagrahaṇasahacaritā vṛkṣavuddhir dravyāntarotpattau kalpate na samudayamātre iti//32//
children.translated_text:
[p.477]
Alternatively, a tree would be [either] the completeness of the aggregate (<s>samudāya</s>), or [merely] an aggregate — that is, [either] the totality of root, trunk, branches, leaves, and so forth, or [merely] a coming-together of aggregated [parts]. In either case, the grasping of the tree as an aggregate is untenable. As for [the first alternative], because other parts obstruct [some] parts, the grasping of all without remainder is untenable. And the grasping based on coming-together is also untenable, because those that have come together are not [all] grasped. Thus this cognition of a tree, accompanied by the grasping of a part, is fit for [postulating] the origination of a different substance (<s>dravyāntara</s>), not for a mere aggregate. //32//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.33: There is doubt regarding the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) because it is [itself] what needs to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>).

children.text: yad uktam avayavisadhbāvād iti, ayam ahetuḥ sādhyatvāt/ sādhyaṃ tāvad etat kāraṇebhyo dravyāntaram utpadyata iti, anupapāditam etat/ evaṃ ca sati vipratipattimātraṃ bhavati vipratipatteś cāvayavini saṃśaya iti//33//
children.translated_text: What was stated — 'because of the existence of the whole' — this is a non-reason (<s>ahetu</s>), because it is [itself] what needs to be proved (<s>sādhya</s>). That something different from the causes — [namely] a different substance — originates: this has not been demonstrated. This being so, there is merely a difference of opinion, and from the difference of opinion, there is doubt regarding the whole. //33//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.34: [There would be] non-grasping of everything if the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) did not exist.

children.text: yady avayavī nāsti sarvasya grahaṇaṃ nopapadyate/ kiṃ tat sarvam? dravyaguṇakarmasāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyāḥ/ kathaṃ kṛtvā? paramāṇusamavasthānaṃ tāvad darśanaviṣayo na bhavaty atīndriyatvād aṇūnām, dravyāntarañ cāvayavibhūtaṃ darśanaviṣayo nāsti, darśanaviṣayasthāś ceme dravyādayo gṛhante te niradhiṣṭhānā na gṛhyeran/ gṛhyante tu kumbho 'yaṃ śyāma eko mahān saṃyuktaḥ spandate asti mṛnmayaś ceti, santi ceme guṇādayo dharmā iti/ tena sarvasya grahaṇāt paśyāmo 'sti dravyāntarabhūto .vayavīti//34//
children.translated_text: If the whole does not exist, the grasping of everything would be untenable. What is that 'everything'? Substance (<s>dravya</s>), quality (<s>guṇa</s>), action (<s>karma</s>), universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), particularity (<s>viśeṣa</s>), and inherence (<s>samavāya</s>). How so? The state of aggregation of atoms (<s>paramāṇu</s>) is not an object of visual perception, since atoms are beyond the senses (<s>atīndriya</s>). And another substance, being a whole (<s>avayavin</s>), does not exist [on the opponent's view] as an object of perception. And these — substance and the rest — which are objects of perception, are grasped; [but] without a substratum, they would not be grasped. Yet they are grasped: 'This is a pot, dark-colored, one, large, conjoined, moving, existent, made of clay' — and these qualities and other properties do exist. Therefore, from the grasping of everything, we see that the whole, being a different substance, does exist. //34//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.35: And because of the applicability of supporting (<s>dhāraṇa</s>) and pulling (<s>ākarṣaṇa</s>).

children.text:
avayavy arthāntarabhūta iti/
saṅgrahakārite vai dhāraṇākarṣaṇe/ saṃgraho nāma saṃyogasahacaritaṃ guṇāntaraṃ snehadravatvakāritam, apāṃ saṃyogād āme kumbhe, agnisaṃyogāt pakve/ yadi tv avayavikārite abhaviṣyatāṃ pāṃśurāśiprabhṛtiśv apy ajñāsyetām/ dravyāntarānutpattau ca tṛṇopalakāṣṭhādiṣu jatusaṃgṛhīteṣv api nābhāviṣyatām iti/
children.translated_text:
The whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is a distinct entity.
Supporting and pulling are caused by cohesion (<s>saṅgraha</s>). Cohesion is a quality distinct [from conjunction], accompanied by conjunction, caused by viscosity (<s>sneha</s>) and fluidity (<s>dravatva</s>) — [arising] from the conjunction with water in an unbaked pot, and from the conjunction with fire in a baked one. If [supporting and pulling] were caused by the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) [alone], they would be known also in heaps of dust and the like. And if no distinct substance were produced, they would not occur even in straw, stones, wood, and so forth that are joined together by lac.

children.text:
% p.499
athāvayavinaṃ pratyācakṣāṇako mā bhūt pratyakṣalopa ity aṇusañcayaṃ darśanaviṣayaṃ pratijānānaḥ kim anuyoktavya iti/ ekam idaṃ dravyam ity ekavuddher viṣayaṃ paryanuyojyaḥ --- kim ekabuddhir abhinnārthaviṣayeti āhosvit bhinnārthaviṣayeti/ abhinnārthaviṣayeti cet ---
children.translated_text:
[p.499]
Now, one who denies the whole, claiming 'let there not be the loss of perception' [i.e. trying to preserve perception], and who asserts that an aggregate of atoms is an object of perception — what should he be asked? He should be questioned about the object of the unitary cognition 'this is one substance': is the unitary cognition directed at an undivided object, or at a divided object? If directed at an undivided object —

children.text:
% cet ---] p.500
arthāntarānujñānād avayavavisiddhiḥ/ nānārthaviṣayeti cet --- bhinneṣv ekadarśanānupapattiḥ anekasminn eka iti vyāhatā buddhir na dṛśyata iti//35//
children.translated_text:
[p.500]
then from the acknowledgment of something different [from the parts], the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is established. If directed at a divided object — then in the case of divided [things], the occurrence of a unitary perception is untenable; a contradictory cognition — 'one' regarding what is many — is not observed. //35//

children.text: NyS_2,1.36: senāvanavat grahaṇam iti cen nātīndriyatvād aṇūnām ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.1.36: If [one says] the grasping [is] like [that of] an army or a forest — no, because atoms are beyond the senses (<s>atīndriya</s>).

children.text: yathā senāṅgeṣu vanāṅgeṣu ca dūrād agṛhyamāṇapṛthaktveṣv ekam idam ity upapadyate buddhiḥ evam aṇuṣu sañciteṣv agṛhyamāṇapṛthaktveṣv ekam idam ity upapadyate buddhir iti/ yathā gṛhyamāṇapṛthaktvānāṃ senāvanāṅgānām ārāt kāraṇāntarataḥ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇam,
children.translated_text: Just as in the case of the members of an army or of a forest, when their individual distinctness is not grasped from a distance, the cognition 'this is one [thing]' is tenable — so too, when atoms are aggregated and their individual distinctness is not grasped, the cognition 'this is one [thing]' is tenable — [so says the opponent]. [Reply:] Just as the non-grasping of the distinctness of the members of an army or forest, whose distinctness is [in principle] graspable, occurs due to distance, i.e. due to another cause,

children.text:
% p.501
yathā gṛhyamāṇajātīnāṃ palāśa iti vā khadira iti vā nārāj jātigrahaṇaṃ bhavati/ yathā gṛhyamāṇapraspandānāṃ nārāt spandagrahaṇam, gṛhyamāṇe cārthajāte pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād ekam iti bhāktaḥ pratyayo bhavati, na tv aṇūnāṃ gṛhyamāṇapṛthaktvānāṃ kāraṇataḥ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād bhākta ekapratyayaḥ, atīndriyatvād aṇūnām iti/
children.translated_text:
[p.501]
just as the grasping of the species (<s>jāti</s>) of those whose species is graspable — [such as] '<s>palāśa</s>' or '<s>khadira</s>' — does not occur from a distance; just as the grasping of the movement of those whose movement is graspable does not occur from a distance; and when, among things being grasped, the distinctness is not grasped, there arises a figurative (<s>bhākta</s>) cognition 'one' — but in the case of atoms, whose distinctness is graspable, the non-grasping of their distinctness is not due to a [similar] cause, so the figurative unitary cognition [does not arise], because atoms are beyond the senses.

children.text:
% p.503
idam eva ca parīkṣyate kim ekapratyayo ṇusañcayaviṣaya āhosvit neti, aṇusañcaya eva senāvanāṅāni/ na ca parīkṣyamāṇam udāharaṇam iti yuktaṃ sādhyatvād iti/
dṛṣṭam iti cen na tadviṣayasya parīkṣopapatteḥ/ yad api manyeta dṛṣṭam idaṃ senāvanāṅgānāṃ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād abhedenaikam iti grahaṇam, na ca dṛṣṭaṃ śakyaṃ pratyākhyātum iti, tac ca naivam, tadviṣayasya parīkṣopapatteḥ --- darśanaviṣaya evāyaṃ parīkṣyate yo 'yam ekam iti pratyayo dṛśyate, sa parīkṣyate kiṃ dravyāntaraviṣayo vā athāṇusañcayaviṣaya iti/ atra darśanam anyatarasya sādhakaṃ na bhavati/ nānābhāve cāṇūnāṃ pṛthaktvasyāgrahaṇād abhedenaikam iti grahaṇam atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayaḥ, yathā sthāṇau puruṣa iti/ tataḥ kim?
children.translated_text:
[p.503]
And this is precisely what is being examined: whether the unitary cognition is directed at an aggregate of atoms or not. The aggregate of atoms is [analogous to] the members of an army or forest. And it is not proper for what is being examined to serve as an illustration, because it is [itself] what needs to be proved.
If [one says] 'it is observed' — no, because the examination of that very subject-matter is tenable. Even if one thinks 'it is observed that, due to non-grasping of the distinctness of members of an army or forest, there is a grasping [of them] as one through non-difference, and what is observed cannot be rejected' — that is not so, because the examination of that very subject-matter is tenable. The very thing that is the object of perception is being examined: this cognition that is seen as 'one' — is it examined [to determine] whether it is directed at a different substance, or at an aggregate of atoms? Here, observation does not establish either alternative. And in the manifoldness of atoms, if, from the non-grasping of distinctness, there is a grasping as 'one' through non-difference, that is a cognition of 'that' in what is 'not that' — like the cognition of a person in a tree-stump. What follows from that?

children.text:
% kim?] p.504
atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayasya pradhānāpekṣitvāt pradhānasiddhiḥ/ sthāṇau puruṣa iti pratyayasya kiṃ pradhānam? so 'sau puruṣe puruṣapratyayaḥ, tasmin sati puruṣasāmānyagrahaṇāt sthāṇau puruṣo .yam iti/ evaṃ nānābhūteṣv ekam iti sāmānyagrahaṇāt pradhāne sati bhavitum arhati/ pradhānaṃ ca sarvasyāgrahaṇād iti nopapadyate/ tasmād abhinna evāyam abhedapratyaya ekam iti/
children.translated_text:
[p.504]
Since the cognition of 'that' in 'not that' is dependent upon a paradigm case (<s>pradhāna</s>), the paradigm is established. What is the paradigm of the cognition 'person' in a tree-stump? It is the cognition of a person in [an actual] person; because in that [actual] case, from the grasping of the universal 'person,' [the cognition arises] 'this is a person,' [and then by analogy] in the tree-stump. Likewise, from the grasping of the universal 'one' in manifold [things], the paradigm [case of actual unity] must exist. And the paradigm — [namely] that the non-grasping of everything [does not occur, i.e. that some unity is indeed grasped] — is untenable [on the opponent's view]. Therefore this unitary cognition 'one' is indeed [directed] at something that is undivided.

children.text:
% p.505
indriyāntaraviṣayeṣv abhedapratyayaḥ pradhānam iti ced, na viśeṣahetvabhāvād dṛṣṭāntāvyavasthā --- śrotrādiviṣayeṣu śabdādiṣv abhinneṣv ekapratyayaḥ pradhānam anekasminn ekapratyayasyeti/ evaṃ ca sati dṛṣṭāntopādānaṃ na vyavatiṣṭhate viśeṣahetvabhāvāt/ aṇuṣu saṃśiteṣv ekapratyayaḥ kim atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayaḥ sthāṇau puruṣapratyayavat, athārthasya tathābhāvāt tasmiṃs tad iti pratyayaḥ yathā śabdasyaikatvād ekaḥ śabda iti viśeṣahetuparigrahaṇam antareṇa dṛṣṭāntau saṃśayam āpādayata iti/ kumbhavatsañcayamātraṃ gandhādayo 'pīty anudāharaṇaṃ gandhādaya iti/
children.translated_text:
[p.505]
If [one says] 'the paradigm for the unitary cognition is in the objects of other senses' — no, because in the absence of a distinguishing reason, the illustration is indeterminate. [The objection is:] In sounds and other objects of hearing and other senses, when they are undivided, the unitary cognition is the paradigm for the [claim that] a unitary cognition [can occur] in what is many. This being so, the citing of the illustration does not stand, because there is no distinguishing reason. Regarding the unitary cognition in aggregated atoms — is it the cognition of 'that' in 'not that,' like the cognition of a person in a tree-stump, or is it the cognition of 'that' in 'that' because the object is truly so, as in the case of 'one sound' due to the unity of the sound? Without the adoption of a distinguishing reason, the two illustrations [merely] produce doubt. Like a pot, a mere aggregate [could explain] odor and the rest as well — [but] the citation of odor and the rest [as examples works against the opponent].

children.text:
% -dāharaṇaṃ gandhādaya iti/] p.507
evaṃ parimāṇasaṃyogaspandajātiviśeṣapratyayān apy anuyoktavyaḥ, teṣu caivaṃ prasaṅga iti/
ekatvabuddhis tasmiṃs tad iti pratyaya iti viśeṣahetur mahad iti pratyayena sāmānādhikaraṇyāt --- ekam idaṃ mahac ceti ekaviṣayau pratyayau samānādhikaraṇau bhavataḥ tena vijñāyate yan mahat tad ekam iti/ aṇusamūhātiśayagrahaṇaṃ mahatpratyaya iti cet so .yam amahatsu aṇuṣu mahatpratyayo 'tasmiṃs tad iti pratyayo bhavatīti/ kiṃ cātaḥ? atasmiṃs tad iti pratyayasya pradhānāpekṣitvāt pradhānasiddhir iti bhavitavyaṃ mahaty eva mahatpratyayeneti/
children.translated_text:
[p.507]
Likewise, one should also challenge [the opponent] regarding the cognitions of size (<s>parimāṇa</s>), conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), movement (<s>spanda</s>), universal (<s>jāti</s>), and particularity (<s>viśeṣa</s>), for in those cases too the same consequence arises.
The unitary cognition [being] the cognition of 'that' in 'not that' has a distinguishing reason: because of co-reference (<s>sāmānādhikaraṇya</s>) with the cognition 'large' — the two cognitions 'this one thing' and 'large' are co-referential, and from that it is known: what is large is one. If [one says] 'the cognition of largeness is the grasping of an excess in the aggregate of atoms' — then this cognition of largeness regarding atoms, which are not large, is a cognition of 'that' in 'not that.' What follows from this? Since the cognition of 'that' in 'not that' is dependent upon a paradigm, the paradigm is established — that the cognition of largeness must [truly] occur in what is [actually] large.

children.text:
% p.508
aṇuḥ śabdo mahān iti ca vyavasāyāt pradhānasiddhir iti cet, na mandatīvratāgrahaṇam iyattānavadhāraṇāt --- yathā dravye aṇuḥ śabdo 'lpo manda ity etasya grahaṇaṃ mahan śabdaḥ paṭus tīvra ity etasya grahaṇam/ kasmāt? iyattānavadhāraṇāt/ na hy ayaṃ mahān śabda iti vyavasyann iyān ayam ity avadhārayati, yathā badarāmalakabilvādīni/
children.translated_text:
[p.508]
If [one says] 'the paradigm is established from the determination "an atom, a [small] sound, is large"' — no, because the grasping of soft and intense [degrees] does not involve the determination of [precise] quantity. Just as in a substance, there is the grasping of 'the sound is atomic, small, soft' and the grasping of 'the sound is large, sharp, intense' — why? Because there is no determination of quantity. For one who determines 'this is a large sound' does not determine 'it is this much,' unlike [the case of] jujube, gooseberry, wood-apple, and the like.

children.text:
% p.509
saṃyukte ime iti ca dvitvasamānāśrayaprāptigrahaṇam --- dvau samudāyāv āśrayaḥ saṃyogasyeti cet ko 'yaṃ samudāyaḥ? prāptir anekasyānekā vā prāptir ekasya samudāya iti cet prāpter agrahaṇaṃ prāptyāśritāyāḥ/ saṃyukte ime vastunī iti nātra dve prāptī saṃyukte gṛhyete/
anekasamūhaḥ samudāya iti cet, na dvitvena samānādhikaraṇasya grahaṇāt/ dvāv imau saṃyuktāv arthāv iti grahaṇe sati nānekasamūhāśrayaḥ saṃyogo gṛhyate/ na ca dvayor aṇvor grahaṇam asti/ tasmān mahatī dvitvāśrayabhūte dravye saṃyogasya sthānam iti/
children.translated_text: [Page 509] And the apprehension of 'these are conjoined' is the grasping of duality having the same substratum as contact — if it be said that two aggregates are the substratum of <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction), then what is this aggregate? If it be said that contact of many, or multiple contacts of one, constitutes an aggregate, then there is no apprehension of contact that is dependent on contact. 'These two things are conjoined' — here two contacts are not apprehended as conjoined. If it be said that a collection of many is an aggregate, no, because what is apprehended is co-located with duality. When the apprehension is 'these two conjoined objects,' <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) having a collection of many as its substratum is not apprehended. Nor is there apprehension of two atoms. Therefore, the locus of <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) is in the large <s>dravya</s> (substance) that serves as the substratum of duality.

children.text:
% p.510
pratyāsattiḥ pratīghātāvasānā saṃyogo nārthāntaram iti cet, nārthāntarahetutvāt saṃyogasya/ śabdarūpādispandānāṃ hetuḥ saṃyogaḥ/ na ca dravyayor guṇāntaropajananam antareṇa śabde rūpādiṣu spande ca kāraṇatvaṃ gṛhyate, tasmād guṇāntaram/ pratyayaviṣayaś cārthāntaraṃ tatpratiṣedho vā, kuṇḍalī gurur akuṇḍalaś chātra iti/ saṃyogabuddheś ca yady arthāntaraṃ na viṣayaḥ arthāntarapratiṣedhas tarhi viṣayaḥ, tatra pratiṣidhyamānavacanam --- saṃyukte dravye iti yad arthāntaram anyatra dṛṣṭam iha pratiṣidhyate tadvaktavyam iti/ dvayor mahator āśritasya grahaṇān nāṇvāśraya iti/
children.translated_text: [Page 510] If it be said that proximity terminating in contact is <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) and not a separate category — no, because <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) is the cause of a separate category. <s>Saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) is the cause of sound, color, and other vibrations. And without the production of a different <s>guṇa</s> (quality) in two <s>dravyas</s> (substances), causality with respect to sound, color, and vibration is not apprehended; therefore it is a distinct <s>guṇa</s> (quality). Moreover, the object of cognition is either a separate category or its negation — as in 'the teacher is one with earrings, the student is one without earrings.' And if the object of the cognition of <s>saṃyoga</s> (conjunction) is not a separate category, then its negation would be the object; in that case, the expression of what is being negated must be stated — that is, one must specify what separate category, seen elsewhere, is being negated here with the expression 'conjoined <s>dravyas</s> (substances).' Since what is apprehended is dependent on two large substances, it is not dependent on atoms.

children.text:
% p.511
jātiviśeṣasya pratyayānuvṛttiliṅgasyāpratyākhyānam, pratyākhyāne vā pratyayavyavasthānupapattiḥ/ vyadhikaraṇasyānabhivyakter adhikaraṇavacanam/ aṇusamavasthānaṃ viṣaya iti cet prāptāprāptasāmarthyavacanam --- kim aprāpte aṇusamavasthāne tadāśrayo jātiviśeṣo gṛhyate atha prāpte iti/ aprāpte grahaṇam iti cet vyavahitasyāṇusamavasthānasyāpy upalabdhiprasaṅgaḥ, vyavahite 'ṇsamavasthāne tadāśrayo jātiviśeṣo gṛhyeta/ prāpte grahaṇam iti cet,
children.translated_text: [Page 511] There is no rejection of the particular universal that has the mark of recurrent cognition; or if there were rejection, the regularity of cognition would be inexplicable. The mention of the substratum is because what resides in a different substratum is not manifest. If it be said that the arrangement of atoms is the object, then the question of the capacity of what is reached and not reached must be stated — is the particular universal dependent on that apprehended when the atomic arrangement is not reached, or when it is reached? If it be said that apprehension occurs when it is not reached, then there would follow the absurd consequence of perceiving even an obstructed atomic arrangement — the particular universal dependent on it would be apprehended even when the atomic arrangement is obstructed. If it be said that apprehension occurs when it is reached,

children.text:
% cet,] p.512
madhyaparabhāgayor aprāptāv anabhivyaktiḥ/ yāvat prāptaṃ bhavati tāvaty abhivyaktir iti cet, tāvato 'dhikaraṇatvam aṇusamavasthānasya/ yāvati prāpte jātiviśeṣe gṛhyate tāvad asyādhikaraṇam iti prāptaṃ bhavati/ tatraikasamudāye pratīyamāne 'rthabhedaḥ/ evaṃ ca sati yo 'yam aṇusamudāyo vṛkṣa iti pratīyate tatra vṛkṣabahutvaṃ pratīyeta, yatra yatra hy aṇusamudāyasya bhāge vṛkṣatvaṃ gṛhyate sa sa vṛkṣa iti/ tasmāt samuditāṇusamavasthānasyārthāntarasya jātiviśeṣābhivyaktiviṣayatvād avayavyarthāntarabhūta iti//39//
children.translated_text: [Page 512] then when the middle and far portions are not reached, there is no manifestation. If it be said that manifestation occurs in so far as there is contact, then to that extent the atomic arrangement serves as the substratum. It follows that so far as the particular universal is apprehended when contacted, to that extent it is its substratum. In that case, when a single aggregate is cognized, there would be a distinction of objects. And this being so, in the aggregate of atoms that is cognized as 'a tree,' a multiplicity of trees would be cognized, for wherever the tree-nature is apprehended in a portion of the atomic aggregate, that portion would be a tree. Therefore, since a separate entity — the atomic aggregate taken together — is the object of the manifestation of the particular universal, the whole (<s>avayavin</s>) is a separate entity. [39]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.37]

children.text:
% p.514
parīkṣitaṃ pratyakṣam/ anumānam idānīṃ parīkṣyate ---
children.translated_text: [Page 514] <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) has been examined. Now <s>anumāna</s> (inference) is examined —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.37: From obstruction, damage, and similarity, because of deviation, <s>anumāna</s> (inference) is not a valid <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge).

children.text: apramāṇam iti ekadāpy arthasya na pratipādakam iti/ rodhād api nadī pūrṇā gṛhyate, tadā copariṣṭād vṛṣṭo deva iti mithyānumānam/ nīḍopaghātād api pipīlikāṇḍasañcāro bhavati, tadā ca bhaviṣyati vṛṣṭir iti mithyānumānam iti/ puruṣo 'pi mayūravāśitam anukaroti tadā 'pi śabdasādṛśyān mithyānumānaṃ bhavati//37//
children.translated_text: 'Not a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge)' means it never establishes an object. Even from an obstruction a river is seen to be full, and then 'it has rained upstream' is a false <s>anumāna</s> (inference). Even from the damage to an anthill, the movement of ant-eggs occurs, and then 'it will rain' is a false <s>anumāna</s> (inference). A man also imitates the cry of a peacock, and then too, from the similarity of the sound, a false <s>anumāna</s> (inference) arises. [37]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.38]
[Page 516]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.38: Because partial error, obstruction, and similarity are different from [genuine inference], they constitute a different category.

children.text: nāyam anumānavyabhicāraḥ, ananumāne tu khalv ayam anumānābhimānaḥ/ katham? nāviśiṣṭo liṅgaṃ bhavitum arhati/ pūrvodakaviśiṣṭaṃ khalu varṣodakaṃ śīgrataratvaṃ srātaso bahutaraphenaphalaparṇakāṣṭhādivahanaṃ copalabhamānaḥ pūrṇatvena nadyā upari vṛṣṭo deva ity anuminoti nodakavṛddhimātreṇa/ pipīlikāprāyasyāṇḍasañcāre bhaviṣyati vṛṣṭir ity anumīyate na kāsāñcid iti/ nedaṃ mayūravāśitaṃ tatsadṛśo 'yaṃ śabda iti viśeṣāparijñānān mithyānumānam iti/ yas tu sadṛśād viśiṣṭāc chabdād viśisṭamayūravāśitaṃ gṛhṇāti tasya viśiṣṭo 'rtho gṛhyamāṇo liṅgam, yathā sarpādīnām iti/ so 'yam anumātur aparādho nānumānasya, yo 'rthaviśeṣeṇānumeyam artham aviśiṣṭārthadarśanena bubhutsata iti//38//
children.translated_text: This is not a deviation of <s>anumāna</s> (inference); rather, this is a mistaken belief that something which is not <s>anumāna</s> (inference) is <s>anumāna</s> (inference). How so? What is undifferentiated cannot serve as a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>). Indeed, one who observes that the rain-water is distinguished from the earlier water by the greater swiftness of the current and the carrying of more foam, fruits, leaves, wood, and the like, infers from the fullness of the river that 'it has rained upstream' — not merely from the rise of water. When ants in large numbers carry their eggs, it is inferred that 'it will rain' — not from just any ants doing so. And 'this is a peacock's cry' — from failure to discern the distinguishing features, this is not a case of the similar sound being a false <s>anumāna</s> (inference). But one who, from a distinct sound distinguished from a similar one, apprehends the distinct cry of a peacock — for him the distinct object apprehended is the logical mark, as in the case of serpents and the like. This is the fault of the one who infers, not of <s>anumāna</s> (inference) itself — namely, one who wishes to ascertain an object to be inferred by a specific characteristic through the observation of an unspecific characteristic. [38]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.39]

children.text:
% p.517
trikālaviṣayam anumānaṃ traikālyagrahaṇād ity uktam/ ata ca ---
children.translated_text: [Page 517] It has been said that <s>anumāna</s> (inference) has the three times as its object, from the apprehension of the three times. And therefore —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.39: The present does not exist, because for a falling object, only the times of 'has fallen' and 'will fall' are applicable.

children.text: vṛntāt pracyutasya phalasya bhūmau pratyāsīdato yadūrdhvaṃ sa patito 'dhvā tatsaṃyuktaḥ kālaḥ patitakālaḥ, yo 'dhastāt sa patitavyo 'dhvā, tatsaṃyuktaḥ kālaḥ patitavyakālaḥ/ nedānīṃ tṛtīyo 'dhvā vidyate yatra patatīti vartamānaḥ kālo gṛhyeta/ tasmād vartamānaḥ kālo na vidyata iti//39//
children.translated_text: For a fruit that has detached from its stalk and is approaching the ground, the path above is the path already fallen, and the time connected with that is the past time; the path below is the path yet to be fallen, and the time connected with that is the future time. Now there is no third path where 'it is falling' — where the present time could be apprehended. Therefore, the present time does not exist. [39]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.40]
[Page 520]

children.text: NyS_2,1.40: tayor apy abhāvo vartamānābhāve tadapekṣatvāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 2.1.40: In the absence of the present, those two also would not exist, because they are dependent on it.

children.text: nādhvavyaṅgyaḥ kālaḥ/ kiṃ tarhi? kriyāvyaṅgyaḥ patatīti/ yadā patanakriyā vyuparatā bhavati sa kālaḥ patitakālaḥ/ yadotpatsyate sa patitavyakālaḥ/
children.translated_text: Time is not indicated by the path. What then? It is indicated by the action — 'it is falling.' When the action of falling has ceased, that time is the past time. When it will arise, that is the future time.

children.text:
% p.521
yadā dravye vartamānā kriyā gṛhyate sa vartamānaḥ kālaḥ/ yadi cāyaṃ dravye vartamānaṃ patanaṃ na gṛhṇāti kasyoparamam utpatsyamānatāṃ vā pratipadyate/ patitaḥ kāla iti bhūtā kriyā, patitavyaḥ kāla iti cotpatsyamānā kriyā, ubhayoḥ kālayoḥ kriyāhīnaṃ dravyam; adhaḥ patatīti kriyāsambaddham/ so 'yaṃ kriyādravyayoḥ sambandhaṃ gṛhṇātīti vartamānaḥ kālaḥ, tadāśrayau cetarau kālau tadahāve na syātām iti//40//
children.translated_text: [Page 521] When the action present in a <s>dravya</s> (substance) is apprehended, that is the present time. And if one does not apprehend the present falling in the <s>dravya</s> (substance), of what does one recognize the cessation or the state of being about to arise? 'Past time' means an action that has ended; 'future time' means an action that is about to arise — in both times the <s>dravya</s> (substance) is devoid of action; 'it is falling downward' means connected with action. Thus, one who apprehends the connection between action and <s>dravya</s> (substance) — that is the present time; and the other two times depend on it, and in its absence they would not exist. [40]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.41]
[Page 522] Moreover —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.41: The past and the future cannot be established through mutual dependence on each other.

children.text: yady atītānāgatāv itaretarāpekṣau sidhyetāṃ pratipadyemahi vartamānavilopam/ nātītāpekṣānāgatasiddhiḥ nāpy anāgatāpekṣātītasiddhiḥ/ kayā yuktyā? kena kalpenātītaḥ katham atītāpekṣānāgatasiddhiḥ, kena ca kalpenānāgata iti naitac chakyaṃ nirvaktum avyākaraṇīyam etad vartamānalopa iti/ yac ca manyeta hrasvadīrghayoḥ sthalanimnayoś chāyātapayoś ca yathetaretarāpekṣayā siddhir evam atītānāgatayor iti, tan nopapadyate viśeṣahetvabhāvāt/ dṛṣṭāntavat pratidṛṣṭānto 'pi prasajyate, yathā rūpasparśau gandharasau netaretarāpekṣau siddhyataḥ evam atītānāgatāv iti netaretarāpekṣā kasyacit siddhir iti/
children.translated_text: If the past and the future were established through mutual dependence on each other, we would accept the elimination of the present. But the future is not established through dependence on the past, nor is the past established through dependence on the future. By what reasoning? By what principle is something past — how then is the future established through dependence on the past? And by what principle is something future? — this cannot be explained; it is inexplicable, this elimination of the present. And if one were to think that just as the short and the long, the elevated and the low, shade and sunlight are established through mutual dependence, so too the past and the future — that does not hold, because there is no distinguishing reason. A counter-example is equally applicable against the example: just as color and touch, smell and taste, are not established through mutual dependence, so too the past and future — nothing is established through mutual dependence.

children.text:
% siddhyataḥ evam ... siddhir iti/] p.523
yasmād ekābhāve ṇyatarābhāvād ubhayābhāvaḥ --- yady ekasyānyatarāpekṣā siddhir anyatarasyedānīṃ kim apekṣā? yady anyatarasyaikāpekṣā siddhir ekasyedānīṃ kim apekṣā? evam ekasyābhāve anyataran na sidhyatīty ubhayābhāvaḥ prasajyate//41//
children.translated_text: [Page 523] Because in the absence of one, from the absence of either, there is the absence of both — if one is established through dependence on the other, then on what does the other now depend? If the other is established through dependence on the one, then on what does the one now depend? Thus, in the absence of one, the other is not established, and the absence of both follows. [41]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.42]

children.text: arthasadbhāvavyaṅgyaś cāyaṃ vartamānaḥ kālaḥ, vidyate dravyaṃ vidyate guṇaḥ vidyate karmeti/ yasya cāyaṃ nāsti, tasya ---
children.translated_text: And this present time is indicated by the existence of objects — 'a <s>dravya</s> (substance) exists,' 'a <s>guṇa</s> (quality) exists,' 'a <s>karma</s> (action) exists.' And for one who does not accept this —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.42: In the absence of the present, there would be no apprehension of anything, because <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) would be impossible.

children.text: pratyakṣam indriyārthasannikarṣajam, na cāvidyamānam asad indriyeṇa sannikṛṣyate/ nacāyaṃ vidyamānaṃ sat kiñcid anujānāti/ pratyakṣanimittaṃ pratyakṣaviṣayaḥ pratyakṣajñānaṃ sarvaṃ nopapadyate, pratyakṣānupapattau tatpūrvakatvād anumānāgamayor anupapattiḥ/ sarvapramāṇavilope sarvagrahaṇaṃ na bhavatīti//42//
children.translated_text: <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) arises from the contact of the sense-organs with objects, and what does not exist, what is unreal, is not brought into contact with the sense-organs. And this [opponent] does not acknowledge anything as existing and real. <s>Pratyakṣa</s> (perception) as a cause, <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) as an object, <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) as knowledge — all would be impossible. And when <s>pratyakṣa</s> (perception) is impossible, since <s>anumāna</s> (inference) and <s>āgama</s> (scripture) presuppose it, they too would be impossible. With the destruction of all <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge), there would be no apprehension of anything whatsoever. [42]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.43]

children.text:
% p.524
ubhayathā ca vartamānaḥ kālo gṛhyate kvacid arthasadbhāvavyaṅgyaḥ yathāsti dravyam iti/ kvacit kriyāsantānavyaṅgyaḥ yathā pacati chinattīti/ nānāvidhā caikārthā kriyā kriyāsantānaḥ kriyābhyāsaś ca/ nānāvidhā caikārthā kriyā pacatīti sthālyadhiśrayaṇam udakāsecanaṃ taṇḍulāvapanam edho'pasarpaṇam agnyabhijvālanaṃ darvīghaṭṭanaṃ maṇḍasrāvaṇam adho'vatāraṇam iti/
chinattīti kriyābhyāsa udyamyodyamya paraśuṃ dāruṇi nipātayan chinattīty ucyate/
children.translated_text: [Page 524] And the present time is apprehended in two ways: sometimes as indicated by the existence of an object, as in 'a <s>dravya</s> (substance) exists'; sometimes as indicated by the continuity of action, as in 'he cooks' or 'he cuts.' A series of diverse actions directed toward a single purpose is a continuity of action, and also a repetition of action. The diverse actions directed toward a single purpose in 'he cooks' are: placing the pot on the fire, pouring water, adding rice, bringing fuel near, kindling the fire, stirring with a ladle, draining the starch, and taking it down. 'He cuts' is a repetition of action — raising the axe again and again and bringing it down on the wood is called 'cutting.'

children.text:
% p.525
yac cedaṃ pacyamānaṃ chidyamānaṃ ca tat kriyamāṇam, tasmin kriyamāṇe ---
children.translated_text: [Page 525] And that which is being cooked or being cut is the thing being acted upon; with respect to that which is being acted upon —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.43: But because what has been done and what remains to be done are both applicable, apprehension is in both ways.

children.text: kriyāsantāno ṇārabdhaś cikīrṣito .āgataḥ kālaḥ pakṣyatīti/ prayojanāvasānaḥ kriyāsantānoparamaḥ atītaḥ kālaḥ apākṣīd iti/
children.translated_text: When the continuity of action has begun but is intended and has arrived — the time is future: 'he will cook.' When the continuity of action terminates with the fulfillment of its purpose — the time is past: 'he cooked.'

children.text:
% kriyāsantānoparamaḥ atītaḥ kālaḥ apākṛīd iti/] p.526
ārabdhakriyāsantāno vartamānaḥ kālaḥ pacatīti/ tatra yā uparatā sā kṛtatā/ yā cikīrṣitā sā kartavyatā/ yā vidyamānā sā kriyamāṇatā/ tad evaṃ kriyāsantānasthas traikālyasamāhāraḥ pacati pacyata iti vartamānagrahaṇena gṛhyate, kriyāsantānasya hy atrāvicchedo 'bhidhīyate nārambho noparama iti/ so 'yam ubhayathā vartamāno gṛhyate apavṛkto vyapavṛktaś cātītānāgatābhyām/ sthitivyaṅgyaḥ --- vidyate dravyam iti/ kriyāsantānāvicchedābhidhāyī ca traikālyānvitaḥ --- pacati chinattīti/ anyaś ca pratyāsattiprabhṛter arthasya vivakṣāyāṃ tadabhidhāyī bahuprakāro lokeṣu utprekṣitavyaḥ/ tasmād asti vartamānaḥ kāla iti//43//
children.translated_text: [Page 526] When the continuity of action has begun — the time is present: 'he cooks.' Therein, what has ceased is the state of having been done (<s>kṛtatā</s>). What is intended is the state of remaining to be done (<s>kartavyatā</s>). What is presently occurring is the state of being done (<s>kriyamāṇatā</s>). Thus, the assemblage of the three times residing within the continuity of action is apprehended by the present-tense expression 'he cooks' or 'it is being cooked,' for what is denoted here is the uninterruptedness of the continuity of action — neither the beginning nor the cessation. Thus the present is apprehended in two ways, distinguished from the past and the future: as indicated by existence — 'a <s>dravya</s> (substance) exists'; and as denoting the uninterruptedness of the continuity of action, encompassing the three times — 'he cooks,' 'he cuts.' And further, when one wishes to express an object beginning with proximity, expressions denoting that are to be recognized in common usage in many forms. Therefore, the present time exists. [43]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.44]
[Page 527]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.44: <s>Upamāna</s> (comparison) is established through partial similarity, not through complete or predominant similarity.

children.text: atyantasādharmyād upamānaṃ na sidhyati/ na caivaṃ bhavati yathā gaur evaṃ gaur iti/
children.translated_text: <s>Upamāna</s> (comparison) is not established through complete similarity, for it never happens that 'a cow is just like a cow.'

children.text:
% gaur iti] p.528
prāyaḥsādharmyād upamānaṃ na sidhyati, na hi bhavati yathānaḍvān evaṃ mahiṣa iti/ ekadeśasādharmyād upamānaṃ na sidhyati, na hi sarveṇa sarvam upamīyata iti//44//
children.translated_text: [Page 528] <s>Upamāna</s> (comparison) is not established through predominant similarity, for it does not hold that 'a buffalo is just like a bull.' <s>Upamāna</s> (comparison) is not established through similarity in one respect alone, for not everything is compared with everything in every respect. [44]
[Commentary on NyS 2.1.45]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.45: Because <s>upamāna</s> (comparison) is established through well-known similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>), the stated objections do not apply.

children.text: na sādharmyasya kṛtsnaprāyālpabhāvam āśrityopamānaṃ pravartate/ kiṃ tarhi?
children.translated_text: <s>Upamāna</s> does not operate by depending on whether the similarity is complete, predominant, or partial. What then?

children.text:
% p.529
prasiddhasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanabhāvam āśritya pravartate/ yatra caitad asti na tatropamānaṃ pratiṣeddhuṃ śakyam/ tasmād yathoktadoṣo nopapadyata iti//45//
children.translated_text: It operates by depending on well-known similarity in establishing the relation of what is to be proved and its proof (<s>sādhyasādhanabhāva</s>). And where this exists, <s>upamāna</s> cannot be denied. Therefore, the stated objections do not apply. // 45 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.46]
Then let <s>upamāna</s> (comparison) be (a form of) inference (<s>anumāna</s>) —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.46: Because what is not directly perceived is established through what is directly perceived.

children.text: yathā dhūmena pratyakṣeṇāpratyakṣasya vahner grahaṇam anumānam, evaṃ gavā pratyakṣeṇāpratyakṣasya gavayasya grahaṇam iti nedam anumānād viśiṣyate//46//
children.translated_text: Just as the apprehension of fire — which is not directly perceived — through smoke which is directly perceived, is inference (<s>anumāna</s>); so too, the apprehension of the <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox) — which is not directly perceived — through the cow which is directly perceived — thus this (<s>upamāna</s>) is not distinguished from inference. // 46 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.47]

children.text:
% p.530
viśiṣyata ity āha/ kayā yuktyā?
children.translated_text: It is distinguished, says (the author). By what reasoning?

children.text: NyS_2,1.47: nāpratyakṣe gavaye pramāṇārtham upamānasya paśyāmaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 2.1.47: We do not see the purpose of <s>upamāna</s> as a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge) with respect to the <s>gavaya</s> which is not directly perceived.

children.text: yadā hy ayam upayuktopamāno godarśī gavayasamānam arthaṃ paśyati tadāyaṃ gavaya ity asya saṃjñāśabdasya vyavasthāṃ pratipadyate na caivam anumānam iti/ parārthaṃ copamānam --- yasya hy upamānam aprasiddhaṃ tadarthaṃ prasiddhobhayena kriyata iti parārtham upamānam iti cet; na,
children.translated_text: For when this person, having been instructed with the comparison, sees a cow and perceives an object similar to a cow, then he comprehends the conventional designation (<s>saṃjñā</s>) — the word 'this is a <s>gavaya</s>.' But inference does not operate in this way. And <s>upamāna</s> serves another's purpose (<s>parārtha</s>) — for the one to whom the comparison is unknown, it is done for his sake by one to whom both are known — if it is objected that <s>upamāna</s> serves another's purpose; no,

children.text:
% p.531
svayam adhyavasāyāt --- bhavati ca bhoḥ svayam adhyavasāyaḥ yathā gaur evaṃ gavaya iti/ nādhyavasāyaḥ pratiṣidhyate upamānaṃ tu tan na bhavati ``prasiddhasādharmyāt sādhyasādhanam upamānam''/ na ca yasyobhayaṃ prasiddhaṃ taṃ prati sādhyasādhanabhāavo vidyata iti//47//
children.translated_text: because of one's own ascertainment — indeed, sir, there is one's own ascertainment: 'Just as a cow is, so is a <s>gavaya</s>.' The ascertainment is not denied; but it is not <s>upamāna</s> — '<s>upamāna</s> is the proof of what is to be proved through well-known similarity.' And for one to whom both are well-known, there is no relation of what is to be proved and its proof. // 47 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.48]
Furthermore —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.48: Because <s>upamāna</s> is established through the subsumption 'thus' (denoting similarity), it is not without distinction (from inference).

children.text: tatheti samānadharmopasaṃhārād upamānaṃ sidhyati nānumānam/ ayaṃ cānayor viśeṣa iti//48//
children.translated_text: <s>Upamāna</s> is established through the subsumption of common properties (expressed by) 'thus' (<s>tathā</s>), not inference. And this is the distinction between the two. // 48 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.49]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.49: Verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is inference (<s>anumāna</s>), because its object, not being (directly) perceived, is to be inferred.

children.text: śabdo 'numānam, na pramāṇāntaram/ kasmāt? śabdārthasyānumeyatvāt/ katham anumeyatvam? pratyakṣato 'nupalabdheḥ/ yathānupalabhyamāno liṅgī mitena liṅgena paścān mīyata iti anumānam/ evaṃ mitena śabdena paścān mīyate artho 'nupalabhyamāna ity anumānaṃ śabdaḥ//
children.translated_text: Verbal testimony is inference, not a separate <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of knowledge). Why? Because the object of verbal testimony is to be inferred. How is it to be inferred? Because it is not perceived directly. Just as the possessor of the mark (<s>liṅgin</s>), not being perceived, is subsequently measured (known) through the perceived mark (<s>liṅga</s>) — that is inference; so too, the object, not being perceived, is subsequently measured (known) through the perceived word — hence verbal testimony is inference.
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.50]
And for this further reason, verbal testimony is inference:
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.50: Because the mode of cognition is not different (from inference).

children.text: pramāṇāntarabhāve dvipravṛttir upalabdhiḥ, anyathā hy upalabdhir anumāne anyathopamāne tad vyākhyātam/ śabdānumānayos tūpalabdhir advipravṛttiḥ yathānumāne tathā śabde 'pi/ viśeṣābhāvād anumānaṃ śabda iti//
children.translated_text: When a <s>pramāṇa</s> is distinct (from others), the mode of cognition (<s>upalabdhi</s>) is different — for the cognition operates differently in inference and differently in comparison; that has been explained. But between verbal testimony and inference, the mode of cognition is not different — as in inference, so also in verbal testimony. Due to the absence of distinction, verbal testimony is inference.
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.51]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.51: And because of the connection (between word and meaning).

children.text: śabdo 'numānam iti vartate/ sambaddhayoś ca śabdārthayoḥ sambandhaprasiddhau śabdopalabdher arthagrahaṇaṃ yathā sambaddhayor liṅgaliṅinoḥ sambandhapratītau liṅgopalabdhau liṅgigrahaṇam iti//
children.translated_text: It is continued that verbal testimony is inference. And when the connection of the two — word and meaning — which are connected, is well-known, the apprehension of meaning from the perception of the word (occurs) — just as when the connection of the mark (<s>liṅga</s>) and the possessor of the mark (<s>liṅgin</s>), which are connected, is recognized, the apprehension of the possessor of the mark (occurs) from the perception of the mark.
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.52]

children.text:
% p.536
yat tāvad arthasyānumeyatvād iti tan na---
children.translated_text: Now, as for the argument 'because the object is to be inferred' — that is not (valid) —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.52: The comprehension of meaning from verbal testimony is due to the authority of the instruction of a reliable person (<s>āpta</s>).

children.text: svargaḥ apsarasaḥ uttarāḥ kuravaḥ sapta dvīpāḥ samudro lokasanniveśa ity evamāder apratyakṣasyārthasya ca śabdamātrāt pratyayaḥ, kiṃ tarhi? āptair ayam uktāḥ śabda ity ataḥ sampratyayaḥ viparyayeṇa sampratyayābhāvāt; na tv evam anumānam iti/
children.translated_text: Heaven, <s>Apsarases</s>, the northern <s>Kurus</s>, the seven continents, the ocean, the arrangement of the worlds — of such objects that are not directly perceived, the cognition does not arise from the mere word; rather, it arises from the fact that 'this word has been uttered by reliable persons (<s>āpta</s>)' — hence the comprehension; and conversely, in the absence (of reliability), there is no comprehension. But inference does not operate in this way.

children.text:
% p.538
yat punar upalabdher advipravṛttitvād iti, ayam eva śabdānumānayor upalabdheḥ pravṛttibhedaḥ; tatra viśeṣe saty ahetur viśeṣābhāvād iti/
children.translated_text: As for the argument 'because the mode of cognition is not different' — this very difference in the mode of operation of cognition between verbal testimony and inference (refutes it); when a distinction exists, the claim 'there is no distinction' is without basis.

children.text:
% p.539
yat punar idaṃ sambandhāc ceti, asti ca śabdārthayoḥ sambandho 'nujñātaḥ, asti ca pratiṣiddhaḥ/ asyedam iti ṣaṣṭhīviśiṣṭasya vākyasyārthaviśeṣo 'nujñātaḥ, prāptilakṣaṇas tu śabdārthayoḥ sambandhaḥ pratiṣiddhaḥ/ kasmāt? pramāṇato 'nupalabdheḥ---pratyakṣatas tāvac chabdārthaprāpter nopalabdhir atīndriyatvāt/ yenendriyeṇa gṛhyate śabdas tasya viṣayabhāvam ativṛtto 'rtho na gṛhyate/ asti cātīndriyaviṣayabhūto 'py arthaḥ samānena cendriyeṇa gṛhyamāṇayoḥ prāptir gṛhyata iti//
children.translated_text: As for the argument 'because of the connection' — there is indeed a connection between word and meaning that is accepted, and there is also one that is rejected. The specific meaning of the sentence distinguished by the sixth case (<s>ṣaṣṭhī</s>) — 'this belongs to that' — is accepted (as a connection). But the connection between word and meaning characterized by physical contact (<s>prāpti</s>) is rejected. Why? Because it is not perceived by any <s>pramāṇa</s>. By direct perception, first of all, the physical contact of word and meaning is not perceived, because it is beyond the senses. The meaning, having transcended the domain of that sense-organ by which the word is grasped, is not grasped (by that same organ). And even when the meaning is a supersensory object, the contact is grasped (only) when both are grasped by the same sense-organ.
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.53]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.53: And because filling, burning, and splitting are not perceived, there is no connection (of physical contact).

children.text:
prāptilakṣaṇe ca gṛhyamāṇe sambandhe śabdārthayoḥ śabdāntike vārthaḥ syāt, arthāntike vā śabdaḥ syāt, ubhayaṃ vobhayatra/ atha khalv ubhayam?
sthānakaraṇābhāvād iti cārthaḥ/ na cāyam anumānato 'py upalabhyate śabdāntike 'rtha iti/ etasmin pakṣe 'py āsyasthānakaraṇoccāraṇīyaḥ śabdas tadantike 'rtha ity annāgnyasiśabdoccāraṇe pūraṇapāhapāṭanāni gṛhyeran, na ca gṛhyante; agrahaṇāt nānumeyaḥ prāptilakṣaṇaḥ sambandhaḥ/
children.translated_text:
And if a connection characterized by physical contact were grasped between word and meaning — either the meaning would be near the word, or the word near the meaning, or both would be in both (locations). But what if both?
The meaning is: because of the absence of the place and articulatory organ (for meaning to be near the word). And this (contact of meaning near word) is also not perceived by inference. In this case too — the word, being articulated by the articulatory organs of the mouth, would have the meaning near it — and then upon uttering the words for food, fire, and sword, filling, burning, and splitting should be perceived; but they are not perceived. Because they are not perceived, the connection characterized by physical contact is not to be inferred.

children.text:
% p.541
arthāntike śabda iti sthānakaraṇāsambhavād anuccāraṇam---sthānaṃ kaṇṭhādayaḥ, karaṇaṃ prayatnaviśeṣaḥ, tasyārthāntike 'nupapattir iti/ ubhayapratiṣedhāc ca nobhayam/ tasmān na śabdenārthaḥ prāpta iti//
children.translated_text: (As for the claim that) the word is near the meaning — because the articulatory organs cannot exist (there), there is no utterance. The articulatory organs are the throat and the rest; the instrument is the specific effort (of articulation); the impossibility of these existing near the meaning (refutes this). And because both (alternatives) are rejected, neither is both (possible). Therefore, meaning is not reached by the word through physical contact.
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.54]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.54: Because of the determinate relation between word and meaning, (the connection) is not denied.

children.text: śabdād arthapratyayasya vyavasthādarśanād anumīyata asti śabdārthasambandho vyavasthākāraṇam/ asambandhe hi śabdamātrād arthamātre pratyayaprasaṅgaḥ/ tasmād apratiṣedhaḥ sambandhasyeti//
children.translated_text: From the observation of the determinate relation of cognition of meaning from words, it is inferred: 'A connection between word and meaning exists as the cause of this determinate relation.' For in the absence of connection, there would be the undesirable consequence that any word whatsoever would produce cognition of any meaning whatsoever. Therefore, the connection is not denied.
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.55]
Here is the resolution —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.55: Not so, because the comprehension of meaning from words is conventional (<s>sāmāyika</s>).

children.text: na sambandhakāritaṃ śabdārthavyavasthānam/ kiṃ tarhi? samayakāritam/ yat tad avocāma asyedam iti ṣaṣṭhīviśiṣṭasya vākyasyārthaviśeṣo 'nujñātaḥ śabdārthayoḥ sambandha iti samayaṃ tam avocāma iti/ kaḥ punar ayaṃ samayaḥ? asya śabdasyedam arthajātam abhidheyam ity abhidhānābhidheyaniyamaniyogaḥ/ tasminn upayukte śabdād arthasampratyayo bhavati/ viparyaye hi śabdaśravaṇa 'pi pratyayābhāvaḥ/ sambandhavādino 'pi cāyam avarjanīya iti/
children.translated_text: The determinate relation between word and meaning is not caused by (physical) connection. What then? It is caused by convention (<s>samaya</s>). What we stated — 'the specific meaning of the sentence distinguished by the sixth case, "this belongs to that," is the accepted connection between word and meaning' — that convention is what we stated. And what is this convention? It is the binding rule (<s>niyoga</s>) that regulates the relation of designation and designated (<s>abhidhānābhidheya</s>): 'to this word, this class of meaning is to be designated.' When that (convention) is employed, the comprehension of meaning from the word occurs. In the contrary case, even upon hearing the word, there is no comprehension. And this is unavoidable even for the proponent of (natural) connection.

children.text:
% p.544
prayujyamānagrahaṇāc ca samayopayogo laukikānām/ samayaparipālanārthaṃ cedaṃ padalakṣaṇāyā vācānvākhyānaṃ vyākaraṇam vākyalakṣaṇāyā vāco 'rthalakṣaṇam,
children.translated_text: And the employment of convention by ordinary people is (established) from the apprehension (of meaning) during actual usage. For the purpose of maintaining convention, grammar (<s>vyākaraṇa</s>) is the analysis of speech (<s>vāc</s>) for the characterization of words (<s>pada</s>), and for the characterization of sentences (<s>vākya</s>) and the characterization of meaning —

children.text:
% lakṣaṇāyā ... 'rthalakṣaṇam,] p.545
padasamūho vākyam arthaparisamāprāv iti/ tad evaṃ prāptilakṣaṇasya śabdārthasambandhasyārthatuṣo 'pi anumānahetur na bhavatīti//55//
children.translated_text: a sentence is a collection of words in which the meaning is fully accomplished. Thus, even the content-satisfaction (meaning-aspect) of the connection between word and meaning characterized by physical contact does not constitute a reason for inference. // 55 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.56]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.56: And because there is no restriction with respect to species and particulars.

children.text: sāmāyikaḥ śabdād arthasampratyayo na svābhāvikaḥ/ ṛṣyāryamlecchānāṃ yathākāmaṃ śabdaviniyogo 'rthapratyāyanāya pravartate/ svābhāvike hi śabdasyārthapratyāyakatve yathākāmaṃ na syād yathā taijasasya prakāśasya rūpapratyayahetutvaṃ na jātiviśeṣe vyabhicaratīti//56//
children.translated_text: The comprehension of meaning from words is conventional, not natural (<s>svābhāvika</s>). <s>Ṛṣis</s> (sages), <s>Āryas</s> (civilized people), and <s>Mlecchas</s> (barbarians) employ words at will for the purpose of communicating meaning. If the capacity of words to communicate meaning were natural, the employment at will would not occur — just as the capacity of luminous fire to cause the cognition of visible form does not vary with species and particulars. // 56 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.57]
In the rites for obtaining a son (<s>putrakāmeṣṭi</s>), in fire-oblations (<s>havana</s>), and in repetitions (<s>abhyāsa</s>) —
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.57: The non-validity of that (verbal testimony) arises from the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and redundancy.

children.text: tasyeti śabdaviśeṣam evādhikurute bhagavān ṛṣiḥ/ śabdasya pramāṇatvaṃ na sambhavati/ kasmāt? anṛtadoṣāt---putrakameṣṭau ``putrakāmaḥ putreṣṭyā yajeta'' iti; neṣṭau saṃsthitāyāṃ putrajanma dṛśyate/ dṛṣṭārthasya vākyasyānṛtatvād adṛṣṭārtham api vākyam ``agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāma'' ityādy anṛtam iti jñāyate/
children.translated_text: By 'that' (<s>tasya</s>), the venerable sage refers specifically to verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>). Verbal testimony cannot be a valid means of knowledge. Why? Because of the defect of falsehood — in the rite for obtaining a son: 'One who desires a son should sacrifice with the <s>Putreṣṭi</s> sacrifice.' But upon completion of the sacrifice, no birth of a son is observed. Since a statement whose result can be observed is false, even a statement whose result cannot be observed — such as 'One who desires heaven should offer the <s>Agnihotra</s>' — is known to be false.

children.text:
% p.548
vihitavyāghātadoṣāc ca, havane ``udite hotavyam anudite hotavyam samayādhyuṣite hotavyam'' iti vidhāya vihitaṃ vyāhanti---``śyāvo 'syāhutim abhyavaharati ya udite juhoti, śabalo 'syāhutim abhyavaharati yo 'nudite juhoti śyāvaśabalau vāsyāhutim abhyavaharato yaḥ samayādhyuṣite juhoti''/ vyāghātāc cānyataran mithyeti/
children.translated_text: And because of the defect of contradiction with what has been prescribed — in the fire-oblation, having prescribed 'one should offer when (the sun has) risen, one should offer when not risen, one should offer when (the sun is) on the horizon,' (the text) contradicts what was prescribed: 'a dark (demon) devours his oblation if he offers when risen; a spotted (demon) devours his oblation if he offers when not risen; both the dark and spotted devour his oblation if he offers when on the horizon.' And because of the contradiction, one of them must be false.

children.text:
% p.549
punaruktadoṣāc ca, abhyāse deśyamāne ``triḥ prathamām anvāha trir uttamām'' iti punaruktadoṣo bhavati/ punaruktaṃ ca pramattavākyam iti/ tasmād apramāṇaṃ śabdo 'nṛtavyāghātapunaruktadoṣebhya iti//57//
children.translated_text: And because of the defect of redundancy — when repetition is taught: 'He recites the first (verse) three times, the last three times' — the defect of redundancy arises. And redundant speech is the speech of a careless person. Therefore, verbal testimony is not a valid means of knowledge, because of the defects of falsehood, contradiction, and redundancy. // 57 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.58]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.1.58: Not so, because of the deficiency in the ritual action, the performer, or the instruments.

children.text: nānṛtadoṣaḥ putrakāmeṣṭiau/ kasmāt? karmakartṛsādhanavaiguṇyāt/ iṣṭyā pitarau saṃyujyamānau putraṃ janayata iti/ iṣṭeḥ karaṇaṃ sādhanam, pitarau kartārau, saṃyogaḥ karma, trayāṇāṃ guṇayogāt putrajanma, vaiguṇyād viparyayaḥ/ iṣṭyāśrayaṃ tāvad karmavaiguṇyaṃ samīhābhreṣaḥ, kartṛvaiguṇyam avidvān prayoktā kapūyācaraṇaś ca/
children.translated_text: There is no defect of falsehood in the rite for obtaining a son (<s>putrakāmeṣṭi</s>). Why? Because of the deficiency in the ritual action (<s>karma</s>), the performer (<s>kartṛ</s>), or the instruments (<s>sādhana</s>). Through the sacrifice, the parents being conjoined produce a son. The sacrifice is the instrument (<s>karaṇa</s>, <s>sādhana</s>); the parents are the performers (<s>kartṛ</s>); the conjunction is the ritual action (<s>karma</s>). From the proper condition of all three, a son is born; from their deficiency, the opposite (result follows). The deficiency of ritual action dependent on the sacrifice is faulty intention (<s>samīhābhreṣa</s>); the deficiency of the performer is an unlearned officiant or one of impure conduct.

children.text:
% p.551
sādhanavaiguṇyaṃ havir asaṃkṛtam upahatam iti, mantrā nyūnādhikāḥ svaravarṇahīnā iti, dakṣiṇā durāgatā hīnā ninditā ceti/ athopajanāśrayaṃ karmavaiguṇyaṃ mithyāsamprayogaḥ, kartṛvaiguṇyaṃ yonivyāpado bījopaghātaś ceti/ sādhanavaiguṇyam iṣṭāv abhihitam/ loke ca ``agnikāmo dāruṇī mathnīyāt'' iti vidhivākyam, tatra karmavaiguṇyaṃ mithyābhimanthanam, kartṛvaiguṇyaṃ prajñāprayatnataḥ pramādaḥ, sādhanavaiguṇyam ārdraṃ suṣiraṃ dāviti, tatra phalaṃ na niṣpadyata iti nānṛtadoṣaḥ, guṇayogena phalaniṣpattidarśanāt/ na cedaṃ laukikād bhidyate ``putrakāmaḥ putreṣṭyā yajeta'' iti//58//
children.translated_text: The deficiency of instruments includes: the oblation (<s>havis</s>) being unpurified or damaged; the <s>mantras</s> being deficient or excessive, lacking in accent or phonemes; and the sacrificial fee (<s>dakṣiṇā</s>) being ill-gotten, insufficient, or censured. And for the deficiency of the ritual action dependent on procreation: faulty copulation, deficiency of the performer being disorders of the womb and damage to the seed. The deficiency of instruments has been stated in connection with the sacrifice. And in the world too, the prescriptive statement 'one who desires fire should churn the fire-sticks' — there, deficiency of action is faulty churning; deficiency of the performer is carelessness in intelligence and effort; deficiency of instruments is the fire-sticks being wet, hollow, or burnt. In such cases, the result is not produced — yet there is no defect of falsehood, because the production of the result is observed when the conditions are proper. And this (Vedic statement) 'one who desires a son should sacrifice with the <s>Putreṣṭi</s>' does not differ from the worldly (example). // 58 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.1.59]
[Page break]
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.59: Because a fault is stated when, having accepted (the prescribed time), one breaks the time-specification.

children.text: na vyāghāto havana ity anuvartate/ yo 'bhyupagataṃ havanakālaṃ bhinatti tato 'nyatra juhoti tatrāyam abhyupagatakālabhede doṣa ucyate ``śyāvo 'syāhutim abhyavaharati ya udite juhoti''/ tad idaṃ vidhibhreṣe nindāvacanam iti//59//
children.translated_text: There is no contradiction — 'offering' continues (from the previous sūtra). One who breaks the accepted time of offering and offers at another time — in that case, a fault is stated regarding the breach of the accepted time: 'The dark one carries away his oblation, he who offers after sunrise.' This is a statement of censure in the case of deviation from the injunction. //59//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.60]
[Note: p.554]
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.60: And because restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) is justified.

children.text:
punaruktadoṣo 'bhyāse neti prakṛtam/
anarthako 'bhyāsaḥ punaruktam, arthavān abhyāso 'nuvādaḥ/ yo 'yam abhyāsaḥ ``triḥ prathamām anvāha trir uttamām'' ity anuvāda upapadyate arthavattvāt/ trirvacanena hi prathamottamayoḥ pañcadaśatvaṃ sāmidhenīnāṃ bhavati/
children.translated_text: The subject under discussion is that the fault of redundancy (<s>punaruktadoṣa</s>) does not apply to repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>). Purposeless repetition is redundancy (<s>punarukta</s>); purposeful repetition is restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>). The repetition found in 'he recites the first three times, the last three times' is justified as restatement, because it is purposeful. For through the threefold recitation, the number fifteen of the <s>sāmidhenī</s> verses is obtained for both the first and the last.

children.text:
% daśatvaṃ sāmidhenīnāṃ bhavati/] p.555
tathā ca mantrābhivādaḥ ``idam ahaṃ bhrātṛvyaṃ pañcadaśāvareṇa vāgvajreṇāvabodhe yo 'smān dveṣṭi yaṃ ca vayaṃ dviṣma'' iti pañcadaśa sāmidhenīr vajramantro 'bhivadati tad abhyāsam antareṇa na syād iti//60//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.555] And there is a <s>mantra</s>-invocation: 'With this fifteen-fold thunderbolt of speech I strike down this rival — him who hates us and him whom we hate.' The thunderbolt-<s>mantra</s> invokes fifteen <s>sāmidhenī</s> verses; that would not be possible without the repetition. //60//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.61]
[Note: p.556]
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.61: And because meaning is grasped through the division of sentences.
Verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) is a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇa</s>), just as in ordinary life. //61//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.62]
And the division of <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> sentences is threefold —
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.62: Because of the distribution (of Brāhmaṇa sentences) into injunction (<s>vidhi</s>), explanatory passage (<s>arthavāda</s>), and restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>).

children.text: tridhā khalu brāhmaṇavākyāni viniyuktāni---vidhivacanāny arthavādavacanāni anuvādavacanānīti//62//
children.translated_text: Indeed, <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> sentences are distributed in three ways — injunctive sentences (<s>vidhivacanāni</s>), explanatory sentences (<s>arthavādavacanāni</s>), and restatement sentences (<s>anuvādavacanāni</s>). //62//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.63]
[Note: p.557] Among these —
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.63: An injunction (<s>vidhi</s>) is that which enjoins.

children.text: yad vākyaṃ vidhāyakaṃ codakaṃ sa vidhiḥ/ vidhis tu niyogo 'nujñā vā/ yathā ``agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāmaḥ'' ityādi//63//
children.translated_text: That sentence which is enjoining, which is prompting — that is an injunction (<s>vidhi</s>). An injunction is either a mandatory command (<s>niyoga</s>) or a permission (<s>anujñā</s>). For example: 'One who desires heaven should offer the <s>Agnihotra</s>,' and so on. //63//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.64]
[Note: p.559]

children.text: NyS_2,1.64: stutir nindā parakṛtiḥ purākalpa ity arthavādaḥ ||
children.translated_text: Nyāyasūtra 2.1.64: Praise (<s>stuti</s>), censure (<s>nindā</s>), the practice of another (<s>parakṛti</s>), and precedent (<s>purākalpa</s>) — these constitute explanatory passage (<s>arthavāda</s>).

children.text: vidheḥ phalavādalakṣaṇā yā praśaṃsā sā stutiḥ sampratyayārthā, stūyamānaṃ śraddadhīteti, pravartikā ca, phalaśravaṇāt pravartate---``sarvajitā vai devāḥ sarvam ajayan sarvasyāptyai sarvasya jityai sarvam evaitenāptenāpnoti sarvaṃ jayati'' iti evamādi/ aniṣṭaphalavādo nindā varjanārthā ninditaṃ na samācared iti
