children.translated_text: Praise (<s>stuti</s>) is commendation that describes the result of an injunction; its purpose is to produce conviction — 'one would believe what is being praised' — and it is also motivating, for one acts upon hearing of the result: 'By the <s>Sarvajit</s> sacrifice, the gods conquered everything; for the attainment of all, for the conquest of all, one conquers all and attains all by this (sacrifice)' — such and similar passages. Censure (<s>nindā</s>) is the statement of undesirable results, intended for avoidance — 'one should not practice what is censured.'

children.text:
% p.560
sa eṣa vāva prathamo yajño yajñānāṃ yaj jotiṣṭomo ya etenādiṣṭvānyana yajate garttapatyam eva taj jīyate vā pramīyate vā ity evamādiḥ/
anyakartṛkasya vyāhatasya vidher vādaḥ parakṛtiḥ ``hutvā vapām evāgre 'bhighārayanti atha pṛṣad ājyaṃ taduha carakādhvaryavaḥ pṛṣadājyam evāgre 'bhidhārayanti agneḥ prāṇāḥ pṛṣadājyastomam ity evam abhidadhati'' ity evamādi/
aitihyasamācarito vidhiḥ purākalpa iti/ ``tasmād vā etena brāhmaṇā bahiṣ pavamānaṃ sāmastomama stoṣan yone yajñaṃ pratanavāmahe ity evamādi/
kathaṃ purākṛtipurākalpāv arthavādāv iti? stutinindāvākyenābhisambandhād vidhyāśrayasya kasyacid arthasya dyotanād arthavāda iti//64//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.560] 'This indeed is the first among sacrifices — the <s>Jyotiṣṭoma</s>; he who, having sacrificed with this, sacrifices with another, either falls into a pit or perishes' — such and similar passages. The practice of another (<s>parakṛti</s>) is the statement of a conflicting injunction attributed to another practitioner: 'Having offered the omentum, they first pour (ghee); then (they pour) curd-mixed ghee. The <s>Caraka</s>-<s>Adhvaryus</s>, however, first pour curd-mixed ghee, saying "curd-mixed ghee is the breath of <s>Agni</s>"' — such and similar passages. Precedent (<s>purākalpa</s>) is an injunction based on tradition and practice: 'Therefore, <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> with this <s>Bahiṣpavamāna</s> <s>Sāmastoma</s> shall chant — "we who extend the sacrifice"' — such and similar passages. How are <s>parakṛti</s> and <s>purākalpa</s> (classified as) <s>arthavāda</s>? Because they are connected with praise and censure statements, and because they illuminate some matter that depends on an injunction, they are <s>arthavāda</s>. //64//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.65]
[Note: p.561]
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.65: Restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) is the re-expression of what has been enjoined by an injunction.

children.text: vidhyanuvacanaṃ cānuvādo vihitānuvacanaṃ ca/ pūrvaḥ śabdānuvādo 'paro 'rthānuvādaḥ/ yathā punaruktaṃ dvividham evam anuvādo 'pi/ kimarthaṃ punar vihitam anūdyate? adhikārārtham; vihitam adhikṛtya stutir bodhyate nindā vā, vidhiśeṣo vābhidhīyate/
children.translated_text: The re-expression of an injunction is restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>), and the re-expression of what has been enjoined is also (restatement). The former is restatement of the word, the latter is restatement of the meaning. Just as redundancy (<s>punarukta</s>) is twofold, so too is restatement. For what purpose, then, is what has been enjoined restated? For the purpose of topicalization (<s>adhikāra</s>) — having topicalized what was enjoined, praise or censure is conveyed, or an additional injunction is stated.

children.text:
% p.562
vihitānantarārtho 'pi cānuvādā bhavati/ evam anyad apy utprekṣaṇīyam/
loke 'pi ca vidhir arthavādo 'nuvāda iti ca trividhaṃ vākyam/ odanaṃ paced iti vidhivākyam/ arthavādavākyam---āyurvarco balaṃ sukhaṃ pratibhānaṃ cānne pratiṣṭhitam/ anuvādaḥ---pacatu pacatu bhavān ity abhyāsaḥ, kṣipraṃ pacyatām iti vā; aṅga pacyatām ity adhyeṣaṇārtham, pacyatām eveti cāvadhāraṇārtham/
yathā laukike vākye vibhāgenārthagrahaṇāt pramāṇatvam evam vedavākyānām api vibhāgenārthagrahaṇāt pramāṇatvaṃ bhavitum arhatīti//65//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.562] Restatement also serves the purpose of what follows upon what was enjoined. Other (functions) too should be inferred in this way. In ordinary life as well, there is a threefold (classification of) sentences: injunction, explanatory statement, and restatement. 'One should cook rice' is an injunctive sentence. An explanatory sentence: 'Longevity, splendor, strength, happiness, and brilliance are established in food.' Restatement: 'Cook, cook, sir!' — this is repetition; or 'Let it be cooked quickly!' — (expressing urgency); 'Please let it be cooked' — for the purpose of request; and 'It must indeed be cooked' — for the purpose of emphasis. Just as in ordinary sentences, the status of being a means of valid knowledge (<s>pramāṇya</s>) is established through the grasping of meaning by means of division, so too it deserves to be the case for Vedic sentences that their status as a means of valid knowledge is established through the grasping of meaning by means of division. //65//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.66]
[Note: p.563]
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.66: There is no distinction between restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) and redundancy (<s>punarukta</s>), because repetition of words is justified (in both cases).

children.text: punaruktam asādhu sādhur anuvāda iti ayaṃ viśeṣo nopapadyate/ kasmāt? ubhayatra hi pratītārthaḥ śabdo 'bhyasyate caritārthasya śabdasyābhyāsād ubhayam asādhv iti//66//
children.translated_text: The distinction that 'redundancy is improper, restatement is proper' is not justified. Why? Because in both cases, a word whose meaning has already been understood is repeated; and from the repetition of a word that has fulfilled its purpose, both are improper. //66//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.67]
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.67: There is no non-distinction (between them), because of repetition, like the instruction to go faster and faster.

children.text: nānuvādapunaruktayor aviśeṣaḥ/ kasmāt? arthavato 'bhyāsasyānuvādabhāvāt/ arthavān abhyāso 'nuvādaḥ, śīghrataragamanopadeśavat/ śīghraṃ śīghraṃ gamyatām iti kriyātiśayo 'bhyāsenaivocyate/
children.translated_text: There is no non-distinction between restatement (<s>anuvāda</s>) and redundancy (<s>punarukta</s>). Why? Because purposeful repetition has the nature of restatement. Purposeful repetition is restatement, like the instruction to go faster and faster. 'Go quickly, quickly!' — the intensification of action is expressed through repetition itself.

children.text:
%śayo 'bhyāsenaivocyate/] p.564
udāharaṇārthaṃ cedam/ evam anyo 'py abhyāsaḥ pacati pacatīti kriyānuparamaḥ/ grāmo grāmo ramanīya iti vyāptiḥ/ pari pari trigartebhyo vṛṣṭo deva iti parivarjanam/ adhy adhi kuḍyaṃ niṣaṇṇam iti sāmīpyam/ tiktaṃ tiktam iti prakāraḥ/ evam anuvādasya stutinindāśeṣavidhiṣv adhikārārthatā vihitānantarārthatā ceti//67//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.564] And this is (stated) for the purpose of illustration. Likewise, other repetitions too (have purpose): 'He cooks, he cooks' — (indicates) non-cessation of the action; 'Village after village is delightful' — (indicates) universality; 'All around, all around from the <s>Trigartas</s>, <s>Deva</s> has rained' — (indicates) exclusion; 'Upon, upon the wall it sat' — (indicates) proximity; 'Bitter, bitter' — (indicates) intensity of quality. Thus, the purpose of restatement is topicalization in the context of praise, censure, and supplementary injunctions, and also serving the purpose of what follows upon what was enjoined. //67//
[Section: NySBh_2,1.68]

children.text: kiṃ punaḥ pratiṣedhahetūddhārād eva śabdasya pramāṇatvaṃ sidhyati? na, ataś ca---
children.translated_text: But is the validity of verbal testimony (<s>śabda</s>) as a means of knowledge established merely by refuting the objections? No, and therefore —
[Note: p.565]
Nyāyasūtra 2.1.68: And its validity is like the validity of <s>mantra</s>s and <s>Āyurveda</s>, because of the authority of the trustworthy (<s>āpta</s>).

children.text: kiṃ punar āyurvedasya prāmāṇyam? yat tad āyurvedenopadiśyate idaṃ kṛtveṣṭam adhigacchati, idaṃ varjayitvāniṣṭaṃ jahāti, tasyānuṣṭhīyamānasya tathābhāvaḥ satyārthatāviparyayaḥ/ mantrapadānāṃ ca viṣayabhūtāśanipratiṣedhārthānāṃ prayoge 'rthasya tathābhāva etatprāmāṇyam/ kiṃkṛtam etat? āptaprāmāṇyakṛtam/ kiṃ punar āptānāṃ prāmāṇyam? sākṣātkṛtadharmatā bhūtadayā yathābhūtārthacikhyāpayiṣeti/
children.translated_text: What then is the validity of <s>Āyurveda</s>? That which is taught by <s>Āyurveda</s> — 'by doing this, one attains what is desired; by avoiding this, one escapes what is undesired' — when that is practiced, the result corresponds accordingly: this is its truth-bearing nature, the absence of falsity. And regarding <s>mantra</s> words, which are employed for the purpose of counteracting poisons, <s>Rākṣasas</s>, and lightning — when applied, the result corresponds accordingly: this is their validity. What is the basis of this? It is based on the authority of the trustworthy (<s>āptaprāmāṇya</s>). What then is the authority of the trustworthy? It is having directly realized <s>dharma</s>, having compassion for beings, and the desire to communicate things as they are.

children.text:
% yathābhūtārthacikhyāpayiṣeti/] p.566
āptāḥ khalu sākṣātkṛtadharmāṇaḥ idaṃ hātavyam idam asya hānihetur idam asyādhigantavyam idam asyādhigamahetuḥ iti bhūtāny anukampante/ teṣāṃ khalu vai prāṇabhṛtāṃ svayam anavabudhyamānānāṃ nānyad upadeśād avabodhakāraṇam asti/%vai prāṇabhṛtāṃ svayam anavabudhyamānānāṃ nānyad upadeśād avabodhakāraṇam asti/] p.567
na cānavabodhe samīhā varjanaṃ vā, na vākṛtvā svastibhāvaḥ, nāpy asyānya upakārako 'py asti/ hanta vayam ebhyo yathādarśanaṃ yathābhūtam upadiśyāmaḥ ta ime śrutvā pratipadyamānā heyaṃ hāsyanty adhigantavyam evādhigamiṣyantīti/ evam āptopadeśaḥ etena trividhenāptaprāmāṇyena parigṛhīto 'nuṣṭhīyamāno 'rthasya sādhako bhavati; evam āptopadeśaḥ pramāṇam/ evam āptāḥ pramāṇam/
dṛṣṭārthenāptopadeśenāyurvedenādṛṣṭārtho vedabhāgo 'numātavyaḥ pramāṇam ity āptaprāmāṇyasya hetoḥ samānatvād iti/ asyāpi caikadeśo ``grāmakāmo yajeta'' ity evamādir dṛṣṭārthaḥ, tenānumātavyam iti/
loke ca bhūyān upadeśāśrayo vyavahāraḥ/ laukikasyāpy upadeṣṭur upadeṣṭavyārthajñānena parānujighṛkṣayā yathābhūtārthacikhyāpayiṣayā ca prāmāṇyam,
children.translated_text: [Note: p.566] Indeed, the trustworthy ones (<s>āpta</s>s), having directly realized <s>dharma</s>, show compassion for beings (thinking): 'This is to be abandoned, this is the cause of its abandonment; this is to be attained, this is the means of its attainment.' [Note: p.567] For those living beings who do not understand on their own, there is no other cause of understanding than instruction. And without understanding, there is neither purposeful activity nor avoidance; and without acting, there is no well-being; nor is there any other benefactor for them. 'Come, let us instruct them as we have seen, as things truly are; and they, having heard and having acted accordingly, will abandon what is to be abandoned and will attain what is to be attained.' Thus the instruction of the trustworthy (<s>āptopadeśa</s>), supported by this threefold authority of the trustworthy, when practiced, becomes an accomplisher of the goal. Thus the instruction of the trustworthy is a means of valid knowledge. Thus the trustworthy are authoritative. From the instruction of the trustworthy that has a visible purpose — namely <s>Āyurveda</s> — the portion of the <s>Veda</s> whose purpose is invisible is to be inferred as a means of valid knowledge, because the basis, namely the authority of the trustworthy, is the same. And even in this (<s>Veda</s>), a portion such as 'one who desires a village should sacrifice' and so on has a visible purpose, from which inference should be drawn. And in the world, most practical activity is based on instruction. Even for a worldly instructor, authority comes from knowledge of the matter to be taught, from the desire to benefit others, and from the desire to communicate things as they are,

children.text:
% jñānena parānujighṛkṣayā yathābhūtārthacikhyāpayiṣayā ca prāmāṇyam,] p.568
tatparigrahād āptopadeśaḥ pramāṇam iti/
draṣṭṛpravaktṛsāmānyāc cānumānam/ ya evāptā vedārthānāṃ draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca ta evāyurvedaprabhṛtīnām ity āyurvedaprāmāṇyavad vedaprāmāṇyam anumātavyam iti/
nityatvād vedavākyānāṃ pramāṇatve tatprāmāṇyam āptaprāmāṇyād ity ayuktam/ śabdasya vācakatvād arthapratipattau pramāṇatvaṃ na nityatvād/ nityatve hi sarvasya sarveṇa vacanāc chabdārthavyavasthānupapattiḥ/ nānityatve vācakatvam iti ced na, laukikeṣv adarśanāt/ te 'pi nityā iti cet na, anāptopadeśād arthavisaṃvādo 'nupapannaḥ/ nityatvād dhi śabdaḥ pramāṇam iti/
children.translated_text: [Note: p.568] and since this is accepted, the instruction of the trustworthy is a means of valid knowledge. And the inference is based on the commonality between the seer and the speaker: those very trustworthy ones who are the seers and speakers of Vedic meanings are also (the seers and speakers) of <s>Āyurveda</s> and the like — therefore, the validity of the <s>Veda</s> is to be inferred like the validity of <s>Āyurveda</s>. (Objection:) Since Vedic sentences are eternal, it is inappropriate (to say) that their validity as means of knowledge comes from the authority of the trustworthy. (Reply:) The status of verbal testimony as a means of knowledge for apprehending meaning comes from its capacity to signify (<s>vācakatva</s>), not from its eternality. For if (everything were) eternal, then since anything could signify anything, the fixed relation between word and meaning would be unjustified. (Objection:) If it is said that the capacity to signify does not exist in the non-eternal — no, because this is not seen in ordinary (non-eternal) words. (Objection:) If it is said that those (ordinary words) are also eternal — no, because the falsity of instruction by the non-trustworthy would be unexplained. For (the opponent holds that) verbal testimony is a means of knowledge because of the eternality of words.

children.text:
%śabdaḥ pramāṇam iti/] p.569
anityaḥ sa iti cet? aviśeṣavacanam/ anāptopadeśo laukiko na nitya iti kāraṇaṃ vācyam iti/ yathāyogaṃ cārthasya pratyāyanād nāmadheyaśabdānāṃ loke prāmāṇyaṃ nityatvāt prāmāṇyānupapattiḥ/ yatrārthe nāmadheyaśabdo niyujyate loke tasya niyogasāmarthyāt pratyāyako bhavati, na nityatvāt/ manvantarayugāntantareṣu cātītānāgateṣu sampradāyābhyāsaprayogāvicchedo vedānāṃ nityatvam,
children.translated_text: [Note: p.569] (Objection:) If it is said that it (the ordinary word) is non-eternal? That statement makes no distinction (i.e., applies equally to Vedic words). One must state the reason why non-trustworthy instruction in the ordinary world is not eternal. And since words, including names, accomplish the communication of meaning as appropriate in the world, their validity comes (from convention), and validity based on eternality is unjustified. The word-as-name becomes a communicator in the world by virtue of the force of the convention to which it is assigned, not because of eternality. And the eternality of the <s>Vedas</s> consists in the unbroken continuity of tradition, practice, and usage across past and future <s>Manvantaras</s> and <s>Yugas</s>,

children.text:
% cātītānāgateṣu sampradāyābhyāsaprayogāvicchedo vedānāṃ nityatvam,] p.570
āptaprāmāṇyāc ca prāmāṇyam; laukikeṣu śabdeṣu caitat samānam iti//68//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.570] and their validity comes from the authority of the trustworthy; and this is the same for ordinary words as well. //68//
Thus ends the first <s>āhnika</s> (lesson) of the second <s>adhyāya</s> (chapter) of the <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> by <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
[Note: p.572]
[Section: NySBh_2,2.1]

children.text:
atha dvitīyādhyāyasya dvitīyam āhnikam
ayathārthaḥ pramāṇoddeśa iti matvāha---
children.translated_text: Now begins the second <s>āhnika</s> (lesson) of the second <s>adhyāya</s> (chapter). Thinking that the enumeration of <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) is inaccurate, (the opponent) says —

Nyāyasūtra 2.2.1: There are not (only) four, because of the validity of tradition (<s>aitihya</s>), presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>), inclusion (<s>sambhava</s>), and non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) (as means of knowledge).

children.text: na catvāry eva pramāṇāni/ kiṃ tarhi? aitihyam arthāpattiḥ sambhavo 'bhāva ity etāny api pramāṇāni,
children.translated_text: There are not only four means of valid knowledge. What then? Tradition (<s>aitihya</s>), presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>), inclusion (<s>sambhava</s>), and non-existence (<s>abhāva</s>) — these too are means of valid knowledge.

children.text:
% pramāṇāni,] p.573
tāni kasmān noktāni/ itihocur ity anirdiṣṭapravaktṛkam pravādapāramparyam aitihyam/ arthād āpattir arthāpattiḥ/ āpattiḥ prāptiḥ prasaṅgaḥ/ yatrābhidhīyamāne 'rthe yo 'nyo 'rthaḥ prasajyate so 'rthāpattiḥ/ yathā megheṣv asatsu vṛṣṭir na bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: [Note: p.573] Why were they not mentioned (among the four)? 'So they say' — a transmitted teaching without an identified speaker is tradition (<s>aitihya</s>). Presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>) is the arrival at a meaning from (another) meaning; 'arrival' means obtainment, implication. When, upon a certain meaning being stated, another meaning necessarily follows — that is presumption (<s>arthāpatti</s>). For example: 'When there are no clouds, rain does not occur.'

children.text:
% bhavatīti] p.574
kim atra prasajyate? satsu bhavatīti/ sambhavo nāmāvinābhāvino 'rthasya sattāgrahaṇād anyasya sattāgrahaṇam/ yathā droṇasya sattāgrahaṇād āḍhakasya sattāgrahaṇam, āḍakasya sattāgrahaṇāt prasthasyeti/ abhāvo virodhy abhūtaṃ bhūtasya, avidyamānaṃ varṣakarma vidyamānasya vāyvabhrasaṃyogasya pratipādakam, vidhārake hi vāyvabhrasaṃyoge gurutvād apāṃ patanakarma na bhavatīti//1//
children.translated_text: What is entailed here? 'When (certain things) exist, (certain effects) come about.' <s>Sambhava</s> (inclusion) is the apprehension of the existence of one thing from the apprehension of the existence of another thing with which it has an inseparable relation. Just as from the apprehension of the existence of a <s>droṇa</s> (measure) one apprehends the existence of an <s>āḍhaka</s> (smaller measure), and from the existence of an <s>āḍhaka</s> one apprehends the existence of a <s>prastha</s> (still smaller measure). <s>Abhāva</s> (non-existence) is what is contradictory — the non-existent (serves as the indicator) of the existent: the non-existing rain-action is the indicator of the existing conjunction of wind and clouds, for when the sustaining conjunction of wind and clouds exists, the downward action of water due to gravity does not occur. // 1 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.2]

children.text:
% p.575
satyam etāni pramāṇāni, na tu pramāṇāntarāṇi/ pramāṇāntaraṃ ca manyamānena pratiṣedha ucyate/ so 'yam---
children.translated_text: True, these are valid means of knowledge, but they are not additional <s>pramāṇas</s>. And the denial is stated against one who considers them to be additional <s>pramāṇas</s>. This is —

<s>NyS</s> 2.2.2: <s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is not denied (as a <s>pramāṇa</s>), because <s>aitihya</s> (tradition) does not differ from it in nature; and <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>sambhava</s> (inclusion), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) are not denied (as <s>pramāṇas</s>) because they do not differ from inference (<s>anumāna</s>) in nature.

children.text: anupapannaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ katham? ``āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ'' iti/ na ca śabdalakṣaṇam aitihyād vyāvartate; so 'yaṃ bhedaḥ sāmānyāt saṃgṛhyata iti/ pratyakṣeṇāpratyakṣasya sambaddhasya pratipattir anumānam/
children.translated_text: The denial is unwarranted. How? '<s>Śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is the instruction of a trustworthy person (<s>āpta</s>).' And the definition of <s>śabda</s> is not distinguished from <s>aitihya</s> (tradition); that distinction is subsumed under the general (definition). The apprehension of something imperceptible that is connected with something perceptible is inference (<s>anumāna</s>).

children.text:
% sambaddhasya pratipattir anumānam/] p.576
tathā cārthāpattisambhavābhāvaḥ/ vākyārthasampratyayenānabhihitasyārthasya pratyanīkabhāvād grahaṇam arthāpattir anumānam eva/ avinābhāvavṛttyā ca sambaddhayoḥ samudāyasamudāyinoḥ samudāyenetarasya grahaṇaṃ sambhavaḥ,
children.translated_text: And likewise <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption), <s>sambhava</s> (inclusion), and <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence). The apprehension of an unstated meaning from the understanding of a sentence's meaning, through the contradictory nature (of what is stated with what is observed) — that is <s>arthāpatti</s>, and it is nothing but inference. And the apprehension of one of two things — the aggregate and its component — that are connected by an inseparable relation through that (inseparable) relation, from the aggregate — that is <s>sambhava</s>,

children.text:
% vṛttyā ca sambaddhayoḥ samudāyasamudāyinoḥ samudāyenetarasya grahaṇaṃ sambhavaḥ,] p.577
tad apy anumānam eva/ asmin satīdaṃ nopapadyata iti virodhitve prasiddhe kāryānupapattyā kāraṇasya pratibandhakam anumīyate/ so 'yaṃ yathārtha eva pramāṇoddeśa iti//2//
children.translated_text: and that too is nothing but inference. When 'given the presence of this, that is not possible' — i.e., when the contradiction is established — the obstruction of the cause is inferred from the impossibility of the effect. Thus this enumeration of <s>pramāṇas</s> is perfectly accurate. // 2 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.3]

children.text:
% p.578
satyam etāni pramāṇāni na tu pramāṇāntarāṇīty uktam, atrārthāpatteḥ pramāṇabhāvābhyanujñā nopapadyate/ tathā hīyam---
children.translated_text: True, it has been said that these are <s>pramāṇas</s> but not additional ones. But the acknowledgment of <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) as a <s>pramāṇa</s> at all is untenable. For indeed this —
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.3: <s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is not a valid means of knowledge, because of its non-conclusiveness (<s>anaikāntikatva</s>).

children.text: asatsu megheṣu vṛṣṭir na bhavatīti satsu bhavatīty etad arthād āpadyate, satsv api caikadā na bhavati/ seyam arthāpattir apramāṇam iti//3//
children.translated_text: 'When clouds are absent, rain does not occur; therefore when (clouds) are present, (rain) occurs' — this is what is presumed from the meaning. But even when (clouds) are present, sometimes (rain) does not occur. Thus <s>arthāpatti</s> is not a valid means of knowledge. // 3 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.4]
There is no non-conclusiveness of <s>arthāpatti</s> —
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.4: Because the supposition of non-<s>arthāpatti</s> as <s>arthāpatti</s> (is responsible for the alleged defect).

children.text:
asati kāraṇe kāryaṃ notpadyata iti vākyāt pratyanīkabhūto 'rthaḥ sati kāraṇe kāryam utpadyata ity arthād āpadyate/ abhāvasya hi bhāvaḥ pratyanīka iti/ so 'yaṃ kāryotpādaḥ sati kāraṇe 'rthād āpadyamāno na kāraṇasya sattāṃ vyabhicarati/ na khalv asati kāraṇe kāryam utpadyate tasmān nānaikāntikī/
yat tu sati kāraṇe nimittapratibandāt kāryaṃ notpadyata iti kāraṇadharmo 'sau na tv arthāpatteḥ prameyam/ kiṃ tarhy asyāḥ prameyam? sati kāraṇe kāryam utpadyata iti yo 'sau kāryotpādaḥ kāraṇasya sattāṃ na vyabhicatati tad asyāḥ prameyam/ evaṃ tu saty anarthāpattāv arthāpattyabhimānaṃ kṛtvā pratiṣedha ucyata iti/
children.translated_text:
From the statement 'in the absence of the cause, the effect does not arise,' the contradictory meaning — 'in the presence of the cause, the effect arises' — is what is presumed from the meaning. For the contradictory of non-existence is existence. This arising of the effect, being presumed from meaning when the cause is present, does not deviate from the existence of the cause. For indeed, in the absence of the cause, the effect does not arise — therefore it is not non-conclusive.
As for the fact that when the cause is present, the effect sometimes does not arise due to obstruction by another condition — that is a property of the cause, not the object measured by <s>arthāpatti</s>. What then is its object? 'When the cause is present, the effect arises' — this arising of the effect, which does not deviate from the existence of the cause — that is its object. Thus, by treating what is not <s>arthāpatti</s> as <s>arthāpatti</s>, the denial is stated.

children.text: % saty anarthāpattāv arthāpattyabhimānaṃ kṛtvā pratiṣedha ucyata iti/] p.580
children.translated_text: [Page break]
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.5]
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.5: And the denial itself lacks validity, because of (its own) non-conclusiveness.

children.text: arthāpattir na pramāṇam anaikāntikatvād iti vākyaṃ pratiṣedhaḥ/ tenānenārthāpatteḥ pramāṇatvaṃ pratiṣidhyate na sadbhāvaḥ, evam anaikāntiko bhavati/ anaikāntikatvād apramāṇenānena na kaścid arthaḥ pratiṣidhyata iti//5//
children.translated_text: The statement '<s>arthāpatti</s> is not a valid means of knowledge because of its non-conclusiveness' — that statement is the denial. By it, the validity of <s>arthāpatti</s> as a <s>pramāṇa</s> is denied, not its existence. Thus it (the denial) is non-conclusive. Since it is non-conclusive and therefore not a valid means of knowledge, nothing can be denied by it. // 5 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.6]

children.text:
% p.581
atha manyase niyataviṣayeṣv artheṣu svaviṣaye vyabhicāro bhavati, na ca pratiṣedhasya sadbhāvo viṣayaḥ? evaṃ tarhi---
children.translated_text: Now, if you think: with respect to objects having a fixed domain, deviation occurs within its own domain, and the existence (of a thing) is not the domain of denial? In that case —
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.6: Or, if that (denial) has validity, then there is no invalidity of <s>arthāpatti</s>.

children.text: arthāpatter api kāryotpādena kāraṇasattāyā avyabhicāro viṣayaḥ/ na ca kāraṇadharmo nimittapratibandhāt kāryānutpādakatvam iti//6//
children.translated_text: The domain of <s>arthāpatti</s> too is the non-deviation of the existence of the cause from the arising of the effect. And the property of the cause — that the effect does not arise due to the obstruction of a condition — (is not a counter-example). // 6 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.7]

children.text:
% p.582
abhāvasya tarhi pramāṇabhāvābhyanujñā nopapadyate/ katham iti?
children.translated_text: Then the acknowledgment of <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) as a valid means of knowledge is untenable. How so?
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.7: <s>Abhāva</s> (non-existence) is not a valid means of knowledge, because its object of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) is not established.

children.text: abhāvasya bhūyasi prameye lokasiddhe vaiyātyād ucyate nābhāvaprāmāṇyaṃ prameyāsiddher iti//7//
children.translated_text: Because the object of knowledge of <s>abhāva</s> is not well-established among the many well-known objects of knowledge in the world, it is said: <s>abhāva</s> is not a valid means of knowledge because its object is not established. // 7 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.8]
But since the subject has many aspects, one particular aspect is cited as an example —

<s>NyS</s> 2.2.8: The object of <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) is established, because among marked things, the unmarked are recognized through the mark of being without marks (<s>alakṣaṇalakṣitatva</s>).

children.text:
% p.584
tasyābhāvasya sidhyati prameyam/ katham? lakṣiteṣu vāsaḥsu anupādeyeṣv upādeyānām alakṣitānām alakṣaṇalakṣitatvād lakṣaṇābhāvena lakṣitatvād iti/ ubhayasannidhāv alakṣitāni vāsāṃsy ānayeti prayukto yeṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣaṇāni na bhavanti tāni lakṣaṇābhāvena pratipadyate, pratipadya cānayati, pratipattihetuś ca pramāṇam iti//8//
children.translated_text: The object of that <s>abhāva</s> is indeed established. How? Among marked garments — those not to be taken — the unmarked ones that are to be taken are recognized through 'being characterized by the absence of marks.' When both (types) are present, one who is told 'bring the unmarked garments' recognizes those garments in which marks do not exist through the absence of marks, and having recognized them, brings them. And the cause of recognition is a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). // 8 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.9]

children.text: NyS_2,2.9: asaty arthe nābhāva iti cen nānyalakṣaṇopapatteḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 2.2.9: If (it is objected that) there is no <s>abhāva</s> when the thing does not exist — no, because of the fitness of an alternative explanation.

children.text: yatra bhūtvā kiñcin na bhavati tatra tasyābhāva upapadyate/ na cālakṣiteṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣitāni bhūtvā na bhavanti, tasmāt teṣu lakṣaṇābhāvo 'nupapanna iti/
children.translated_text: Where something, having existed, ceases to exist — there the <s>abhāva</s> (non-existence) of that thing is warranted. But in the unmarked garments, the marks did not first exist and then cease to exist; therefore the absence of marks in them is unwarranted — (so the objection goes).

children.text:
%'nupapanna iti] p.585
nānyalakṣaṇopapatteḥ---yathāyam anyeṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣaṇānām upapattiṃ paśyati naivam alakṣiteṣu/ so 'yaṃ lakṣaṇābhāvaṃ paśyann abhāvenārthaṃ pratipadyata iti//9//
children.translated_text: No, because of the fitness of an alternative explanation: just as one perceives the fitness (occurrence) of marks in other garments but not so in the unmarked ones — that person, perceiving the absence of marks, apprehends the meaning through non-existence. // 9 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.10]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.10: This is a non-reason with respect to the unmarked, because of the (marks') establishment in those (marked garments).

children.text: teṣu vāsaḥsu lakṣiteṣu siddhir vidhyamānatā yeṣāṃ bhavati na teṣām abhāvo lakṣaṇānām/ yāni ca lakṣiteṣu vidyante lakṣaṇāni teṣām alakṣiteṣv abhāva ity ahetuḥ/ yāni khalu bhavanti teṣām abhāvo vyāhata iti//10//
children.translated_text: In those marked garments, marks have their existence established. The non-existence is not of those (marks that exist in the marked garments). And the absence in the unmarked garments of the marks that exist in the marked ones — this is a non-reason (<s>ahetu</s>). For indeed, the non-existence of things that exist is contradictory. // 10 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.11]
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.11: No, because the establishment depends on the state of marks (being present in some and not in others).

children.text: na brūmo yāni lakṣaṇāni bhavanti teṣām abhāva iti, kin tu keṣucil lakṣaṇāny avasthitāni anavasthitāni keṣucit, apekṣamāṇo yeṣu lakṣaṇānāṃ bhāvaṃ na paśyati tāni lakṣaṇābhāvena pratipadyata iti//11//
children.translated_text: We do not say 'the non-existence of marks that exist.' Rather, marks are situated in some (garments) and not situated in others; one who, looking (at them), does not perceive the existence of marks in certain ones, recognizes those through the absence of marks. // 11 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.12]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 2.2.12: And because of the fitness of non-existence prior to origination.

children.text: abhāvadvaitaṃ khalu bhavati prāk cotpatter avidyamānatā, utpannasya cātmano hānād avidyamānatā/ tatrālakṣiteṣu vāsaḥsu prāg utpatter avidyamānatālakṣaṇo lakṣaṇānām abhāvo netara iti//12//
children.translated_text: There are indeed two kinds of non-existence: the non-existence prior to origination, and the non-existence after the destruction of what has been produced. Of these, the absence of marks in the unmarked garments is non-existence characterized by non-existence prior to origination — not the other kind. // 12 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 2.2.13]

children.text:
% p.588
``āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ'' iti pramāṇabhāve viśeṣaṇaṃ bruvatā nānāprakāraḥ śabda iti jñāpyate/ tasmin sāmanyena vicāraḥ---kiṃ nityo 'thānitya iti/
vimarśahetvanuyoge ca vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ/ ākāśaguṇaḥ śabdao vibhur nityo 'bhivyaktidharmaka ity eke/
children.translated_text:
By stating a qualifier for the valid-means-of-knowledge status in '<s>śabda</s> (verbal testimony) is the instruction of a trustworthy person,' it is indicated that <s>śabda</s> (sound/word) is of many kinds. Regarding this, the general inquiry is: is (sound) permanent or impermanent?
And regarding the grounds for deliberation, from the conflict of views, there is doubt. Some say: sound is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s> (space), pervasive, permanent, and having the nature of manifestation.

children.text:
% p.589
gandhādisahavṛttir dravyeṣu sanniviṣṭo gandhādivad avasthito 'bhivyaktidharmaka ity apare/
ākāśaguṇaḥ śabda utpattinirodhadharmako buddhivad ity apare/
mahābhūtasaṃkṣobhajaḥ śabdo 'nāśrita utpattidharmako nirodhadharmaka ity anye/ ataḥ saṃśayaḥ kim atra tattvam iti//
children.translated_text:
Others say: (sound) co-exists with smell and the like, is situated in substances, is established like smell and the like, and has the nature of manifestation.
Others say: sound is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s>, having the nature of origination and cessation, like cognition (<s>buddhi</s>).
Yet others say: sound is born from the agitation of the great elements (<s>mahābhūtas</s>), is unsubstrated, has the nature of origination and cessation. Hence there is doubt: what is the truth here?

children.text:
% p.594
anityaḥ śabda ity uttaram/ katham?---
children.translated_text: The answer is: sound is impermanent. How?

children.text: NyS_2,2.13: ādhimattvād aindriyakatvāt kṛtakavad upacārāc ca ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 2.2.13: Because it has an origin (<s>ādimat</s>), because it is perceptible by the senses (<s>aindriyaka</s>), because it is treated like something produced (<s>kṛtakavat</s>), and because of conventional usage (<s>upacāra</s>).

children.text:
ādir yoniḥ kāraṇam ādīyate asmād iti/ kāraṇavad anityaṃ dṛṣṭam/ saṃyogavibhāgajaś ca śabdaḥ kāraṇavattvād anitya iti/ kā punar iyam arthadeśanā kāraṇavattvād iti? utpattidharmakatvāt; anityaḥ śabda iti---bhūtvā na bhavati vināśadharmaka iti/
sāṃśayikam etat---kim utpattikāraṇaṃ saṃyogavibhāgau śabdasya, āhosvid abhivyaktikāraṇam ity ata āha---aindriyakatvāt/ indriyapratyāsattigrāhya aindriyakaḥ/
kim ayaṃ vyañjakena samānadeśo 'bhivyajyate rūpādivat atha saṃyogajāc chabdāc chabdasantāne sati śrotrapratyāsanno gṛhyata iti? saṃyoganivṛttau śabdagrahaṇāt na vyañjakena samānadeśasya grahaṇam---dāruvraścane dāruparaśusaṃyoganivṛttau dūrasthena śabdo gṛhyate/ na ca vyañjakābhāve vyaṅgyagrahaṇaṃ bhavati,
children.translated_text:
<s>Ādi</s> means origin, cause — 'it originates from this.' What has a cause has been observed to be impermanent. And sound, born from conjunction and disjunction, is impermanent because of having a cause. What then is this designation 'because of having a cause'? It means: because of having the nature of being produced. Sound is impermanent — that is, having come into being, it ceases to be; it has the nature of destruction.
This is doubtful: are conjunction and disjunction the cause of the production of sound, or the cause of its manifestation? Hence (the sūtra) says: 'because it is perceptible by the senses.' <s>Aindriyaka</s> means: apprehensible through the proximity of a sense organ.
Is it manifested in the same location as its manifester, like color and the like, or is it grasped when, from a sound born of conjunction, a sound-continuum reaches the proximity of the ear? Since sound is perceived even after the cessation of conjunction — in the splitting of wood, when the conjunction of wood and axe has ceased, a person at a distance perceives the sound — there is no perception of something in the same location as its manifester. And without the manifester, there is no perception of the manifested;

children.text:
% ca vayñjakābhāve vyaṅgyagrahaṇaṃ bhavati,] p.596
tasmān na vyañjakaḥ saṃyogaḥ, utpādake tu saṃyoge saṃyogajāc chabdāc chabdasantāne sati śrotrapratyāsannasya grahaṇam iti yuktaṃ saṃyoganivṛttau śabdasya grahaṇam iti/
children.translated_text: therefore conjunction is not the manifester. Rather, when conjunction is the producer, and from the sound born of conjunction a sound-continuum reaches the proximity of the ear, the perception is (appropriately explained). Thus the perception of sound even after the cessation of conjunction is warranted.

children.text:
% p.600
itaś ca śabda utpadyate nābhivyajyate---kṛtakavad upacārāt/ tīvraṃ mandam iti kṛtakam upacaryate, tīvraṃ sukhaṃ mandaṃ sukhaṃ tīvraṃ duḥkhaṃ mandaṃ duḥkham iti, upacaryate ca tīvraḥ śabdo mandaḥ śabda iti/
children.translated_text: And furthermore, sound is produced, not manifested — because of conventional usage like produced things (<s>kṛtakavat</s>). Produced things are conventionally described as 'intense' or 'mild' — 'intense pleasure, mild pleasure, intense pain, mild pain' — and sound too is conventionally described as 'intense sound' or 'mild sound.'

children.text:
% p.603
vyañjakasya tathābhāvād grahaṇasya tīvramandatā rūpavad iti ced na abhibhavopapatteḥ---saṃyogasya vyañjakasya tīvramandatayā śabdagrahaṇasya tīvramandatā bhavati na tu śabdo bhidyate yathā prakāśasya tīvramandatayā rūpagrahaṇasyeti, tac ca na, evam abhibhavopapatteḥ---tīvro bherīśabdo mandaṃ tantrīśabdam abhibhavati na mandaḥ/ na ca śabdagrahaṇam abhibhāvakam, śabdaś ca na bhidyate, śabde tu bhidyamāne yukto 'bhibhavaḥ/ tasmād utpadyate śabdo nābhivyajyata iti/
children.translated_text: If (one objects): because of the corresponding nature of the manifester, the intensity and mildness belong to the perception, like color — no, because of the fitness of suppression (<s>abhibhava</s>). (The objection is:) due to the intensity or mildness of the conjunction that is the manifester, there is intensity or mildness of the perception of sound, but sound itself is not differentiated — just as due to the intensity or mildness of light, the perception of color (varies). But that is not so, because of the fitness of suppression: an intense drum-sound suppresses a mild string-sound, not the mild one (the intense). And it is not the perception of sound that suppresses, but sound itself; if sound were not differentiated, suppression would not be warranted. Therefore, sound is produced, not manifested.

children.text:
% p.604
abhibhavānupapattiś ca vyañjakasamānadeśasyābhivyaktau prāptyabhāvāt---vyañjakena samānadeśe 'bhivyajyate śabda ity etasmin pakṣe nopapadyate 'bhibhavaḥ/ na hi bherīśabdena tantrīsvanaḥ prāpta iti/
children.translated_text: And suppression is unwarranted on the view that sound is manifested in the same location as the manifester, because of the absence of contact — on the view that sound is manifested in the same location as its manifester, suppression is not possible. For the drum-sound has not reached (the location of) the string-sound.

children.text:
% p.605
aprāpte 'bhibhava iti cet śabdamātrābhibhavaprasaṅgaḥ---atha manyeta asatyām prāptāv abhibhavo bhavatīti, evaṃ sati yathā bherīśabdaḥ kañcit tantrīsvanam abhibhavati evam antikasthopādānam iva davīyaḥstho pādānān api tantrīsvanān abhibhaved aprāpter aviśeṣāt/ tatra kvacid eva bheryāṃ praṇāditāyāṃ sarvalokeṣu samānakālās tantrīsvanā na śrūyeran iti/ nānābhūteṣu śabdasantāneṣu satsu śrotrapratyāsattibhāvena kasyacic chabdasya tīvreṇa mandasyābhibhavo yukta iti/
children.translated_text: If [one argues that] there is overpowering without [the sound having] reached [the ear], then the consequence would be the overpowering of mere sound [universally] — if one were to think that overpowering occurs even when there is no reaching, then just as a drum-sound overpowers a certain lute-sound, so too a lute-sound far away would overpower just as one near at hand, since there is no distinction due to non-reaching. In that case, whenever a drum is sounded anywhere, all lute-sounds in all worlds at the same time would not be heard. [Rather,] when there are diverse continua of sounds, the overpowering of a faint sound by an intense one through proximity to the ear is reasonable.

children.text:
% mandasyābhibhavo yukta iti/] p.606
kaḥ punar ayam abhibhavo nāma? grāhyasamānajātīyagrahaṇakṛtam agrahaṇam abhibhavaḥ; yatholkāprakāśasya grahaṇārhasyādityaprakāśeneti//13//
children.translated_text: But what is this 'overpowering'? <s>Abhibhava</s> (overpowering) is the non-apprehension caused by the apprehension of something of the same kind as what is apprehensible — just as [the non-apprehension of] the light of a torch, which is apprehensible, [is caused] by the light of the sun. //13//

children.text: NyS_2,2.14: na ghaṭābhāvasāmānyanityatvān nityeṣv apy anityavad upacārāc ca ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.14: [Sound is] not [proved non-eternal] because of the eternality of the absence of a pot, which is a universal [property]; and because of figurative usage even in the case of eternal [things], as with non-eternal [things].

children.text: na khalu ādimattvād anityaḥ śabdaḥ/ kasmāt? vyabhicārāt/ ādimataḥ khalu ghaṭābhāvasya dṛṣṭaṃ nityatvam/ katham ādimān? kāraṇavibhāgebhyo hi ghaṭo na bhavati/ katham asya nityatvam? yo 'sau kāraṇavibhāgebhyo na bhavati na tasyābhāvo bhāvena kadācin nivartyata iti/ yad apy aindriyakatvāt, tad api vyabhicarati, aindriyakaṃ ca sāmānyaṃ nityaṃ ceti/ yad api kṛtakavad upacārād iti, etad api vyabhicarati; nityeṣv anityavad upacāro dṛṣṭaḥ---tathā hi bhavati vṛkṣasya pradeśaḥ kambalasya pradeśaḥ evam ākāśasya pradeśaḥ ātmanaḥ pradeśa iti bhavatīti//14//
children.translated_text: Sound is certainly not non-eternal because of having a beginning. Why? Because of deviation [of the reason]. For the eternality of the absence of a pot, which has a beginning, is observed. How does it have a beginning? Because from the separation of causes, the pot does not exist. How is its [absence] eternal? That which does not exist due to the separation of causes — its absence is never terminated by an existent [entity]. And as for [the argument from] being perceivable by the senses, that too deviates, since the universal is perceivable by the senses and yet eternal. And as for [the argument from] figurative usage as with produced things, that too deviates; figurative usage as with non-eternal things is seen even in the case of eternal things — for it is said 'a region of a tree,' 'a region of a blanket,' and likewise 'a region of space,' 'a region of the <s>ātman</s> (self).' //14//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.15: There is no deviation, because of the distinction between the real and the figurative senses of 'eternal.'

children.text: nityam ity atra kiṃ tāvat tattvam? arthāntarasyānutpattidharmakasyātmahānānupapattir nityatvam, tac cābhāve nopapadyate/ bhāktaṃ tu bhavati yat tatrātmānam ahāsīd yad bhūtvā na bhavati na jātu tat punar bhavati, tatra nitya iva nityo ghaṭābhāva ity ayaṃ padārtha iti/ tatra yathājātīyakaḥ śabdo na tathājātīyakaṃ kāryaṃ kiṃcin nityaṃ dṛśyata ity avyabhicāraḥ//
children.translated_text: What then is the real [sense of] 'eternal' here? The impossibility of the self-destruction of something that is a distinct entity and not subject to origination — that is eternality, and this does not apply to an absence. But the figurative [sense] is: that which has not destroyed itself, which having existed does not cease to exist, and which never comes into being again — there, as if eternal, the absence of a pot is eternal — this is the [figurative] meaning. In that case, no product of the same kind as sound is seen to be eternal in the real sense — this is the non-deviation. //

children.text:
% p.609
yad api sāmānyanityatvād itīndriyapratyāsattigrāhyam aindriyakam iti---
children.translated_text: And as for [the argument that] because of the eternality of the universal, what is perceivable as proximate to the senses is perceivable by the senses —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.16: Because of the qualification by inference from continuity.

children.text: nityeṣv avyabhicāra iti prakṛtam/ nendriyagrahaṇasāmarthyāc chabdasyānityatvam/ kiṃ tarhi indriyapratyāsattigrāhyatvāt santānānumānaṃ tenānityatvam iti //
children.translated_text: 'There is no deviation in the case of eternal [things]' is the context. The non-eternality of sound is not [established] from the mere capacity of being perceived by the senses. Rather, because of being perceivable through proximity to the senses, there is inference from continuity, and thereby non-eternality. //

children.text: yad api nityeṣv apy anityavad upacārād iti/ na---
children.translated_text: And as for [the argument about] figurative usage even in the case of eternal things as with non-eternal things — no —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.17: Because 'region' is used to denote the causal substance.

children.text:
nityeṣv apy avyabhicāra iti/ evam ākāśapradeśaḥ ātmapradeśa iti nātrākāśātmanoḥ kāraṇadravyam abhidhīyate yathā kṛtakasya/ kathaṃ hy avidyamānam abhidhīyate,
avidyamānatā ca pramāṇato 'nupalabdheḥ/ kiṃ tarhi tatrābhidhīyate? saṃyogasyāvyāpyavṛttitvam---paricchinnena dravyenākāśasya saṃyogo nākāśaṃ vyāpnoti avyāpya vartata iti, tad asy kṛtakena dravyeṇa sāmānyam/ na hy āmalakayoḥ saṃyoga āśrayaṃ vyāpnoti/ sāmānyakṛtā ca bhaktir ākāśasya pradeśa iti/ anenātmapradeśo vyākhyātaḥ/ saṃyogavac ca śabdabuddhyādīnām avyāpyavṛttitvam iti/ parīkṣitā ca tīvramandatā śabdatattvaṃ na bhaktikṛteti/
children.translated_text: 'There is no deviation even in the case of eternal [things].' In expressions like 'a region of space' and 'a region of the <s>ātman</s>,' what is denoted is not the causal substance of space and the <s>ātman</s> as in the case of produced things. For how can what is non-existent be denoted? And its non-existence is [established] because it is not apprehended through any <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge). What then is denoted there? The non-pervasive occurrence of contact — a contact of space with a delimited substance does not pervade space, it occurs non-pervasively — and that is its commonality with a produced substance. For the contact of two <s>āmalakas</s> (myrobalans) does not pervade [their] substratum. And the figurative [usage of] 'a region of space' is made due to this commonality. By this, 'a region of the <s>ātman</s>' is also explained. And like contact, the non-pervasive occurrence of sound, cognition, and the like [is also explained]. And the intensity and faintness [of sound] has been examined — it is the real nature of sound, not produced by figurative usage.

children.text:
% p.613
kasmāt punaḥ sūtrakārasyāsminn arthe sūtraṃ na śrūyata iti? śīlam idaṃ bhavgavataḥ sūtrakārasya bahuṣv adhikaraṇeṣu dvau pakṣau na vyavasthāpayati tatra śāstrasiddhāntāt tattvāvadhāraṇaṃ pratipattum arhatīti manyate/ śāstrasiddhāntas tu nyāyasamākhyātam anumataṃ bahuśākham anumānam iti//17//
children.translated_text: But why then is no <s>sūtra</s> by the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the aphorisms) heard on this topic? It is the practice of the venerable <s>sūtrakāra</s> that in many topics he does not establish both sides — he considers that one should arrive at the determination of truth from the established doctrine of the <s>śāstra</s> (treatise). And the established doctrine of the treatise is inference, which is approved and has many branches, as explained by the <s>Nyāya</s> [system]. //17//

children.text:
% p.614
athāpi khalv idam asti idaṃ nāstīti kuta etat pratipattavyam iti? pramāṇata upalabdher anupalabdheś ceti/ avidyamānas tarhi śabdaḥ---
children.translated_text: Now indeed, how is it to be understood that 'this exists' or 'this does not exist'? Through <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) — from apprehension and non-apprehension. Therefore, sound is non-existent —

children.text: NyS_2,2.18: prāg uccāraṇād anupalabdher āvaraṇādyanupalabdheś ca ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.18: Because of non-apprehension prior to utterance, and because of the non-apprehension of an obstruction and the like.

children.text: prāg uccāraṇān nāsti śabdaḥ/ kasmāt? anupalabdheḥ/ ``sato nupalabdhir āvaraṇādibhyaḥ'' etan nopapadyate/ kasmāt? āvaraṇādīnām anupalabdhikāraṇānām agrahaṇāt---anenāvṛtaḥ śabdo nopalabhyata asannikṛṣṭaś cendriyavyavadhānād ity evamādi anupalabdhikāraṇaṃ na gṛhyata iti so 'yam anuccārito nāstīti/ uccāraṇam asya vyañjakaṃ tadabhāvād prāg uccāraṇād anupalabdhir iti/ kim idam uccāraṇaṃ nāmeti? vivakṣājanitena prayatnena koṣṭhyasya vāyoḥ preritasya kaṇṭhatālvādipratighātaḥ,
children.translated_text: Sound does not exist prior to utterance. Why? Because of non-apprehension. '[But] the non-apprehension of an existent [is due] to obstruction and the like' — this is not tenable. Why? Because the causes of non-apprehension such as obstruction are not perceived — one cannot say 'sound is not apprehended because it is covered by this' or 'because the sense organ is obstructed when it is not in contact' and so forth; no cause of non-apprehension is perceived — therefore, it does not exist when not uttered. Utterance is its manifester; from the absence of that, there is non-apprehension prior to utterance. But what is this 'utterance'? The striking against the throat, palate, and the like, of the air in the chest propelled by effort born of the desire to speak;

children.text:
% prayatnena koṣṭhyasya vāyoḥ preritasya kaṇṭhatālvādipratighātaḥ,] p.615
yathāsthānaṃ pratighātād varṇābhivyaktir iti/ saṃyogaviśeṣo vai pratighātaḥ, pratiṣiddhaṃ ca saṃyogasya vyañjakatvam, tasmān na vyañjakābhāvād agrahaṇam, api tv abhāvād eveti/ so 'yam uccāryamāṇaḥ śrūyate śrūyamāṇaś cābhūtvā bhavatīti anumīyate/ ūrdhvaṃ coccāraṇān na śrūyate sa bhūtvā na bhavati abhāvān na śrūyata iti/ katham? āvaraṇādyanupalabdher ity uktam/ tasmād utpattitirobhāvadharmakaḥ śabda iti//18//
children.translated_text: from striking at the appropriate locations, there is the manifestation of phonemes. But striking is a particular kind of contact, and it has been refuted that contact can be a manifester; therefore, the non-apprehension is not due to the absence of a manifester, but due to sheer non-existence. This [sound], being heard when being uttered, is inferred to come into being having not existed before. And after utterance it is not heard — it ceases to exist, not being heard due to its non-existence. How? Because of the non-apprehension of an obstruction and the like, as stated. Therefore, sound is subject to origination and disappearance. //18//

children.text: evaṃ ca sati tattvaṃ pāṃśubhir ivāvakirann idam āha---
children.translated_text: And in this situation, as if throwing dust on the truth, he says —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.19: From the non-apprehension of its non-apprehension, the tenability of obstruction [follows].

children.text: yady anupalambhād āvaraṇaṃ nāsti, āvaraṇānupalabdhir api tarhy anupalambhāt nāstīti tasyā abhāvād apratiṣiddham āvaraṇam iti/ kathaṃ punar jānīte bhavān nāvaraṇānupalabdhir upalabhyata iti?
children.translated_text: If obstruction does not exist because of non-apprehension, then the non-apprehension of obstruction also does not exist because of non-apprehension; and from the absence of that [non-apprehension of obstruction], obstruction is not refuted. But how does the honorable [opponent] know that the non-apprehension of obstruction is not apprehended?

children.text:
% iti] p.616
kim atra jñeyaṃ pratyātmavedanīyatvāt samānam---ayaṃ khalv āvaraṇam anupalambhamānaḥ pratyātmam eva saṃvedayate nāvaraṇam upalabha iti, yathā kuḍyenāvṛtasyāvaraṇam upalabhamānaḥ pratyātmam eva saṃvedayate/ seyam āvaraṇopalabdhivad āvaraṇānupalabdhir api saṃvedyaiveti/ evaṃ ca saty apahṛtaviṣayam uttaravākyam astīti//16//
children.translated_text: What is there to know, since it is known to each person individually — for indeed, one who does not apprehend an obstruction knows within himself 'I do not apprehend an obstruction,' just as one whose [view] is obstructed by a wall, apprehending the obstruction, knows within himself. Thus the non-apprehension of obstruction, like the apprehension of obstruction, is indeed known [through self-awareness]. This being so, the counter-statement has had its subject-matter removed [and is therefore valid]. //16//
But the proponent of universals says by way of concession —

children.text: NyS_2,2.20: anupalambhād apy anupalabdhisadbhāvān nāvaraṇānupapattir anupalambhāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.20: Even from non-apprehension, since non-apprehension [itself] exists, there is no untenable obstruction due to non-apprehension.

children.text: yathānupalambhamānāpy āvaraṇānupalabdhir asti evam anupalabhyamānam apy āvaraṇam astīti yady abhyanujānāti bhavān anupalabhyamānāvaraṇānupalabdhir astīti abhyanujñāya ca vadati nāsty āvaraṇam anupalambhād iti, etasminn apy abhyanujñāvāde pratipattiniyamo nopapadyata iti//20//
children.translated_text: Just as the non-apprehension of obstruction exists even though not apprehended, so too obstruction exists even though not apprehended. If you accept that the non-apprehension of obstruction exists even when not apprehended, and having accepted this, you say 'obstruction does not exist because of non-apprehension,' then even in this argument by concession, a restriction of understanding is untenable. //20//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.21: Since non-apprehension is of the nature of non-apprehension, [the argument from non-apprehension of obstruction] is not a [valid] reason.

children.text: yad upalabhyate tad asti, yan nopalabhyate tan nāsti, ity anupalambhātmakam asad iti vyavasthitam/ upalabdhyabhāvaś cānupalabdhir iti seyam abhāvatvān nopalabhyate/ sac ca khalv āvaraṇaṃ tasyopalabdhyā bhavitavyaṃ na copalabhyate tasmān nāstīti/
children.translated_text: It is established that what is apprehended exists, and what is not apprehended does not exist — thus the non-existent is of the nature of non-apprehension. And non-apprehension is the absence of apprehension — this, being of the nature of absence, is not apprehended. But if obstruction were existent, it should be apprehended, and it is not apprehended; therefore it does not exist.

children.text:
% khalv āvaraṇaṃ tasyopalabdhyā bhavitavyaṃ na copalabhyate tasmān nāstīti/] p.619
tatra yad uktaṃ nāvaraṇānupapattir anupalambhād ity ayuktam iti//21//
children.translated_text: In that case, what was stated — 'there is no untenable obstruction due to non-apprehension' — is unreasonable. //21//

children.text: atha śabdasya nityatvaṃ pratijānānaḥ kasmād dhetoḥ pratijānīte---
children.translated_text: Now, one who maintains the eternality of sound — on what grounds does he maintain it?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.22: Because of intangibility.

children.text: asparśam ākāśaṃ nityaṃ dṛṣṭam iti tathā ca śabda iti//22//
children.translated_text: Space is observed to be intangible and eternal; and so too is sound. //22//

children.text:
so 'yam ubhayataḥ savyabhicāraḥ---sparśavāṃś cāṇur nityaḥ, asparśaṃ ca karmānityaṃ dṛṣṭam/
asparśatvād ity etasya sādhyasādharmyeṇodāharaṇam---
children.translated_text: This [reason] deviates in both directions — an atom is tangible and eternal, and <s>karma</s> (action) is intangible and non-eternal. The example by similarity with the <s>sādhya</s> (what is to be proved) for 'because of intangibility' —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.23: Not so, because of the non-eternality of <s>karma</s> (action).
The example by dissimilarity with the <s>sādhya</s> —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.24: Not so, because of the eternality of atoms.
Because of the deviation in both examples, it is not a [valid] reason. //24//
Then this is the reason —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.25: Because of transmission.

children.text: sampradīyamānam avasthitaṃ dṛṣṭam, sampradīyate ca śabda ācaryeṇāntevāsane, tasmād avasthita iti//25//
children.translated_text: What is transmitted is observed to be enduring; and sound is transmitted from teacher to pupil; therefore it is enduring. //25//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.26: [This] is not a [valid] reason, because of the non-apprehension of [sound] in the interval between [the two].

children.text: yena sampradīyate yasmai ca, tayor antarāle 'vasthānam asya kena liṅgenopalabhyate/ sampradīyamāno 'hy avasthitaḥ sampradātur apaiti sampradānaṃ ca prāpnotīty avarjanīyam etat//26//
children.translated_text: Between the one who transmits and the one to whom it is transmitted, by what mark is the endurance [of sound] in the interval apprehended? For what is transmitted, not being enduring, departs from the transmitter and reaches the recipient — this is unavoidable. //26//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.27: Because of teaching, [the objection is] not refuted.

children.text: adhyayanaṃ liṅgam, asati sampradāne 'dhyāpanaṃ na syād iti//27//
children.translated_text: Teaching is the mark [of transmission]; without transmission, teaching would not be possible. //27//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.28: Because teaching [applies] to either of the two positions, [the objection is] not refuted.

children.text: samānam adhyāpanam ubhayoḥ pakṣayoḥ saṃśayānivṛtteḥ, kim ācāryasthaḥ śabdo 'ntevāsinam āpadyate tad adhyāpanam,
children.translated_text: Teaching is common to both positions, since doubt is not resolved — is it the case that the sound residing in the teacher reaches the pupil, and that is teaching,

children.text:
% m āpadyate tad adhyāpanam,] p.623
āhosvin nṛtyopadeśavad gṛhītasyānukaraṇam adhyāpanam iti/ evam adhyāpanam aliṅgaṃ sampradānasyeti//28//
children.translated_text: or is teaching the imitation of what has been learned, like instruction in dance? Thus, teaching is not a mark of transmission. //28//
Then this is the reason —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.29: Because of repetition.

children.text:
abhyasyamānam avasthitaṃ dṛṣṭam/
pañcakṛtvaḥ paśyatīti rūpam avasthitaṃ punaḥ punar dṛśyate/ bhavati ca śabde 'bhyāsaḥ---daśakṭtvo 'dhīto 'nuvāko viṃśatikṛtvo 'dhīta iti/ tasmād avasthitasya punaḥ punar uccāraṇam abhyāsa iti//29//
children.translated_text: What is repeated is seen to be stable (persistent). 'He sees five times' — the form (color) is stable and is seen again and again. And there is repetition (practice) regarding words: 'the passage has been studied ten times, (or) studied twenty times.' Therefore, the repeated utterance of what is stable is <s>abhyāsa</s> (repetition). // 29 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.30: Even if they are different, (the objection fails) because of the figurative usage of the word '<s>abhyāsa</s>' (repetition).

children.text: anavasthāne 'py abhyāsasyābhidhānaṃ bhavati dvir nṛtyatu bhavān trir nṛtyatu bhavān iti, dvir anṛtyat trir anṛtyad dvir agnihotraṃ juhoti dvir bhuṅkte//30//
children.translated_text: Even in the absence of persistence, the designation '<s>abhyāsa</s>' (repetition) is used: 'let the gentleman dance twice, let the gentleman dance three times' — he danced twice, he danced three times, he offers the <s>agnihotra</s> twice, he eats twice. // 30 //

children.text: evaṃ vyabhicārāt pratiṣiddhahetāv anyaśabdasya prayogaḥ pratiṣidhyate---
children.translated_text: Thus, when the reason has been refuted through deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>), the use of the word 'different' (<s>anya</s>) is denied —

children.text: NyS_2,2.31: anyad anyasmād ananyatvād ananyad ity anyatābhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.31: Something different from another — since it is not non-different from itself — is not non-different; thus there is no (real) difference.

children.text: yad idam anyad iti manyase tat svārthenānanyatvād anyan na bhavati, evam anyatāyā abhāvaḥ/ tatra yad uktam anyatve 'py abhyāsopacārād iti etad ayuktam iti//31//
children.translated_text: What you consider to be 'different' — that, not being non-different from its own meaning, is not (truly) different. Thus there is the absence of difference. Therefore, the statement 'even if different, (there is) the figurative usage of repetition' — this is improper. // 31 //
Against one who denies the use of a word (like 'different'), the use of another word (like 'non-different') is denied —

children.text: NyS_2,2.32: tadabhāve nāsty ananyatā tayor itaretarāpekṣasiddheḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.32: In the absence of that ('different'), 'non-different' does not exist either, since they are mutually dependent for their establishment.

children.text: anyasmād ananyatām upapādayati bhavān, upapādya cānyat pratyācaṣṭe ananyad iti ca śabdam anujānāti, prayuṅkte cānanyad ity etat samāsapadam, anyaśadbo 'yaṃ pratiṣedhena saha samasyate/ yadi cātrottaraṃ padaṃ nāsti kasyāyaṃ pratiṣedhena saha samāsaḥ? tasmāt tayor anyānanyaśabdayor itaro 'nanyaśabda itaram anyaśabdam apekṣamāṇaḥ sidhyatīti tatra yad uktam anyatāyā abhāva iti etad ayuktam iti//32//
children.translated_text: You establish non-difference from 'different,' and having established it, reject 'different' and accept the word 'non-different,' and employ it. But '<s>ananya</s>' (non-different) is a compound word — the word '<s>anya</s>' (different) combined with a negation (<s>pratiṣedha</s>). If the latter constituent does not exist, with what does the negation form a compound? Therefore, of these two words — 'different' and 'non-different' — 'non-different' depends on the word 'different' for its establishment. Hence the statement 'there is no difference' — this is improper. // 32 //
Let sound then be permanent —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.33: Because no cause of destruction is perceived.

children.text: yad anityaṃ tasya vināśaḥ kāraṇād bhavati yathā loṣṭasya kāraṇadravyavibhāgāt/ śabdaś ced anityas tasya vināśo yasmāt kāraṇād bhavati tad upalabhyeta, na copalabhyate tasmān nitya iti//33//
children.translated_text: What is impermanent undergoes destruction from a cause — just as a clod (is destroyed) by the separation of its constituent substance. If sound is impermanent, the cause from which its destruction comes should be perceived; but it is not perceived. Therefore, it is permanent. // 33 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.34: Since no cause of non-hearing is perceived, the consequence would be perpetual hearing.

children.text: yathā vināśakāraṇānupalabdher avināśaprasaṅga evam aśravaṇakāraṇānupalabdheḥ satataṃ śravaṇaprasaṅgaḥ/ vyañjakābhāvād aśravaṇam iti cet? pratiṣiddhaṃ vyañjakam/ atha vidyamānasya nirnimittam aśravanam iti vidyamānasya nirnimitto vināśa iti/ samānaś ca dṛṣṭavirodho nimittam antareṇa vināśe cāśravaṇe ceti//34//
children.translated_text: Just as from the non-perception of a cause of destruction follows the consequence of non-destruction, likewise from the non-perception of a cause of non-hearing follows the consequence of perpetual hearing. If (you say) non-hearing is due to the absence of a manifesting agent (<s>vyañjaka</s>) — the manifesting agent has been refuted. If then non-hearing of what exists is without a cause — then destruction of what exists would also be without a cause. And the observed contradiction is the same whether destruction or non-hearing is without a cause. // 34 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.35: Since the non-perception (of a cause of destruction) does not hold when (such a cause) is being perceived (through inference), the argument is invalid (<s>anapadeśa</s>).

children.text: anumānāc copalabhyamāne śabdasya vināśakāraṇe vināśakāraṇānupalabdher asattvād ity anapadeśaḥ, yathā yasmād viṣāṇī tasmād aśva iti/ kim anumānam iti cet? santānopapattiḥ/ upapāditaḥ śabdasantānaḥ saṃyogavibhāgajāc chabdāc chabdāntaraṃ tato 'ntat tato 'py anyad iti/ tatra kāryaḥ śabdaḥ kāraṇaśabdaṃ niruṇaddhi pratighātidravyasaṃyogas tv antyasya śabdasya nirodhakaḥ/
children.translated_text: Since the cause of sound's destruction is being perceived through inference, the claim that 'no cause of destruction is perceived' is invalid — like saying 'because it has horns, therefore it is a horse.' What is the inference? The establishment of a succession (<s>santāna</s>). The succession of sounds has been established: from the sound born of conjunction and disjunction, another sound arises, from that another, from that yet another. There, the effect-sound suppresses the cause-sound, while the contact with an obstructing substance is the suppressor of the final sound.

children.text:
% pratighātidravyasaṃyogas tv antyasya śabdasya nirodhakaḥ/] p.629
dṛṣṭaṃ hi tiraḥpratikuḍyam antikasthenāpy aśravaṇaṃ śabdasya śravaṇaṃ dūrasthenāpy asati vyavadhāne iti/
children.translated_text: For it is observed that sound is not heard by one nearby who is behind a wall, while it is heard by one far away when there is no obstruction.

children.text:
% p.630
ghaṇṭāyām abhihanyamānāyāṃ tāras tārataro mando mandatara iti śrutibhedān nānāśabdasantāno 'vicchedena śrūyate/ tatra nitye śabde ghaṇṭāstham anyagataṃ vāvasthitaṃ santānavṛtti vābhivyaktikāraṇaṃ vācyam,
children.translated_text: When a bell is struck, a succession of different sounds is heard without interruption — high-pitched, higher-pitched, soft, softer — distinguished by auditory differences. If sound is permanent, the cause of manifestation (<s>abhivyakti</s>) — whether located in the bell, or elsewhere in a stable position, or operating as a succession — must be stated,

children.text:
% santānavṛtti vābhivyaktikāraṇaṃ vācyam,] p.631
yena śrutisantāno bhavatīti śabdabhede vāsati śrutibheda upapādayitavya iti/ anitye tu śabde ghaṇṭāsthaṃ santānavṛtti saṃyogasahakāri nimittāntaraṃ saṃskārabhūtaṃ paṭu mandam anuvartate tastānuvṛttyā śabdasantānānuvṛttiḥ, paṭumandabhāvāc ca tīvramandatā śabdasya, tatkṛtaś ca śrutibheda iti//35//
children.translated_text: by which the succession of auditory perceptions occurs; and the auditory difference must be explained either by a difference in sounds (or otherwise). But if sound is impermanent, another instrumental cause, located in the bell, operating as a succession, acting as an auxiliary to conjunction — a <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) — follows the intensity and softness. Through its continuation, the sound-succession continues; and from the states of intensity and softness, the sharpness and softness of the sound (arise); and from that, the difference in auditory perception. // 35 //

children.text:
% p.633
na vai nimittāntaraṃ saṃskāra upalabhyate/ anupalabdher nāstīti?
children.translated_text: Indeed, no other instrumental cause, namely <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression), is perceived. Because it is not perceived, does it not exist?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.36: Because of the pressing of the hand, in the absence of sound, there is no non-perception (of <s>saṃskāra</s>).

children.text: pāṇikarmaṇā pāṇighaṇṭāpraśleṣo bhavati tasmiṃś ca sati śabdasantāno notpadyate ataḥ śravaṇānupapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: Through the action of the hand, there is a pressing (<s>praśleṣa</s>) of the hand against the bell; when this occurs, the sound-succession does not arise — hence the impossibility of hearing.

children.text:
% ataḥ śravaṇānupapattiḥ/] p.634
tatra pratighātidravyasaṃyogaḥ śabdasya nimittāntaraṃ saṃskārabhūtaṃ niruṇaddhīty anumīyate; tasya ca nirodhāc chabdasantāno notpadyate/ anutpattau śrutivicchedo yathā pratighātidravyasaṃyogād iṣoḥ kriyāhetau saṃskāre niruddhe gamanābhāva iti/ kampasantānasya sparśanendriyagrāhyasya coparamaḥ/ kāṃsyapātrādiṣu pāṇisaṃśleṣo liṅgaṃ saṃskārasantānasyeti/ tasmān nimittāntarasya saṃskārabhūtasya nānupalabdhir iti//36//
children.translated_text: There, it is inferred that the contact with an obstructing substance suppresses the other instrumental cause, the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression); and from its suppression, the sound-succession does not arise. In the absence of arising, there is an interruption of auditory perception — just as when the <s>saṃskāra</s> that is the cause of motion is suppressed by the contact with an obstructing substance, the arrow ceases to move. There is also the cessation of the vibration-succession, which is perceptible by the tactile sense-organ. The pressing of the hand against bronze vessels and the like is the inferential mark of the succession of <s>saṃskāra</s>. Therefore, it is not the case that the other instrumental cause, the <s>saṃskāra</s>, is unperceived. // 36 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.37: If, from the non-perception of a cause of destruction, there is persistence — then the consequence would be the permanence of that (auditory perception too).

children.text: yadi yasya vināśakāraṇaṃ nopalabhyate tad avatiṣṭhate, avasthānāc ca tasya nityatvaṃ prasajyate; evaṃ yāni khalv imāni śabdaśravaṇāni śabdābhivyaktaya iti matam, na teṣāṃ vināśakāraṇaṃ bhavatopapādyate, anupapādanād avasthānam avasthānāt teṣāṃ nityatvaṃ prasajyata iti/ atha naivam, na tarhi vināśakāraṇānupalabdheḥ śabdasyāvasthānān nityatvam iti//37//
children.translated_text: If whatever has no perceived cause of destruction persists, and from persistence its permanence follows — then these very auditory perceptions of sound, which you consider to be manifestations (<s>abhivyakti</s>) of sound, have no cause of destruction demonstrated by you. From the failure to demonstrate (such a cause), they persist; and from their persistence, the consequence would be their permanence. If this is not (accepted), then neither is sound permanent merely from the persistence caused by non-perception of a cause of destruction. // 37 //

children.text: kampasamānāśrayasyānunādasya pāṇipraśleṣāt kampavat kāraṇoparamād abhāvaḥ/ vaiyadhikaraṇye hi pratighātidravyapraśleṣāt samānādhikaraṇasyaivoparamaḥ syād iti---
children.translated_text: Resonance (<s>anunāda</s>), which shares the same substrate as vibration, ceases like vibration itself from the cessation of its cause through the pressing of the hand. But if (sound and vibration) have different substrates, then from the pressing of an obstructing substance, only what shares the same substrate would cease —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.38: Because (it is) intangible, the refutation does not hold.

children.text: yad idaṃ nākāśaguṇaḥ śabda iti pratiṣidhyate ayam anupapannaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ, asparśatvāc chabdāśrayasya/ rūpādisamānadeśasyāgrahaṇe śabdasantānopapatter asparśavyāpidravyāśrayaḥ śabda iti jñāyate na kampasamānāśraya iti//38//
children.translated_text: This denial — that sound is not a quality of <s>ākāśa</s> (space) — is untenable, because the substrate of sound is intangible. Since the sound-succession is established even without the apprehension (of sound) at the same location as color and the like, it is known that sound has an intangible substance as its substrate — not one sharing the same substrate as vibration. // 38 //

children.text:
% p.637
pratidravyaṃ rūpādibhiḥ saha sanniviṣṭaḥ śabdaḥ samānadeśo vyajyata iti nopapadyate/ katham?---
children.translated_text: It is untenable that sound, co-located with color and the like in each substance, is manifested at the same location. How?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.39: Because another type of differentiation is possible, (even) in the aggregate.

children.text: santānopapatteś ceti cārthaḥ/ tad vyākhyātam/ yadi rūpādayaḥ śabdāś ca pratidravyaṃ samastāḥ samuditāḥ samuditās tasmin samāse samudāye yo yathājātīyakaḥ sanniviṣṭas tasya tathā jātīyasyaiva grahaṇena bhavitavyaṃ śabde rūpādivat/ tatra yo 'yaṃ vibhāga ekadravye nānārūpā bhinnaśrutayo vidharmāṇaḥ śabdā abhivyajyamānāḥ śrūyante yac ca vibhāgāntaraṃ sarūpāḥ samānaśrutayaḥ sadharmāṇaḥ śabdās tīvramandadharmatayā bhinnāḥ śrūyante tad ubhayaṃ nopapadyate, nānābhūtānām utpadyamānānām ayaṃ dharmo naikasya vyajyamānasyeti/
children.translated_text: And because the succession is possible — this is the meaning of 'and.' That has been explained. If colors and sounds are aggregated together in each substance, combined in that aggregate — then, of one that is co-present according to its class, only the apprehension of (something of) that very class should occur, as with color and the like in the case of sound. Now, there is this differentiation: in a single substance, sounds of different forms, different auditory qualities, and different properties are heard as being manifested. And there is another differentiation: sounds of the same form, same auditory quality, and same properties are heard as differentiated by the property of intensity and softness. Both of these are not possible — this is the characteristic of diverse entities being produced, not of a single entity being manifested.

children.text:
% bhūtānām utpadyamānānām ayaṃ dharmo naikasya vyajyamānasyeti/] p.638
asti cāyaṃ vibhāgo vibhāgāntaraṃ ca, tena vibhāgopapatter manyāmahe na pratidravyaṃ rūpādibhiḥ saha śabdaḥ sanniviṣṭo vyajyata iti//39//
children.translated_text: And this differentiation and the other differentiation do exist. Therefore, from the possibility of (this) differentiation, we hold that sound is not co-present with color and the like in each substance, being manifested (from them). // 39 //

children.text: dvividhaś cāyaṃ śabdo varṇātmako dhvanimātraś ca/ tatra varṇātmani tāvat---
children.translated_text: And this sound is of two kinds: consisting of phonemes (<s>varṇātmaka</s>) and consisting of mere noise (<s>dhvanimātra</s>). Regarding that which consists of phonemes —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2.2.40: Doubt (arises) from the teaching of both transformation (<s>vikāra</s>) and substitution (<s>ādeśa</s>).

children.text: dadhy atreti kecit ikāra itvaṃ hitvā yatvam āpadyata iti vikāraṃ manyante/ kecid ikārasya prayoge viṣayakṛte yad ikāraḥ sthānaṃ jahāti tatra yakārasya prayogaṃ bruvate/ saṃhitāyāṃ viṣaye ikāro na prayujyate tasya sthāne yakāraḥ prayujyate sa ādeśa iti ubhayam idam upadiśyate/ tatra na jñāyate kiṃ tattvam iti/
children.translated_text: In (the sandhi of) '<s>dadhy atra</s>' — some think that the <s>i</s>-vowel, abandoning its i-nature, undergoes transformation (<s>vikāra</s>) into <s>y</s>. Others state that when the <s>i</s>-vowel, in the domain of its usage, leaves its place, the <s>y</s>-consonant is employed in that place. In (the domain of) <s>saṃhitā</s> (euphonic combination), the <s>i</s>-vowel is not employed; in its place, the <s>y</s>-consonant is employed — this is substitution (<s>ādeśa</s>). Both of these are taught. The question is: which is the reality?

children.text:
% p.639
ādeśopadeśas tattvam/ vikāropadeśe hy anvayasyāgrahaṇād vikārānanumānam---saty anvaye kiñcin nivartate kiñcid upajāyata iti śakyeta vikāro 'numātum/ na cānvayo gṛhyate tasmād vikāro nāstīti/
bhinnakaraṇayoś ca varṇayor aprayoge prayogopapattiḥ---vivṛtakaraṇa ikāra īṣatspṛṣṭakaraṇo yakāraḥ, tāv imau pṛthakkaraṇākhyena prayatnenoccāraṇīyau, tayor ekasyāprayoge 'nyasya prayoga upapanna iti/
avikāre cāviśeṣaḥ/ yatremāv ikārayakārau na vikārabhūtau---yatate, yacchati, prāyaṃsta, iti, ikāra idam iti ca, yatra ca vikārabhūtau iṣṭyā dadhy āhareti, ubhayatra prayoktur aviśeṣo yatnaḥ śrotuś ca śrutir ity ādeśopapattiḥ/
children.translated_text:
The teaching of substitution (<s>ādeśa</s>) is the reality. For in the teaching of transformation (<s>vikāra</s>), since continuity (<s>anvaya</s>) is not apprehended, transformation cannot be inferred — (only) if there were continuity could one infer a transformation, where something persists while something is removed and something new arises. But continuity is not apprehended; therefore transformation does not exist.
And the possibility of the usage of one when the other — which has a different articulatory organ — is not used: the <s>i</s>-vowel has an open articulatory organ, and the <s>y</s>-consonant has a slightly-touching articulatory organ. These two are to be pronounced with different articulatory efforts. When one of them is not used, the usage of the other is possible.
And there is no distinction in non-transformation. Where these <s>i</s>-vowel and <s>y</s>-consonant are not transformations of each other — (as in) '<s>yatate</s>' (he strives), '<s>yacchati</s>' (he controls), '<s>prāyaṃsta</s>' (they departed), '<s>iti</s>' (thus), '<s>ikāra</s>' (the letter i), '<s>idam</s>' (this) — and where they are transformations — (as in) '<s>iṣṭyā dadhy āhara</s>' (bring the curd for the sacrifice) — in both cases the effort of the speaker and the auditory perception of the listener are without distinction. Hence substitution is established.

children.text:
% p.640
prayujyamānāgrahaṇāc ca/ na khalv ikāraḥ prayujyamāno yakāratām āpadyamāno gṛhyate/ kiṃ tarhi? ikārasya prayoge yakāraḥ prayujyate, tasmād avikāra iti/
avikāre ca na śabdānvākhyānalopaḥ/ na vikriyante varṇā iti/ na caitasmin pakṣe śabdānvākhyānasyāsambhave yena varṇavikāraṃ pratipadyemahīti/
na khalv varṇasya varṇāntaraṃ kāryam, na hi ikārād yakāra utpadyate yakārād vā ikāraḥ/ pṛthaksthānaprayatnotpādyā hīme varṇāḥ teṣām anyonyasya sthāne prayujyata iti yuktam/ etāvac caitat pariṇāmo vā vikāraḥ syāt kāryakāraṇabhāvo vā/ ubhayaṃ ca nāsti tasmāt na santi varṇavikārāḥ/
varṇasamudāyavikārānupapattivac ca varṇavikārānupapattiḥ---``aster bhūḥ'' ``bruvo vacir'' iti yathā varṇasamudāyasya dhātulakṣaṇasya kvacid viṣaye varṇāntarasamudāyo na pariṇāmo na kāryaṃ śabdāntarasya sthāne śabdāntaraṃ prayujyate tathā varṇasya varṇānataram iti//40//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.640]
And because the [phoneme] being employed is not apprehended [as undergoing transformation]. Indeed, the <s>i-kāra</s> (vowel 'i') when being employed is not apprehended as turning into a <s>ya-kāra</s> (semivowel 'y'). What then? When the <s>i-kāra</s> is to be employed, a <s>ya-kāra</s> is employed [in its place]; therefore it is not a modification.
And when there is no modification, there is no loss of etymological explanation of words. Phonemes are not modified. And in this position, there is no impossibility of etymological explanation such that we should accept phonemic modification.
Indeed, one phoneme is not the product of another phoneme — for the <s>ya-kāra</s> does not arise from the <s>i-kāra</s>, nor the <s>i-kāra</s> from the <s>ya-kāra</s>. Since these phonemes are produced by distinct points of articulation and efforts, it is proper that one is employed in the place of the other. And this much [can be said]: modification would be either transformation or a cause-effect relation, and neither of these obtains; therefore there are no phonemic modifications.
And just as the modification of a group of phonemes is untenable, so is the modification of phonemes — just as in '<s>aster bhūḥ</s>' and '<s>bruvo vacir</s>,' the replacement of one group of phonemes constituting a verbal root by another group in a certain domain is neither transformation nor a product — one word is employed in the place of another — so too one phoneme [is employed in the place of] another. //40//
[Section: NySBh_2,2.41]

children.text:
% p.641
itaś ca na santi varṇavikārāḥ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.641]
Moreover, there are no phonemic modifications because —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.41: When the original form increases, the modification increases.

children.text: prakṛtyanuvidhānaṃ vikāreṣu dṛṣṭam, yakāre hrasvadīrghānuvidhānaṃ nāsti yena vikāratvam anumīyata iti//41//
children.translated_text: Conformity to the original is observed in modifications. In the <s>ya-kāra</s>, there is no conformity to short and long [forms of <s>i-kāra</s>], by which its status as a modification could be inferred. //41//
[Section: NySBh_2,2.42]
[Note: p.642]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.42: Because modifications are apprehended as less, equal, or greater, this is not a valid reason.

children.text: dravyavikārā nyūnāḥ samāḥ adhikāś ca gṛhyante/ tadvad ayaṃ vikāro nyūnaḥ syād iti//42//
children.translated_text: Modifications of substances are apprehended as less, equal, or greater. Similarly, this [alleged phonemic] modification would be [only] less [than the original]. //42//
[Section: NySBh_2,2.43]

children.text: NyS_2,2.43: dvividhasyāpi hetor abhāvād asādhanaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 2,2.43: Since both types of reason are absent, the example fails to prove [the thesis].

children.text:
atra nodāharaṇasādharmyād dhetur asti na vaidharmyāt/ anupasaṃhṛtaś ca hetunā dṛṣṭānto na sādhaka iti/
pratidṛṣṭānte cāniyamaḥ prasajyeta/ yathānuḍuhaḥ sthāne 'śvo voḍhuṃ niyukto na tadvikāro bhavati evam ivarṇasya sthāne yakāraḥ prayukto na vikāra iti/ na cātra niyamahetur asti---dṛṣṭāntaḥ sādhako na pratidṛṣṭānta iti//43//
children.translated_text:
Here, neither through positive concomitance with the example is there a reason, nor through negative concomitance. And an example not subsumed under the reason is not probative.
