children.translated_text: In a calf just born, the desire for milk is apprehended as a sign of activity. And that (desire) does not occur without the practice of eating. By what reasoning? For it is observed that in embodied beings afflicted by hunger, the desire for food arises from the connection with memory produced by the practice of eating. And this (desire) in one just born is not possible without the practice (of eating) in a previous body.

children.text:
% jātamātrasyopapadyate/] p.746
tenānumīyate bhūtapūrvaṃ śarīraṃ yatrānenāhāro 'bhyasta iti/ sa khalv ayam ātmā pūrvaśarīrāt pretya śarīrāntaram āpannaḥ kṣutpīḍitaḥ pūrvābhyastam āhāram anusmaran stanyam abhilaṣati/ tasmān na dehabhedād ātmā bhidyate bhavaty evorddhvaṃ dehabhedād iti//21//
children.translated_text: Therefore it is inferred that there existed a previous body in which this one practiced eating. This very self (<s>ātman</s>), having departed from the previous body and obtained another body, being afflicted by hunger, remembering the previously practiced food, desires milk. Therefore, the self is not destroyed by the destruction of the body — it continues to exist after the destruction of the body. // 21 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.22: Like the approach of iron to a magnet, so is that approach (of the infant to the breast).

children.text: yathā khalv ayo 'bhyāsam antareṇāyaskāntam upasarpati, evam āhārābhyāsam antareṇa bālaḥ stanyam abhilaṣati//22//
children.translated_text: Just as iron approaches a magnet without (prior) practice, so too a child desires milk without the practice of eating. // 22 //

children.text:
% p.747
kim idam ayaso 'yaskāntābhisarpaṇaṃ nirnimittam atha nimittād iti? nirnimittaṃ tāvat ---
children.translated_text: Is this approach of iron to a magnet without a cause, or from a cause? If without a cause —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.23: (It is) not (without a cause), because of the absence of activity elsewhere.

children.text: yadi nirnimittam, loṣṭādayo 'py ayaskāntam upasarpeyuḥ/ na jātu niyame kāraṇam astīti/ atha nimittāt, tat kenopalabhyate iti/ kriyāliṅgaḥ kriyāhetuḥ, kriyāniyamaliṅgaś ca kriyāhetuniyamaḥ, tenānyatra pravṛttyabhāvaḥ, bālasyāpi niyatam upasarpaṇakriyopalabhyate/ na ca stanyābhilāṣaliṅgam anyad āhārābhyāsakṛtāt smaraṇāubandhāt/ nimittaṃ dṛṣṭāntenopapādyate,
children.translated_text: If it were without a cause, clods and the like should also approach a magnet. And there could never be a cause for any restriction. If then it is from a cause — by what is that (cause) apprehended? The cause of an activity is inferred from the activity, and the restriction of the cause of activity is inferred from the restriction of activity. Therefore, (there must be a cause for) the absence of activity elsewhere. In the case of the infant too, a restricted approach-activity is observed. And there is no other inferential mark for the desire for milk apart from the connection with memory produced by the practice of eating. The cause is established by an example,

children.text:
% dṛṣṭāntenopapādyate,] p.748
na cāsati nimitte kasyacid utpattiḥ/ na ca dṛṣṭānto dṛṣṭam abhilāṣahetuṃ bādhate/ tasmād ayaso 'yaskāntābhigamanam adṛṣṭānta iti/
ayasaḥ khalv api nānyatra pravṛttir bhavati, na jātv ayo loṣṭam upasarpati, kiṃkṛito 'sya niyama iti? yadi kāraṇaniyamāt, sa ca kriyāniyamaliṅgaḥ/ evaṃ bālasyāpi niyataviṣayo 'bhilāṣaḥ kāraṇaniyamād bhavitum arhati/ tac ca kāraṇam abhyastasmaraṇam anyad veti dṛṣṭena viśiṣyate/ dṛṣṭo hi śarīriṇām abhastasmaraṇād āhārābhilāṣa iti//23//
children.translated_text:
and there is no origination of anything without a cause. And the example does not contradict the observed cause of desire. Therefore, the approach of iron to a magnet is not a (valid) counter-example.
Moreover, iron too has no activity toward anything else — iron never approaches a clod. What causes its restriction? If (you say) it is from the restriction of the cause — that too is inferred from the restriction of activity. Likewise, the infant's desire too, being restricted to a specific object, should be from the restriction of a cause. And whether that cause is the memory of practice or something else — this is distinguished by what is observed. For the desire for food in embodied beings is observed to arise from the memory of practice. // 23 //
And for this further reason, the self (<s>ātman</s>) is permanent. Why?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.24: Because birth without attachment (<s>vītarāga</s>) is not observed.

children.text: sarāgo jāyata ity arthād āpadyate/ ayaṃ jāyamāno rāgānubhaddho jāyate, rāgasya pūrvānubhūtaviṣayānucintanaṃ yoniḥ, pūrvānubhavaś ca viṣayāṇām anyasmin janmani śarīram antareṇa nopapadyate/
children.translated_text: From the content, it follows that one is born with attachment (<s>sarāga</s>). This being born is born connected with attachment (<s>rāga</s>). The source of attachment is the recollection of previously experienced objects. And the prior experience of objects in another birth is not possible without a body.

children.text:
% śarīram antareṇa nopapadyate/] p.749
so 'yam ātmā pūrvaśarīrānubhūtān viṣayān anusmaran teṣu teṣu rajyate, tathā cāyaṃ dvayor janmanoḥ pratisandhiḥ/ evaṃ pūrvaśarīrasya pūrvatareṇa pūrvatarasya pūrvatamenetyādinānādiś cetanasya śarīrayogaḥ, anādiś ca rāgānubandha iti siddhaṃ nityatvam iti//24//
children.translated_text: This self (<s>ātman</s>), remembering the objects experienced in the previous body, becomes attached to those very objects. And thus there is a connection (<s>pratisandhi</s>) between two births. In this way, the previous body (was connected) with the one before it, and that one with the one still earlier — thus the connection of the conscious being with a body is beginningless, and the connection with attachment is beginningless. Hence the permanence (of the self) is established. // 24 //

children.text:
% p.750
kathaṃ punar jñāyate pūrvānubhūtaviṣayānucintanajanito jātasya rāgaḥ, na punaḥ ---
children.translated_text: But how is it known that the attachment of the newborn arises from the recollection of previously experienced objects, and not —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.25: Like the origination of a substance with its qualities, so is its (<s>rāga</s>'s) origination.

children.text: athotpattidharmakasya dravyasya guṇāḥ kāraṇata utpadyante tathotpattidharmakasyātmano rāgaḥ kutaścid utpadyate/ atrāyam uditānuvādo nidarśanārthaḥ//25//
children.translated_text: If the qualities of a substance that is subject to origination arise from a cause, then likewise the attachment of the self, which is subject to origination, arises from some cause. Here, this recapitulation of what has been stated serves the purpose of illustration. // 25 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.26: Not so, because attachment and the rest have volition (<s>saṅkalpa</s>) as their cause.

children.text: na khalu saguṇadravyotpattivad utpattir ātmano rāgasya ca/ kasmāt? saṅkalpanimittatvād rāgādīnām/ ayaṃ khalu prāṇināṃ viṣayān āsevamānānāṃ saṅkalpajanito rāgo gṛhyate, saṅkalpaś ca pūrvānubhūtaviṣayānucintanayoniḥ/ tenānumīyate jātasyāpi pūrvānubhūtārthacintanakṛto rāga iti/ ātmotpādādhikaraṇāt tu rāgotpattir bhavantī saṅkalpād anyasmin rāgakāraṇe sati vācyā kāryadravyaguṇavat/ na cātmotpādaḥ siddho nāpi saṅkalpād anyad rāgakāraṇam asti/
children.translated_text: The origination of the self and of its attachment is not like the origination of a substance with its qualities. Why? Because attachment and the rest have volition (<s>saṅkalpa</s>) as their cause. For in living beings experiencing objects, attachment born of volition is observed; and volition has as its source the recollection of previously experienced objects. Therefore it is inferred that even in the newborn, attachment is produced by the reflection on previously experienced objects. But if the origination of attachment were to come from the origination of the self, this would need to be stated when there is a cause of attachment other than volition — as in the case of the qualities of an effect-substance. But neither is the origination of the self established, nor is there any cause of attachment other than volition.

children.text:
% nāpi saṅkalpād anyad rāgakāraṇam asti/] p.751
tasmād ayuktaṃ saguṇadravyotpattivat tayor utpattir iti/
athāpi saṅkalpād anyad rāgakāraṇaṃ dharmādharmalakṣaṇam adṛṣṭam upādīyate, tathāpi pūrvaśarīrayogo 'pratyākhyeyaḥ/ tatra hi tasya nirvṛttiḥ nāsmin janmani/
tanmayatvād rāga iti/ viṣayābhyāsaḥ khalv ayaṃ bhāvanāhetuḥ tanmayatvam ucyate iti/ jātiviśeṣāc ca rāgaviśeṣa iti/ karma khalv idaṃ jātiviśeṣanirvartakaṃ tādarthyāt tācchabdyaṃ vijñāyate/ tasmād anupapannaṃ saṅkalpād anyad rāgakāraṇam iti//26//
children.translated_text:
Therefore the statement 'like the origination of a substance with its qualities, so is their origination' is untenable.
Even if an unseen force (<s>adṛṣṭa</s>) characterized by <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> is adduced as a cause of attachment other than volition — even so, the connection with a previous body cannot be denied. For the arising of that (unseen force) was in a previous life, not in this birth.
(The objection that) 'attachment is due to absorption (<s>tanmayatva</s>)' — but this practice with objects is what is called <s>tanmayatva</s> (absorption), and it is the cause of habitual disposition (<s>bhāvanā</s>). And (the objection that) 'a specific attachment comes from a specific birth' — but this <s>karma</s> (action), being the producer of a specific birth, is understood through its purposiveness to bear the name (of that birth). Therefore, it is untenable that there is a cause of attachment other than volition. // 26 //

children.text:
% p.752
anādiś cetanasya śarīrayoga ity uktam, svakṛtakarmanimittaṃ cāsya śarīraṃ sukhaduḥkhādhiṣṭhānam/ tat parīkṣyate --- kiṃ ghrāṇādivad ekaprakṛtikam uta nānāprakṛtīti/ kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ? vipratipatteḥ saṃśayaḥ/ pṛthivyādīni bhūtāni saṅkhyāvikalpena śarīraprakṛtir iti pratijānata iti/ kiṃ tatra tattvam?
children.translated_text: It has been stated that the connection of the conscious being with a body is beginningless, and this body — the seat of pleasure and pain — is caused by one's own actions (<s>karma</s>). This is now examined: is it made of a single material cause, like the sense of smell and the others, or of multiple material causes? Whence the doubt? The doubt arises from conflicting views. Those who claim that the elements — earth and the rest — in various numbers constitute the material cause of the body (disagree). What is the truth there?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.27: The body is earthen (<s>pārthiva</s>), because a different quality (namely, smell) is perceived.

children.text: tatra mānuṣaṃ pārthivam/ kasmāt? guṇāntaropalabdheḥ/ gandhavatī pṛthivī gandhavac ca śarīram/ abādīnām agandhatvāt tatprakṛtyagandhaṃ syāt/ na tv idam abādibhir asampṛktayā pṛthivyārabdhaṃ ceṣṭendriyārthāśrayabhāvena kalpate ity ataḥ pañcānāṃ bhūtānāṃ saṃyoge sati śarīraṃ bhavati/ bhūtasaṃyogo hi mithaḥ pañcānāṃ na niṣiddha iti/ āpyataijasavāyavyāni lokāntare śarīrāṇi teṣv api bhūtasaṃyogaḥ puruṣārthatantra iti/ sthālyādidravyaniṣpattāv api niḥsaṃśayo nābādisaṃyogam antarena niṣpattir iti//27//
children.translated_text: Among these, the human body is earthen. Why? Because a different quality is perceived. Earth possesses smell, and the body possesses smell. Since water and the rest are devoid of smell, (a body) made from them as its material cause would be devoid of smell. However, this body, made from earth unmixed with water and the rest, is not adequate to function as the substrate of effort, sense-organs, and their objects. Therefore, the body comes into being when there is a conjunction of all five elements. For the mutual conjunction of the five elements is not prohibited. Bodies of water, fire, and air exist in other worlds; in those too, the conjunction of elements is subservient to the purposes of the person (<s>puruṣa</s>). Even in the production of substances like pots, there is undoubtedly no production without the conjunction of water and the rest. // 27 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.28: (The body is) of earth, water, and fire, because their qualities are perceived.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.29: And it is of four elements (<s>cāturbhautika</s>), because inhalation and exhalation are perceived.
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.30: From smell, moisture, heat, arrangement, and the provision of space — it is of five elements (<s>pāñcabhautika</s>).

children.text: ta ime sandigdhā hetava ity upekṣitavān sūtrakāraḥ/ kathaṃ sandigdhāḥ? sati ca prakṛtibhāve bhūtānāṃ dharmopalabdhir asati ca saṃyogāpratiṣedhāt sannihitānām iti, yathā sthālyām udakatejovāyvākāśānām iti/ tad idam anekabhūtaprakṛti śarīram agandham arasam arūpam asparśaṃ ca prakṛtyanuvidhānāt syāt,
children.translated_text: These are doubtful reasons, and therefore the <s>sūtrakāra</s> (author of the sūtras) has set them aside. How are they doubtful? Because the perception of the properties of the elements is possible both when they constitute the material cause and when, in a state of conjunction (merely), they are present without their being the material cause (being refuted) — just as water, fire, air, and space are present in a pot. Therefore, this body, if made of multiple elements as its material cause, would be devoid of smell, taste, color, and touch due to following the nature of its (respective) material causes,

children.text:
% -m arūpam asparśaṃ ca prakṛtyanuvidhānāt syāt,] p.755
na tv idam itthambhūtam/ tasmāt ``pārthivaṃ guṇāntaropalabdheḥ''//28-29-30//
children.translated_text: but in fact the body is not like that. Therefore, '(the body is) earthen, because a different quality is perceived.' // 28-29-30 //
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.31: And because of the authority of scripture (<s>śruti</s>).

children.text: ``sūryaṃ te cakṣurgacchatād'' ity atra mantre ``pṛthivīṃ te śarīram'' iti śrūyate/ tad idaṃ prakrtau vikārasya pralayābhidhānam iti/
children.translated_text: In the <s>mantra</s> 'let your eye go to the sun,' it is heard: 'let your body (go) to the earth.' This is the statement of the dissolution of the modification into its material cause.

children.text:
% prakrtau vikārasya pralayābhidhānam iti/] p.757
``sūryaṃ te cakṣuḥ spṛṇomi'' ity atra mantrāntare ``pṛthivīṃ te śarīraṃ spṛṇomīti'' śrūyate/ seyaṃ kāraṇād vikārasya spṛtir abhidhīyata iti/ sthālyādiṣu ca tulyajātīyānām ekakāryārambhadarśanād bhinnajātīyānām ekakāryārambhānupapattiḥ//31//
children.translated_text: In another <s>mantra</s> — 'I reunite your eye with the sun' — it is heard: 'I reunite your body with the earth.' This is the statement of the reunion of the modification with its cause. And since in the production of substances like pots, only things of the same class are seen to participate in a single effect, the participation of things of different classes in a single effect is not possible. // 31 //

children.text: athedānīm indriyāṇi prameyakrameṇa vicāryante --- kim āvyaktikāny āhosvid bhautikānīti/
children.translated_text: Now the sense organs (<s>indriya</s>) are examined according to the order of the objects of knowledge (<s>prameya</s>) — are they derived from <s>avyakta</s> (the unmanifest, i.e., <s>prakṛti</s>) or are they elemental (<s>bhautika</s>)?
Whence the doubt?

children.text: NyS_3,1.32: kṛṣṇasāre saty upalambhād vyatiricya copalambhāt saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.32: Doubt arises because of perception when the eye's pupil (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>) exists, and also perception separate from it.

children.text: kṛṣṇasāraṃ bhautikam, tasminn anupahate rūpopalabdhiḥ upahate cānupalabdhir iti/ vyatiricya kṛṣṇasāram avasthitasya viṣayasya upalambho na kṛṣṇasāraprāptasya/ na cāprāpyakāritvam indriyāṇām, tad idam abhautikatve vibhutvāt sambhavati/ evam ubhayadharmopalabdheḥ saṃśayaḥ//32//
children.translated_text: The pupil (<s>kṛṣṇasāra</s>) is elemental (<s>bhautika</s>). When it is unimpaired, color is perceived; when it is impaired, (color is) not perceived. But perception of a distant object occurs separate from the pupil — not (only) what is reached by the pupil. And the sense organs are not non-contact-operative (<s>aprāpyakārin</s>). This (distant perception) is possible if they are non-elemental, due to their being all-pervasive (<s>vibhu</s>). Thus, from the perception of properties of both (views), doubt arises. // 32 //
(The sense organs are) non-elemental (<s>abhautika</s>), he says. Why?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.33: Because both the great and the minute are apprehended.

children.text: mahad iti mahattaraṃ mahattamaṃ copalabhyate yathā nyagrodhaparvatādi/ aṇv iti aṇutaram aṇutamaṃ ca gṛhyate yathā nyagrodhadhānādi/ tadubhayam upalabhyamānaṃ cakṣuṣo bhautikatvaṃ bādhate/ bhautikaṃ hi yāvat tāvad eva vyāpnoti/ abhautikaṃ tu vibhutvāt sarvavyāpakam iti//33//
children.translated_text: 'Great' means that what is greater and greatest is perceived — such as a banyan tree, a mountain, and so on. 'Minute' means that what is more minute and most minute is apprehended — such as a grain of rice, a sesame seed, and so on. The perception of both contradicts the elemental nature of the eye. For what is elemental pervades only as far as it extends. But what is non-elemental, being all-pervasive (<s>vibhu</s>), pervades everything. // 33 //

children.text:
% p.762
na mahadaṇugrahaṇamātrād abhautikatvaṃ vibhutvaṃ cendriyāṇāṃ śakyaṃ pratipattum/ idaṃ khalu ---
children.translated_text: The non-elemental nature and all-pervasiveness of the sense organs cannot be established merely from the apprehension of the great and the minute. Rather —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.34: The apprehension of those (great and minute objects) is due to the specific contact of the visual ray (<s>raśmi</s>) with the object.

children.text: tayor mahadaṇvor grahaṇaṃ cakṣūraśmer arthasya ca sannikarṣaviśeṣād bhavati yathā pradīparaśmer arthasya ceti/
children.translated_text: The apprehension of both the great and the minute occurs due to the specific contact of the visual ray of the eye with the object — just as (it occurs) with the ray of a lamp and an object.

children.text:
% -r arthasya ceti/] p.763
raśmyarthasannikarṣaś cāvaraṇaliṅgaḥ/ cākṣuṣo hi raśmiḥ kuḍyādibhir āvṛtam arthaṃ na prakāśayati yathā pradīparaśmir iti//34//
children.translated_text: And the contact of the ray with the object is inferred from obstruction. For the visual ray does not illuminate an object that is obstructed by a wall and the like — just as the ray of a lamp (does not). // 34 //
Given that (the visual ray's existence) is to be inferred from obstruction, (the opponent) says —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.35: From the non-perception of that (obstruction), the argument is invalid.

children.text: rūpasparśavad dhi tejaḥ, mahattvād anekadravyavattvād rūpavattvāc copalabdhir iti pradīpavat pratyakṣata upalabhyeta cākṣuṣo raśmir yadi syād iti//35//
children.translated_text: For fire has form and touch; and apprehension [is possible] because of being large, being present in many substances, and possessing form — thus, like lamp-light, the visual ray would be directly perceived if it existed. //35//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.36: The non-apprehension of what is inferred through perception is not a reason for its non-existence.

children.text: sannikarṣapratiṣedhārthenāvaraṇena liṅgenānumīyamānasya raśmer yā pratyakṣato 'nupalabdhir nāsāv abhāvaṃ pratipādayati yathā candramasaḥ parabhāgasya prthivyāś cādhobhāgasya//36//
children.translated_text: The non-apprehension through direct perception of the visual ray, which is inferred through the inferential mark of an obstruction whose purpose is to prevent contact, does not establish its non-existence — just as [one cannot infer the non-existence of] the far side of the moon or the underside of the earth. //36//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.37: And [there is] a restriction of apprehension due to the distinction between the properties of substance and quality.

children.text: bhinnaḥ khalv ayaṃ dravyadharmo guṇadharmaś ca, mahadanekadravyavac ca viṣaktāvayavam āpyaṃ dravyaṃ pratyakṣato nopalabhyate sparśas tu śīto gṛhyate/ tasya dravyasyānubandhād hemantaśiśirau kalpyete tathāvidham eva ca taijasaṃ dravyam anudbhūtarūpaṃ saha rūpeṇa nopalabhyate,
children.translated_text: Indeed, the property of a substance and the property of a quality are different. A large watery substance present in many substances, with attached parts, is not apprehended through direct perception, but its cold touch is perceived. From the connection with that substance, the winter and cold seasons are inferred. Likewise, a fiery substance of that kind, whose form is unmanifest, is not apprehended together with its form,

children.text:
% kalpyete tathāvidham ... nopalabhyate,] p.766
sparśas tv asyoṣṇa upalabhyate tasya dravyasyānubandhād grīṣmavasantau kalpyete//37//
children.translated_text: but its hot touch is apprehended. From the connection with that substance, the summer and spring seasons are inferred. //37//
But where this [apprehension of form] does occur —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.38: The apprehension of form [occurs] because of inherence in many substances and because of a special [quality of] form.

children.text: tatra rūpaṃ ca dravyaṃ ca tadāśrayaḥ pratyakṣata upalabhyate/ rūpaviśeṣas tu yadbhāvāt kvacid rūpopalabdhiḥ yadabhāvāc ca dravyasya kvacid anupalabdhiḥ sa rūpadharmo 'yam udbhava samākhyāta iti/ anudbhūtarūpaś cāyaṃ nāyano raśmiḥ, tasmāt pratyakṣato nopalabhyata iti/
children.translated_text: There, both form and the substance that is its substratum are apprehended through direct perception. The special [quality of] form, from whose presence there is apprehension of form in some cases and from whose absence there is non-apprehension of a substance in other cases — that property of form is called <s>udbhava</s> (manifestation). And this visual ray has unmanifest form; therefore it is not apprehended through direct perception.

children.text:
% iti/] p.767
dṛṣṭaś ca tejaso dharmabhedaḥ, udbhūtarūpasparśaṃ pratyakṣaṃ tejo yathā ādityaraśmayaḥ/ udbhūtarūpam anudbhūtasparśaṃ ca pratyakṣaṃ yathā pradīparaśmayaḥ/ udbhūtasparśam anudbhūtarūpam apratyakṣaṃ yathābādisaṃyuktaṃ tejaḥ/ anudbhūtarūpasparśo 'pratyakṣaś cākṣuṣo raśmir iti//38//
children.translated_text: And a distinction in the properties of fire has been observed: fire with manifest form and touch is directly perceptible, like the rays of the sun; that with manifest form but unmanifest touch is perceptible, like the rays of a lamp; that with manifest touch but unmanifest form is imperceptible, like fire connected with a spit and the like; and the visual ray, with unmanifest form and touch, is imperceptible. //38//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.39: And the arrangement of the sense organs, brought about by <s>karma</s> (action), is dependent on the purpose of the person.

children.text: yathā cetanasyārtho viṣayopalabdhibhūtaḥ sukhaduḥkhopalabdhibhūtaś ca kalpyate tathendriyāṇi vyūḍhāni, viṣayaprāptyarthaś ca raśmeś cākṣuṣasya vyūhaḥ/ rūpasparśānabhivyaktiś ca vyavahāraprakḷptyarthā, dravyaviśeṣe ca pratīghātād āvaraṇopapattir vyavahārārthā/ sarvadravyāṇāṃ viśvarūpo vyūha indriyavat karmakāritaḥ puruṣārthatantraḥ/ karma tu dharmādharmabhūtaṃ cetanasyopabhogārtham iti/
children.translated_text: Just as the purpose of the conscious being — consisting in the apprehension of objects and the experience of pleasure and pain — is conceived, so the sense organs are arranged; and the arrangement of the visual ray is for the purpose of reaching objects. The non-manifestation of form and touch serves the purpose of establishing practical usage, and the obstruction by a particular substance makes the tenability of an obstruction serve practical purposes. The multiform arrangement of all substances, like that of the sense organs, is brought about by <s>karma</s> and is dependent on the purpose of the person. And <s>karma</s>, being of the nature of <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), is for the purpose of the conscious being's experience.

children.text:
% p.768
avyabhicārāc ca pratīghāto bhautikadharmaḥ/ yaś cātvaraṇopalambhād indriyasya dravyaviśeṣe pratighātaḥ sa bhautikadharmo na bhūtāni vyabhicarati, nābautikaṃ pratighātadharmakaṃ dṛṣṭam iti/ apratighātas tu vyabhicārī bhautikābhautikayoḥ samānatvād iti/
yad api manyeta pratighātād bhautikānīndriyāṇi, apratighātād abhautikānīti prāptam? dṛṣṭaś cāpratighātaḥ kācābhrapaṭalasphaṭikāntaritopalabdheḥ/ tan na yuktam/ kasmāt? yasmād bhautikam api na pratihanyate, kācābhrapaṭalasphaṭikāntaritaprakāśāt pradīparaśmīnām, sthālyādiṣu pācakasya tejaso 'pratighātaḥ//39//
children.translated_text: And obstruction is a property of material elements, due to its invariable [correlation with them]. The obstruction of a sense organ by a particular substance, [known] from the apprehension of obstruction, is a property of material elements — it does not deviate from material elements, and nothing non-elemental with the property of obstruction is observed. But non-obstruction is deviant, since it is common to both elemental and non-elemental [entities]. Even if one were to think that because of obstruction the sense organs are elemental, and because of non-obstruction they are non-elemental — this is established? Non-obstruction is observed in the case of apprehension through glass, mica-sheets, and crystal. But this is not correct. Why? Because even an elemental thing is not obstructed — [as seen from] the light of lamp-rays through glass, mica-sheets, and crystal; and [from] the non-obstruction of cooking fire through pots and the like. //39//
And non-apprehension is tenable due to a difference in cause —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.40: The non-apprehension of that [visual ray] is like the non-apprehension of the light of a torch at midday.

children.text: yathā ``anekadravyeṇa samavāyād rūpaviśeṣāc copalabdhir'' iti saty upalabdhikāraṇe madhyandinolkāprakāśo nopakabhyate ādityaprakāśenābhibhūtaḥ, evaṃ mahadanekadravyavattvād rūpaviśeṣāc copalabhir iti saty upalabdhikāraṇe cākṣuṣo raśmir nopalabhyate nimittāntarataḥ// tac ca vyākhyātam anudbhūtarūpasparśasya dravyasya pratyakṣato 'nupalabdhir iti//40//
children.translated_text: Just as, when the cause of apprehension exists — namely, 'apprehension is due to inherence in many substances and a special [quality of] form' — the light of a torch at midday is not apprehended, being overpowered by the light of the sun, so too, when the cause of apprehension exists — namely, being large, being present in many substances, and having a special form — the visual ray is not apprehended due to another reason. And that has been explained: the non-apprehension through direct perception of a substance with unmanifest form and touch. //40//

children.text: atyantānupalabdhiś cābhāvakāraṇam/ yo hi bravīti loṣṭaprakāśo madhyandine ādityaprakāśābhibhavān nopalabhyata iti, tasyaitat syāt?
children.translated_text: But absolute non-apprehension is a reason for non-existence. For one who says that the light of a clod of earth is not apprehended at midday because of being overpowered by the light of the sun — would this hold?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.41: No, because it is not apprehended even at night.

children.text: apy anumānato 'nupalabdher iti/ evam atyantānupalabdher loṣṭaprakāśo nāsti, na tv evaṃ cakṣuṣo raśmir iti//41//
children.translated_text: That is, because it is not apprehended even through inference. Thus, from absolute non-apprehension, the light of a clod of earth does not exist; but the visual ray is not like this. //41//
And this [non-apprehension] is of a tenable kind —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.42: Since the apprehension of objects [requires] the assistance of external light, the non-apprehension is due to non-manifestation.

children.text: bāhyena prakāśenānugṛhītaṃ cakṣuḥ viṣayagrāhakaṃ tadabhāve 'nupalabdhiḥ/ sati ca prakāśānugrahe śītasparśopalabdhau ca satyāṃ tadāśrayasya dravyasya cakṣuṣā 'grahaṇaṃ rūpasyānudbhūtatvāt,
children.translated_text: The eye, assisted by external light, apprehends objects; in the absence of that, there is non-apprehension. And when the assistance of light is present and cold touch is perceived, the non-apprehension of the substance that is its substratum by the eye is due to the unmanifest nature of its form;

children.text:
% prakāśānugrahe ...] p.771
seyaṃ rūpānabhivyaktito rūpāśrayasya dravyasyānupalabdhir dṛṣṭā/ tatra yad uktaṃ ``tadanupalabdher ahetur'' iti etad ayuktam//42//
children.translated_text: this non-apprehension of the substance that is the substratum of form, due to the non-manifestation of form, has been observed. In that case, what was stated — 'the non-apprehension of that is not a [valid] reason' — this is unreasonable. //42//

children.text: kasmāt punar abhibhavo 'nupalabdhikāraṇaṃ cākṣuṣasya raśmer nocyata iti?
children.translated_text: But why is overpowering not stated as the cause of non-apprehension of the visual ray?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.43: And because overpowering [applies only] when there is manifestation.

children.text: bāhyaprakāśānugrahanirapekṣatāyāṃ ceti cārthaḥ/ yad rūpam abhivyaktam udbhūtaṃ bāhyaprakāśānugrahaṃ ca nāpekṣate tadviṣayo 'bhibhavaḥ, viparyaye 'bhibhavābhāvāt/ anudbhūtarūpatvāc cānupalabhyamānaṃ bāhyaprakāśānugrahāc copalabhyamānaṃ nābhibhūyata iti/
children.translated_text: The meaning of 'and' is: when there is independence from the assistance of external light. Overpowering applies to that form which is manifest, which is prominent, and which does not require the assistance of external light — because in the opposite case, overpowering is absent. And what is not apprehended because of having unmanifest form but is apprehended through the assistance of external light is not overpowered.

children.text:
% -nupalabhyamānaṃ] p.772
evam upapannam asti cākṣuṣo raśmir iti//43//
children.translated_text: Thus it is established that the visual ray exists. //43//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.44: And from the observation of visual rays of nocturnal creatures.

children.text: dṛśyante hi naktaṃ nayanaraśmayo naktañcarāṇāṃ vṛṣadaṃśaprabhṛtīnām, tena śeṣasyānumānam iti/ jātibhedavad indriyabheda iti cet? dharmabhedamātraṃ cānupapannam āvaraṇasya prātipratiṣedhārthasya darśanād iti//44//
children.translated_text: For the visual rays of nocturnal creatures such as cats and the like are seen at night; from that, the existence of the rest is inferred. If [one objects that] just as there is a difference in species, there is a difference in sense organs? But the [hypothesis of] a mere difference in properties is untenable, since obstruction, which serves as a counter-argument, is observed. //44//
The contact of sense organ and object as the cause of cognition is untenable. Why?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.45: [The sense organ] apprehends without reaching [the object], since there is apprehension through glass, mica-sheets, and crystal [as intervening substances].

children.text: tṛṇādi sarpad dravyaṃ kāce abhrapaṭale vā pratihataṃ dṛṣt'm, avyavahitena sannikṛṣyate vyāhanyate vai prāptir vyavadhāneneti/ yadi ca raśmyarthasannikarṣo grahaṇahetuḥ syāt na vyavahitasya sannikarṣa ity agrahaṇaṃ syāt/ asti ceyaṃ kācābhrapaṭalasphaṭikāntaritopalabdhiḥ sā jñāpayati aprāpyakārīṇīndriyāṇi ata evābhautikāni, prāpyakāritvaṃ hi bhautikadharma iti//45//
children.translated_text: A moving substance like grass and the like is observed to be obstructed by glass or mica-sheets; direct contact is obstructed, for reaching is impeded by an intervening substance. If the contact of the ray with the object were the cause of apprehension, then there would be non-apprehension of what is separated by an intervening substance, since there would be no contact. But this apprehension through glass, mica-sheets, and crystal does exist — it indicates that the sense organs act without reaching [the object], and for this very reason are non-elemental, since acting-upon-contact is a property of material elements. //45//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.46: [This] is not refuted, because of the non-apprehension of what is separated by a wall.
If the sense organs act without reaching [the object], then there should be no non-apprehension of what is separated by a wall. //46//
But even if [the sense organ] acts upon contact, there would be no apprehension through glass, mica-sheets, and crystal?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.47: The tenability of contact [is established] because there is no obstruction.

children.text: na ca kāco 'bhrapaṭalaṃ vā nayanaraśmiṃ viṣṭabhnāti so 'pratihanyamānaḥ sannikṛṣyata iti//47//
children.translated_text: Neither glass nor mica-sheets obstruct the visual ray; not being obstructed, it makes contact. //47//

children.text:
% p.776
yaś ca manyate na bhautikasyāpratighāta iti tan na ---
children.translated_text: And [to] one who thinks that there is no non-obstruction of an elemental thing — that is not so —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.48: Because the sun's ray is not impeded even through crystal, and [there is] no impediment to combustion.

children.text: ādityaraśmer avighātāt sphaṭikāntarite 'py avighātāt, dāhye 'vighātāt/ avighātād iti ca padābhisambandhād vākyabheda iti/ prativākyaṃ cārthabheda iti/ ādityaraśmiḥ kumbhādiṣu na pratihanyate, avighātāt kumbhastham udakaṃ tapati/ prāptau hi dravyāntaraguṇasya uṣṇasya sparśasya grahaṇaṃ tena ca śītasparśābhibhava iti/ sphaṭikāntarite 'pi prakāśanīye pradīparaśmīnām apratighātaḥ, apratighātāt prāptasya grahaṇam iti/ bharjanakapālādisthaṃ ca dravyam āgneyena tejasā dahyate tatrāvighātāt prāptiḥ, prāptau tu dāho nāprāpyakāri teja iti/
children.translated_text: Because the sun's ray is not impeded, even through crystal it is not impeded, and combustion is not impeded. 'Because of non-impediment' forms a separate sentence through connection with each word, and there is a different meaning for each sentence. The sun's ray is not obstructed by pots and the like; because of non-impediment, it heats the water inside a pot. For upon reaching, there is the apprehension of a hot touch, which is a quality of another substance, and thereby the overpowering of cold touch. Even through crystal, the rays of a lamp are not obstructed in illuminating what is to be illuminated; because of non-obstruction, what has reached is apprehended. And a substance placed in a frying pan and the like is burned by fiery heat; because of non-impediment there, there is reaching; and upon reaching, combustion — fire does not act without reaching.

children.text:
% p.777
avighātād iti ca kevalaṃ padam upādīyate, ko 'yam avighāto nāma? avyuhyamānāvayavena vyavadhāyena dravyeṇa sarvato dravyasyāviṣṭhmbhaḥ kriyāhetor apratibandhaḥ prāpter apratiṣedha iti/ dṛṣṭaṃ hi kalaśaniṣaktānām apāṃ bahiḥ śītasparśasya grahaṇam/ na cendriyeṇāsannikṛṣṭasya dravyasya sparśopalabdhiḥ/ dṛṣṭau ca praspandaparisravau/ tatra kācābhrapaṭalādibhir nayanaraśmer apratighātād vibhidyārthena saha sannikarṣād upapannaṃ grahaṇam iti//48//
children.translated_text: The mere word 'non-impediment' is employed — what is this non-impediment? The non-obstruction of a substance in all directions by an intervening substance whose parts are not displaced; the non-obstruction of the cause of motion; the non-prevention of reaching. For the apprehension of cold touch externally from water contained in a jar is observed. And there is no apprehension of the touch of a substance that is not in contact with the sense organ. And vibration and seepage are observed. Therefore, the apprehension [through glass and the like] is tenable because the visual ray, not being obstructed by glass, mica-sheets, and the like, penetrates and makes contact with the object. //48//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.49: Because the consequence of mutual interchange of properties [would follow].

children.text: kācābhrapaṭalādivad vā kuḍyādibhir apratighātaḥ, kuḍyādivad vā kācābhrapaṭalādibhiḥ pratighāta iti prasajyate, niyame kāraṇaṃ vācyam iti//49//
children.translated_text: Either there would be non-obstruction by walls and the like, just as by glass, mica-sheets, and the like; or there would be obstruction by glass, mica-sheets, and the like, just as by walls and the like — this follows as a consequence. A reason for the restriction must be stated. //49//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,1.50: The apprehension of that [through transparent substances] is like the apprehension of form in mirrors and water, due to the natural transparency [of those substances].

children.text: ādarśodakayoḥ prasādo rūpaviśeṣaḥ svo dharmo niyamadarśanāt, prasādasya vā svo dharmo rūpopalambhanam/ yathā ādarśapratihatasya parāvṛttasya nayanaraśmeḥ svena mukhena sannikarṣe sati svamukhopalambhanaṃ pratibimbagrahaṇākhyam ādarśarūpānugrahāt tannimittaṃ bhavati,
children.translated_text: The transparency of mirrors and water is a special form, their own property, as seen from the observed restriction; or rather, the apprehension of form is the natural property of transparency. Just as the visual ray, reflected back from a mirror, when in contact with one's own face, apprehends one's own face — this apprehension, called the grasping of a reflection, occurs due to the assistance of the form of the mirror and is caused by it;

children.text:
% -karṣe sati ...] p.779
ādarśarūpopaghāte tadabhāvāt, kuḍyādiṣu ca pratibimbagrahaṇaṃ na bhavati evaṃ kācābhrapaṭalādibhir avighātaś cakṣūraśmeḥ kuḍyādibhiś ca pratighāto dravyasvabhāvaniyamād iti//50//
children.translated_text: when the form of the mirror is damaged, that [reflection] is absent because of the absence [of the assisting form]; and in walls and the like, the grasping of a reflection does not occur. Similarly, the non-impediment of the visual ray by glass, mica-sheets, and the like, and the obstruction by walls and the like, is due to the restriction inherent in the nature of the substances. //50//
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.51]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.51: For it is impossible to command or forbid things that are perceived or inferred.

children.text: pramāṇasya tattvaviṣayatvāt/ na khalu bhoḥ parīkṣamāṇena dṛṣṭānumitā arthāḥ śakyā niyoktum evaṃ bhavateti,
children.translated_text: Because a <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) has truth as its object. Indeed, sir, things perceived and inferred cannot be commanded by an examiner to 'be thus,'

children.text:
% niyoktum evaṃ bhavateti,] p.780
nāpi pratiṣeddhum evaṃ na bhavateti/ na hīdam upapadyate rūpavad gandho 'pi cākṣuṣo bhavatv iti, gandhavad vā rūpaṃ cākṣuṣaṃ mā bhūd iti, agnipratipattivat dhūmenodakapratipattir api bhavatv iti, udakāpratipattivad vā dhūmenāgnipratipattir api mā bhūd iti/ kiṃ kāraṇam? yathā khalv arthā bhavanti ya eṣāṃ svo bhāvaḥ svo dharma iti tathābhūtāḥ pramāṇena pratipadyanta iti/ tathābhūtaviṣayakaṃ hi pramāṇam iti/ imau khalu niyogapratiṣedhau bhavatā deśitau kācābhrapaṭalādivad vā kuḍyādibhir apratighāto bhavatu kuḍyādivad vā kācābhrapaṭalādibhir apratighāto mā bhūd iti/ na, dṛṣṭānumitāḥ khalv ime dravyadharmāḥ, pratighātāpratighātayor hy upalabdhī vyavasthāpike/ vyavahitānupalabdhyānumīyate kuḍyādibhiḥ pratighātaḥ, vyavahitopalabdhyānumīyate kācābhrapaṭalādibhir apratighāta iti//51//
children.translated_text: nor can they be forbidden to 'not be thus.' For this is not tenable: 'Let smell, like color, also be an object of sight,' or 'Like smell, let color also not be an object of sight'; or 'Like the apprehension of fire from smoke, let there also be apprehension of water from smoke,' or 'Like the non-apprehension of water, let there also be no apprehension of fire from smoke.' Why? Because things exist as they are — their own nature, their own property — and as such they are apprehended by a <s>pramāṇa</s>. For a <s>pramāṇa</s> has as its object things as they actually are. Now, these commands and prohibitions of yours have been taught as if saying: 'Let there be non-obstruction by crystal, mica-sheet, and the like, as by walls,' or 'Let there not be non-obstruction by walls and the like, as by crystal, mica-sheet, and the like.' No — for these are indeed properties of substances that are perceived and inferred. The perceptions of obstruction and non-obstruction are the determiners. Non-obstruction by walls and the like is inferred from the non-perception of what is behind them; non-obstruction by crystal, mica-sheet, and the like is inferred from the perception of what is behind them. // 51 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.52]

children.text:
% p.781
athāpi khalv ekam idam indriyaṃ bahūnīndriyāṇi vā? kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ?
children.translated_text: Now, is there one sense organ or many? Whence the doubt?

children.text: NyS_3,1.52: sthānānyatve nānātvād avayavinānāsthānatvāc ca saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.1.52: Doubt (arises) from the plurality (of sense organs) when the locations are different, and from the fact that a whole (<s>avayavin</s>) can be in different locations.

children.text: bahūni dravyāṇi nānāsthānāni dṛśyante, nānāsthānaś ca sann eko 'vayavī ceti/ tenendriyeṣu bhinnasthāneṣu saṃśaya iti//52//
children.translated_text: Many substances are seen in different locations; and a single whole, being in different locations, (is also seen). Hence there is doubt regarding the sense organs that are in different locations. // 52 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.53]
There is one sense organ —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.53: Because of the non-difference of skin (<s>tvac</s>).

children.text:
tvag ekam indriyam ity āha/ kasmāt? avyatirekāt/ na tvacā kiñcid indriyādhiṣṭhānaṃ na prāptam, na cāsatyāṃ tvaci kiñcid viṣayagrahaṇaṃ bhavati, yayā satvendriyasthānāni vyāptāni yasyāṃ ca satyāṃ viṣayagrahaṇaṃ bhavati sā tvag ekam indriyam iti/
nendriyāntarārthānupalabdheḥ/ sparśopalabdhilakṣaṇāyāṃ satyāṃ tvaci gṛhyamāṇe tvagindriyeṇa sparśe indriyāntarārthā rūpādayo na gṛhyante andhādibhiḥ/ na sparśagrāhakāt indriyād indriyāntaram astīti sparśavad andhādibhir gṛhyeran rūpādayaḥ, na ca gṛhyante tasmān naikam indriyaṃ tvag iti/
children.translated_text:
Skin (<s>tvac</s>) is one sense organ, it is said. Why? Because of non-difference. No location of a sense organ is not reached by skin, and without skin there is no apprehension of any sense-object. That which pervades the locations of all sense organs, and in the presence of which sense-object apprehension occurs — that skin is one sense organ.
(Reply:) Not so, because the objects of other sense organs are not perceived (by skin alone). When skin — characterized by the perception of touch — is being perceived by the tactile organ, other sense objects such as color and the like are not perceived by blind persons and the like. Since there is no other sense organ beyond the touch-perceiving organ, blind persons and others should perceive color and the like just like touch — but they do not perceive them. Therefore, skin is not the one sense organ.

children.text:
% p.784
tvagavayavaviśeṣeṇa dhūmopalabdhivat tadupalabdhiḥ/ yathā tvaco 'vayavaviśeṣaḥ kaścic cakṣuṣi sannikṛṣṭo dhūmasparśaṃ gṛhṇāti nānyaḥ, evaṃ tvaco 'vayavaviśeṣā rūpādigrāhakās teṣām upaghātād andhādibhir na gṛhyante rūpādaya iti/ vyāhatatvād ahetuḥ/ tvagavyatirekād ekam indriyam ity uktvā ``tvag avayavaviśeṣeṇa dhūmopalabdhivad rūpādyupalabdhir'' ity ucyate/ evaṃ ca sati nānābhūtāni viṣayagrāhakāṇi viṣayavyavasthānāt tadbhāve viṣayagrahaṇasya bhāvāt tadupaghāte cābhāvāt, tathā ca pūrvo vāda uttareṇa vādeṇa vyāhanyata iti/
sandigdhaś cāvyatirekaḥ/ pṛthivyādibhir api bhūtair indriyādhiṣṭhānāni vyāptāni, na ca teṣv asatsu viṣayagrahaṇaṃ bhavatīti/ tasmān na tvag anyad vā sarvaviṣayam ekam indriyam iti//53//
children.translated_text:
(Objection:) Perception of those (other objects) occurs through special parts of skin, like the perception of smoke (through a specific organ). Just as a particular part of skin, proximate to the eye, perceives the touch of smoke but another (part) does not, similarly, particular parts of skin are the perceivers of color and the like; due to their impairment, color and the like are not perceived by blind persons and the like. (Reply:) This is a non-reason because it is self-contradictory. Having said 'skin is one sense organ because of non-difference,' then saying 'perception of color and the like occurs through special parts of skin, like the perception of smoke' — given this, since the perceivers of sense-objects are diverse, differentiated by their objects, and since perception exists when they exist and is absent when they are impaired, the earlier thesis is contradicted by the later one.
And the non-difference (of skin) is doubtful. For the locations of sense organs are pervaded by other elements — earth and the rest — as well, and without them being present, sense-object apprehension does not occur. Therefore, neither skin nor anything else is one sense organ for all objects. // 53 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.54]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.54: No (one sense organ), because of the non-simultaneous perception of objects.

children.text: ātmā manasā sambadhyate, mana indriyeṇa, indriyaṃ sarvārthaiḥ sannikṛṣṭam iti, ātmendriyamanorthasannikarṣebhyo yugapad grahaṇāni syuḥ/ na ca yugapad rūpādayo gṛhyante tasmān naikam indriyaṃ sarvaviṣayam astīti/ asāhacaryāc ca viṣayagrahaṇānāṃ naikam indriyaṃ sarvaviṣayakam, sāhacarye hi viṣayagrahaṇānām andhādyanupapattir iti//54//
children.translated_text: The <s>ātman</s> (self) is connected with <s>manas</s> (mind), <s>manas</s> with the sense organ, and the sense organ is in contact with all its objects — thus from the contacts of self, sense organ, mind, and object, there should be simultaneous apprehensions. But color and the like are not perceived simultaneously; therefore there is no one sense organ for all objects. And from the non-co-occurrence of sense-object perceptions, there is no one all-encompassing sense organ; for if there were co-occurrence, the impossibility of blindness and the like (would follow). // 54 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.55]
[Page break]

children.text: NyS_3,1.55: vipratiṣedhāc ca na tvag ekā ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.1.55: And because of the contradiction, skin is not one (sense organ).

children.text: na khalu tvag ekam indriyaṃ vyāghātāt --- tvacā rūpāṇy aprāptāni gṛhyanta ity aprāpyakāritve sparśādiṣv apy evaṃ prasaṅgaḥ/ sparśādīnāṃ ca prāptānāṃ grahaṇād rūpādīnāṃ prāptānāṃ grahaṇam iti prāptam/
children.translated_text: Skin is indeed not one sense organ, because of the contradiction: since colors are perceived by skin without physical contact, the consequence would be that touch and the like too (are perceived) without contact. And since touch and the like are perceived through contact, it follows that color and the like should also be perceived through contact.

children.text:
% p.787
prāpyāprāpyakāritvam iti cet? āvaraṇānupapatter viṣayamātrasya grahaṇam/ athāpi manyeta prāptāḥ sparśādayas tvacā gṛhyante rūpāṇi tv aprāptānīti? evaṃ sati nāsty āvaraṇam, āvaraṇānupapatteś ca rūpamātrasya grahaṇaṃ vyavahitasya cāvyavahitasya ceti/ dūrāntikānuvidhānaṃ ca rūpopalabdhyanupalabdhyor na syāt/ aprāptaṃ tvacā gṛhyate rūpam iti dūre rūpasyāgrahaṇam antike ca grahaṇam ity etan na syād iti//55//
children.translated_text: (Objection:) It operates both with and without contact? (Reply:) Then there would be no obstruction, and there would be the perception of any object whatsoever. Or if you think: touch and the like are perceived by skin through contact, but colors without contact? In that case there is no obstruction; and since there is no obstruction, there would be the perception of color alone, whether obstructed or unobstructed. And the conformity to distance and proximity in the perception and non-perception of color would not exist. Since color is perceived by skin without contact, the non-perception of color at a distance and the perception nearby — this would not obtain. // 55 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.56]

children.text: pratiṣedhāc ca nānātvasiddhau sthāpanāhetur apy upādīyate ---
children.translated_text: And from the refutation, when plurality is established, the reason for the positive thesis is also adopted —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.56: Because of the fivefold purpose of the sense organs.

children.text: arthaḥ prayojanam, tat pañcavidham indriyāṇām, sparśanenendriyeṇa sparśagrahaṇe sati na tenaiva rūpaṃ gṛhyata iti rūpagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ cakṣur anumīyate/
children.translated_text: Purpose means function, and that is fivefold for the sense organs. When the sense of touch perceives touch, color is not perceived by that same organ — hence the eye is inferred as having the function of perceiving color.

children.text:
% tenaiva rūpaṃ gṛhyata iti rūpagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ cakṣur anumīyate/] p.788
sparśarūpagrahaṇe ca tābhyām eva na gandho gṛhyata iti gandhagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ ghrāṇam anumīyate/ trayāṇāṃ grahaṇe na tair eva raso gṛhyata iti rasagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ rasanam anumīyate/ na ca caturṇāṃ grahaṇe tair eva śabdaḥ śrūyata iti śabdagrahaṇaprayojanaṃ śrotram anumīyate/ evam indriyaprayojanasyānitaretarasādhanasādhyatvāt pañcaivendriyāṇi//56//
children.translated_text: And when touch and color are perceived, smell is not perceived by those same (organs) — hence the nose is inferred as having the function of perceiving smell. When three (types of objects) are perceived, taste is not perceived by those — hence the tongue is inferred as having the function of perceiving taste. And when four (types) are perceived, sound is not heard by those — hence the ear is inferred as having the function of perceiving sound. Thus, since the functions of the sense organs are not mutually interchangeable as means and objects (of proof), there are five and only five sense organs. // 56 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.57]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.57: No, because of the multiplicity of those objects.

children.text: na khalv indriyārthapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇīti sidhyati/ kasmāt? teṣām arthānāṃ bahutvāt/ bahavaḥ khalv ime indriyārthāḥ, sparśās tāvat śītoṣnānuṣṇāśītā iti/ rūpāṇi śuklaharitādīni/ gandhā iṣṭāniṣṭopekṣaṇīyāḥ/ rasāḥ kaṭukādayaḥ, śabdā varṇātmāno dhvanimātrāś ca bhinnāḥ/ tad yasyendriyārthapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇi tasyendriyārthabahutvād bahūni indriyāṇi prasajyanta iti//57//
children.translated_text: It is not established that there are five sense organs merely because of the fivefold purpose of the sense organs. Why? Because of the multiplicity of those objects. For these sense-objects are indeed many: touches are cold, hot, and neither-cold-nor-hot. Colors are white, green, and the like. Smells are pleasant, unpleasant, and neutral. Tastes are pungent and the like. Sounds are those consisting of phonemes and those consisting of mere noise — (all) different. Therefore, for one who holds that there are five sense organs because of the fivefold purpose, the consequence would be many sense organs because of the multiplicity of objects. // 57 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.58]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.58: There is no refutation of smells and the like, because of the non-difference of smell-ness and the like (as general categories).

children.text: gandhatvādibhiḥ svasāmānyaiḥ kṛtavyavasthānāṃ gandhādīnāṃ yāni gandhādigrahaṇāni tāny asamānasādhanasādhyatvād grāhakāntarāṇi na prayojayanti/ arthasamūho 'numānamukto nārthaikadeśaḥ/
children.translated_text: Smells and the like, whose classification is determined by their own generalities such as smell-ness and the like — the perceptions of smell and the like, not being mutually interchangeable as means and objects (of proof), do not require additional perceiving organs. The inference is based on the aggregate of objects, not on a particular portion of objects.

children.text:
% -mukto nārthaikadeśaḥ/] p.790
arthaikadeśaṃ cāśritya viṣayapañcatvamātraṃ bhavān pratiṣedhati tasmād ayukto 'yaṃ pratiṣedha iti/
kathaṃ punar gandhatvādibhiḥ svasāmānyaiḥ kṛtavyavasthā gandhādaya iti? sparśaḥ khalv ayaṃ trividhaḥ śīta uṣṇo 'nuṣṇāśītaś ca sparśatvena svasāmānyena saṃgṛhītaḥ/ gṛhyamāṇe ca śītasparśe noṣṇasyānuṣṇāśītasya vā sparśasya grahaṇaṃ grāhakāntaraṃ prayojayati sparśabhedānām ekasādhanasādhyatvād yenaiva śītasparśo gṛhyate tenaivetarāv apīti/ evaṃ gandhatvena gandhānām, rūpatvena rūpāṇām, rasatvena rasānām, śabdatvena śabdānām iti/ gandhādigrahaṇāni punar asamānasādhanasādhyatvād grāhakāntarāṇāṃ prayojakāni/ tasmād upapannam indriyārthapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇīti//58//
children.translated_text:
And you, relying on a particular portion of objects, deny only the fivefold (division) of sense-objects; therefore this denial is unwarranted.
But how are smells and the like classified by their own generalities such as smell-ness? Touch is indeed of three kinds — cold, hot, and neither-cold-nor-hot — yet is subsumed by its own generality 'touch-ness.' And when cold touch is being perceived, the non-perception of hot or neither-cold-nor-hot touch does not require an additional perceiving organ, because the sub-types of touch share the same means and object (of proof) — that very (organ) by which cold touch is perceived, by that same (organ) the others are also (perceived). Similarly, smells by 'smell-ness,' colors by 'color-ness,' tastes by 'taste-ness,' sounds by 'sound-ness.' But the perceptions of smell and the like, not sharing the same means and objects (of proof), do require additional perceiving organs. Therefore it is established: because of the fivefold purpose of the sense organs, there are five sense organs. // 58 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.59]
If generality is what subsumes, then the consequence for the sense organs is —
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.59: There would be oneness (of the sense organs), because of the non-difference of 'being-an-object' (as a general category).

children.text: viṣayatvena hi sāmānyena gandhādayaḥ saṅgṛhītā iti//59//
children.translated_text: For smells and the like are subsumed by the generality 'being-an-object' (<s>viṣayatva</s>). // 59 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.60]
[Page break]
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.60: No, because of the fivefold (distinction based on) cognition-as-mark, location, mode-of-operation, configuration, and material cause.

children.text:
na khalu viṣayatvena sāmānyena kṛtavyavasthā viṣayā grāhakāntaranirapekṣā ekasādhanagrāhyā anumīyante, anumīyante ca pañca gandhādayo gandhatvādibhiḥ svasāmānyaiḥ kṛtavyavasthā indriyāntaragrāhyāḥ, tasmād asambaddham etat/ ayam eva cārtho 'nūdyate buddhilakṣaṇapañcatvād iti/
buddhaya eva lakṣaṇāni viṣayagrahaṇaliṅgatvāt indriyāṇām, tad etat ``indriyārthapañcatvāt'' ity etasmin sūtre kṛtabhāṣyam iti/ tasmād buddhilakṣaṇapañcatvāt pañcendriyāṇi/
children.translated_text:
It is not the case that objects whose classification is determined by the generality 'being-an-object' are inferred as being independent of additional perceiving organs and as being apprehensible by a single means. Rather, the five (types) — smell and the like — are inferred as having their classification determined by their own generalities such as smell-ness, and as being apprehensible by different sense organs. Therefore this (objection) is irrelevant. And this very point is reiterated as 'because of the fivefold (distinction based on) cognition-as-mark.'
Cognitions themselves are the marks — since they are the indicators of the sense organs by virtue of their apprehending sense-objects. This has been commented upon in the <s>sūtra</s> 'because of the fivefold purpose of the sense organs.' Therefore, because of the fivefold (distinction of) cognition-as-mark, there are five sense organs.

children.text:
% p.792
adhiṣṭhānāny api khalu pañcendriyāṇām, sarvaśarīrādhiṣṭhānaṃ sparśanaṃ sparśagrahaṇaliṅgam, kṛṣṇasārādhiṣṭhānaṃ cakṣuḥ bahirniḥsṛtaṃ rūpagrahaṇaliṅgam, nāsādhiṣṭhānaṃ ghrāṇam, jihvādhiṣṭhānaṃ rasanam, karṇacchidrādhiṣṭhānaṃ śrotram, gandharasarūpasparśaśabdagrahaṇaliṅgatvād iti/
gatibhedād apīndriyabhedaḥ/ kṛṣṇasāropanibaddhaṃ cakṣur bahirniḥsṛtya rūpādhikaraṇāni dravyāṇi prāpnoti/ sparśanādīni tv indriyāṇi viṣayā evāśrayopasarpaṇāt pratyāsīdanti/ santānavṛttyā śabdasya śrotrapratyāsattir iti/
ākṛtiḥ khalu parimāṇam iyattā sā pañcadhā/ svasthānamātrāṇi ghrāṇarasanasparśanāni viṣayagrahaṇenānumeyāni/ cakṣuḥ kṛṣṇasārāśrayaṃ bahirniḥsṛtaṃ viṣayavyāpi/ śrotraṃ nānyad ākāśāt, tac ca vibhu śabdamātrānubhavānumeyaṃ puruṣasaṃskāropagrahaṇāc cādhiṣṭhānaniyamena śabdasya vyañjakam iti/
children.translated_text:
The locations (<s>adhiṣṭhānas</s>) of the five sense organs are also (five): the sense of touch, whose location is the entire body, is indicated by the apprehension of touch; the eye, whose location is the black pupil, extends outward and is indicated by the apprehension of color; the nose, whose location is the nasal (cavity), is indicated by the apprehension of smell; the tongue, whose location is the tongue, is indicated by the apprehension of taste; the ear, whose location is the ear-cavity, is indicated by the apprehension of sound.
The sense organs are also distinguished by their modes of operation (<s>gati</s>). The eye, bound to the black pupil, extends outward and reaches the substances that are the substrates of color. But the other sense organs — touch and the rest — the objects themselves approach the substrate (of the organ). The proximity of sound to the ear occurs through a continuum-operation.
Configuration (<s>ākṛti</s>) means magnitude, extent — and that is fivefold. The nose, tongue, and touch-organ are confined to their respective locations and are to be inferred from their apprehension of sense-objects. The eye, having its substrate in the black pupil, extends outward and pervades the objects. The ear is nothing other than <s>ākāśa</s> (space) — it is all-pervasive, to be inferred from the experience of all sounds; and because of its support by the individual's bodily constitution (<s>saṃskāra</s>), it manifests sound with a restriction to its location.

children.text:
% p.793
jātir iti yoniṃ pracakṣate/ pañca khalv indriyayonayaḥ pṛthivyādīni bhūtāni, tasmāt prakṛtipañcatvād api pañcendriyāṇīti siddham//60//
children.translated_text: <s>Jāti</s> (material cause) means origin. The five origins of the sense organs are the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) — earth and the rest. Therefore, because of the fivefold material cause as well, five sense organs is established. // 60 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.1.61]
But how is it known that the sense organs have the elements as their material cause and not the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>)?
<s>NyS</s> 3.1.61: Identity (of the sense organs with the elements) is established because of the perception of specific elemental qualities.

children.text: dṛṣṭo hi vāyvādīnāṃ bhūtānāṃ guṇaviśeṣābhivyaktiniyamaḥ/ vāyuḥ sparśavyañjakaḥ, āpo rasavyañjikāḥ, tejo rūpavyañjakam, pārthivaṃ kiñcid dravyaṃ kasyacid dravyasya gandhavyañjakam/ asti cāyam indriyāṇāṃ bhūtaguṇaviśeṣopalabdhiniyamaḥ tena bhūtaguṇaviśeṣopalabdher manyāmahe bhūtaprakṛtīnīndriyāṇi nāvyaktaprakṛtīnīti//61//
children.translated_text: For a fixed rule is observed regarding the manifestation of specific qualities by the elements (<s>bhūtas</s>) such as wind and the rest. Wind (<s>vāyu</s>) manifests touch, water (<s>āpas</s>) manifests taste, fire (<s>tejas</s>) manifests color, and a certain earthy (<s>pārthiva</s>) substance manifests the smell of a certain substance. And there is this fixed rule that the sense organs apprehend specific qualities of the elements; therefore, from the fixed apprehension of specific elemental qualities, we hold that the sense organs have the elements as their material cause, not the unmanifest (<s>avyakta</s>). //61//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.62]

children.text:
% p.795
gandhādayaḥ pṛthivyādiguṇā ity uddiṣṭam uddeśaś ca pṛthivyādīnām ekaguṇatve cānekaguṇatve ca samāna ity ata āha ---
children.translated_text: [Note: p.795] It has been stated that smell and the rest are the qualities of earth and the rest, and the enumeration of earth and the rest is the same whether they have one quality or many qualities; therefore (the sūtra) says —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.62: Of smell, taste, color, touch, and sound — (earth has qualities) up to and including touch.
[Section: NySBh_3,1.63]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.63: For water, fire, and wind, the preceding ones are successively removed; and for space (<s>ākāśa</s>), the last (quality remains).

children.text: sparśaparyantānām iti vibhaktivipariṇāmaḥ/ ākāśasyottaraḥ śabdaḥ sparśaparyantebhya iti/
children.translated_text: 'Up to and including touch' — this is a transformation of the case ending. For space, the last (quality), sound, (remains) after removing (the qualities) up to and including touch.

children.text:
% iti/] p.796
kathaṃ tarhi tarabnirdeśaḥ? svatantraviniyogasāmarthyāt/ tenottaraśabdasya parārthābhidhānaṃ vijñāyate/ uddeśasūtre hi sparśaparyantebhyaḥ paraḥ śabda iti/ tantraṃ vā sparśasya vivakṣitatvāt --- sparśaparyanteṣu niyukteṣu yo 'nyas taduttaraḥ śabda iti//62-63//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.796] How then is the comparative suffix (-tara) to be explained? By the force of the independent syntactic connection. Thereby it is understood that the word 'last' (<s>uttara</s>) denotes what is beyond the others. For in the enumeration sūtra, (the meaning is:) sound is beyond (those qualities) up to and including touch. Alternatively, the syntactic device is because touch is the intended (focus) — when (the qualities) up to and including touch have been assigned, what is other than that, the last, is sound. //62-63//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.64]
[Note: p.797]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.64: (This assignment is) not (correct), because not all qualities are apprehended.

children.text: nāyaṃ guṇaniyogaḥ sādhuḥ/ kasmāt? yasya bhūtasya ye guṇā na te tadātmakenendriyeṇa sarve upalabhyante/ pārthivena hi ghrāṇena sparśaparyantā na gṛhyante gandha eva eko gṛhyate evaṃ śeṣeṣv apīti//64//
children.translated_text: This assignment of qualities is not valid. Why? Because the sense organ that is of the same nature as an element does not apprehend all the qualities of that element. For through the earthen organ of smell, (the qualities) up to and including touch are not grasped — only smell alone is grasped; likewise for the rest as well. //64//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.65]
How then should these qualities be assigned?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.65: Because each successive (element) possesses one quality at a time, the non-apprehension of those (qualities) by the successively (higher elements is explained).

children.text: gandhādīnām ekaiko yathākramaṃ pṛthivyādīnām ekaikasya guṇaḥ, ataḥ ``tadanupalabdhiḥ'' teṣāṃ tayoḥ tasya cānupalabdhiḥ ---
children.translated_text: Of smell and the rest, each one in order is a quality of each one of earth and the rest; therefore 'the non-apprehension of those' — that is, the non-apprehension of those (three), of those two, and of that one —

children.text:
% teṣāṃ tayoḥ tasya cānupalabdhiḥ ---] p.798
ghrāṇena rasarūpasparśānāṃ rasanena rūpasparśayoḥ cakṣuṣā sparśasyeti/
kathaṃ tarhy anekaguṇāni bhūtāni gṛhyanta iti?
saṃsargāc cānekaguṇagrahaṇam/ abādisaṃsargāc ca pṛthivyāṃ rasādayo gṛhyante evaṃ śeṣeṣv apīti//65//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.798] (namely,) the non-apprehension of taste, color, and touch by the organ of smell; of color and touch by the organ of taste; of touch by the eye. How then are the elements with multiple qualities apprehended? The apprehension of multiple qualities is due to association (<s>saṃsarga</s>). Through the association of earth with water and the rest, taste and the other (qualities) are apprehended in earth; likewise in the case of the rest as well. //65//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.66]

children.text:
% p.799
niyamas tarhi na prāpnoti saṃsargasyāniyamāt caturguṇā pṛthivī triguṇā āpo dviguṇaṃ teja ekaguṇo vāyur iti/ niyamaś copapadyate/ katham?
children.translated_text: [Note: p.799] Then a fixed rule would not obtain, since there is no fixed rule regarding association — (the rule) that earth has four qualities, water has three qualities, fire has two qualities, and wind has one quality. Yet a fixed rule is justified. How?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.66: For the lower is pervaded by the higher.

children.text: pṛthivyādīnāṃ pūrvapūrvam uttareṇottareṇa viṣṭam ataḥ saṃsarganiyama iti/ tac caitad bhūtasṛṣṭau veditavyaṃ naitarhīti//66//
children.translated_text: Among earth and the rest, each preceding one is pervaded by each succeeding one; hence the fixed rule of association. And this is to be understood as (applying) at the time of the creation of the elements, not at the present time. //66//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.67]
[Note: p.800]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.67: (This is) not (correct), because of the perceptibility of earthy and watery (substances).

children.text: neti trisūtrīṃ pratyācaṣṭe/ kasmāt? pārthivasya dravyasyāpy asya ca pratyakṣaṭvāt/ mahatvānekadravyatvād rūpāc copalabdhir iti taijasam eva dravyaṃ pratyakṣaṃ syāt na pārthivam āpyaṃ vā rūpābhāvāt/ taijasavat tu pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt na saṃsargād anekaguṇagrahaṇaṃ bhūtānām iti/ bhūtāntararūpakṛtaṃ ca pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvaṃ bruvataḥ pratyakṣo vāyuḥ prasajyate niyame vā kāraṇam ucyatām iti/
children.translated_text: The word 'not' (<s>na</s>) rejects the preceding three sūtras. Why? Because earthy substances and watery substances are perceptible. Since apprehension (requires) magnitude, multiplicity of substances, and color — only fiery substances alone should be perceptible, not earthy or watery substances, because they lack (their own) color. But since earthy and watery substances are perceptible just like fiery substances, the apprehension of multiple qualities is not due to association of elements. And for one who maintains that the perceptibility of earthy and watery substances is caused by the color of another element (fire), the consequence would follow that wind is also perceptible — or else a reason for the restriction must be stated.

children.text:
% p.801
rasayor vā pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt --- pārthivo rasaḥ ṣaḍvidhaḥ, āpyo madhura eva; na caitat saṃsargād bhavtitum arhati/ rūpayor vā pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt taijasarūpānugṛhītayoḥ, saṃsarge hi vyañjakam eva rūpaṃ na vyaṅgyam astīti/ ekānekavidhatve ca pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvād rūpayoḥ/ pārthivaṃ haritalohitapītādyanekavidhaṃ rūpam, āpyaṃ tu śuklam aprakāśakam, na caitad ekaguṇānāṃ saṃsarge saty upapadyata iti/ udāharaṇamātraṃ caitat, ataḥ paraṃ prapañcaḥ /
sparśayor vā pārthivataijasayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt/ pārthivo 'nuṣnāśītaḥ sparśaḥ, uṣṇas taijasaḥ pratyakṣaḥ, na caitad ekaguṇānām anuṣṇāśītasparśena vāyunā saṃsargeṇopapadyata iti/
atha vā pārthivāpyayor dravyayor vyvasthitaguṇayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt/ caturguṇaṃ pārthivaṃ dravyaṃ triguṇam āpyaṃ pratyakṣam, tena tatkāraṇam anumīyate tathābhūtam iti/ tasya kāryaṃ liṅgaṃ kāraṇabhāvād dhi kāryabhāva iti/ evaṃ taijasavāyavyayor dravyayoḥ pratyakṣatvād guṇavyavasthāyāḥ tatkāraṇe dravye vyavasthānumānam iti/
dṛṣṭaś ca vivekaḥ pārthivāpyayoḥ pratyakṣatvāt/ pārthivaṃ dravyam abādibhir viyuktaṃ pratyakṣato gṛhyate,
children.translated_text: [Note: p.801] Or, because of the perceptibility of the tastes of earthy and watery substances — earthly taste is sixfold, while watery taste is only sweet; and this cannot be due to association. Or, because of the perceptibility of the colors of earthy and watery substances, which are aided by fiery color — for in association, only the manifesting color exists, not the manifested (color). And because of the perceptibility of the colors of earthy and watery substances in their single and manifold forms — earthly color is manifold: green, red, yellow, and so on, while watery color is white and non-luminous; and this is not possible when single-quality (elements) are in association. And this is merely by way of illustration; beyond this, (there is further) elaboration. Or, because of the perceptibility of the touches of earthy and fiery substances — earthy touch is neither hot nor cold, while fiery (touch) is hot and perceptible; and this is not possible through association with wind, which has (only) a neither-hot-nor-cold touch and a single quality. Alternatively, because earthy and watery substances are perceptible with their qualities in fixed arrangement — an earthy substance with four qualities and a watery substance with three qualities are perceptible; and from that, their cause is inferred to be of the same nature. The effect is the inferential mark of the cause, for the nature of the effect arises from the nature of the cause. Likewise, from the perceptibility of fiery and aerial substances, the fixed arrangement of qualities is inferred in their causal substance. And a separation is observed from the perceptibility of earthy and watery substances — an earthy substance is perceived as separated from water and the rest,

children.text:
% gṛhyate,] p.802
āpyaṃ ca parābhyām, taijasaṃ ca vāyunā, na caikaikaguṇaṃ gṛhyata iti/ niranumānaṃ tu ``viṣṭaṃ hy aparaṃ pareṇa'' ity etad iti/ nātra liṅgam anumāpakaṃ gṛhyata iti yenaitad evaṃ pratipadyemahi/
yac coktaṃ viṣṭaṃ hy aparaṃ pareṇeti bhūtasṛṣṭau veditavyaṃ na sāmpratam iti niyamakāraṇābhāvād ayuktam/ dṛṣṭaṃ ca sāmpratam aparaṃ pareṇa viṣṭam iti, vāyunā ca viṣṭaṃ teja iti/ viṣṭatvaṃ saṃyogaḥ, sa ca dvayoḥ samānaḥ, vāyunā ca viṣṭatvāt sparśavat tejo na tu tejasā viṣṭatvād rūpavān vāyur iti niyamakāraṇaṃ nāstīti/ dṛṣṭaṃ ca taijasena sparśena vāyavyasya sparśasyābhibhavād agrahaṇam iti, na ca tenaiva tasyābhibhava iti//67//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.802] and a watery substance from the other two, and a fiery substance from wind; and (they are) not perceived as having only a single quality each. However, the statement 'for the lower is pervaded by the higher' is without inferential support; no inferential mark that would warrant apprehension is grasped here by which we could accept this. And the statement that 'the lower is pervaded by the higher' is to be understood at the time of elemental creation and not at present — this is untenable because there is no reason for the restriction. For it is observed even at present that the lower is pervaded by the higher — fire is pervaded by wind. Pervasion means conjunction (<s>saṃyoga</s>), and that is the same for both; and because fire is pervaded by wind, fire has touch — but it does not follow that wind has color because it is pervaded by fire; hence there is no reason for the restriction. And it is observed that, due to the overwhelming of the aerial touch by the fiery touch, (the aerial touch) is not apprehended; but the converse overwhelming does not occur. //67//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.68]

children.text: tad evaṃ nyāyaviruddhaṃ pravādaṃ pratiṣidhya ``na sarvaguṇānupalabdher'' iti coditaṃ samādhīyate ---
children.translated_text: Having thus refuted the doctrine that contradicts proper reasoning with 'not, because not all qualities are apprehended,' the objection raised is now resolved —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.68: Because of the predominance of each preceding quality in succession, each (sense organ) has that as its primary (function).

children.text:
tasmān na sarvaguṇopalabdhiḥ, ghrāṇādīnāṃ pūrvaṃ pūrvaṃ gandhāder guṇasyotkarṣāt tat tat pradhānam/ kā pradhānatā? viṣayagrāhakatvam/ ko guṇotkarṣaḥ? abhivyaktau samarthatvam/ yathā bāhyānāṃ pārthivāpyataijasānāṃ dravyāṇāṃ caturguṇatriguṇadviguṇānāṃ na sarvaguṇavyañjakatvaṃ gandharasarūpotkarṣāt tu yathākramaṃ gandharasarūpavyañjakatvam,
% bāhyānāṃ ...] p.803
evaṃ ghrāṇa rasanacakṣuṣā.ṃ caturguṇatriguṇadviguṇānāṃ na sarvaguṇagrāhakatvam, gandharasarūpotkarṣāt tu yathākramaṃ gandharasarūpagrāhakatvam/ tasmād ghrāṇādibhir na sarveṣāṃ guṇānām upalabdhir iti/
yas tu pratijānīte gandhaguṇatvād ghrāṇaṃ gandhasya grāhakam evaṃ rasanādiṣv apīti, tasya yathāguṇayogaṃ ghrāṇādibhir guṇagrahaṇaṃ prasajyata iti//68//
children.translated_text: Therefore, there is no apprehension of all qualities — because for the organ of smell and the rest, each preceding quality such as smell has predominance in succession, that (quality) is the primary one for each (organ). What is this 'being primary'? It is the capacity to grasp (its own) object. What is the 'predominance of quality'? It is the capacity for manifestation. Just as external earthy, watery, and fiery substances with four, three, and two qualities respectively do not manifest all qualities, but manifest smell, taste, and color respectively due to the predominance of smell, taste, and color, [Note: p.803] so too the organs of smell, taste, and sight with four, three, and two qualities respectively do not grasp all qualities, but grasp smell, taste, and color respectively due to the predominance of smell, taste, and color. Therefore, all qualities are not apprehended by the organ of smell and the rest. However, one who maintains that the organ of smell grasps smell because it has smell as its quality — and likewise for the organ of taste and the rest — for such a person, the consequence follows that each organ grasps qualities according to its own quality-endowment. //68//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.69]

children.text:
% p.804
kiṃkṛtaṃ punar vyavasthānam --- kiñcit pārthivam indriyaṃ na sarvāṇi, kānicid āpyataijasavāyavyāni indriyāṇi na sarvāṇīti?
children.translated_text: [Note: p.804] What then determines the arrangement — that a certain sense organ is earthy and not all (are), that certain ones are watery, fiery, and aerial and not all?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.69: But that arrangement is due to predominance (<s>bhūyastva</s>).

children.text: arthanirvṛttisamarthasya pravibhaktasya dravyasya saṃsargaḥ puruṣasaṃskārakārito bhūyastvam/ dṛṣṭo hi prakarṣe bhūyastvaśabdaḥ, yathā prakṛṣṭo viṣayo bhūyān ity ucyate/ yathā pṛthagarthakriyāsamarthāni puruṣasaṃskāravaśād viṣauṣadhimaṇiprabhṛtīni dravyāṇi nirvartyante, na sarvaṃ sarvārtham; evaṃ pṛthagviṣayagrahaṇasamarthāni ghrāṇādīni nirvartyante na sarvaviṣayagrahaṇasamarthānīti//69//
children.translated_text: The association of a substance that is capable of accomplishing a purpose and that is differentiated — impelled by the <s>saṃskāra</s> (accumulated merit) of the person — is predominance (<s>bhūyastva</s>). For the word '<s>bhūyastva</s>' (predominance) is observed (to be used) in the sense of excellence, as when an excellent object is called 'predominant.' Just as substances such as poisons, medicines, gems, and the like, each capable of distinct functions, are produced through the force of the person's accumulated impressions, and not everything serves every purpose — likewise, the organ of smell and the rest, each capable of grasping a distinct object, are produced (through such impressions), not as capable of grasping all objects. //69//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.70]

children.text:
% p.805
svaguṇān nopalabhanta indriyāṇi/ kasmād iti cet?
children.translated_text: [Note: p.805] The sense organs do not apprehend their own qualities. If (one asks) why?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.70: Because those possessing qualities function as sense organs (together) with (those very) qualities.

children.text: svān gandhādīn nopalabhante ghrāṇādīni/ kena kāraṇeneti cet? svaguṇaiḥ saha ghrāṇādīnām indriyabhāvāt/ ghrāṇaṃ svena gandhena samānārthakāriṇā saha bāhyaṃ gandhaṃ gṛhṇāti tasya svagandhagrahaṇaṃ sahakārivaikalyān na bhavati, evaṃ śeṣāṇām api//70//
children.translated_text: The organ of smell and the rest do not apprehend their own smell and the rest. For what reason? Because the organ of smell and the rest function as sense organs together with their own qualities. The organ of smell grasps external smell together with its own smell, which cooperates (in the act of grasping); the apprehension of its own smell does not occur due to the absence of a cooperating factor. Likewise for the rest as well. //70//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.71]

children.text: yadi punar gandhaḥ sahakārī ca syād ghrāṇasya grāhyaś cety ata āha ---
children.translated_text: But if smell were both a cooperating factor and an object of apprehension for the organ of smell — therefore (the sūtra) says:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.71: And because that (sense organ) is not apprehended by that very (sense organ).

children.text:
% p.806
na guṇopalabdhir indriyāṇām/ yo brūte --- yathā bāhyaṃ dravyaṃ cakṣuṣā (corr.; cakṣaṣā, ed.) gṛhyate tathā tenaiva cakṣuṣā tad eva cakṣur gṛhyatām iti, tādṛṅ idam; tulyo hy ubhayatra pratipattihetvabhāva iti//71//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.806] The sense organs do not apprehend (their own) qualities. One who says 'just as an external substance is grasped by the eye, let that very eye be grasped by that very eye' — this is the same (kind of argument); for in both cases there is an equal absence of the basis for apprehension. //71//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.72]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.72: (This is) not (so), because of the apprehension of sound as (the ear's own) quality.

children.text: svaguṇān nopalabhanta indriyāṇīti etan na bhavati/ upalabhyate hi svaguṇaḥ śabdaḥ śrotreṇeti//72//
children.translated_text: The claim that the sense organs do not apprehend their own qualities is not valid. For the ear does apprehend sound, which is its own quality. //72//
[Section: NySBh_3,1.73]
[Note: p.807]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.1.73: The apprehension of that (sound by the ear) is due to the dissimilarity of qualities between the two substances.

children.text: na śabdena guṇena saguṇam ākāśam indriyaṃ bhavati/ na śabdaḥ śabdasya vyañjakaḥ, na ca ghrāṇādīnāṃ svaguṇagrahaṇaṃ pratyakṣam, nāpy anumīyate/ anumīyate tu śrotreṇākāśena śabdasya grahaṇam, śabdaguṇatvaṃ ca ākāśasyeti/ pariśeṣaś cānumānaṃ veditavyam/ ātmā tāvat śrotā na karaṇam, manasaḥ śrotratve badhiratvābhāvaḥ, pṛthivyādīnāṃ ghrāṇādibhāve sāmarthyam, śrotrabhāve cāsāmarthyam/
children.translated_text: <s>Ākāśa</s> (space), which possesses sound as its quality, does not become a sense organ (merely) because of that quality. Sound is not the manifester of sound, nor is the apprehension of their own qualities by the organ of smell and the rest directly perceived, nor is it inferred. But it is inferred that the ear, being <s>ākāśa</s>, apprehends sound, and that sound is a quality of <s>ākāśa</s>. And the method of residual elimination (<s>pariśeṣa</s>) should be understood as inference. The self (<s>ātman</s>) is the hearer, not the instrument (of hearing); if the mind (<s>manas</s>) were the organ of hearing, there would be no deafness; earth and the rest have the capacity to be the organ of smell and the rest, but lack the capacity to be the organ of hearing.

children.text:
% sāmarthyam, śrotrabhāve cāsāmarthyam/] p.808
asti cedaṃ śrotram ākāśaṃ ca śiṣyate, pariśeṣād ākāśaṃ śrotram iti//73//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.808] And this organ of hearing exists, and <s>ākāśa</s> (space) remains (as the only candidate); therefore, by elimination, <s>ākāśa</s> is the organ of hearing. //73//
Thus ends the first <s>āhnika</s> (lesson) of the third <s>adhyāya</s> (chapter) of the revered <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> by <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
[Note: p.809] Now begins the second <s>āhnika</s> (lesson) of the third <s>adhyāya</s> (chapter).
[Section: NySBh_3,2.1]

children.text: parīkṣitānīndriyāṇy arthāś ca, buddher idānīṃ parīkṣākramaḥ, sā kim anityā nityā veti/ kutaḥ saṃśayaḥ?
children.translated_text: The sense organs and their objects have been examined. Now comes the turn of the examination of cognition (<s>buddhi</s>): is it impermanent or permanent? What gives rise to the doubt?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3.2.1: Doubt (arises) from the similarity of (cognition) with action (<s>karman</s>) and space (<s>ākāśa</s>).

children.text: asparśavattvaṃ tābhyāṃ samāno dharma upalabhyate buddhau, viśeṣaś copajanāpāyadharmavattvam, viparyayaś ca yathāsvam anityanityayos tasyāṃ buddau nopalabhyate, tena saṃśaya iti//1//
children.translated_text: Intangibility is apprehended as a common property of both [<s>buddhi</s> and <s>ākāśa</s>] in cognition; the differentia is the property of arising and perishing, and its opposite — belonging respectively to the impermanent and the permanent — is not apprehended in that cognition; hence there is doubt. //1//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.2]

children.text: anupapannarūpaḥ khalv ayaṃ saṃśayaḥ/ sarvaśarīriṇāṃ hi pratyātmavedanīyā anityā buddhiḥ sukhādivat/
