children.translated_text: But this doubt is of an untenable form. For the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect) of all embodied beings is impermanent, being individually experienced by each self, like pleasure and the rest.

children.text:
% sukādivat] p.810
bhavati ca saṃvittiḥ --- jñāsyāmi jānāmi ajñāsiṣam iti/ na copajanāpāyāv antareṇa traikālyavyāktiḥ, tataś ca traikālyavyakter anityā buddhir ity etat śiddham/ pramāṇasiddhaṃ cedaṃ śāstare 'py uktam --- `indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam', `yugapaj jñānānutpattir manaso liṅgam ityevamādi/ tasmāt saṃśayaprakriyānupapattir iti/
dṛṣṭipravādopālambhārthan tu prakaraṇam/ evaṃ hi paśyantaḥ pravadanti sāṅkhyāḥ --- puruṣasyāntaḥkaraṇabhūtā nityā buddhir iti/ sādhanaṃ ca pracakṣate ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.810 — sukādivat]
And there is awareness: 'I shall know, I know, I knew.' And without arising and perishing, the threefold temporal distinction is not possible; hence from the threefold temporal distinction, the impermanence of <s>buddhi</s> is established. And this, established by <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge), is also stated in the treatise — '<s>indriyārthasannikarṣotpannam</s>' (arising from the contact of sense organ and object), 'the non-origination of simultaneous cognitions is the mark of <s>manas</s>' and so forth. Therefore, the procedure of raising this as a doubt is untenable.
However, this section is for the purpose of criticizing a doctrinal position. For the <s>Sāṅkhyas</s> hold and assert this view: the <s>buddhi</s> (intellect), which is the inner instrument of <s>puruṣa</s> (the conscious self), is permanent. And they state the proof —
[Note: p.811]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.2: Because of the recognition of objects.

children.text: kiṃ punar idaṃ pratyabhijñānam? yaṃ pūrvam ajñāsiṣam arthaṃ tam imaṃ jānāmīti jñānyoḥ samāne 'rthe pratisandhijñānaṃ pratyabhijñānam, etac cāvasthitāyā buddher upapannam/ nānātve tu buddhibhedeṣūtpannāpavargiṣu pratyabhijñānānupapattiḥ nānyajñātam anyaḥ pratyabhijānātīti//2//
children.translated_text: What is this recognition (<s>pratyabhijñāna</s>)? 'The object that I previously knew — I now know this very same one' — the connecting cognition regarding the same object between two cognitions is recognition. And this is possible for a <s>buddhi</s> that persists. But if [cognitions are] diverse — when distinct cognitions arise and perish — recognition is untenable, for what is known by one [cognition] is not recognized by another. //2//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.3]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.3: This is not a valid reason, because it is equal to what is to be proved (<s>sādhyasama</s>).

children.text: yathā khalu nityatvaṃ buddheḥ sādhyam evaṃ pratyabhijñānam apīti/ kiṃ kāraṇam? cetanadharmasya karaṇe 'nupapattiḥ/ puruṣadharmaḥ khalv ayaṃ jñānaṃ darśanam upalabdhir bodhaḥ pratyayaḥ adhyavasāya iti/
children.translated_text: Just as the permanence of <s>buddhi</s> is what is to be proved, so too is the recognition [of objects]. Why? Because [knowledge as] a property of the conscious [self] is untenable in an instrument. For this — knowledge, seeing, apprehension, understanding, cognition, determination — is a property of <s>puruṣa</s> (the conscious self).

children.text:
% adhyavasāya iti] p.812
cetano hi pūrvajñātam arthaṃ pratyabhijānāti, tasyaitasmād dhetor nityatvaṃ yuktam iti/ karaṇacaitanyābhyupagame tu cetanasvarūpaṃ vacanīyaṃ nānirdiṣṭasvarūpam ātmāntaraṃ śakyam astīti pratipattum/ jñānaṃ ced buddher antaḥkaraṇasyābhyupagamyate cetanasyedānīṃ kiṃ svarūpaṃ ko dharmaḥ kiṃ tattvam? jñānena ca buddhau vartamānenāyaṃ cetanaḥ kiṃ karotīti?
cetayate iti cet na, jñānād arthāntaravacanam --- puruṣaś cetayate buddhir jānātīti nedaṃ jñānād arthāntaram ucyate, cetayate jānīte buddhyate paśyati upalabhate ity eko 'yam artha iti/ buddhir jñpayatīti cet addhā --- jānīte puruṣo buddhir jñāpayatīti satyam etat/ evaṃ cābhyupagame jñānaṃ puruṣasyeti siddhaṃ bhavati na buddher antaḥkaraṇasyeti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.812 — adhyavasāya iti]
For it is the conscious being who recognizes a previously known object; its permanence is properly established by this reason. But if consciousness is attributed to the instrument [i.e., <s>buddhi</s>], then the nature of the conscious being must be stated — one cannot accept a different self whose nature has not been specified. If knowledge is attributed to <s>buddhi</s> as the inner instrument, then what is the nature, what is the property, what is the essence of the conscious being? And what does this conscious being do when knowledge resides in <s>buddhi</s>?
If [one says] 'it is conscious' (<s>cetayate</s>) — no, that would be stating something different from knowledge. [Objection:] '<s>Puruṣa</s> is conscious, <s>buddhi</s> knows' — this is not stated as something different from knowledge; 'is conscious, knows, cognizes, sees, apprehends' — this is one and the same meaning. If [one says] '<s>buddhi</s> makes known' — indeed, '<s>puruṣa</s> knows, <s>buddhi</s> makes known' — this is true. And given this acceptance, it is established that knowledge belongs to <s>puruṣa</s>, not to <s>buddhi</s> as the inner instrument.

children.text:
%813
pratipuruṣaṃ ca śabdāntaravyavasthāpratijñāne pratiṣedhahetuvacanam/ yaś ca pratijānīte --- kaścit puruṣaś cetayate, kaścid buddhyate, kaścid upalabhate, kaścit paśyatīti; puruṣāntarāṇi khalv imāni cetano boddhopalabdhā draṣṭeti naikasyaite dharmā iti atra kaḥ pratiṣedhahetur iti?
arthasyābheda iti cet samānam/ abhinnārthā ete śabdā iti tatra vyavasthānupapattir ity evaṃ cen manyase, samānaṃ bhavati --- puruṣaś cetayate buddhir jānīte ity atrāpy artho na bhidyate tatrobhayoś cetanatvād anyataralopa iti/ yadi punar budhyate 'nayeti bodhanaṃ buddhiḥ mana evocyate tac ca nityam,
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.813]
And the statement of the reason for refuting the claim that different words [for cognition] are established for each person. One who claims: 'some person is conscious, some cognizes, some apprehends, some sees' — [arguing that] these are different persons — 'the conscious one, the cognizer, the apprehender, the seer' — that these are not properties of one [being] — what is the reason for refuting this?
If [one says] 'because the meaning is not different' — the same [applies to your case]. If you think there is no basis for the distinction because these words have the same meaning — the same applies: in 'the person is conscious, <s>buddhi</s> knows' there too the meaning is not different, since both [imply] consciousness, and one of the two should be eliminated. But if [one says] '<s>buddhi</s> means that by which one cognizes — it is cognition [itself]' — then it is just <s>manas</s> (mind) that is being referred to, and that is permanent.

children.text:
% evocyate tac ca nityam,] p.814
astv etad evam, na tu manaso viṣayapratyabhijñānān nityatvam/ dṛṣṭaṃ hi karaṇabhede jñātur ekatvāt pratyabhijñānaṃ `savyadṛṣṭasyetareṇa pratyabhijñānād' iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.814 — evocyate tac ca nityam,]
Let this be so. But the permanence of <s>manas</s> is not [established] from the recognition of objects. For recognition is observed when there is a difference of instrument but unity of the knower — 'because of the recognition of what was seen by the left [eye] by means of the other [eye].'

children.text:
% p.815
cakṣurvat pradīpavac ca; pradīpāntaradṛṣṭasya pradīpāntareṇa pratyabhijñānam iti/ tasmāj jñātur ayaṃ nityatve hetur iti//3//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.815]
And like the eye, like a lamp — there is recognition of what was seen by one lamp by means of another lamp. Therefore, this [recognition] is a reason for the permanence of the knower [not the instrument]. //3//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.4]

children.text: yac ca manyate buddher avasthitāyā yathāviṣayaṃ vṛttayo jñānāni niścaranti vṛttiś ca vṛttimato nānyeti, tac ca ---
children.translated_text: And as for the view that from <s>buddhi</s>, which is persisting, cognitions issue forth as operations directed to their respective objects, and that an operation is not different from that which has the operation — that too [is addressed] —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.4: No, because [all objects] would be grasped simultaneously.

children.text: vṛttivṛttimator ananyatve vṛttimato 'vasthānād vṛttīnām avasthānam iti yānīmāni viṣayagrahaṇāni tāny avatiṣṭanta iti yugapad viṣayāṇāṃ grahaṇaṃ prasajyata iti//4//
children.translated_text: If the operation and that which has the operation are not different, then since that which has the operation persists, the operations too would persist — and thus these apprehensions of objects would persist, and the simultaneous grasping of objects would follow. //4//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.5]
[Note: p.816]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.5: And if there is no recognition, the destruction [of the inner instrument] would follow.

children.text: atīte ca pratyabhijñāne vṛttimān apy atīta ity antaḥkaraṇasya vināśaḥ prasajyate, viparyaye ca nānātvam iti//5//
children.translated_text: And when recognition has ceased, that which has the operations too has ceased — thus the destruction of the inner instrument would follow. And in the opposite case [where operations differ from their possessor], there would be multiplicity. //5//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.6]

children.text: avibhu caikaṃ manaḥ paryāyeṇendriyaiḥ saṃyujyata iti ---
children.translated_text: And the single <s>manas</s> (mind), being non-pervasive, conjoins with the sense organs in succession — therefore —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.6: Because of successive operation, there is no simultaneous grasping.
Of the objects of the sense organs — [and this shows] the difference between the operation and that which has the operation.
[Note: p.817]
[Section: NySBh_3,2.7]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.7: And non-recognition is due to engagement with a different object.

children.text: apratyabhijñānam anupalabdhiḥ/ anupalabdhiś ca kasyācid arthasya viṣayāntaravyāsakte manasy upapadyate vṛttivṛttimator nānātvāt, ekatve hi anarthako vyāsaṅga iti//7//
children.translated_text: Non-recognition means non-apprehension. And non-apprehension of some object is possible when <s>manas</s> is engaged with a different object, because of the difference between the operation and that which has the operation. For if they were identical, engagement [with a different object] would be purposeless. //7//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.8]
And if the inner instrument were pervasive, [there would be no need for] successive conjunction with the sense organs —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.8: No, because there is no movement.

children.text: prāptānīndriyāṇy antaḥkaraṇeneti prāptyarthasya gamanasyābhāvaḥ/ tatra kramavṛttitvābhāvād ayugapad grahaṇānupapattir iti/
children.translated_text: The sense organs are [already] reached by the inner instrument — hence there is absence of movement, which serves the purpose of reaching. Therefore, because of the absence of successive operation, the non-simultaneous grasping [of objects] would be untenable.

children.text:
% p.818
gatyabhāvāc ca pratiṣiddhaṃ vibhuno 'ntaḥkaraṇasyāyugapadgrahaṇaṃ na liṅgāntareṇānumīyate iti/ yathā cakṣuṣo gatiḥ pratiṣiddhā sannikṛṣṭaviprakṛṣṭayos tulyakālagrahaṇāt pāṇicandramasor vyavadhānena pratīghāte so'numīyata iti so 'yaṃ nāntaḥ karaṇe vivādo na tasya nityatve/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.818]
And since movement has been denied, the non-simultaneous grasping by the pervasive inner instrument is not inferred by any other mark. Just as movement of the eye is denied because of the equal-time grasping of near and far [objects], and because obstruction through an intervening object between the hand and the moon is inferred — this dispute concerns the inner instrument, not its permanence.

children.text:
% karaṇe vivādo na tasya nityatve] p.819
siddhaṃ hi mano 'ntaḥkaraṇaṃ nityaṃ ceti/ kva tarhi vivādaḥ? tasya vibhutve, tac ca pramāṇato 'nupalabdheḥ pratiṣiddham iti/ ekaṃ cāntaḥkaraṇaṃ nānā caitā jñānātmakā vṛttayaḥ, cakṣurvijñānaṃ ghrāṇavijñānaṃ rūpavijñānaṃ gandhavijñānam/ etac ca vṛttivṛttimator ekatve 'nupapannam iti/ puruṣo jānīte nāntaḥkaraṇam iti/ etena viṣayāntaravyāsaṅgaḥ pratyuktaḥ/ viṣayāntaragrahaṇalakṣaṇo viṣayāntaravyāsaṅgaḥ puruṣasya nāntaḥkaraṇasyeti, kenacid indriyeṇa sannidhiḥ kenacid asannidhir ity ayaṃ tu vyāsaṅgo 'nujñāyate manasa iti//8//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.819 — karaṇe vivādo na tasya nityatve]
For it is established that <s>manas</s> is the inner instrument and is permanent. Where then is the dispute? It is about its pervasiveness, and that is denied because it is not apprehended by any <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge). The inner instrument is one, but these cognitive operations are many — visual cognition, olfactory cognition, form-cognition, odor-cognition. And this is untenable if the operation and that which has the operation are identical. It is the <s>puruṣa</s> (conscious self) who knows, not the inner instrument. By this, the engagement with a different object is also answered: the engagement with a different object, characterized by the grasping of another object, belongs to <s>puruṣa</s>, not to the inner instrument. But this engagement is conceded for <s>manas</s> — that it is proximate to one sense organ and not proximate to another. //8//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.9]

children.text:
% p.820
ekam antaḥkaraṇaṃ nānā vṛttaya iti/ saty abhede vṛtter idam ucyate ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.820]
The inner instrument is one, the operations are many — given non-difference of the operation [from its possessor], this is said —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.9: Like the false apprehension of difference in a crystal, so the false apprehension of difference in that [<s>buddhi</s>].

children.text: tasyāṃ vṛttau nānātvābhimānaḥ, yathā dravyāntaropahite sphaṭike anyatvābhimāno nīlo lohita iti; evaṃ viṣayāntaropadhānād iti/
children.translated_text: There is a false apprehension of multiplicity in that operation — just as in a crystal affected by another substance, there is a false apprehension of difference: 'it is blue, it is red'; similarly, because of the superimposition of different objects.

children.text:
% p.821
na hetvabhāvāt/ sphaṭikānyatvābhimānavad ayaṃ jñāneṣu nānātvābhimāno gauṇo na punar gandhādyanyatvābhimānavad iti hetur nāsti hetvabhāvād anupapanna iti/ samāno hetvabhāva iti cet na jñānānāṃ krameṇopajanāpāyadarśanāt --- krameṇa hīndriyārtheṣu jñānāny upajāyante cāpayanti ceti dṛśyate/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.821]
This is not [valid], because of the absence of a reason. This false apprehension of multiplicity in cognitions, like the false apprehension of difference in a crystal, is metaphorical (secondary), but not like the false apprehension of difference in odor and the like — there is no reason [for this]; because of the absence of a reason, [the argument] is untenable. If [one objects that] the absence of a reason is the same [in both cases] — no, because the arising and perishing of cognitions is observed in succession. For it is observed that cognitions regarding the objects of the sense organs arise and perish in succession.

children.text:
% cāpayanti ceti dṛśyate/] p.822
tasmād gandhādyanyatvābhimānavad ayaṃ jñāneṣu nānātvābhimāna iti//9//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.822 — cāpayanti ceti dṛśyate/]
Therefore, this apprehension of multiplicity in cognitions is like the [genuine] apprehension of difference in odor and the like [i.e., it is real, not illusory]. //9//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.10]

children.text:
% p.823
sphaṭikānyatvābhimānavad ity etad amṛṣyamāṇaḥ kṣaṇikavādy āha ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.823]
Not accepting [the analogy] 'like the false apprehension of difference in a crystal,' the proponent of momentariness (<s>kṣaṇikavādin</s>) says —

children.text: NyS_3,2.10: sphaṭike 'py aparāparotpatteḥ kṣaṇikatvād vyaktīnām ahetuḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.10: Even in a crystal, because of the successive origination [of different instances], and because particulars are momentary, this is not a valid reason.

children.text:
% p.824
sphaṭikasyābhedenāvasthitasyopadhānabhedān nānātvābhimāna ity ayam avidyamānahetukaḥ pakṣaḥ/ kasmāt? sphaṭike 'py aparāparotpatteḥ/ sphaṭike 'pi anyā vyaktaya utpadyante anyā nirudhyanta iti/ katham? kṣaṇikatvād vyaktīnām/ kṣaṇaś cālpīyān kālaḥ kṣaṇasthitikāḥ kṣaṇikāḥ/ kathaṃ punar gamyate kṣaṇikā vyaktaya iti? upacayāpacayaprabandhadarśanāc charīrādiṣu/ paktinirvṛttasyāhārarasasya śarīre rudhirādibhāvenopacayo 'pacayaś ca prabandhena pravarttate/ upacayād vyaktīnām utpādaḥ, apacayād vyaktinirodhaḥ/ evaṃ ca saty avayavapariṇāmabhedena vṛddhiḥ śarīrasya kālāntare gṛhyate iti so 'yaṃ vyaktiviśeṣadharmo vyaktimātre veditavya iti//10//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.824]
The position that there is a false apprehension of multiplicity due to differences in superimposition while the crystal persists without difference — this is a position without a valid basis. Why? Because even in a crystal there is successive origination. Even in a crystal, different particulars arise and different ones cease. How? Because particulars are momentary. A <s>kṣaṇa</s> (moment) is the smallest unit of time; things lasting [only] a moment are momentary. But how is it known that particulars are momentary? From the observation of the process of accretion and decay in bodies and the like. The nutrient essence of food that is digested proceeds in the body through a continuous process of accretion in the form of blood and the like, and [correspondingly] decay. From accretion comes the origination of particulars; from decay, the cessation of particulars. This being so, the growth of the body apprehended at a later time through differences in the transformation of parts — this property of particular instances should be understood as applying to all particulars. //10//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.11]
[Note: p.825]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.11: Because there is no reason for the restriction, acknowledgment should follow what is observed.

children.text: sarvāsu vyaktiṣu upacayāpacayaprabandhaḥ śarīravad iti nāyaṃ niyamaḥ/ kasmāt? hetvabhāvāt/ nātra pratyakṣam anumānaṃ vā pratipādakam astīti/ tasmād yathādarśanam abhyanujñā/ yatra yatropacayāpacayaprabandho dṛśyate, tatra tatra vyaktīnām aparāparotpattir upacayāpacayaprabandhadarśanenābhyanujñāyate,
children.translated_text: That there is a process of accretion and decay in all particulars, as in bodies — this restriction does not hold. Why? Because of the absence of a reason. There is neither perception nor inference to establish this. Therefore, acknowledgment should follow what is observed. Wherever a process of accretion and decay is observed, there the successive origination of particulars is acknowledged on the basis of observing the process of accretion and decay,

children.text:
% r upacayāpacayaprabandhadarśanenābhyanujñāyate,] p.826
yathā śarīrādiṣu/ yatra yatra na dṛśyate tatra tatra pratyākhyāyate yathā grāvaprabhṛtiṣu/ sphaṭike 'py upacayāpacayaprabandho na dṛśyate, tasmād ayuktaṃ sphaṭike 'py aparāprotpattir iti/ yathā cārkasya kaṭukimnā sarvadravyāṇāṃ kaṭukimānām āpādayet tādṛg etad iti//11//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.826 — r upacayāpacayaprabandhadarśanenābhyanujñāyate,]
as in bodies and the like. Wherever it is not observed, there it is denied — as in stones and the like. In a crystal too, the process of accretion and decay is not observed; therefore, the claim that even in a crystal there is successive origination is untenable. Just as one would make all substances as pungent as the <s>arka</s> [plant] — that is what this amounts to. //11//
[Section: NySBh_3,2.12]

children.text: yaś cāśeṣanirodhenāpūrvotpādaṃ niranvayaṃ dravyasantāne kṣaṇikatāṃ manyate tasyaitat ---
children.translated_text: And for one who holds that through complete destruction and unprecedented origination, there is momentariness in a substance-continuum without any continuity — for such a person, this [is stated] —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.12: Not so, because the causes of origination and destruction are apprehended.

children.text: utpattikāraṇaṃ tāvad upalabhyate avayavopacayo valmīkādīnām, vināśakāraṇaṃ copalabhyate ghaṭādīnām avayavavibhāgaḥ/
children.translated_text: The cause of origination, namely the accretion of parts, is apprehended in ant-hills and the like; and the cause of destruction, namely the separation of parts, is apprehended in pots and the like.

children.text:
% labhyate ghaṭādīnām avayavavibhāgaḥ/] p.827
yasya tv anapacitāvayavaṃ nirudhyate anupacitāvayavaṃ cotpadyate tasyāśeṣanirodhe niranvaye vāpūrvotpāde na kāraṇam ubhayatrāpy upalabhyate iti//12//
children.translated_text:
[Note: labhyate ghaṭādīnām avayavavibhāgaḥ/] p.827
But for that which is destroyed without diminishment of parts and arises without augmentation of parts, no cause is perceived in either case — neither in its complete destruction without remainder, nor in its unprecedented origination. // 12 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.13]
[Note: 829]

children.text: NyS_3,2.13: kṣīravināśe kāraṇānupalabdhivad dadhyutpattivac ca tadupapattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.2.13: Its possibility is like the non-perception of the cause of the destruction of milk and like the origination of curd.

children.text: yathānupalabhyamānaṃ kṣīravināśakāraṇaṃ dadhyutpattikāraṇaṃ cābhyanujñāyate tathā sphaṭike parāparāsu vyaktiṣu vināśakāraṇam utpādakāraṇaṃ cābhyanujñeyam iti//13//
children.translated_text: Just as the cause of the destruction of milk and the cause of the origination of curd are granted even though they are not perceived, so too the cause of destruction and the cause of origination in the successive manifestations of crystal and the like should be granted. // 13 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.14]
[Note: p.830]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.14: Because the cause is grasped through its inferential mark, there is no non-perception.

children.text: kṣīravināśaliṅgaṃ kṣīravināśakāraṇaṃ dadhyutpattiliṅgaṃ dadhyutpattikāraṇaṃ ca gṛhyate 'to nānupalabdhiḥ, viparyayas tu sphaṭikādiṣu dravyeṣu aparāparotpattau vyaktīnāṃ na liṅgam astīty anutpattir eveti//14//
children.translated_text: The cause of the destruction of milk is grasped through the inferential mark of milk's destruction, and the cause of the origination of curd is grasped through the inferential mark of curd's origination — therefore there is no non-perception. But the opposite holds for substances like crystal and the like: in the successive origination of manifestations, there is no inferential mark — therefore there is simply no origination. // 14 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.15]

[Note: p.846]
Here someone offers a response —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.15: Not so with regard to milk, because of transformation and the appearance of other qualities.

children.text:
payasaḥ pariṇāmo na vināśa ity eka āha/ pariṇāmaś cāvasthitasya dravyasya pūrvadharmanivṛttau dharmāntarotpattir iti/
guṇāntaraprādurbhāva ity apara āha/ satā dravyasya pūrvaguṇanivṛttau guṇāntaram utpadyata iti/ sa khalv ekapakṣībhāva iva//15//
children.translated_text:
One says: the transformation of milk is not its destruction. And transformation is the arising of a new property when the prior property of a persisting substance ceases.
Another says: 'the appearance of other qualities' — when the prior quality of an existing substance ceases, another quality arises. But this is indeed like taking one side only. // 15 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.16]

[Note: p.847]
But here is the refutation —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.16: The observation that a different substance arises from a different arrangement (of parts) is an inference for the cessation of the prior substance.

children.text: saṃmūrchanalakṣaṇād avayavavyūhād dravyāntare dadhni utpanne gṛhyamāṇe pūrvaṃ payodravyam avayavavibhāgebhyo nivṛttam ity anumīyate, yathā mṛdavayavānāṃ vyūhāntarād dravyāntare sthālyām utpannāyāṃ pūrvaṃ mṛtpiṇḍadravyaṃ mṛdavayavavibhāgebhyo nivarttate iti/ mṛdvac cāvayavānvayaḥ payodadhnor nāśeṣanirodhe niranvayo dravyāntarotpādo ghaṭata iti//16//
children.translated_text: When a different substance, curd, characterized by solidification, arises from a different arrangement of parts and is perceived, it is inferred that the prior substance, milk, has ceased from the separation of its parts — just as when a different substance, a pot, arises from a different arrangement of the parts of clay, the prior substance, the lump of clay, ceases from the separation of the clay-parts. And as with clay, the continuity of parts (exists) for milk and curd — it is not the case that the origination of a different substance occurs without remainder and without continuity. // 16 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.17]

children.text:
% p.848
abhyanujñāya ca niṣkāraṇaṃ kṣīravināśaṃ dadhyutpādaṃ ca pratiṣedha ucyate ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.848]
Having granted the causeless destruction of milk and origination of curd, the refutation is stated —

children.text: NyS_3,2.17: kvacid vināśakāraṇānupalabdheḥ kvacic copalabdher anekāntaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.2.17: Because the cause of destruction is sometimes not perceived and sometimes perceived, this is <s>anekānta</s> (non-conclusive).

children.text: kṣīradadhivan niṣkāraṇau vināśotpādau sphaṭikavyaktīnām iti nāyam ekānta iti/ kasmāt? hetvabhāvāt/ nātra hetur asti akāraṇau vināśotpādau sphaṭikādivyaktīnāṃ kṣīradadhivat, na punar yathā vināśakāraṇabhāvāt kumbhasya vināśa utpattikāraṇabhāvāc cotpattiḥ evaṃ sphaṭikādivyaktīnāṃ vināśotpattikāraṇabhāvād vināśotpattibhāva iti/
children.translated_text: The claim that 'the destruction and origination of the manifestations of crystal are without cause, like those of milk and curd' is not conclusive. Why? Because of the absence of a reason. There is no reason here (to say) that the destruction and origination of the manifestations of crystal and the like are without cause, like those of milk and curd; (rather,) just as the destruction of a pot occurs because of the existence of a cause of destruction, and its origination because of the existence of a cause of origination, so too the destruction and origination of the manifestations of crystal and the like occur because of the existence of causes of destruction and origination.

children.text:
% p.849
niradhiṣṭhānaṃ ca dṛṣṭāntavacanam/ gṛhyamāṇayor vināśotpādayoḥ sphaṭikādiṣu syād ayam āśrayavān dṛṣṭāntaḥ kṣīravināśakāraṇānupalabdhivad dadhyutpattivac ceti, tau tu na gṛhyete/ tasmān niradhiṣṭhāno 'yaṃ dṛṣṭānta iti/
abhyanujñāya ca sphaṭikasyotpādavināśau yo 'tra sādhakas tasyābhyanujñānād apratiṣedhaḥ/ kumbhavan na niṣkāraṇau vināśotpādau sphaṭikādīnām ity anujñeyo 'yaṃ dṛṣṭāntaḥ pratiṣeddham aśakyatvāt/ kṣīradadhivat tu niṣkāraṇau vināśotpādāv iti śakyo 'yaṃ pratiṣeddhuṃ kāraṇato vināśotpattidarśanāt/ kṣīradadhnor vināśotpattī paśyatā tatkāraṇam anumeyaṃ kāryaliṅgaṃ hi kāraṇam iti//17//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.849]
And the citation of the example is without basis. If destruction and origination in crystal and the like were perceived, this example — 'like the non-perception of the cause of the destruction of milk and like the origination of curd' — would have a basis; but those two are not perceived. Therefore this example is without basis.
And having granted the origination and destruction of crystal: from the granting of the argument that establishes them, there is no refutation. 'The destruction and origination of crystal and the like are not without cause, like a pot' — this example should be granted, since it cannot be refuted. But 'the destruction and origination are without cause, like those of milk and curd' — this can be refuted, because destruction and origination are observed to have causes. One who observes the destruction and origination of milk and curd should infer their cause, for the effect is the inferential mark of the cause. // 17 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.18]

children.text:
% p.850
upapannam anityā buddhir iti/ idaṃ tu cintyate kasyeyaṃ buddhir ātmeindriyamano 'rthānāṃ guṇa iti/ prasiddho 'pi khalv ayam arthaḥ parīkaṣāśeṣaṃ pravarttayāmīti prakriyate/ so 'yaṃ buddhau sannikarṣotpatteḥ saṃśayaḥ viśeṣasyāgrahaṇād iti/ tatrāyaṃ viśeṣaḥ
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.850]
It is established that cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) is impermanent. But this is to be considered: of what is this cognition a quality — of <s>ātman</s>, sense-organ, <s>manas</s> (mind), or the object? Although this matter is well-known, it is taken up in order to complete the examination. The doubt here is regarding the contact from which cognition arises, since the distinguishing feature is not grasped. And here is the distinguishing feature —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.18: (Cognition is) not (a quality) of the sense-organs or the objects, because knowledge persists even when they are destroyed.

children.text: nendriyāṇām vā guṇo jñānaṃ teṣāṃ vināśo 'pi jñānasya bhāvāt/ bhavati khalv idam indriye 'rthe ca vinaṣṭe jñānam adrākṣam iti/ na ca jñātari vinaṣthe jñānaṃ bhavitum arhati/ anyat khalu vai tad indriyārthasannikarṣajaṃ jñānaṃ yad indriyārthavināśe na bhavati/
children.translated_text: Knowledge is not a quality of the sense-organs, because knowledge exists even when they are destroyed. For there is this knowledge when the sense-organ and the object are destroyed: 'I saw (it).' And knowledge cannot exist when the knower is destroyed. The knowledge born of the contact of sense-organ and object is one thing — it does not exist when the sense-organ and object are destroyed.

children.text:
% bhavati] p.851
idam anyad ātmamanaḥsannikarṣajam, tasya yukto bhāva iti/smṛtiḥ khalv iyam adrākṣam iti pūrvadṛṣṭaviṣayā/ na ca vijñātari naṣṭe pūrvopalabdheḥ smaraṇaṃ yuktam, na cānyadṛṣṭam anyaḥ smarati/ na ca manasi jñātary abhyupagamyamāne śakyam indriyārthayor jñātṛtvaṃ pratipādayitum//18//
children.translated_text:
[Note: bhavati] p.851
The other (knowledge) is born of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>; its existence is appropriate. This memory, 'I saw (it),' has a previously seen object as its content. And it is not appropriate that there be recollection of a previous apprehension when the knower is destroyed, nor does someone else remember what another saw. And when <s>manas</s> is accepted as the knower, it is not possible to establish that the sense-organs and objects are knowers. // 18 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.19]
Then let cognition be a quality of <s>manas</s> (mind) —

children.text: NyS_3,2.19: yugapaj jñeyānupalabdheś ca na manasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.2.19: And because objects of knowledge are not perceived simultaneously, (cognition is) not (a quality) of <s>manas</s>.

children.text: yugapaj jñeyānupalabdhir antaḥkaraṇasya liṅgam, tatra yugapaj jṇeyānupalabdhyā yad anumīyate antaḥkaraṇam, na tasya guṇo jñānam/ kasya tarhi? jñasya vaśitvāt/
children.translated_text: The non-simultaneous perception of objects of knowledge is the mark of the inner instrument (<s>antaḥkaraṇa</s>). That inner instrument which is inferred from the non-simultaneous perception of objects of knowledge — cognition is not its quality. Whose then? Of the knower, because of his mastery.

children.text:
% p.852
vaśī jñātā vaśyaṃ karaṇam, jñānaguṇatve ca karaṇabhāvanivṛttiḥ/ ghrāṇādisādhanasya ca jñātur gandhādijñānabhāvād anumīyate antaḥkaraṇasādhanasya sukhādijñānaṃ smṛtiś ceti/ tatra yaj jñānaguṇaṃ manaḥ sa ātmā, yat tu sukhādyupalabdhisādhanam antaḥkaraṇaṃ manas tad iti saṃjñābhedamātraṃ nārthabheda iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.852]
The knower is the master; the instrument is the subordinate. And if (cognition) were a quality of the instrument, its instrumental status would be negated. And since the knower who uses the nose and other instruments has knowledge of smell and the like, it is inferred that (he also has) knowledge of pleasure and the like and memory through the instrument of the inner organ. And as for that <s>manas</s> which has cognition as its quality — that is the <s>ātman</s>; and that which is the inner instrument, the means of perceiving pleasure and the like — that is <s>manas</s>. This is merely a difference in terminology, not a difference in meaning.

children.text:
% p.853
yugapaj jñeyopalabdheś ca yogina iti vā cārthaḥ/ yogī khalu ṛddhau prādurbhūtāyāṃ vikaraṇadharmā nirmāya sendriyāṇi śarīrāntarāṇi teṣu yugapaj jñeyāny upalabhate/ tac caitad vibhau jñātary upapadyate nāṇau manasīti/ vibhutve vā manaso jñānasya nātmaguṇatvapratiṣedhaḥ/ vibhu ca manastadantaḥkaraṇabhūtam iti tasya sarvendriyair yugapat saṃyogād yugapaj jñānāny utpadyerann iti//19//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.853]
Or the word 'and' (in the <s>sūtra</s>) means: 'and because of the simultaneous perception of objects of knowledge by a <s>yogin</s>.' A <s>yogin</s>, when supernatural power has manifested, possessing the property of being free from (ordinary) sense-organs, creates bodies with sense-organs and in those perceives objects of knowledge simultaneously. And this is possible for a knower who is all-pervading, not for an atomic <s>manas</s>. Alternatively, if <s>manas</s> is all-pervading, the denial that knowledge is a quality of <s>ātman</s> does not follow. And if <s>manas</s> is all-pervading, being an inner instrument, then from its simultaneous conjunction with all sense-organs, cognitions would arise simultaneously. // 19 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.20]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.20: Even if (cognition) is a quality of <s>ātman</s>, the same (problem applies).

children.text: vibhur ātmā sarvendriyaiḥ saṃyukta iti yugapaj jñānotpattiprasaṅga iti//20//
children.translated_text: <s>Ātman</s> is all-pervading and conjoined with all sense-organs — so the consequence of simultaneous arising of cognitions (would follow). // 20 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.21]
[Note: p.854]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.21: Because of the absence of the contact of <s>manas</s> with the sense-organs, that (simultaneous arising) does not occur.

children.text: gandhādyupalabdher indriyārthasannikarṣavad indriyamanaḥsannikarṣo 'pi kāraṇam, tasya cāyaugapadyam aṇutvān manasaḥ/ ayaugapadyād anutpattir yugapaj jñānānām ātmaguṇatve 'pīti//21//
children.translated_text: Just as the contact of sense-organ and object is a cause of the perception of smell and the like, so too the contact of sense-organ and <s>manas</s> is a cause; and that (contact) is non-simultaneous because of the atomic nature of <s>manas</s>. Because of the non-simultaneity, there is no simultaneous arising of cognitions even when cognition is a quality of <s>ātman</s>. // 21 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.22]
But what if the cognition of smell and the like arises from the mere contact of <s>ātman</s> with the sense-organs and the objects?
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.22: No, because no originating cause is indicated.

children.text: ātmendriyasannikarṣamātrād gandhādijñānam utpadyate iti, nātrotpattikāraṇam apadiśyate yenaitat pratipadyemahīti//22//
children.translated_text: That the cognition of smell and the like arises from the mere contact of <s>ātman</s> with the sense-organs — no originating cause is indicated here by which we could accept this. // 22 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.23]
[Note: p.855]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.23: And since no cause of destruction is perceived, if (cognition) persists, the consequence would be its permanence.

children.text: ``tadātmaguṇatve 'pi tulyam'' ity etad anena samuccīyate/ dvividho hi guṇanāśahetuḥ, guṇānām āśrayābhāvo virodhī ca guṇaḥ/ nityatvād ātmano 'nupapannaḥ pūrvaḥ, virodhī ca buddher guṇo na gṛhyate --- tasmād ātmaguṇatve sati buddher nityatvaprasaṅgaḥ//23//
children.translated_text: This is combined with the statement 'even if (cognition) is a quality of <s>ātman</s>, the same (problem applies).' For the cause of the destruction of qualities is twofold: the absence of the substratum of the qualities, and an opposing quality. The first is inapplicable because of the permanence of <s>ātman</s>; and no quality opposing cognition is perceived — therefore, if cognition is a quality of <s>ātman</s>, the consequence would be its permanence. // 23 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.24]
[Note: p.856]

children.text: NyS_3,2.24: anityatvagrahād buddher buddhyantarād vināśaḥ śabdavat ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.2.24: Because impermanence of cognition is grasped, the destruction of cognition is by another cognition, like sound.

children.text: anityā buddhir iti sarvaśarīriṇāṃ pratyātmavedanīyam etat/ gṛhyate ca buddhisantānaḥ tatra buddher buddhyantaraṃ virodhī guṇa ity anumīyate yathā śabdasantāne śabdaḥ śabdāntaravirodhīti//24//
children.translated_text: That cognition is impermanent is known by direct experience to all embodied beings. And a succession of cognitions is perceived; therein it is inferred that one cognition is an opposing quality (to another), just as in the succession of sounds, one sound is opposed by another. // 24 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.25]

children.text:
% p.857
asaṅkhyeyeṣu jñānakāriteṣu saṃskāreṣu smṛtihetuṣv ātmasamaveteṣv ātmamanasoś ca sannikarṣe samāne smṛtihetau sati na kāraṇasyāyaugapadyam astīti yugapat smṛtayaḥ prādurbhaveyuḥ yadi buddhir ātmaguṇaḥ syād iti/ tatra kaścit sannikarṣasyāyaugapadyam upapādayiṣyann āha ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.857]
Since the <s>saṃskāras</s> (impressions) — which are innumerable, produced by cognition, causes of memory, and inherent in the <s>ātman</s> — exist, and since the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, which is the common cause of memory, exists, and since there is no non-simultaneity of the cause, memories would arise simultaneously if cognition were a quality of <s>ātman</s>. Thereupon, someone attempting to establish the non-simultaneity of the contact says —

children.text: NyS_3,2.25: jñānasamavetātmapradeśasannikarṣān manasaḥ smṛtyutpatter na yugapadutpattiḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.2.25: Because memory arises from the contact of <s>manas</s> with the parts of <s>ātman</s> that are invested with knowledge(-impressions), there is no simultaneous arising.

children.text: jñānasādhanaḥ saṃskāro jñānam ity ucyate jñānasaṃskṛtair ātmapradeśaiḥ paryāyeṇa manaḥ sannikṛṣyate/ ātmamanaḥsannikarṣāt smṛtayo 'pi paryāyeṇa bhavantīti//25//
children.translated_text: The <s>saṃskāra</s> (impression) that is the means of knowledge is called 'knowledge' — <s>manas</s> contacts in succession the parts of <s>ātman</s> that are invested with knowledge-impressions. From the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, memories too arise in succession. // 25 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.26]
[Note: p.858]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.26: No, because <s>manas</s> operates within the body.

children.text: sadehasyātmano manasā saṃyogo vipacyamānakarmāśayasahito jīvanam iṣyate/ tatrāsya prāk prāyaṇād antaḥśarīre vartamānasya manasaḥ śarīrād bahirjñānasaṃskṛtair ātmapradeśaiḥ saṃyogo nopapadyata iti//26//
children.translated_text: The conjunction of <s>manas</s> with the <s>ātman</s> that has a body, together with the ripening <s>karma</s>-store, is accepted as life. And for this (being), before death, while <s>manas</s> operates within the body, its conjunction with the parts of <s>ātman</s> invested with knowledge-impressions that are outside the body is not possible. // 26 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.27]
[Note: p.859]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.27: (This reason is) invalid, because (the operation of <s>manas</s> within the body) is itself what needs to be proven.

children.text: vipacyamānakarmāśayamātraṃ jīvanam, evaṃ ca sati sādhyam antaḥśarīravṛttitvaṃ manasa iti//27//
children.translated_text: Life is merely the ripening <s>karma</s>-store; this being so, the operation of <s>manas</s> within the body is itself what needs to be proven. // 27 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.28]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.28: Because the maintenance of the body by one who is remembering is possible, there is no refutation.

children.text: susmūrṣayā khalv ayaṃ manaḥ praṇidadhānaś cirād api kaṃcid arthaṃ smarati, smarataś ca śarīradhāraṇaṃ dṛśyate/ ātmamanaḥsannikarṣajaś ca prayatno dvividhaḥ --- dhārakaḥ prerakaś ca, niḥsṛte ca śarīrād bahir manāsi dhārakasya prayatnasyābhāvād gurutvāt patanaṃ syāt śarīrasya smarata iti//28//0
children.translated_text: For a person, applying <s>manas</s> with the desire to remember, remembers some object even after a long time; and the maintenance of the body of one who is remembering is observed. And the effort born of the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> is of two kinds — sustaining and impelling. And when <s>manas</s> goes outside the body, due to the absence of the sustaining effort, the body of one who is remembering would fall because of gravity. // 28 //
[Section: NySBh_3,2.29]
[Note: p.860]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.29: No, because of the swift movement of <s>manas</s>.

children.text: āśugati manaḥ tasya bahiḥśarīrātmapradeśena jñānasaṃskṛtena sannikarṣaḥ, pratyāgatasya ca prayatnotpādanam ubhayaṃ yujyata iti/ utpādya vā dhārakaṃ prayatnaṃ śarīrān niḥsaraṇaṃ manasaḥ, atas tatropapannaṃ dhāraṇam iti//29//
children.translated_text: <s>Manas</s> (mind) is swift-moving; its contact [is possible] through a region of the <s>ātman</s> (self) outside the body that is endowed with <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) from knowledge; and when it has returned, the production of effort — both are tenable. Or, having first produced the sustaining effort, the mind exits from the body; hence sustaining [of the remembered object] there is tenable. //29//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.30: Not so, because there is no fixed time for remembering.

children.text:
kiñcit kṣipraṃ smaryate kiñcic cireṇa/ yadā cireṇa, tadā susmūrṣayā manasi dhāryamāṇe cintāprabandhe sati kasyacid arthasya liṅgabhūtasya cintanam ārādhitaṃ smṛtihetur bhavati/ tatraitac ciraniścarite manasi nopapadyata iti/
śarīrasaṃyogānapekṣaś cātmamanaḥsaṃyogo na smṛtihetuḥ śarīrasya bhogāyatanatvāt/
children.translated_text: Some things are remembered quickly, others after a long time. When [something is remembered] after a long time, while the mind is being held [in concentration] with the desire to remember, during a continuous chain of thought, the contemplation of some object that serves as an inferential mark succeeds and becomes the cause of memory. In that case, this is not tenable if the mind has departed [from the body] for a long time. And the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s>, independent of connection with the body, is not the cause of memory, since the body is the locus of experience.

children.text:
% p.861
upabhogāyatanaṃ puruṣasya jñātuḥ śarīraṃ na tato niścaritasya manasa ātmasaṃyogamātraṃ jñānasukhādīnām utpattau kalpate, kḷptau vā śarīravaiyarthyam iti//30//
children.translated_text: The body is the locus of experience for the <s>puruṣa</s> (person), the knower; therefore, the mere contact of the mind that has departed from the body with the <s>ātman</s> cannot serve as the cause of the origination of knowledge, pleasure, and the like — and if it could, the body would be rendered purposeless. //30//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.31: And there is no special contact through the impulsion of the self, chance, or the [mind's own] cognizance.

children.text: ātmapreraṇena vā manaso bahiḥ śarīrāt saṃyogaviśeṣaḥ syāt, yadṛcchayā vā, ākasmikatayā jñatayā vā manasaḥ? sarvathā cānupapattiḥ/ katham? smartavyatvāt, icchātaḥ smaraṇāj jñānāsambhavāc ca/ yadi tāvad ātmā amuṣyārthasya smṛtihetuḥ saṃskāraḥ amuṣminn ātmadeśe samavetas tena manaḥ saṃyujyatām iti manaḥ prerayati tadā smṛta evāsāv artho bhavati na smartavyaḥ/ na cātmapratyakṣa ātmapradeśaḥ saṃskāro vā, tatrānupapannātmapratyakṣeṇa saṃvittir iti/ susmūrṣayā cāyaṃ manaḥ praṇidadhānaś cirād api kañcid arthaṃ smarati nākasmāt, jñatvaṃ ca manaso nāsti jñānapratiṣedhād iti//31//
children.translated_text: Would the special contact [of the mind with the self] outside the body occur through the impulsion of the <s>ātman</s>, or by chance, or accidentally, or through the cognizance of the mind? In all cases it is untenable. How? Because [the object] is to be remembered, because remembering is volitional, and because knowledge [in the mind] is impossible. If the <s>ātman</s> impels the mind [saying] 'Let the mind be conjoined with that region of the self where the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression), which is the cause of memory of such-and-such an object, inheres,' then that object is already remembered, not yet-to-be-remembered. And neither the region of the <s>ātman</s> nor the <s>saṃskāra</s> is directly perceived by the <s>ātman</s>; hence awareness through direct perception of the <s>ātman</s>, which is untenable, [cannot establish this]. And one who concentrates the mind with the desire to remember eventually remembers some object, not suddenly; and the mind has no cognizance, since cognition [belonging to the mind] has been refuted. //31//
And this —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.32: [This is] analogous to [the case of] the pain in the foot of one whose mind is absorbed, [explained] by a special contact.

children.text:
yadā khalv ayaṃ vyāsaktamanāḥ kvacid deśe śarkarayā kaṇṭakena vā pādavyathanam āpnoti tadā ātmamanaḥ saṃyogaviśeṣa eṣitavyaḥ, dṛṣṭaṃ hi duḥkhaṃ duḥkhavedanaṃ ceti/ tatrāyaṃ samānaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ yadṛcchayā tu na viśeṣo nākasmikī kriyā nākasmikaḥ saṃyoga iti/
karmādṛṣṭam upabhogārthaṃ kriyāhetur iti cet samānam/ karmādṛṣṭaṃ puruṣasthaṃ puruṣopabhogārthaṃ manasi kriyāhetuḥ evaṃ duḥkhaṃ duḥkhasaṃvedanaṃ ca sidhyatīty evaṃ cen manyase, samānam --- smṛtihetāv api saṃyogaviśeṣo bhavitum arhati/ tatra yad uktam ``ātmapreraṇayadṛcchājñatābhiś ca na saṃyogaviśeṣaḥ'' ity ayam apratiṣedha iti/ pūrvas tu pratiṣedho ``nāntaḥśarīravṛttitvān manasa'' iti//32//
children.translated_text: When indeed one whose mind is absorbed somewhere experiences pain in the foot from a pebble or thorn, then a special contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> must be sought, since pain and the sensation of pain are observed. Here the same refutation [applies]. And indeed there is no special contact by chance — no action is causeless, no contact is causeless. If [one argues that] the unseen force of <s>karma</s>, [being] for the purpose of experience, is the cause of action — then the same [applies to memory]. If you think that the unseen force of <s>karma</s>, residing in the person, being for the person's experience, is the cause of action in the mind, and that thus pain and the sensation of pain are established — then the same [applies]: a special contact can also be the cause of memory. In that case, the statement 'there is no special contact through the impulsion of the self, chance, or cognizance' is not a [valid] refutation. But the earlier refutation — 'because the mind does not operate outside the body' — [still holds]. //32//

children.text:
%863
kaḥ khalv idānīṃ kāraṇayaugapadyasadbhāve yugapad asmaraṇasya hetur iti?
children.translated_text: Now then, when the simultaneity of causes is present, what is the reason for not remembering simultaneously?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.33: The non-simultaneous remembering is due to the non-simultaneity of concentration, knowledge of inferential marks, and the like.

children.text: yathā khalv ātmamanasoḥ sannikarṣaḥ saṃskāraś ca smṛtihetur evaṃ praṇidhānaṃ liṅgādijñānāni tāni ca na yugapadbhavanti tatkṛtā smṛtīnāṃ yugapad anutpattir iti/ pratibhavat tu praṇidhānādyanapekṣe smārte yaugapadyaprasaṅgaḥ/ yat khalv idaṃ prātibham iva jñānaṃ praṇidhānādyanapekṣaṃ smārttam utpadyate kadācit tasya yugapadutpattiprasaṅgo hetvabhāvāt/ sataḥ smṛtihetor asaṃvedanāt prātibhena samānābhimānaḥ/ bahvarthaviṣaye vai cintāprabandhe kaścid evārthaḥ kasyacit smṛtihetuḥ,
children.translated_text: Just as the contact of <s>ātman</s> and <s>manas</s> and <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) are causes of memory, so too are concentration, knowledge of inferential marks, and the like; and these do not occur simultaneously — hence the non-simultaneous origination of memories caused by them. But regarding intuitive [knowledge], which does not depend on concentration and the like — the consequence of simultaneity would follow for memorial [knowledge]. Indeed, the memorial knowledge that sometimes arises like intuitive knowledge, independent of concentration and the like — for that, the consequence of simultaneous origination [would follow], due to the absence of a [restricting] cause. Since the actual cause of memory is not perceived, one has the same impression as with intuitive [knowledge]. In a continuous chain of thought about many objects, some particular object becomes the cause of memory of another;

children.text:
% cintāprabandhe kaścid evārthaḥ kasyacit smṛtihetuḥ,] p.864
tasyānucintanāt tasya smṛtir bhavati/ na cāyaṃ smartā sarvaṃ smṛtihetuṃ saṃvedayate evaṃ me smṛtir utpanneti/ asaṃvedanāt prātibham iva jñānam idaṃ smārtam iti abhimanyate, na tv asti praṇidhānādyanapekṣaṃ smārtam iti/
prātibhe katham iti cet puruṣakarmaviśeṣād upabhogavan niyamaḥ/ prātibham idānīṃ jñānaṃ yugapat kasmān notpadyate? yathopabhogārthaṃ karma yugapadupabhogaṃ na karoti evaṃ puruṣakarmaviśeṣaḥ pratibhāhetur na yugapad anekaṃ prātibhaṃ jñānam utpādayati/
hetvabhāvād ayuktam iti cet, na karaṇasya pratyayaparyāye sāmarthyāt/ ``upabhogavan niyama'' ity asti dṛṣṭānto hetur nāstīti cen manyase? na, karaṇasya pratyayaparyāye sāmarthyāt/ naikasmin jñeye yugapad anekaṃ jñānam utpadyate, na cānekasmin/ tad idaṃ dṛṣṭena pratyayaparyāyeṇānumeyaṃ karaṇasāmarthyam itthambhūtam iti na jñātuḥ vikaraṇadharmaṇo dehanānātve pratyayayaugapadyād iti/
children.translated_text: from contemplating it, the memory of that [other object] arises. And this person who remembers does not perceive every cause of memory, [thinking] 'thus my memory has arisen.' Because [the cause] is not perceived, one regards this memorial knowledge as if it were intuitive — but there is no memorial knowledge independent of concentration and the like. As for how [this works] in the case of intuitive knowledge: the restriction is like [that of] experience, due to the particular <s>karma</s> of the person. Why does intuitive knowledge not arise simultaneously now? Just as <s>karma</s> for the purpose of experience does not produce simultaneous experience, so too the particular <s>karma</s> of the person, which is the cause of intuition, does not produce multiple intuitive cognitions simultaneously. If [one objects that] this is unreasonable due to the absence of a cause — no, because of the capacity [of the instrument] in the sequence of cognitions. '[The restriction is] like experience' — if you think there is an example but no reason, that is not so, because of the capacity of the instrument in the sequence of cognitions. Not multiple cognitions of a single object arise simultaneously, nor [multiple cognitions] of many objects. This capacity of the instrument, which is to be inferred through the observed sequence of cognitions, is of such a nature — therefore it is not [the case that] the knower, who has the property of being without [additional] instruments, would have simultaneous cognitions due to the multiplicity of bodies.

children.text:
% pratyayaparyāyeṇānumeyaṃ karaṇasāmarthyam itthambhūtam iti na jñātuḥ vikaraṇadharmaṇo dehanānātve pratyayayaugapadyād iti/] p.865
ayaṃ ca dvitīyaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ, avasthitaśarīrasya cānekajñānasamavāyād ekapradeśe yugapad anekārthasmaraṇaṃ syāt/ kvacid deśe 'vasthitaśarīrasya jñātur indriyārthaprabandhena jñānam anekam ekasminn ātmapradeśe samavaiti/ tena yadā manaḥ saṃyujyate tadā jñātapūrvasyānekasya yugapat smaraṇaṃ prasajyate pradeśasaṃyogaparyāyābhāvād iti/ ātmapradeśānām adravyāntaratvād ekārthasamavāyasyāviśeṣe sati smṛtiyaugapadyapratiṣedhānupapattiḥ/
children.translated_text: And this is the second refutation: since one who is established in a body has the inherence of multiple cognitions [in the self], there would be simultaneous remembering of multiple objects in a single region [of the self]. For a knower established in a body, multiple cognitions inhere in a single region of the <s>ātman</s> through the successive [operation of] sense organs and objects. When the mind is conjoined with that [region], the simultaneous remembering of the multiple previously known [objects] would follow, since there is no sequence of contact with different regions. Since the regions of the <s>ātman</s> are not different substances, and since there is no distinction in the inherence of a single object [in them], the prevention of simultaneous memory is untenable.

children.text:
% p.866
śabdasantāne tu śrotrādhiṣṭhānapratyāsattyā śabdaśravaṇavat saṃskārapratyāsattyā manasaḥ smṛtyutpatter na yugapad utpattiprasaṅgaḥ/ pūrva eva tu pratiṣedho nānekajñānasamavāyād ekapradeśe yugapat smṛtiprasaṅga iti//33//
children.translated_text: But in the case of a continuum of sounds, just as hearing occurs through the proximity of the sound to the locus of the ear, so too memory arises in the mind through the proximity of the <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) — hence there is no consequence of simultaneous origination. But the earlier refutation [holds]: there is no consequence of simultaneous memory from the inherence of multiple cognitions in a single region. //33//

children.text: puruṣadharmo jñānam antaḥkaraṇasyecchādveṣaprayatnasukhaduḥkhāni dharmā iti kasyacid darśanam, tat pratiṣidhyate ---
children.translated_text: Some hold the view that knowledge is a property of the person, while desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain are properties of the inner organ — this is refuted:
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.34: Because desire and aversion are the causes of initiation and cessation, for the knower.

children.text: ayaṃ khalu jānāti tāvad idaṃ me sukhasādhanam idaṃ me duḥkhasādhanam iti jñātvā svasya sukhasādhanam āptum icchati, duḥkhasādhanaṃ hātum icchati, prāptīcchāprayuktasyāsya sukhasādhanāvāptaye samīhāviśeṣa ārambhaḥ, jihāsāprayuktasya duḥkhasādhanaparivarjanaṃ nivṛttiḥ, evaṃ jñānecchāprayatnadveṣasukhaduḥkhānām ekenābhisambandhaḥ/ ekakartṛkatvaṃ jñānecchāpravṛttīnāṃ samānāśrayatvaṃ ca/ tasmāj jñasyecchādveṣaprayatnasukhaduḥkhāni dharmā nācetanasyeti/ ārambhanivṛttyoś ca pratyagātmani dṛṣṭatvāt paratrānumānaṃ veditavyam iti//34//
children.translated_text: Indeed, this [person] first knows: 'this is a means to my pleasure, this is a means to my pain.' Having known, he desires to obtain what is a means to his pleasure and desires to avoid what is a means to his pain. For one impelled by the desire to obtain, the particular endeavor to achieve the means of pleasure is initiation; for one impelled by the desire to avoid, the avoidance of the means of pain is cessation. Thus, knowledge, desire, effort, aversion, pleasure, and pain are all connected with a single [entity]. The agency of knowledge, desire, and activity is single, and their substratum is the same. Therefore, desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, and pain are properties of the knower, not of something unconscious. And since initiation and cessation are observed in one's own self, the inference regarding others should be understood. //34//
Here the proponent of elemental consciousness says —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.35: Since [initiation and cessation] are the marks of those [desire and aversion], the denial of desire and aversion in earthly and other [elements] is not [established].

children.text: ārambhanivṛttiliṅgāv icchādveṣāv iti yasyārambhanivṛttī tasyecchādveṣau tasya jñānam iti prāptaṃ pārthivāpy ataijasavāyavīyānāṃ śarīrāṇām ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣajñānair yoga iti caitanyam//35//
children.translated_text: Desire and aversion are marked by initiation and cessation — thus, wherever there is initiation and cessation, there are desire and aversion, and wherever there are these, there is knowledge. Since initiation and cessation are observed in bodies made of earth, fire, and air, their connection with desire, aversion, and knowledge [follows] — hence consciousness [of elements is established]. //35//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.36: Because initiation and cessation are observed in axes and the like.

children.text: śarīre caitanyanivṛttiḥ/ ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣajñānair yoga iti prāptaṃ paraśvādeḥ karaṇasyārambhanivṛttidarśanāc caitanyam iti/ atha śarīrasyecchādibhir yogaḥ, paraśvādes tu karaṇasyārambhanivṛttī vyabhicarataḥ, na tarhy ayaṃ hetuḥ pārthivāpy ataijasavāyavīyānāṃ śarīrāṇām ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣajñānair yoga iti/
children.translated_text: [This argues for] the cessation of consciousness in the body. Since initiation and cessation are observed, and connection with desire, aversion, and knowledge is established — then from the observation of initiation and cessation of an axe, which is an instrument, consciousness [of the axe would follow]. Now, if the body has connection with desire and the like, while the initiation and cessation of an instrument like an axe deviate [from this rule], then this is not a [valid] reason: that from the observation of initiation and cessation of bodies made of earth, fire, and air, there is connection with desire, aversion, and knowledge.

children.text:
% p.869
ayaṃ tarhy anyo 'rthaḥ --- talliṅgatvād icchādveṣayoḥ pārthivādyeṣv apratiṣedhaḥ/ pṛthivyādīnāṃ bhūtānām ārambhas tāvat trasasthāvaraśarīreṣu tadavayavavyūhaliṅgaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣaḥ loṣṭādiṣu ca liṅgābhāvāt pravṛttiviśeṣābhāvo nivṛttiḥ/ ārambhanivṛttiliṅgāv icchādveṣāv iti pārthivādyeṣv aṇuṣu taddarśanād icchādveṣayogas tadyogāj jñānayoga iti siddhaṃ bhūtacaitanyam iti/
kumbhādiṣv anupalabdher ahetuḥ/ kumbhādimṛdavayavānāṃ vyūhaliṅgaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣa ārambhaḥ, sikatādiṣu pravṛttiviśeṣābhāvo nivṛttiḥ/ na ca mṛtsikatānām ārambhanivṛttidarśanād icchādveṣaprayatnajñānair yogaḥ/ tasmāt talliṅgatvād icchādveṣayor ity ahetur iti//36//
children.translated_text: Then this is another meaning — since [initiation and cessation] are the marks of those [desire and aversion], the denial of desire and aversion in earthly and other [elements] is not [valid]. As for the elements earth and the rest: their initiation in mobile and immobile bodies is a particular activity marked by the arrangement of their parts; and in clods and the like, the absence of such particular activity due to the absence of a mark is cessation. Since desire and aversion are marked by initiation and cessation, from the observation of these in the atoms of earth and the like, there is connection with desire and aversion, and from that connection, connection with knowledge — thus elemental consciousness is established. [But] this is not a [valid] reason because of non-apprehension in pots and the like. For the particular activity that is initiation, marked by the arrangement of parts of clay atoms, [is seen in] pots; and the absence of particular activity in sand and the like is cessation. Yet the connection of clay and sand with desire, aversion, effort, and knowledge [does not follow] from the observation of their initiation and cessation. Therefore, the [argument] 'since [these] are the marks of desire and aversion' is not a [valid] reason. //36//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 3,2.37: But restriction and non-restriction are the distinguishing factors of those [desire and aversion].

children.text: tayor icchādveṣayor niyamāniyamau viśeṣakau bhedakau/ jñasyecchādveṣanimitte pravṛttinivṛttī na svāśraye/
children.translated_text: Restriction and non-restriction are the distinguishing factors — the differentiators — of those desire and aversion. The activity and cessation caused by the desire and aversion of a knower do not [occur] in their own substratum;

children.text:
% pravṛttinivṛttī na svāśraye/] p.870
kiṃ tarhi? prayojyāśraye/ tatra prayujyamāneṣu bhūteṣu pravṛttinivṛttī staḥ na sarveṣv ity aniyamopapattiḥ/
yasya tu jñatvād bhūtānām icchādveṣanimitte ārambhanivṛttī svāśraye tasya niyamaḥ syāt, yathā bhūtānāṃ guṇāntaranimittā pravṛttir guṇapratibandhāc ca nivṛttir bhūtamātre bhavati niyamena, evaṃ bhūtamātre jñānecchādveṣanimitte pravṛttinivṛttī svāśraye syātām, na tu bhavataḥ tasmāt prayojakāśritā jñānecchādveṣaprayatnāḥ, prayojyāśraye tu pravṛttinivṛttīti siddham/
children.translated_text: rather, in the substratum of what is to be employed. There, among the elements being employed, activity and cessation occur — but not in all [elements]; hence the tenability of non-restriction. But for one for whom, because the elements are knowers, the initiation and cessation caused by desire and aversion occur in their own substratum — for him there should be restriction. Just as the activity of elements caused by other qualities, and the cessation due to the obstruction of qualities, occurs in elements universally with restriction, so too activity and cessation caused by knowledge, desire, and aversion should occur in their own substratum in all elements universally — but they do not. Therefore, knowledge, desire, aversion, and effort belong to the employer, while activity and cessation [occur] in the substratum of what is employed — this is established.

children.text:
% p.871
ekaśarīre tu jñātṛbahutvaṃ niranumānam/ bhūtacaitanikasyaikaśarīre bahūni bhūtāni jñānecchādveṣaprayatnaguṇānīti jñātṛbahutvaṃ prāptam/ om iti bruvataḥ pramāṇaṃ nāsti, yathā nānāśarīreṣu nānā jñātāro buddhyādiguṇavyavasthānāt, evam ekaśarīre 'pi buddhyādivyavasthānumānaṃ syāj jñātṛbahutvasyeti/
children.translated_text: But the multiplicity of knowers in a single body is without inferential support. For the proponent of elemental consciousness, since there are many elements with the qualities of knowledge, desire, aversion, and effort in a single body, the multiplicity of knowers would follow. There is no <s>pramāṇa</s> (valid means of knowledge) for one who assents to this. Just as in different bodies there are different knowers, established from the arrangement of cognition and other qualities, so too in a single body, from the arrangement of cognition and the like, there might be an inference for the multiplicity of knowers —

children.text:
% p.872
dṛṣṭaś ca anyaguṇanimittaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣo bhūtānāṃ so 'numānam anyatrāpi/ dṛṣṭaḥ karaṇalakṣaṇeṣu bhūteṣu paraśvādiṣu upādānalakṣaṇeṣu ca mṛtprabhṛtiṣv anyaguṇanimittaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣaḥ/ so 'numānam anyatrāpi trasasthāvaraśarīreṣu/ tadavayavavyūhaliṅgaḥ pravṛttiviśeṣo bhūtānām anyaguṇanimitta iti/ sa ca guṇaḥ prayatnasamānāśrayaḥ saṃskāro dharmādharmasamākhyātaḥ sarvārthaḥ puruṣārthārādhanāya prayojako bhūtānāṃ prayatnavad iti/
ātmāstitvahetubhir ātmanityatvahetubhiś ca bhūtacaitanyapratiṣedhaḥ kṛto veditavyaḥ/ ``nendriyārthayos tadvināśe 'pi jjānāvasthānād''iti ca samānaḥ pratiṣedha iti/ kriyāmātraṃ kriyoparamamātraṃ cārambhanivṛttī ity abhipretyoktam ``talliṅgatvād icchādveṣayoḥ pārthivādyeṣv apratiṣedhaḥ''/ anyathā tv ime ārambhanivṛttī ākhyāte, na ca tathāvidhe pṛthivyādiṣu dṛśyete/ tasmād ayuktam ``talliṅgatvād icchādveṣayoḥ pārthivādyeṣv apratiṣedha''iti//37
children.translated_text:
And the purposeful variation of activity in beings that is observed to be caused by other qualities — that is an inference (applicable) elsewhere as well. In beings characterized as instruments — such as axes and the like — and in beings characterized as materials — such as clay and the like — a purposeful variation of activity caused by other qualities is observed. That is an inference (applicable) elsewhere as well — in the bodies of mobile and immobile beings. The inferential mark of this purposeful variation in beings, caused by another quality, is the arrangement of their parts. And that quality, which shares the same substrate as effort (<s>prayatna</s>), is a latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) called <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit), which, being all-purposive, impels beings toward the accomplishment of the person's goals, just like effort.
By the reasons establishing the existence of the <s>ātman</s> and by the reasons establishing the permanence of the <s>ātman</s>, the denial of consciousness in material elements has been accomplished — this should be understood. And the refutation 'not (consciousness belongs to the senses), because knowledge persists even when the sense-organs and their objects are destroyed' — that same refutation applies here. It was stated with the understanding that initiation and cessation are merely action and mere cessation of action: 'because desire and aversion are marked by the same signs, they are not denied in earthy and other (entities).' But initiation and cessation are explained differently (from how they occur in beings), and they are not seen in earth and the like of that (conscious) kind. Therefore, it is untenable (to say) 'because desire and aversion are marked by the same signs, they are not denied in earthy and other (entities).' // 37
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.2.38]

children.text:
% p.873
bhūtendriyamanasāṃ samānaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ, manas tūdāharaṇamātram/
children.translated_text: The same refutation (of consciousness) applies to the elements, sense-organs, and mind; the mind is mentioned merely as an illustration.

children.text: NyS_3,2.38: yathoktahetutvāt pāratantryād akṛtābhyāgamāc ca na manasaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 3.2.38: Not of the mind (<s>manas</s>) — because of the reasons stated (above), because of its dependence, and because of (the consequence of) the accrual of what was not done.

children.text:
``icchādveṣaprayatnasukhaduḥkhajñānāny ātmano liṅgam''ity ataḥ prabhṛti yathoktaṃ saṅgṛhyate, tena bhūtendriyamanasāṃ caitanyapratiṣedhaḥ/
pāratantryāt --- paratantrāṇi bhūtendriyamanāṃsi dhāraṇapreraṇavyūhanakriyāsu prayatnavaśāt pravarttante, caitanye punaḥ svatantrāṇi syur iti/
children.translated_text:
From 'desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and knowledge are the marks of the <s>ātman</s>' onward, what has been stated is summarized — by that, the denial of consciousness in the elements, sense-organs, and mind (is established).
Because of dependence — the elements, sense-organs, and mind, being dependent (<s>paratantra</s>), operate in the activities of sustaining, impelling, and arranging through the power of effort; but if they were conscious, they would be independent.

children.text:
% p.874
akṛtābhyāgamāc ca --- ``pravṛttir vāgbuddhiśarīrārambha''iti caitanye bhūtendriyamanasāṃ parakṛtaṃ karma puruṣeṇopabhujyata iti syāt, acaitanye tu tatsādhanasya svakṛtakarmaphalopabhogaḥ puruṣasyety upapadyata iti//38//
children.translated_text: And because of the (consequence of) the accrual of what was not done — 'Activity is the initiation of speech, mind, and body' — if the elements, sense-organs, and mind were conscious, then the <s>karma</s> done by another would be experienced by the person (<s>puruṣa</s>). But when they are non-conscious, the person's experience of the fruit of his own <s>karma</s>, through them as instruments, is established. // 38 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.2.39]
Now, this is the concluding summary of what has been established —
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.39: By the method of residue (<s>pariśeṣa</s>), and because of the applicability of the reasons stated.

children.text:
ātmaguṇo jñānam iti prakṛtam/ pariśeṣo nāma `prasaktapratiṣedhe anyatrāprasaṅgāc chiṣyamāṇe sampratyayaḥ''/ bhūtendriyamanasāṃ pratiṣedhe dravyāntaraṃ na prasajyate śiṣyate cātmā tasya guṇo jñānam iti jñāyate/
yathoktahetūpapatteś ceti ``darśanasparśanābhyām ekārthagrahaṇād''ityevamādīnām ātmapratipattihetūnām apratiṣedhād iti/ pariśeṣajñāpanārthaṃ prakṛtasthāpanādijñānārthaṃ ca yathoktahetūpapattivacanam iti/
atha vā upapatteś ceti hetvantaram evedam/ nityaḥ khalv ayam ātmā, yasmād ekasmin śarīre dharmaṃ caritvā kāyasya bhedāt svarge deveṣūpapadyate, adharmaṃ caritvā dehabhedāt narakeṣūpapadyata iti/ upapattiḥ śarīrāntaraprāptilakṣaṇā, sā sati sattve nitye cāśrayavatī, buddhiprabandhamātre tu nirātmake nirāśrayā nopapadyata iti/ ekasattvādhiṣṭhānaś cānekaśarīrayogaḥ saṃsāra upapadyate, śarīraprabandhocchedaś cāpavargo muktir ity upapadyate/ buddhisantatimātre tv ekasattvānupapatter na kaścid dīrgham adhvānaṃ sandhāvati na kaścic charīraprabandhād vimucyata iti saṃsārāpavargānupapattir iti/ buddhisantatimātre ca sattvabhedāt sarvam idaṃ prāṇivyavahārajātam apratisaṃhitam avyāvṛttam apariniṣṭhaṃ ca syāt,
children.translated_text:
It is the topic (under discussion) that knowledge is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>. Residue (<s>pariśeṣa</s>) means: 'when what is connected (with an erroneous thesis) has been denied, the conviction settles on what remains, because there is no other possibility.' When consciousness has been denied in the elements, sense-organs, and mind, no other substance is applicable; the <s>ātman</s> remains — and it is known that knowledge is its quality.
'And because of the applicability of the reasons stated' — since the reasons for the cognition of the <s>ātman</s>, such as 'from the apprehension of a single object through sight and touch,' have not been denied. The statement about the applicability of the reasons as stated serves the purpose of indicating the method of residue and of establishing, etc. the topic.
Alternatively, 'because of applicability' is itself a separate reason. For this <s>ātman</s> is permanent, since, having practiced <s>dharma</s> (merit) in one body, upon the dissolution of that body, it is born (<s>upapadyate</s>) among the gods in heaven; and having practiced <s>adharma</s> (demerit), upon the dissolution of the body, it is born in the hells. Birth (<s>upapatti</s>), characterized by the attainment of another body — that, being possessed of a substrate, exists when a permanent entity exists; but in the case of a mere continuum of cognitions (<s>buddhiprabandha</s>), which is selfless (<s>nirātmaka</s>), it would be without a substrate and would not be established. And <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration), which is the connection of a single entity with multiple bodies, is established (on this view); and <s>apavarga</s> (liberation), the cessation of the continuum of bodies, is also established. But in the case of a mere continuum of cognitions, since a single entity is not established, no one transmigrates through a long course, and no one is liberated from the continuum of bodies — hence <s>saṃsāra</s> and <s>apavarga</s> are not established. And in the case of a mere continuum of cognitions, because of the difference of entities (at each moment), this entire class of activities of living beings would be uncoordinated, undiscriminated, and unsettled,

children.text:
% -jātam apratisaṃhitam avyāvṛttam apariniṣṭhaṃ ca syāt,] p.876
tataḥ smaraṇābhāvāt nānyadṛṣṭam anyaḥ smaratīti/ smaraṇaṃ ca khalu pūrvajñātasya samānena jñātrā grahaṇam ajñāsiṣam amum arthaṃ jñeyam iti/ so .yam eko jñātā pūrvajñātam arthaṃ gṛhṇāti tac cāsya grahaṇaṃ smaraṇam iti, tad buddhiprabandhamātre nirātmake nopapadyate//39//
children.translated_text: and therefore there would be no remembering — 'what was experienced by one is not remembered by another.' And remembering is indeed the apprehension of a previously known object by the same knower: 'I did not know this object that is to be known.' This one knower apprehends the previously known object, and that apprehension of his is remembering — and that is not established in the case of a mere continuum of cognitions without a self. // 39 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.2.40]
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.40: But remembering belongs to the <s>ātman</s>, because of its nature as knower.

children.text: upapadyata iti/ ātmana eva smaraṇaṃ na buddhisantatimātrasyeti/ tuśabdo 'vadhāraṇe/ katham? jñasvabhāvatvāt/ jña iti asya svabhāvaḥ svo dharmaḥ/ ayaṃ khalu jñāsyati jānāti ajñāsīd iti trikālaviṣayeṇānekena jñānena sambadhyate,
children.translated_text: (This) is established. Remembering belongs to the <s>ātman</s> alone, not to a mere continuum of cognitions. The word 'but' (<s>tu</s>) is for emphasis. How? Because of its nature as knower (<s>jñasvabhāva</s>). 'Knower' (<s>jña</s>) is its nature, its own property. For this (self) is connected with multiple cognitions across three times: 'he will know, he knows, he knew' —

children.text:
% jñāsyati jānāti ... sambadhyate,] p.877
tac cāsya trikālaviṣayaṃ jñānaṃ pratyātmavedanīyaṃ jñāsyāmi jānāmi ajñāsiṣam iti varttate, tad yasyāyaṃ svo dharmas tasya smaraṇaṃ na buddhiprabandhamātrasya nirātmakasyeti//40//
children.translated_text: and this three-time cognition of his is experienced by each individual self: 'I shall know, I know, I knew.' That whose own property this is — to that belongs remembering, not to a mere continuum of cognitions without a self. // 40 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.2.41]

children.text: smṛtihetūnām ayaugapadyād yugapad asmaraṇam ity uktam/ atha kebhyaḥ smṛtir utpadyata iti? smṛtiḥ khalu ---
children.translated_text: It has been stated that because of the non-simultaneity of the causes of memory, there is no simultaneous remembering. Now, from what causes does memory arise? Memory indeed —

<s>NyS</s> 3.2.41: (Memory arises) from attention (<s>praṇidhāna</s>), binding (<s>nibandha</s>), repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>), mark (<s>liṅga</s>), sign (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>), similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>), possession (<s>parigraha</s>), support (<s>āśraya</s>), the supported (<s>āśrita</s>), relation (<s>sambandha</s>), succession (<s>ānantarya</s>), separation (<s>viyoga</s>), joint effect (<s>ekakārya</s>), opposition (<s>virodha</s>), superiority (<s>atiśaya</s>), attainment (<s>prāpti</s>), obstruction (<s>vyavadhāna</s>), pleasure (<s>sukha</s>), pain (<s>duḥkha</s>), desire (<s>icchā</s>), aversion (<s>dveṣa</s>), fear (<s>bhaya</s>), need (<s>arthitva</s>), action (<s>kriyā</s>), attachment (<s>rāga</s>), merit (<s>dharma</s>), and demerit (<s>adharma</s>).

children.text: susmūrṣayā manaso dhāraṇaṃ praṇidhānaṃ susmūrṣitaliṅgacintanaṃ cārthasmṛtikāraṇam/ nibandhaḥ khalv ekagranthopayamo 'rthānām, ekagranthopayatāḥ khalv arthā anyonyasmṛtihetava ānupūrvyeṇetarathā vā bhavantīti/
children.translated_text: Attention (<s>praṇidhāna</s>) — the fixation of the mind through the desire to remember, and the contemplation of the mark of what is desired to be remembered — is the cause of memory of the object. Binding (<s>nibandha</s>) is the arrangement of objects under a single heading; objects arranged under a single heading become causes of mutual remembering, in sequence or otherwise.

children.text:
% ānupūrvyeṇetarathā vā bhavatīti/] p.878
dhāraṇaśāstrakṛto vā prajñāteṣu vastuṣu smartavyānām upanikṣepo nibandha iti/
abhyāsas tu samāne viṣaye jñānānām abhyāvṛttiḥ, abhyāsajanitaḥ saṃskāra ātmaguṇo 'bhyāsaśabdenocyate, sa ca smṛtihetuḥ samāna iti/
liṅgaṃ punaḥ saṃyogi samavāyy ekārthasamavāyi virodhi ceti/ yathā dhūmo 'gneḥ, gor viṣāṇam, pāṇiḥ pādasya, rūpaṃ sparśasya abhūtaṃ bhūtasyeti/
lakṣaṇaṃ paśvavayavasthaṃ gotrasya smṛtihetuḥ, vidānām idaṃ gargāṇām idam iti/ sādṛśyaṃ citragataṃ pratirūpakaṃ devadattasyetyevamādi/ parigrahāt svena vā svāmī svāminā vā svaṃ smaryate/ āśrayād grāmaṇyā tadadhīnaṃ saṃsmarati/ āśritāt tadadhīnena grāmaṇyam iti/ sambandhād antevāsinā yuktaṃ guruṃ smarati, ṛtvijā yājyam iti/
children.translated_text:
Or, binding is the method of placing what is to be remembered among known objects, as prescribed by the science of retention (<s>dhāraṇāśāstra</s>).
Repetition (<s>abhyāsa</s>) is the recurring occurrence of cognitions with respect to the same object; the latent impression (<s>saṃskāra</s>) generated by repetition, being a quality of the <s>ātman</s>, is called by the word 'repetition' — and it is a cause of memory, similarly.
Mark (<s>liṅga</s>) means: what is conjoined, what is inherent, what is co-inherent in the same entity, and what is opposed. For example: smoke (reminds one) of fire; a horn of a cow; a hand of a foot; visible form of touch; what has not occurred of what has occurred.
Sign (<s>lakṣaṇa</s>) — a characteristic located in an individual member of a lineage — is a cause of memory of the lineage: 'this is (the mark) of the <s>Viḍas</s>, this of the <s>Gargas</s>.' Similarity (<s>sādṛśya</s>) — a likeness in a painting serves as a cause of remembering <s>Devadatta</s> and the like. From possession (<s>parigraha</s>) — by one's own property the owner is remembered, or by the owner, one's property. From the support (<s>āśraya</s>) — a village headman remembers those dependent on him. From the supported (<s>āśrita</s>) — by one dependent, the headman (is remembered). From relation (<s>sambandha</s>) — by a student, the teacher with whom he is associated is remembered; by a sacrificial priest, the patron.

children.text:
% yājyam iti/] p.879
ānantaryād iti karaṇīyeṣv artheṣu/ viyogād yena viyujyate tadviyogapratisaṃvedī bhṛśaṃ smarati/ ekakāryāt kartrantaradarśanāt kartrantare smṛtiḥ/ virodhāt, vijigīṣamāṇayor anyataradarśanād anyataraḥ smaryate/ atiśayād yenātiśaya utpāditaḥ/ prāpteḥ yato 'nena kiṃcit prāptam āptavyaṃ vā bhavati tam abhīkṣṇaṃ smarati/ vyavadhānāt kośādibhir asiprabhṛtīni smaryante/
children.translated_text: From succession (<s>ānantarya</s>) — in tasks that follow one after another. From separation (<s>viyoga</s>) — one who perceives the separation from someone remembers that person intensely. From joint effect (<s>ekakārya</s>) — from seeing one co-worker, another co-worker is remembered. From opposition (<s>virodha</s>) — when two are in rivalry, from seeing one, the other is remembered. From superiority (<s>atiśaya</s>) — one by whom one has been surpassed (is remembered). From attainment (<s>prāpti</s>) — one from whom something has been obtained or is to be obtained, one remembers him constantly. From obstruction (<s>vyavadhāna</s>) — by sheaths and the like, swords and other (weapons) are remembered.

children.text:
% kośādibhir asiprabhṛtīni smaryante/] p.880
sukhaduḥkhābhyāṃ taddhetuḥ smaryate/ icchādveṣābhyāṃ yam icchati yaṃ ca dveṣṭi taṃ smarati/ bhayād yato bibheti/ arthitvād yenārthī bhojanenācchādanena vā/ kriyayā rathena rathakāraṃ smarati/ rāgād yasyāṃ striyāṃ rakto bhavati tām abhīkṣṇaṃ smarati/ dharmāj jātyantarasmaraṇam iha cādhītaśrutāvadhāraṇam iti/ adharmāt prāganubhūtaduḥkhasādhanaṃ smarati/ na caiteṣu nimitteṣu yugapat saṃvedanāni bhavantīti yugapad asmaraṇam iti/ nidarśanaṃ cedaṃ smṛtihetūnāṃ na parisaṅkhyānam iti//41//
children.translated_text: From pleasure and pain — their cause is remembered. From desire and aversion — what one desires and what one hates, one remembers. From fear — that which one fears. From need (<s>arthitva</s>) — that which one needs, whether food or clothing. From action (<s>kriyā</s>) — by a chariot, one remembers the chariot-maker. From attachment (<s>rāga</s>) — the woman to whom one is attached, one constantly remembers. From <s>dharma</s> (merit) — the remembering of other births, and here, the retaining of what has been studied and heard. From <s>adharma</s> (demerit) — one remembers the previously experienced means of suffering. And since there is no simultaneous perception of these causes, there is no simultaneous remembering. And this is an illustration of the causes of memory, not an exhaustive enumeration. // 41 //
[Commentary on <s>NyS</s> 3.2.42]

children.text:
% p.881
anityāyāṃ ca buddhāv utpannāpavargitvāt kālāntarāvāsthānāc ca anityānāṃ saṃśayaḥ kim utpatpannāpavargiṇī buddhiḥ śabdavat āhosvit kālāntarāvasthāyinī kumbhavad iti/ utpannāpavargiṇīti pakṣaḥ parigṛhyate/kasmāt?
children.translated_text: And cognition (<s>buddhi</s>) being impermanent — since impermanent things either perish immediately upon arising or persist for some time — there is a doubt: 'Is cognition one that perishes immediately upon arising, like sound? Or does it persist for some time, like a pot?' The position that it perishes immediately upon arising is adopted. Why?
<s>NyS</s> 3.2.42: Because of the apprehension of action, which is non-persisting.

children.text: karmaṇo 'navasthāyino grahaṇād iti/ kṣiptasyeṣor āpatanāt kriyāsantāno gṛhyate, pratyarthaniyamāc ca buddhīnāṃ kriyāsantānavad buddhisantānoupapattir iti/ avasthitagrahaṇe ca vyavadhīyamānasya pratyakśanivṛtteḥ/ avasthite ca kumbhe gṛhyamāṇe santānenaiva buddhir vartate prāg vyavadhānāt tena vyavahite pratyakṣaṃ jñānaṃ nivartate,
children.translated_text: Because of the apprehension of non-persisting action.
