children.translated_text: [Note: p.944] and his <s>dharma</s>, having as its fruit the eightfold sovereignty (<s>aiśvarya</s>) beginning with <s>aṇimā</s> (the power of becoming minute), conforms to his will and sets in motion the <s>dharma</s> and <s>adharma</s> accumulations operating in each individual self, as well as the elements beginning with earth. And thus, the creative power of <s>Īśvara</s>, without loss of (the results of) his own deeds, should be understood as the fruit of his own actions. And he is like a trustworthy authority (<s>āpta</s>) — just as a father (cares for) his children, so <s>Īśvara</s>, being like a father, (cares for) beings. And no other nature than that of the self is possible (for him). Indeed, no property that would serve as an inferential mark can be established for him apart from cognition. And from scripture (<s>āgama</s>), <s>Īśvara</s> is a seer, a knower, and omniscient. But who is able to establish an <s>Īśvara</s> who is indescribable, who transcends the domain of perception, inference, and scripture, by means of the inferential marks of the self such as cognition and the rest?

children.text:
% liṅgair nirupākhyam īśvaraṃ pratyakṣānumānāgamaviṣayātītaṃ kaḥ śakta upapādayitum/] p.945
svakṛtābhyāgamalopena ca pravartamānasyāsya yad uktaṃ pratiṣedhajātam akarmanimitte śarīrasarge tat sarvaṃ prasajyate iti//21//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.945] And for one who operates without loss of (the results of) his own deeds, all the objections that have been stated regarding the creation of the body without action as the cause would apply. //21//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.22]
[Note: p.958] Now another says —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.22: Things originate without a cause, because of the observation of the sharpness of thorns and the like.
The origination of the body and the like is without a cause. Why? Because of the observation of the sharpness of thorns and the like. The sharpness of the thorn,

children.text:
% p.959
taikṣṇyam, parvatadhātūnāṃ citratā, grāvṇāṃ ślakṣṇatā, nirnimittaṃ ca upādānavac ca dṛṣṭaṃ tathā śarīrādisargo .pīti//22//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.959] the variegation of mountain minerals, the smoothness of stones — (these are) observed to be without a cause yet as if having a material cause; likewise the creation of the body and the rest. //22//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.23]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.23: Not from the causeless, because (even) what is called 'causeless' has a cause.

children.text: animittato bhāvotpattir ity ucyate yataś cotpadyate tannimittam/ animittasya nimittatvān nānimittā bhāvotpattir iti//23//
children.translated_text: It is said that things originate without a cause — but that from which (something) originates is its cause. Since what is (called) causeless has a cause, the origination of things is not causeless. //23//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.24]
[Note: p.960]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.24: There is no refutation, because the cause and the denial of a cause are different things.

children.text: anyad dhi nimittam anyac ca nimittapratyākhyānam, na ca pratyākhyānam eva pratyākhyeyaṃ
children.translated_text: For the cause is one thing and the denial of a cause is another, and the denial itself is not what is being denied —

children.text:
% p.961
yathānudakaḥ kamaṇḍalur iti nodakapratiṣedha udakaṃ bhavatīti/ sa khalv ayaṃ vādo 'karmanimittaḥ śarīrādisarga ity etasmān na bhidyate, abhedāt tatpratiṣedhenaiva pratiṣiddho veditavya iti//24//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.961] just as (saying) 'the water-pot is without water' is not a denial of water (such that) water comes into being (from the denial). This doctrine — that the creation of the body and the like is without action as a cause — is not different from (the previously refuted view), and since there is no difference, it should be understood as refuted by the same refutation. //24//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.25]
[Note: p.962] Others, however, think —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4.1.25: Everything is impermanent, because it has the nature of origination and destruction.

children.text: kim anityaṃ nāma? yasya kadācid bhāvas tad anityam/ utpattidharmakam anutpannaṃ nāsti vināśadharmakaṃ ca vinaṣṭaṃ nāsti/ kiṃ punaḥ sarvam? bhautikaṃ ca śarīrādi
children.translated_text: What is meant by 'impermanent'? That which exists at some time but not at another is impermanent. That which has the nature of origination does not exist before it has originated, and that which has the nature of destruction does not exist after it has been destroyed. But is everything [impermanent]? The material, such as the body and so forth,

children.text:
% p.963
abhautikaṃ ca buddhyādi, tad ubhayam utpattivināśadharmakaṃ vijñāyate, tasmāt tat sarvam anityam iti//25//
children.translated_text: [Page 963] and the non-material, such as <s>buddhi</s> (cognition) and so forth — both of these are known to have the nature of origination and destruction; therefore all of that is impermanent. [25]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.26]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.26: Not so, because impermanence itself would be impermanent.

children.text: yadi tāvat sarvasyānityatā nityā, tannityatvān na sarvam anityam/ athānityā tasyām avidyamānāyāṃ sarvaṃ nityam iti//26//
children.translated_text: If, on the one hand, the impermanence of everything is permanent, then because of that permanence, not everything is impermanent. If, on the other hand, it is impermanent, then when that [impermanence] ceases to exist, everything would be permanent. [26]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.27]
[Page 964]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.27: The impermanence of that [impermanence] is like fire, which perishes along with the combustible it destroys.

children.text: tasyā anityatāyā apy anityatvam/ katham? yathā agnir dāhyaṃ vināśyānuvinaśyati evaṃ sarvasyānityatā sarvaṃ vināśyānuvinaśyatīti//27//
children.translated_text: That impermanence too is itself impermanent. How so? Just as fire perishes along with the combustible that it destroys, so too the impermanence of everything perishes along with everything that it destroys. [27]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.28]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.28: The permanent cannot be denied, because things are established according to how they are apprehended.

children.text: ayaṃ khalu vādo nityaṃ pratyācaṣṭe, nityasya ca pratyākhyānam anupapannam/ kasmāt? yathopalabdhi vyavasthānāt/ yasyotpattivināśadharmakatvam upalabhyate pramāṇatas tad anityam,
children.translated_text: This doctrine indeed denies the permanent, but the denial of the permanent is untenable. Why? Because things are established according to how they are apprehended. That whose nature of origination and destruction is apprehended through <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge) is impermanent,

children.text:
% p.965
yasya nopalabhyate tadviparītam/ na ca paramasūkṣmāṇāṃ bhūtānām ākāśakāladigātmamanasāṃ tadguṇānāṃ ca keṣāñcit sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyānāṃ cotpattivināśadharmakatvaṃ pramāṇata upalabhyate, tasmān nityāny etānīti//28//
children.translated_text: [Page 965] and that whose [origination and destruction] is not apprehended is the opposite [i.e., permanent]. And the nature of origination and destruction of the supremely subtle elements, of <s>ākāśa</s> (space), <s>kāla</s> (time), <s>dik</s> (direction), <s>ātman</s> (self), and <s>manas</s> (mind), and of certain of their <s>guṇas</s> (qualities), and of <s>sāmānya</s> (universals), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particulars), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) is not apprehended through <s>pramāṇa</s> (means of valid knowledge); therefore these are permanent. [28]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.29]
[Page 966] Here is another extreme view:
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.29: Everything is permanent, because the five elements are permanent.

children.text: bhūtamātram idaṃ sarvaṃ tāni ca nityāni bhūtocchedānupapatter iti//29//
children.translated_text: All this is nothing but elements, and they are permanent, since the annihilation of elements is untenable. [29]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.30]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.30: Not so, because causes of origination and destruction are observed.

children.text: utpattikāraṇaṃ copalabhyate vināśakāraṇaṃ ca, tat sarvanityatve vyāhanyate iti//30//
children.translated_text: Causes of origination are observed and causes of destruction are observed; that is contradicted by [the thesis of] the permanence of everything. [30]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.31]
[Page 967]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.31: There is no refutation, because [what originates and perishes] falls under the definition of those [elements].

children.text: yasyotpattivināśakāraṇam upalabhyate iti manyase, na tad bhūtalakṣaṇahīnam arthāntaraṃ gṛhyate, bhūtalakṣaṇāvarodhād bhūtamātram idam ity ukto 'yaṃ pratiṣedha iti//31//
children.translated_text: What you consider to have observed causes of origination and destruction — that is not grasped as something different devoid of the defining characteristics of elements. Because it falls under the defining characteristics of elements, the refutation stated [above] — that 'all this is nothing but elements' — [stands]. [31]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.32]
[Page 968]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.32: Not so, because origination and its cause are observed.

children.text:
kāraṇasamānaguṇasyotpattiḥ kāraṇaṃ copalabhyate/ na caitad ubhayaṃ nityaviṣayam, na cotpattitatkāraṇopalabdhiḥ śakyā pratyākhyātum, na cāviṣayā kācid upalabdhiḥ/ upalabdhisāmarthyāt kāraṇena samānaguṇaṃ kāryam utpadyate ity anumīyate, sa khalūpalabdher viṣaya iti/ evaṃ ca tallakṣaṇāvarodhopapattir iti/
utpattivināśakāraṇaprayuktasya jñātuḥ prayatno dṛṣṭa iti/ prasiddhaś cāvayavī taddharmā/ utpattivināśadharmā cāvayavī siddha iti/
children.translated_text: Origination is [the arising] of something possessing qualities similar to its cause, and the cause is observed. Neither of these two pertains to what is permanent. Nor can the observation of origination and its cause be denied, nor is any observation without an object. By the force of observation, it is inferred that an effect possessing qualities similar to the cause is produced — that indeed is the object of observation. And thus the inclusion under their [i.e., the elements'] defining characteristics is established. [The opponent argues:] the effort of a knower impelled by a cause of origination and destruction is seen [to exist]. And the <s>avayavin</s> (composite whole) possessing those properties is well-established. And the <s>avayavin</s> (composite whole) having the properties of origination and destruction is established.

children.text:
% p.969
śabdakarmabuddhyādīnāṃ cāvyāptiḥ/ pañcabhūtanityatvāt tallakṣaṇāvarodhāc cety anena śabdakarmabuddhisukhaduḥkhecchādveṣaprayatnāś ca na vyāptāḥ tasmād anekāntaḥ/
svapnaviṣayābhimānavan mithyopalabdhir iti cet bhūtopalabdhau tulyam/ yathā svapne viṣayābhimāna evam utpattikāraṇābhimāna iti/ evaṃ caitad bhūtopalabdhau tulyaṃ pṛthivyādyupalabdhir api svapnaviṣayābhimānavat prasajyate/
children.translated_text: [Page 969] And [there is] non-pervasion with respect to <s>śabda</s> (sound), <s>karma</s> (action), <s>buddhi</s> (cognition), and so forth. By [the arguments] 'because the five elements are permanent' and 'because it falls under the definition of those,' <s>śabda</s> (sound), <s>karma</s> (action), <s>buddhi</s> (cognition), <s>sukha</s> (pleasure), <s>duḥkha</s> (pain), <s>icchā</s> (desire), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>prayatna</s> (effort) are not covered; therefore [the thesis] is inconclusive. [The opponent says:] 'Like the false apprehension of dream-objects, the observation [of origination] is erroneous' — if so, the same applies to the observation of elements. Just as in a dream there is merely the false apprehension of objects, so too there would be merely the false apprehension of a cause of origination. And this equally applies to the observation of elements — the observation of earth and so forth would also be like the false apprehension of dream-objects.

children.text:
% p.970
pṛthivyādyabhāve sarvavyavahāravilopa iti cet tad itaratra samānam --- utpattivināśakāraṇopalabdhiviṣayasyāpy abhāve sarvavyavahāravilopa iti, so 'yaṃ nityānām atīndriyatvād aviṣayatvāc cotpattivināśayoḥ svapnaviṣayābhimānavad ity ahetur iti//32//
children.translated_text: [Page 970] [The opponent says:] 'If earth and so forth did not exist, all practical activity would cease' — if so, the same applies to the other side: if the objects of observation of causes of origination and destruction also did not exist, all practical activity would cease. Thus this [argument] — that because permanent entities are beyond the sense-organs and because origination and destruction are not objects [of perception], [their observation] is like the false apprehension of dream-objects — is a fallacious reason. [32]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.33]

children.text: avasthitasyopādānasya dharmamātraṃ nivartate dharmamātram upajāyate sa khalūtpattivināśayor viṣayaḥ/
children.translated_text: [The Sarvāstitvavādin says:] Of a persisting substratum, only a property ceases and only a property arises — that indeed is the object of origination and destruction.

children.text:
% -śayor viṣayaḥ/] p.971
yac copajāyate tat prāg apy upajananād asti, yac ca nivartate tan nivṛttam apy astīti, evaṃ ca sarvasya nityatvam iti?
children.translated_text: [Page 971] And that which arises exists even before its arising, and that which ceases continues to exist even after its cessation — and thus everything is permanent. [Is this so?]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.33: Not so, because [then] determination would be impossible.

children.text: ayam upajanaḥ iyaṃ nivṛttir iti vyavasthā nopapadyate, upajātanivṛttayor vidyamānatvāt/ ayaṃ dharma upajāto 'yaṃ nivṛtta iti sadbhāvāviśeṣād avyavasthā, idānīm upajananivṛttī nedānīm iti kālavyavasthā nopapadyate sarvadā vidyamānatvāt asya dharmasyopajananivṛttī nāsyeti vyavasthānupapattiḥ,
children.translated_text: The determination 'this is origination' and 'this is cessation' would be impossible, since both the originated and the ceased would [always] be existent. The determination 'this property has originated, that has ceased' — owing to there being no distinction in their existence, there would be indeterminacy. [The determination] 'origination and cessation [occur] now, not at another time' — such temporal determination would be impossible, since [the property] exists at all times. [The determination] 'origination and cessation belong to this property, not to that one' — such determination would be impossible,

children.text:
% -jananivṛttī nāsyeti vyavasthānupapattiḥ,] p.972
ubhyor aviśeṣāt/ anāgato 'tīta iti ca kālavyavasthānupapattiḥ, vartamānasya sadbhāvalakṣaṇatvāt/ avidyamānasyātmalābha upajano vidyamānasyātmahānaṃ nivṛttir ity etasmin sati naite doṣāḥ/ tasmād yad uktaṃ prāg apy upajanād asti nivṛttaṃ cāsti tad ayuktam iti//33//
children.translated_text: [Page 972] since there is no distinction between the two. And the temporal determination 'future' and 'past' would be impossible, since the present is defined by existence. [But] if origination is the coming into being of what was non-existent, and cessation is the loss of being of what was existent, then these defects do not arise. Therefore, the statement that [something] exists even before origination and exists [even after] cessation is untenable. [33]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.34]
Here is another extreme view:
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.34: Everything is separate, because the defining characteristics of entities are distinct.

children.text: sarvaṃ nānā na kaścid eko bhāvo vidyate/ kasmāt? bhāvalakṣaṇapṛthaktvāt --- bhāvasya lakṣaṇam abhidhānam, yena lakṣyate bhāvaḥ sa samākhyāśabdaḥ, tasya pṛthagviṣayatvāt/
children.translated_text: Everything is manifold; no single entity exists. Why? Because the defining characteristics of entities are distinct — the defining characteristic of an entity is its designation, that by which the entity is characterized, namely the conventional word; because that [word] has distinct referents.

children.text:
% p.973
sarvo bhāvasamākhyāśabdaḥ samūhavācī, kumbha iti saṃjñāśabdo gandharasarūpasparśasamūhe budhnapārśvagrīvādisamūhe ca varttate, nidarśanamātraṃ cedam iti//34//
children.translated_text: [Page 973] Every conventional word for an entity denotes a collection. The designating word '<s>kumbha</s>' (pot) applies to a collection of smell, taste, color, and touch, and to a collection of base, sides, neck, and so forth — and this is merely an illustration. [34]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.35]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.35: Not so, because a single entity is produced from multiple defining characteristics.

children.text: anekavidhalakṣaṇair iti madhyamapadalopī samāsaḥ/ gandhādibhiś ca guṇair budhnādibhiś cāvayavaiḥ sambaddha eko bhāvo niṣpadyate, guṇavyatiriktaṃ ca dravyam avayavātiriktaś cāvayavīti/ vibhaktanyāyaṃ caitad ubhayam iti//35//
children.translated_text: 'Multiple defining characteristics' — this is a compound with elision of the middle term [meaning 'of multiple kinds of defining characteristics']. From <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) such as smell and so forth, and from parts such as the base and so forth, a single entity is produced in conjunction [with them]. And <s>dravya</s> (substance) is distinct from <s>guṇa</s> (quality), and the <s>avayavin</s> (composite whole) is distinct from the parts. And both of these have been established by separate reasoning. [35]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.36]
[Page 974] Moreover —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.36: There is no refutation, precisely because of the established determinate use of defining characteristics.

children.text:
na kaścid eko bhāva ity ayuktaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ kasmāt? lakṣaṇavyavasthānād eva/ yad iha lakṣaṇaṃ bhāvasya saṃjñāśabdabhūtaṃ tad ekasmin vyavasthitam, yaṃ kumbham adrākṣaṃ taṃ spṛśāmi yam evāsprākṣaṃ taṃ paśyāmīti nāṇusamūho gṛhyate iti/ aṇusamūhe cāgṛhyamāṇe yad gṛhyate tad ekam eveti/
athāpy etad anūktam nāsty eko bhāvo yasmāt samudāyaḥ, ekānupapatter nāsty eva samūhaḥ --- nāsty eko bhāvo yasmāt samūhe bhāvaśabdaprayogaḥ;ekasya cānupapatteḥ
children.translated_text: The denial that 'no single entity exists' is untenable. Why? Precisely because of the established determinate use of defining characteristics. The defining characteristic of an entity, being the conventional word, is established as referring to a single thing: 'the pot I saw is the one I touch; the very one I touched is the one I see' — it is not a collection of atoms that is grasped. And when no collection of atoms is grasped, what is grasped is a single entity. Furthermore, even this [argument] remains unsaid: [you say] 'there is no single entity because there is a collection'; [but] since the one is impossible, there is no collection either — [you say] 'there is no single entity because the word 'entity' is used for the collection'; and since the one is impossible,

children.text:
% p.975
samūho nopapadyate ekasamuccayo hi samūha iti/ vyāhatatvād anupapannaṃ --- nāsty eko bhāva iti yasya pratiṣedhaḥ pratijñāyate, samūhe bhāvaśabdaprayogād iti hetuṃ bruvatā sa evābhyanujñāyate, ekasamuccayo hi samūha iti/ samūhe bhāvaśabdaprayogād iti ca samūham āśritya pratyekaṃ samūhipratiṣedho nāsty eko bhāva iti/ so 'yam ubhayato vyāghātād yatkiñcanavāda iti//36//
children.translated_text: [Page 975] the collection is impossible, for a collection is the aggregation of ones. Because it is self-contradictory, [the position] is untenable — the thesis that is asserted is 'there is no single entity,' but by stating the reason 'because the word 'entity' is used for the collection,' that very [single entity] is implicitly acknowledged, for a collection is the aggregation of ones. And [the thesis] 'there is no single entity because the word 'entity' is used for the collection' denies each individual member while depending on the collection. Thus this is a mere arbitrary statement due to self-contradiction from both sides. [36]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.37]
[Page 977] Here is yet another extreme view:
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.37: Everything is non-existence, because mutual non-existence among entities is established.

children.text: yāvad bhāvajātaṃ tat sarvam abhāvaḥ/ kasmāt? bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddheḥ/ ``asan gaur aśvātmanā'' anaśvo gauḥ ``asann aśvo gavātmanā agaur aśvaḥ'' ity asatpratyayasya pratiṣedhasya ca bhāvaśabdena sāmānādhikaraṇyāt sarvam abhāva iti//37//
children.translated_text: Whatever class of entities there is, all of it is non-existence. Why? Because mutual non-existence among entities is established. 'A cow is non-existent as a horse' — a cow is a non-horse; 'a horse is non-existent as a cow' — a horse is a non-cow. Because the cognition of non-existence and the denial are co-referential with the word 'entity,' everything is non-existence. [37]
[Commentary on NyS 4.1.38]

children.text:
% p.978
pratijñāvākye padayoḥ pratijñāhetvoś ca vyāghātād ayuktam/ anekasyāśeṣatā sarvaśabdasyārtho, bhāvapratiṣedhaś cābhāvaśabdasyārthaḥ/ pūrvaṃ sopākhyam uttaraṃ nirupākhyaṃ tatra
children.translated_text: [Page 978] [This is] untenable because of the contradiction in the words of the thesis and between the thesis and the reason. The meaning of the word 'all' is the totality of the manifold; and the meaning of the word 'non-existence' is the negation of an entity. The former [term] has positive content, the latter has no positive content; how then

children.text:
% p.979
samupākhyāyamānaṃ kathaṃ nirupākhyam abhāvaḥ syād iti? na jātv abhāvo nirupākhyo 'nekatayāśeṣatayā śakyaḥ pratijñātum iti/ sarvam etad abhāva iti cet --- yad idaṃ sarvam iti manyase tadabhāva iti? evaṃ cet anivṛtto vyāghātaḥ, anekam aśeṣaṃ ceti nābhāve pratyayena śakyaṃ bhavitum/ asti cāyaṃ pratyayaḥ sarvam iti, tasmān nābhāva iti/
pratijñāhetvoś ca vyāghātaḥ --- sarvam abhāva iti bhāvapratiṣedhaḥ pratijñā, bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddher iti hetuḥ/ bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvam anujñāyāśritya ca itaretarābhāvasiddhyā sarvam abhāva ity ucyate/ yadi sarvam abhāvo bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddher iti nopapadyate/ atha bhāveṣv itaretarābhāvasiddhiḥ, sarvam abhāva iti nopapadyate/
children.translated_text: [Page 979] can that which is being positively designated be non-existence, which has no positive content? Non-existence, having no positive content, can never be asserted as manifold and exhaustive. [If the opponent says:] 'all this is non-existence' — do you mean 'what you consider all this to be, that is non-existence'? If so, the contradiction is not resolved, for what is manifold and exhaustive cannot be identified with non-existence. And this cognition 'all' does exist; therefore it is not non-existence. And there is contradiction between the thesis and the reason: 'everything is non-existence' — this negation of entities is the thesis; 'because mutual non-existence among entities is established' is the reason. By acknowledging mutual non-existence among entities and relying on [that very] establishment of mutual non-existence, it is said that 'everything is non-existence.' If everything is non-existence because mutual non-existence among entities is established, then [the reason itself] is untenable. And if the establishment of mutual non-existence among entities [holds], then 'everything is non-existence' is untenable.
[Page 980] And [here is] the connection with the <s>sūtra</s>:
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.38: Not so, because of the self-established nature of entities.

children.text: na sarvam abhāvaḥ/ kasmāt? svena bhāvena sadbhāvād bhāvānām/ svena dharmeṇa bhāvā bhavantīti pratijñāyate/ kaś ca svo dharmo bhāvānām? dravyaguṇakarmaṇāṃ sadādisāmānyam, dravyāṇāṃ kriyāvad ityevamādiviśeṣaḥ, sparśaparyantāḥ pṛthivyā iti ca; pratyekaṃ cānanto bhedaḥ/ sāmānyaviśeṣasamavāyānāṃ ca viśiṣṭā dharmā gṛhyante/
children.translated_text: Not everything is non-existence. Why? Because entities exist by their own nature, by their own being. It is maintained that entities exist by their own properties. And what are the own properties of entities? For <s>dravya</s> (substance), <s>guṇa</s> (quality), and <s>karma</s> (action), [there are] <s>sāmānya</s> (universals) such as existence and so forth; for substances, [there are] <s>viśeṣas</s> (particulars) such as 'possessing activity' and so forth; and [there are properties] such as 'ending with touch' for earth; and for each [entity] the distinctions are endless. And the distinctive properties of <s>sāmānya</s> (universals), <s>viśeṣa</s> (particulars), and <s>samavāya</s> (inherence) are [also] grasped.

children.text:
% p.981
so 'yam abhāvasya nirupākhyatvāt sampratyāyako 'rthabhedo na syāt? asti tv ayam, tasmān na sarvam abhāva iti/
atha vā na svabhāvasiddher bhāvānām iti svarūpasiddher iti/ gaur iti prayujyamāne śabde jātiviśiṣṭaṃ dravyaṃ gṛhyate, nābhāvamātram/ yadi ca sarvam abhāvaḥ gaur ity abhāvaḥ pratīyeta, gośabdena cābhāva ucyeta/ yasmāt tu gośabdaprayoge dravyaviśeṣaḥ pratīyate nābhāvas tasmād ayuktam iti/
atha vā na svabhāvasiddher iti/ asan gaur aśvātmaneti gavātmanā kasmān nocyate? avacanād gavātmanā gaur astīti svabhāvasiddhiḥ, anaśvo 'śva iti vā gaur agaur iti vā kasmān nocyate? avacanāt svena rūpeṇa vidyamānatā dravyasyeti vijñāyate/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.981]
Could it be that since non-existence is without designation, there is no meaningful distinction that could produce understanding? But there is such [a distinction]; therefore, not everything is non-existence.
Alternatively, 'not because of the self-nature establishment of existents' means 'not because of the establishment through their own form.' When the word 'cow' is employed, a substance qualified by a universal is apprehended, not mere non-existence. And if everything were non-existence, non-existence would be cognized [when one hears] 'cow,' and non-existence would be denoted by the word 'cow.' But since a particular substance, not non-existence, is cognized when the word 'cow' is employed, [the thesis that everything is non-existence] is untenable.
Alternatively, 'not because of self-nature establishment': the cow is non-existent as having the nature of a horse — why is it not said [to be non-existent] as having the nature of a cow? Because it is not so said, the self-nature establishment [obtains]: the cow exists with its own nature. Why is it not said 'the non-horse is a horse' or 'the cow is a non-cow'? Because it is not so said, it is understood that a substance exists through its own form.

children.text:
% p.982
avyatirekapratiṣedhe ca bhāvena asatpratyayasāmānādhikaraṇyam bhāve saṃyogādisambandho vyatirekaḥ/ atra avyatirekaḥ abhedākhyasambandhaḥ tatpratiṣedhe sadā ca asatpratyayasāmānādhikaraṇyam, yathā na santi kuṇḍe badarāṇīti/ asan gaur aśvātmanā anaśvo gaur iti ca gavāśvayor avyatirekaḥ pratiṣidhyate gavāśvayor ekatvaṃ nāstīti/ tasmin pratiṣidhyamāne bhāvena gavā sāmānādhikaraṇyam asatpratyayasya asan gaur aśvātmaneti, yathā na santi kuṇḍe badarāṇīti kuṇḍe badarasaṃyoge pratiṣidhyamāne sadbhir asatpratyayasya sāmānādhikaraṇyam iti//38//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.982]
And when the negation of non-difference [is considered]: there is co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence with an existent; in the existent, there is the relation of conjunction and the like, [which constitutes] difference. Here, non-difference is the relation called identity; when that is negated, there is always co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence [with an existent] — as in 'there are no jujubes in the pot.' 'The cow is non-existent as having the nature of a horse; the cow is a non-horse' — thus the non-difference of cow and horse is negated, [meaning] the identity of cow and horse does not exist. When that is negated, there is co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence with the existent cow — 'the cow is non-existent as having the nature of a horse' — just as when the conjunction of jujubes in the pot is negated in 'there are no jujubes in the pot,' there is co-referentiality of the cognition of non-existence with the existing [pot]. //38//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.39]
[Note: p.983]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.39: There is no self-nature establishment, because [things] are relative.

children.text: apekṣākṛtam āpekṣikam/ hrasvāpekṣākṛtaṃ dīrghaṃ dīrghāpekṣākṛtaṃ hrasvam, na svenātmanāvasthitaṃ kiñcit/ kasmāt? apekṣāsāmarthyāt/ tasmān na svabhāvasiddhir bhāvānām iti//39//
children.translated_text: That which is produced by dependence is relative. Long is produced by dependence on the short, and short is produced by dependence on the long — nothing exists in its own nature. Why? Because of the power of dependence [to determine things]. Therefore, there is no self-nature establishment of existents. //39//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.40]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.40: This is untenable because of self-contradiction.

children.text: yadi hrasvāpekṣākṛtaṃ dīrghaṃ hrasvam anāpekṣikam/ kim idānīm apekṣya hrasvam iti gṛhyate? atha dīrghāpekṣākṛtaṃ hrasvam, dīrgham anāpekṣikam? evam itaretarāśrayayor ekābhāve anyatarābhāvād ubhayābhāva iti apekṣāvyavasthānupapannā/
children.translated_text: If long is produced by dependence on the short, the short is non-relative. With respect to what, then, is it apprehended as short? But if short is produced by dependence on the long, the long is non-relative? Thus, since when one of the two mutually dependent [terms] is absent, the other is absent too, both are absent — hence the establishment of [the relation of] dependence is untenable.

children.text:
% retarāśrayayor ekābhāve anyatarābhāvād ubhayābhāva iti apekṣāvyavasthānupapannā/] p.984
svabhāvasiddhāv asatyāṃ samayoḥ parimaṇḍalayor vā dravyayor āpekṣike dīrghatvahrasvatve kasmān na bhavataḥ? apekṣāyām anapekṣāyāṃ ca dravyayor abhedaḥ/ yāvatī dravye apekṣamāṇe tāvatī evānapekṣamāṇe nānyataratra bhedaḥ/ āpekṣikatve tu saty anyataratra viśeṣopajanaḥ syād iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.984 — retarāśrayayor ekābhāve anyatarābhāvād ubhayābhāva iti apekṣāvyavasthānupapannā/]
And if there is no self-nature establishment, why do longness and shortness not [arise] in two equal or spherical substances through relativity? Whether dependent or non-dependent, the two substances do not differ — to whatever extent the substance [is what it is] when being depended upon, to that same extent it is when not being depended upon; there is no difference in either case. But if there were relativity, a distinguishing feature would arise in one of them.

children.text:
% p.985
kim apekṣāsāmarthyam iti cet? dvayor grahaṇe 'tiśayagrahaṇopapattiḥ/ dve dravye paśyann ekatra vidyamānam atiśayaṃ gṛhṇāti tad dīrgham iti vyavasyati, yac ca hīnaṃ gṛhṇāti tad dhrasvam iti vyavasyatīti/ etac cāpekṣāsāmarthyam iti//40//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.985]
What is the power of dependence? When two things are grasped, the apprehension of superiority is possible. Perceiving two substances, one grasps the superiority present in one and determines 'that is long,' and grasps the inferiority [in the other] and determines 'that is short.' And this is the power of dependence. //40//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.41]

children.text:
% p.986
atheme saṅkhyaikāntavādāḥ ---
sarvam ekaṃ sadaviśeṣāt/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.986]
Now, these numerical absolutist doctrines —
'Everything is one, because of the absence of distinction in being (<s>sat</s>).'

children.text:
% p.987
sarvaṃ dvedhā nityānityabhedāt/ sarvaṃ tredhā jñātā jñānaṃ jñeyam iti/ sarvaṃ caturddhā pramātā pramāṇaṃ prameyaṃ pramitir iti/ evaṃ yathāsambhavam anye 'pīti/ tatra parīkṣā ---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.987]
'Everything is twofold, because of the distinction into permanent and impermanent.' 'Everything is threefold: knower, knowledge, and the knowable.' 'Everything is fourfold: the measurer, the means of measurement, the measurable, and the act of measurement.' And similarly others as applicable. The examination of these —
[Note: p.988]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.41: Numerical absolutism is not established, because of the impossibility and possibility of the reason.

children.text: yadi sādhyasādhanayor nānātvam, ekānto na siddhyati vyatirekāt/ atha
children.translated_text: If the thing to be proved and the means of proof are different, the absolutism is not established because of the [presence of] difference. But if

children.text:
% p.989
sādhyasādhanayor abhedaḥ? evam apy ekānto na sidhyati sādhanābhāvāt, na hi hetum antareṇa kasyacit siddhir iti//41//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.989]
the thing to be proved and the means of proof are identical? Even so, the absolutism is not established because of the absence of a means of proof — for nothing can be established without a reason. //41//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.42]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.42: Not so, because the reason has the status of a part.

children.text: na saṅkhyaikāntānām asiddhiḥ kasmāt? kāraṇasyāvayavabhāvāt/ avayavaḥ kaścit sādhanabhūta ity avyatirekaḥ/ evaṃ dvaitādīnām apīti//42//
children.translated_text: There is no failure to establish numerical absolutism. Why? Because the reason has the status of a part of the [whole to be] proved. Some part constitutes the means of proof — hence there is non-difference. The same applies to the dualist and other positions. //42//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.43]
[Note: p.990]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.43: This is not a valid reason, because [the whole] has no parts.

children.text: kāraṇasyāvayavabhāvād ity ahetuḥ/ kasmāt? sarvam ekam ity anapavargeṇa pratijñāya kasyacid ekatvam ucyate, tatra vyapavṛkto 'vayavaḥ sādhanabhūto nopapadyate/ evaṃ dvaitādiṣv apīti/
children.translated_text: 'Because the reason has the status of a part' is not a valid reason. Why? Having asserted 'everything is one' without exception, the oneness of something [in particular] is stated — but then a part, separated out [from the whole], that would serve as a means of proof is untenable. The same applies to the dualist and other positions.

children.text:
% p.991
te khalv ime saṅkhyaikāntā yadi viśeṣakāritasyārthabhedavistārasya pratyākhyānena varttante, pratyakṣānumānāgamavirodhān mithyāvādā bhavanti/ athābhyanujñānena varttante? samānadharmakārito 'rthasaṃgraho viśeṣakāritaś cārthabheda iti evam ekāntatvaṃ jahatīti/ te khalv ete tattvajñānapravivekārtham ekāntāḥ parīkṣitā iti//43//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.991]
Indeed, these numerical absolutists — if they proceed by rejecting the manifold differentiation of objects produced by specific features, they become proponents of falsehood, since they contradict perception, inference, and scripture. But if they proceed by accepting [differentiation]? Then the grouping of objects produced by common properties and the differentiation of objects produced by specific features — thus they abandon absolutism. These numerical absolutisms have been examined for the purpose of distinguishing true knowledge. //43//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.44]

[Note: p.992]
After post-mortem existence, [comes] the fruit [of action]. Regarding that —

children.text: NyS_4,1.44: sadyaḥ kālāntare ca phalaniṣpatteḥ saṃśayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.44: There is doubt regarding the fruit, since it may come about immediately or at a later time.

children.text: pacati dogdhīti sadyaḥ phalamodanapayasī, karṣati vapatīti kālāntare phalaṃ
children.translated_text: 'One cooks, one milks' — the fruit [comes] immediately: porridge and milk. 'One ploughs, one sows' — the fruit [comes] at a later time:

children.text:
% p.993
śasyādhigama iti/ asti ceyaṃ kriyā agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāma iti etasyāḥ
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.993]
the acquisition of grain. And there is this action: 'one who desires heaven should offer the <s>agnihotra</s>' —

children.text:
% p.994
phale saṃśayaḥ/ na sadyaḥ kālāntaropabhogyatvāt / svargaḥ phalaṃ śrūyate, tac ca bhinne 'smin dehabhedād utpadyate iti/ na sadyaḥ grāmādikāmānāmü@ārambhaphalam iti//44//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.994]
regarding its fruit there is doubt. It is not immediate, since it is to be enjoyed at a later time. Heaven is declared as the fruit, and that arises after the breakup of this body, due to the difference [between this life and the next]. It is not like the immediate fruit of undertakings motivated by desire for a village and the like. //44//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.45]
[Note: p.995]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.45: There is no fruition at a later time, because of the destruction of the cause.

children.text: dhvastāyāṃ pravṛttau pravṛtteḥ phalaṃ na kāraṇam antareṇotpattum arhati, na khalu vai vinaṣṭāt kāraṇāt kiñcid utpadyate iti//45//
children.translated_text: When the activity has been destroyed, the fruit of that activity cannot arise without a cause. For indeed, nothing arises from a destroyed cause. //45//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.46]

children.text: NyS_4,1.46: prāṅ niṣpatter vṛkṣaphalavat tat syāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.46: Prior to fruition, it would be like the fruit of a tree.

children.text: yathā phalārthinā vṛkṣamūle sekādi parikarma kriyate, tasmiṃś ca pradhvaste pṛthivīdhātur abdhātunā saṃgṛhīta āntareṇa tejasā pacyamāno rasadravyaṃ nirvartayati, sa dravyabhūto raso vṛkṣānugataḥ pākaviśiṣṭo vyūhaviśeṣeṇa sanniviśamānaḥ parṇādi phalaṃ nirvartayati, evaṃ pariṣekādi karma cārthavat/ na ca vinaṣṭāt phalaniṣpattiḥ/ tathā pravṛttyā saṃskāro dharmādharmalakṣaṇo janyate, sa jāto nimittāntarānugṛhītaḥ kālāntare phalaṃ niṣpādayatīti/ uktañ caitat ``pūrvakṛtaphalānubandhāt tadutpattir'' iti//46//
children.translated_text: Just as one desiring fruit performs watering and other acts of cultivation at the root of a tree, and when that [watering] has ceased, the element of earth, taken up by the element of water, being matured by the internal fire, produces a flavorful substance, and that substance in the form of sap, pervading the tree, distinguished by [the process of] maturation, settling in a particular configuration, produces leaves and the like and [then] fruit — thus the watering and other acts of cultivation are purposeful. And the fruit does not arise from something that has been destroyed. Similarly, a <s>saṃskāra</s> (disposition) characterized by <s>dharma</s> (merit) and <s>adharma</s> (demerit) is generated by activity; once generated, being supported by another cause, it produces fruit at a later time. And this has been stated: 'because of the connection with the fruit of what was previously done, its origination [occurs].' //46//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.47]

children.text:
% p.996
tad idaṃ prāṅ niṣpatter niṣpadyamānam---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.996]
Now this, prior to fruition, which is in the process of coming to fruition —

children.text: NyS_4,1.47: nāsan na san na sadasat sadasator vaidharmyāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.47: [The effect prior to its production] is neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, because of the mutual incompatibility of existence and non-existence.

children.text: prāṅ niṣpatter niṣpattidharmakaṃ nāsat, upādānaniyamāt/ kasyacid utpattaye kiñcid upādeyaṃ na sarvaṃ sarvasyety asadbhāve niyamo nopapadyate iti/ na sat, prāṅ utpatter vidyamānasyotpattir anupapanneti/ na, sadasat sadasator vaidharmyāt
children.translated_text: Prior to its production, that which has the property of production is not non-existent — because of the restriction regarding the material cause. For the production of something, something specific must be adopted [as its cause], not everything for everything — and this restriction is untenable if [things prior to production] were [simply] non-existent. It is not existent — because the production of what already exists prior to production is untenable. It is not both existent and non-existent — because of the mutual incompatibility of existence and non-existence.

children.text:
% p.997
sad ity arthābhyanujñā, asad iti arthapratiṣedhaḥ, etayor vyāghāto vaidharmyaṃ vyāghātād avyatirekānupapattir iti//47//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.997]
'Existent' means acknowledgment of the object; 'non-existent' means denial of the object. The contradiction between these two constitutes their incompatibility; from the incompatibility, the impossibility of non-difference [between them] follows. //47//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.48]

children.text: prāg utpatter utpattidharmakam asad ity addhā/ kasmāat?
children.translated_text: Prior to production, that which has the property of production is indeed non-existent. Why?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.48: Because origination and destruction are observed.

children.text:
% p.999
yat punaruktaṃ prāg utpatteḥ kāryaṃ nāsad upādānaniyamād iti---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.999]
As for the statement that prior to production the effect is not non-existent because of the restriction regarding the material cause —
[Section: NySBh_4,1.49]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.49: But that [restriction of the cause to specific effects] when [the effect is] non-existent is established through cognition.

children.text: idam asyotpattaye samarthaṃ na sarvam iti prāg utpatter niyatakāraṇaṃ kāryaṃ buddhyā
children.translated_text: 'This is capable of producing this, not everything [capable of producing] everything' — the effect, prior to production, having a determinate cause, is established through cognition

children.text:
% p.1000
siddham utpattiniyamadarśanāt/ tasmād upādānaniyamasyopapattiḥ sati tu kārye prāg utpatter utpattir eva nāstīti//49//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1000]
from the observation of the restriction of production. Therefore, the restriction regarding the material cause is tenable; but when the effect already exists [prior to production], production itself simply does not exist. //49//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.50]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.50: Because of the difference of locus, [the analogy] 'like the production of fruit in a tree' is not a valid reason.

children.text: mūlasekādi parikarma phalaṃ cobhayaṃ vṛkṣāśrayam, karma ceha śarīre, phalaṃ cāmutra ity āśrayavyatirekād ahetur iti//50//
children.translated_text: The watering and other acts of cultivation at the root, and the fruit — both have the tree as their locus. But here, the action [is performed] in this body, while the fruit [arises] in another [body] — because of the difference of locus, this is not a valid reason. //50//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.51]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.51: There is no refutation, because pleasure has the <s>ātman</s> (self) as its locus.

children.text: prītir ātmapratyakṣatvād ātmāśrayā, tadāśrayam eva karma dharmasaṃjñitam, dharmasyātmaguṇatvāt tasmād āśrayavyatirekānupapattir iti//51//
children.translated_text: Pleasure has the <s>ātman</s> as its locus, since it is directly experienced by the <s>ātman</s>. The action designated as <s>dharma</s> (merit) likewise has that [<s>ātman</s>] as its locus, since <s>dharma</s> is a quality of the <s>ātman</s>. Therefore, the [claim of] difference of locus is untenable. //51//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.52]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.52: Not so, because sons, livestock, wives, ornaments, gold, food, and the like are indicated as the fruit.

children.text: putrādi phalaṃ nirdiśyate na prītiḥ, ``grāmakāmo yajeta'' ``putrakāmo yajete''ti tatra yad uktaṃ prītiḥ phalam ity etad ayuktam iti//52//
children.translated_text: Sons and the like are indicated as the fruit, not pleasure — 'let one who desires a village sacrifice,' 'let one who desires a son sacrifice.' Therefore, the statement that pleasure is the fruit is untenable. //52//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.53]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.53: Because the fruit arises from the connection with those [sons, etc.], there is a figurative attribution of 'fruit' to them.

children.text: putrādisambandhāt phalaṃ prītilakṣaṇam utpadyate iti putrādiṣu phalavadupacāraḥ, yathānne prāṇaśabdo ``annaṃ vai prāṇāḥ''iti//53//
children.translated_text: The fruit, characterized by pleasure, arises from the connection with sons and the rest; hence there is a figurative attribution of 'fruit' to sons and the rest — just as the word '<s>prāṇa</s>' (life-breath) is applied to food: 'food indeed is the life-breaths.' //53//
[Section: NySBh_4,1.54]

children.text:
% p.1006
phalānantaraṃ duḥkham uddiṣṭam, uktaṃ ca ``bādhanālakṣaṇaṃ duḥkham''iti/ tat kim idaṃ pratyātmavedanīyasya sarvajantupratyakṣasya sukhasya pratyākhyānam, āhosvid anyaḥ kalpa iti?
anya ity āha/ katham? na vai sarvalokasākṣikaṃ sukhaṃ śakyaṃ pratyākhyātum/ ayaṃ tu janmamaraṇaprabandhānubhavanimittād duḥkhān nirviṇṇasya duḥkhaṃ jihāsato duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanopadeśo duḥkhahānārtha iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1006]
After the fruit, suffering has been mentioned, and it has been said: 'suffering is characterized by affliction.' Is this a rejection of pleasure, which is individually experienced by each self and directly perceived by all beings, or is it a different interpretation?
It is a different [interpretation], he says. How? Indeed, the pleasure that is witnessed by the whole world cannot be rejected. But this is a teaching of the cultivation of the perception of suffering, for the purpose of abandoning suffering, for one who is disgusted with suffering caused by experiencing the continuous cycle of birth and death, and who desires to abandon suffering.

children.text:
% bhāvanopadeśo duḥkhahānārtha iti/] p.1007
kayā yuktyā? sarve khalu sattvanikāyāḥ sarvāṇy utpattisthānāni sarvaḥ punarbhavo bādhanānuṣakto duḥkhasāhacaryād bādhanālakṣaṇaṃ duḥkham ity uktam ṛṣibhiḥ, duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanam upadiśyate atra ca hetur upādīyate---
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1007 — bhāvanopadeśo duḥkhahānārtha iti/]
By what reasoning? Indeed, all classes of living beings, all places of birth, all rebirths are attended by affliction; because of the association with affliction, suffering is characterized by affliction — thus the <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages) have said. The cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught, and here a reason is adduced —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.54: Because of the connection with manifold affliction, birth itself is suffering.

children.text: janma jāyate iti śarīrendriyabuddhayaḥ śarīrādīnāṃ ca saṃsthānaviśiṣṭānāṃ prādurbhāva utpattiḥ/ vividhā ca bādhanā, hīnā madhyamā utkṛṣṭā ceti/ utkṛṣṭā nārakiṇām, tiraścāṃ tu madhyamā, manuṣyāṇāṃ tu hīnā, devānāṃ hīnatarā vītarāgāṇāṃ ca/ evaṃ sarvam utpattisthānaṃ vividhabādhanānuṣaktaṃ paśyataḥ sukhe tatsādhaneṣu ca śarīrendriyabuddhiṣu duḥkhasaṃjñā vyavatiṣṭhate/
children.translated_text: Birth means 'being born' — (namely) body, sense-organs, and intellects; the manifestation of body and the rest with their specific configurations is origination. And the affliction is manifold: low, middling, and extreme. Extreme for beings in hell; middling for animals; low for humans; and even lower for gods and for those free from passion. Thus, for one who sees that every place of birth is attended by manifold affliction, the perception of suffering (<s>duḥkhasaṃjñā</s>) becomes established with regard to pleasure and its means — body, sense-organs, and intellects.

children.text:
% buddhiṣu duḥkhasaṃjñā vyavatiṣṭhate/] p.1008
duḥkhasaṃjñāvyavasthānāt sarvalokeṣv anabhiratisaṃjñā bhavati/ anabhiratisaṃjñām upāsīnasya sarvalokaviṣayā tṛṣṇā vicchidyate, tṛṣṇāprahāṇāt sarvaduḥkhād vimucyate iti/ yathā viṣayogāt payo viṣam iti budhyamāno nopādatte, anupādadāno maraṇaduḥkhaṃ nāpnoti//54//
children.translated_text:
[Note: buddhiṣu duḥkhasaṃjñā vyavatiṣṭhate/] p.1008
From the establishment of the perception of suffering, the perception of dissatisfaction arises with regard to all worlds. For one who cultivates the perception of dissatisfaction, craving directed toward all worlds is cut off; from the abandonment of craving, one is freed from all suffering. Just as one who understands that milk is poison because of its mixture with poison does not take it, and not taking it, does not incur the suffering of death. // 54 //
[Section: NySBh_4,1.55]

children.text: duḥkhoddeśas tu na sukhasya pratyākhyānam, kasmāt?
children.translated_text: But the designation of suffering is not the rejection of pleasure. Why?
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.55: (This is) not (a rejection of pleasure), because pleasure arises in the intervals.

children.text: na khalv ayaṃ duḥkhoddeśaḥ sukhasya pratyākhyānam/ kasmāt, sukhasyāntarālaniṣpatteḥ/ niṣpadyate khalu bādhanāntarāleṣu sukhaṃ pratyātmavedanīyaṃ śarīriṇām, tad aśakyaṃ pratyākhyātum iti//55//
children.translated_text: This designation of suffering is certainly not a rejection of pleasure. Why? Because pleasure arises in the intervals. For pleasure, to be known through personal experience by embodied beings, does arise in the intervals between afflictions — that cannot be denied. // 55 //
[Section: NySBh_4,1.56]

[Note: p.1009]
Even so —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.56: Because of the non-cessation of affliction, and because of the fault of seeking by one who experiences, there is no refutation.

children.text: sukhasya, duḥkhoddeśeneti prakaraṇāt paryeṣaṇaṃ prārthanā viṣayārjanatṛṣṇā, paryeṣaṇasya doṣo yad ayaṃ vedayamānaḥ prārthayate tac cāsya prārthitaṃ na sampadyate, sampadya vā vipadyate, nyūnaṃ vā sampadyate, bahupratyanīkaṃ vā sampadyate iti etasmāt paryeṣaṇadoṣān nānāvidho mānasaḥ santāpo bhavati evaṃ vedayataḥ paryeṣaṇadoṣād bādhanāyā anivṛttiḥ/ bādhanānivṛtter duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanam upadiśyate / anena kāraṇena duḥkhaṃ janma na tu sukhasyābhāvād iti/
children.translated_text: Of pleasure — since the context is 'the designation of suffering.' Seeking (<s>paryeṣaṇa</s>) is craving, the desire for acquiring objects. The fault of seeking is that this experiencing person desires, and what he desires does not materialize, or having materialized it is lost, or it materializes in a diminished form, or it materializes accompanied by many adversities — from this fault of seeking, manifold mental torment arises. Thus, for one who experiences, because of the fault of seeking, there is non-cessation of affliction. Because of the non-cessation of affliction, the cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught. For this reason, birth is suffering — but not because of the absence of pleasure.

children.text:
% p.1010
athāpy etad anūktam---
``kāmaṃ kāmayamānasya yadā kāmaḥ samṛdhyati/
athainam aparaḥ kāmaḥ kṣipram eva prabādhate//''
``api ced udanemi samantād bhūmim imāṃ labhate sagavāśvām/ na sa tena dhanena dhanaiṣī tṛpyati kin nu sukhaṃ dhanakāme//'' iti//56//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1010]
And furthermore, this has been said:
'When the desire of one who desires is fulfilled, another desire quickly afflicts him.'
'Even if he should gain the entire earth with its cattle and horses, the wealth-craving one is not satisfied by that wealth — what then is the pleasure in the desire for wealth?'
// 56 //
[Section: NySBh_4,1.57]
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.57: And because of the false identification of a modification of suffering as pleasure.

children.text: duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanopadeśaḥ kriyate/ ayaṃ khalu sukhasaṃvedane vyavasthitaḥ sukhaṃ paramapuruṣārthaṃ manyate, na sukhād anyan niḥśreyasam asti sukhe prāpte caritārthaḥ kṛtakaraṇīyo bhavati/ mithyāsaṅkalpāt sukhe tatsādhaneṣu ca viṣayeṣu saṃrajyate, saṃraktaḥ sukhāya ghaṭate, ghaṭamānasyāsya janmajarāvyādhiprāyaṇāniṣṭasaṃyogeṣṭaviyogaprārthitānupapattinimittam anekavidhaṃ yāvad duḥkham utpadyate, taṃ duḥkhavikalpaṃ sukham ity abhimanyate/ sukhāṅgabhūtaṃ dukham, na duḥkham anāsādya śakyaṃ sukham avāptum, tādarthyāt sukham evedam iti sukhasaṃjñopahataprajño jāyasva ceti saṃdhāvatīti saṃsāraṃ
children.translated_text: The teaching of cultivating the perception of suffering is given. For this person, established in the experience of pleasure, considers pleasure to be the supreme purpose of a person (<s>puruṣārtha</s>) — 'there is no higher good beyond pleasure; upon attaining pleasure, one's purpose is fulfilled and one's task is done.' From false conception, he becomes attached to pleasure and to the objects that are its means; being attached, he strives for pleasure; and for him who strives, manifold suffering arises, caused by birth, old age, disease, death, unwanted associations, separation from the desired, and the non-fulfillment of what is sought — he falsely identifies that modification of suffering as pleasure. 'Suffering is a part of pleasure; one cannot attain pleasure without encountering suffering; since it serves that purpose, this is pleasure itself' — thus, with his understanding corrupted by the identification with pleasure, he rushes into 'be born!' and does not transcend <s>saṃsāra</s> (transmigration).

children.text:
% p.1012
nātivarttate/ tad asyāḥ sukhasaṃjñāyāḥ pratipakṣo duḥkhasaṃjñābhāvanam upadiśyate, *duḥkhānuṣaṅgād (corr.; duḥkhānusaṅgād, ed.) duḥkhaṃ janmeti, na sukhasyābhāvāt/
yady evaṃ kasmād duḥkhaṃ janmeti nocyate? so 'yam evaṃ vācye yad evam āha duḥkham eva janmeti tena sukhābhāvaṃ jñāpayatīti janma vinigrahārthīyo vai khalv ayam evaśabdaḥ/ katham? na duḥkhaṃ janma svarūpataḥ, kiṃ tu duḥkhopacārāt; evaṃ sukham apīti etad anenaiva nirvarttyate na tu duḥkham eva janmeti//57//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1012]
Therefore, as the antidote to this identification with pleasure, the cultivation of the perception of suffering is taught — birth is suffering because of its association with suffering, not because of the absence of pleasure.
If so, why is it not simply said 'birth is suffering'? The reason he says 'birth is suffering indeed (<s>eva</s>)' in this way of speaking is that by this he indicates the absence of pleasure — so the word <s>eva</s> here has a restrictive meaning. How so? Birth is not suffering by its own nature; rather it is so by metaphorical usage from suffering. Similarly, (birth is not) pleasure either — this too is established by the same (reasoning). But (the meaning is) not 'birth is exclusively suffering.' // 57 //
[Section: NySBh_4,1.58]

[Note: p.1013]
After the designation of suffering, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) (is discussed). It is objected to —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.58: Because of the persisting connection with debts, afflictions, and activity, <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) does not exist.

children.text: ṛṇānubandhān nāsty apavargaḥ---``jāyamāno ha vai brāhmaṇas tribhir ṛṇair ṛṇavān jāyate, brahmacaryeṇa ṛṣibhyo yajñena devebhyaḥ prajayā pitṛbhya'' iti ṛṇāni, teṣām anubandhaḥ svakarmabhiḥ sambandhaḥ, karmasambandhavacanāt ``jarāmaryaṃ vā etat satraṃ yad agnihotraṃ darśapūrṇam āsau ca'' iti ``jarayā ha vā eṣa tasmāt satrād vimucyate mṛtyunā ha vā'' iti *ṛṇānubandhād (corr.; ṛṇānuvandhād, ed.) apavargānuṣṭhānakālo nāstīty apavargābhāvaḥ/
children.translated_text: Because of the persisting connection with debts, <s>apavarga</s> does not exist — 'A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> is born owing three debts: to the <s>ṛṣis</s> (sages) through <s>brahmacarya</s> (celibacy/study), to the gods through sacrifice, and to the ancestors through progeny.' These are the debts; their persisting connection is the bond through one's own <s>karmas</s>. From the statement about the bond to <s>karma</s>: 'the <s>agnihotra</s> (fire-ritual), the <s>darśapūrṇamāsa</s> (new and full moon rites), and the other (rites) constitute a sacrificial session lasting until old age and death' and 'he is freed from that session either by old age or by death' — because of the persisting connection with debts, there is no time for the practice of <s>apavarga</s> — hence <s>apavarga</s> does not exist.

children.text:
% p.1014
kleśānubandhān nāsty apavargaḥ kleśānubaddha evāyaṃ mriyate, kleśānubaddhaś ca jāyate nāsya kleśānubandhavicchedo gṛhyate/
pravṛttyanubandhān nāsty apavargaḥ---janmaprabhṛty ayaṃ yāvat prāyaṇaṃ vāgbuddhiśarīrārambheṇāvimukto gṛhyate, tatra yad uktaṃ ``duḥkhajanmapravṛttidoṣamithyājñānānām uttarottarāpāye tadanantarābhāvād apavarga'' iti, tad anupapannam iti//58//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1014]
Because of the persisting connection with afflictions (<s>kleśa</s>), <s>apavarga</s> does not exist — this person dies bound to afflictions, and is born bound to afflictions; no severance of his bond to afflictions is perceived.
Because of the persisting connection with activity (<s>pravṛtti</s>), <s>apavarga</s> does not exist — from the moment of birth until death, this person is observed to be unrelieved from the engagement of speech, intellect, and body. In that case, the statement 'from the successive removal of suffering, birth, activity, defect, and false knowledge, there is <s>apavarga</s> through the absence of the next in succession' is untenable. // 58 //
[Section: NySBh_4,1.59]

children.text: atrābhidhīyate/ yat tāvad ṛṇānubandhād iti ṛṇair iva ṛṇair iti---
children.translated_text: Here the reply is given. Regarding the claim 'because of the persisting connection with debts' — (these are) debts only figuratively, 'like debts' —
<s>NyS</s> 4.1.59: Because the primary meaning of the word (debt) is inapplicable, it is a restatement through a secondary word; and (this is established) because censure and praise are applicable.

children.text: ṛṇair iti nāyaṃ pradhānaśabdaḥ/ yatra khalv ekaḥ pratyādeyaṃ dadāti, dvitīyaś ca pratideyaṃ gṛhṇāti tatrāsya dṛṣṭatvāt pradhānam ṛṇaśabdaḥ/ na caitad ihopapadyate, pradhānaśabdānupapatteḥ, guṇaśabdenāyam anuvāda ṛṇair iva ṛṇair iti/
children.translated_text: The word 'debts' (<s>ṛṇa</s>) is not used here in its primary sense. For where one person gives something to be returned and a second person receives what is to be returned — there, because of its being observed (in this context), the word 'debt' is primary. But this does not apply here; because the primary meaning of the word is inapplicable, this is a restatement through a secondary word — 'debts figuratively, like debts.'

children.text:
% nupapatteḥ guṇaśabdenāyam anuvāda ṛṇair iva ṛṇair iti/] p.1015
prayuktopamaṃ caitad yathāgnir māṇavaka iti---anyatra dṛṣṭaś cāyam ṛṇaśabda iha prayujyate, yathāgniśabdo māṇavake/ kathaṃ guṇaśabdenānuvādaḥ? nindāpraśaṃsopapatteḥ/ karmalope ṛṇīva ṛṇādānān nindyate, karmānuṣṭhāne ca ṛṇīva ṛṇadānāt praśasyate sa evopamārtha iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: nupapatteḥ guṇaśabdenāyam anuvāda ṛṇair iva ṛṇair iti/] p.1015
And this is a simile in use, like (saying) 'the boy is a fire.' The word 'debt,' which is observed elsewhere, is employed here — just as the word 'fire' (is employed) for a boy. How is it a restatement through a secondary word? Because censure and praise are applicable. One who omits his <s>karmas</s> is censured as being like a debtor because of incurring a debt; one who performs his <s>karmas</s> is praised as being like a debtor because of paying off a debt — this is the meaning of the simile.

children.text:
% p.1016
jāyamāna iti guṇaśabdo viparyaye 'nadhikārāt/ jāyamāno ha vai brāhmaṇa iti ca guṇaśabdo gṛhasthaḥ sampadyamāno jāyamāna iti; yadāyaṃ gṛhastho jāyate tadā karmabhir adhikriyate mātṛto jāyamānasyānadhikārāt/ yadā tu mātṛto jāyate kumāro na tadā karmabhir adhikriyate arthinaḥ śaktasya cādhikārāt/ arthinaḥ karmabhir adhikāraḥ karmavidhau kāmasaṃyogas mṛteḥ ``agnihotraṃ juhuyāt svargakāma'' ity evamādi/ śaktasya ca (3*) pravṛttisambhavāt śaktasya karmabhir adhikāraḥ pravṛttisambhavāt/ (4*) śaktaḥ khalu vihite karmaṇi pravarttate netara iti/ ubhayābhāvas tu pradhānaśabdārthe/ mātṛto jāyamāne kumāre ubhayam arthitā śaktiś ca na bhavatīti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1016]
'Being born' is a secondary word, since in the reverse case there is no eligibility. 'A <s>brāhmaṇa</s> being born' — this 'being born' is a secondary word: one who comes into being as a householder is 'being born.' For when this person is born as a householder, then he is eligible for <s>karmas</s> — because one who is merely being born from the mother has no eligibility. But when an infant is born from the mother, he is not then eligible for <s>karmas</s>, because eligibility belongs to one who desires and is capable. One who desires is eligible for <s>karmas</s> — in the injunction of <s>karma</s>, there is the conjunction of desire: 'one who desires heaven should offer the <s>agnihotra</s>' and so on. And one who is capable is eligible for <s>karmas</s> because of the possibility of activity — one who is capable engages in prescribed <s>karma</s>, not another. But both (desire and capability) are absent in the primary meaning of the word. When an infant is being born from the mother, neither desire nor capability exists.

children.text:
% p.1017
na bhidyate ca laukikād vākyād vaidikaṃ vākyaṃ prekṣāpūrvakāripuruṣapraṇītatvena/ tatra laukikas tāvad aparīkṣako 'pi na *jātamātraṃ (corr.; jātaprātraṃ, ed.) kumārakam evaṃ brūyād adhīṣva yajasva brahmacaryaṃ careti/ kuta evam ṛṣir upapannānavadyavādī upadeśārthena prayukta upadiśati? na khalu vai narttako 'ndheṣu pravarttate na gāyako badhireṣv iti/
upadiṣṭārthavijñānaṃ copadeśaviṣayaḥ/ yaś copadiṣṭam arthaṃ vijānāti taṃ praty upadeśaḥ kriyate, na caitad asti jāyamānakumāraka iti/ gārhasthyaliṅgaṃ ca mantrabrāhmaṇaṃ karma abhivadati/ yac ca mantrabrāhmaṇaṃ karma abhivadati tat patnīsambandhādinā gārhasthyaliṅgenopapannam, tasmād gṛhastho 'yaṃ jāyamāno 'bhidhīyate iti/
arthitvasya cāvipariṇāme jarāmaryavādopapattiḥ/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1017]
And Vedic speech does not differ from ordinary speech in being composed by persons who act with deliberation. Even an ordinary person who is not a critical examiner would not say to a newly born infant: 'Study! Sacrifice! Practice <s>brahmacarya</s>!' How much less would a <s>ṛṣi</s> (sage), who speaks appropriately and without fault, who is engaged for the purpose of instruction, teach thus? For a dancer does not perform among the blind, nor a singer among the deaf.
And the subject of instruction is the understanding of the meaning taught. Instruction is given to one who can understand the meaning taught, and this does not apply to a newly born infant. And the <s>mantras</s> and <s>brāhmaṇas</s> (Vedic texts) prescribe <s>karma</s> characterized by the marks of householder life. And what the <s>mantras</s> and <s>brāhmaṇas</s> prescribe as <s>karma</s> is appropriate with the marks of householder life such as the relation to a wife and so on. Therefore, this 'one being born' who is referred to is the householder.
And the statement about (the session lasting until) old age and death is appropriate when the desire (for fruits) does not change.

children.text:
% p.1018
yāvac cāsya phalenārthitvaṃ na vipariṇamate na nivartate tāvad anena karmānuṣṭheyam ity upapadyate jarāmaryavādas taṃ pratīti/ jarayā ha vety āyuṣasü@turīyasya caturthasya pravrajyāyuktasya vacanaṃ ``jarayā ha vā eṣa etasmād vimucyate'' iti/ āyuṣas turīyaṃ caturthaṃ pravrajyāyuktaṃ jarety ucyate, tatra hi pravrajyā vidhīyate; atyantajarāsaṃyoge jarayā ha vety anarthakam/ ``aśakto vimucyate'' ity etad api nopapadyate, svayam aśaktasya bāhyāṃ śaktim āha---``antevāsī vā juhuyād brahmaṇā sa parikrītaḥ, kṣīrahotā vā jahuyād dhanena sa parikrīta'' iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1018]
As long as his desire for the fruit does not change or cease, so long he must perform the <s>karmas</s> — thus the statement about (the session lasting until) old age and death is appropriate with regard to him. 'By old age' — this is the statement regarding the fourth quarter of life, which is suited to renunciation (<s>pravrajyā</s>): 'he is freed from this (session) by old age.' The fourth quarter of life, suited to renunciation, is called 'old age,' for renunciation is enjoined therein. In the case of one absolutely afflicted by old age, the statement 'by old age' would be purposeless. And 'the incapable one is freed' is also not appropriate, for he states an external capacity for one who is himself incapable: 'Let the pupil offer the oblation — he is purchased with <s>Brahman</s> (sacred knowledge); or let one who offers with milk offer — he is purchased with wealth.'

children.text:
% p.1019
athāpi vihitaṃ vānūdyeta kāmād vārthaḥ parikalpyeta? vihitānuvacanaṃ nyāyyam iti/ ṛṇavān ivāsvatantro gṛhasthaḥ karmasu pravarttate ity upapannaṃ vākyasya
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1019]
Or should a prescribed (injunction) be restated, or should the meaning be constructed from desire? The restatement of what is prescribed is proper. 'The householder, like a debtor, without independence, engages in <s>karmas</s>' — this is the appropriate force of the statement.

children.text:
% p.1020
sāmarthyam/ phalasya hi sādhanāni prayatnaviṣayo na phalam, tāni sampannāni phalāya kalpante/ vihitaṃ ca jāyamānam, vidhīyate ca jāyamānam, tena yaḥ sambaddhyate so 'yaṃ jāyamāna iti/
pratyakṣavidhānābhāvād iti cen na, pratiṣedhasyāpi pratyakṣavidhānābhāvād iti/ pratyakṣato vidhīyate *gārhasthyaṃ (corr.; gārhathyaṃ, ed.) brāhmaṇena, yadi cāśramāntaram abhaviṣyat tad api vyadhāsyata
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1020]
For the means of attaining the fruit are the domain of effort, not the fruit itself; and those, being accomplished, conduce to the fruit. And the (status of) 'one being born' is prescribed and enjoined; and the one who is connected with that is 'the one being born.'
If it is objected that there is no explicit prescription (of other stages of life)? No, because there is no explicit prescription of the prohibition either. The householder stage is prescribed explicitly for the <s>brāhmaṇa</s>; and if another stage of life existed, it too would have been prescribed

children.text:
% p.1021
pratyakṣataḥ, pratyakṣavidhānābhāvān nāsty āśramāntaram iti/ na, pratiṣedhasyāpi pratyakṣto vidhānābhāvāt/ na pratiṣedho 'pi vai brāhmaṇena pratyakṣato vidhīyate --- na santy āśramāntarāṇi eka eva gṛhasthāśrama iti pratiṣedhasya pratyakṣato 'śravaṇād ayuktam etad iti/
adhikārāc ca vidhānaṃ vidyāntaravat/ yathā śāstrāntarāṇi sve sve 'dhikāre pratyakṣato vidhāyakāni nārthāntarābhāvād evam idaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ gṛhasthaśāstraṃ sve 'dhikāre pratyakṣato vidhāyakaṃ nāśramāntarāṇām abhāvād iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1021]
explicitly; from the absence of explicit prescription, there is no other stage of life — (so one might argue). No, because there is no explicit prescription of the prohibition either. No prohibition is explicitly prescribed by the <s>brāhmaṇa</s> texts — 'there are no other stages of life; the householder stage is the only one' — since such a prohibition is not heard explicitly, this (argument) is improper.
And the prescription arises from eligibility, like in other branches of knowledge. Just as other <s>śāstras</s> (treatises) are prescriptive explicitly in their own domains, and this does not mean that other (domains) do not exist — so too this <s>brāhmaṇa</s> text, being the <s>śāstra</s> of the householder, is prescriptive explicitly in its own domain, and this does not mean that the other stages of life do not exist.

children.text:
% p.1022
ṛgbrāhmaṇaṃ cāpavargābhidhāyy abhidhīyate/ ṛcaś ca brāhmaṇāni cāpavargābhivādīni bhavanti/ ṛcaś ca tāvat ---
``karmabhir mṛtyum ṛṣayo niṣeduḥ prajāvanto draviṇam icchamānāḥ/ athāpare ṛṣayo manīṣiṇaḥ paraṃ karmabhyo 'mṛtatvam ānaśuḥ//''
``na karmaṇā na prajayā dhanena tyāgenaike amṛtatvam ānaśuḥ/ pareṇa nākaṃ nihitaṃ guhāyāṃ vibhrājate yad yatayo viśanti//''
``vedāham etaṃ puruṣaṃ mahāntam ādityavarṇaṃ tamasaḥ parastāt/ tam eva viditvātimṛtyum eti nānyaḥ panthā vidyate 'yanāya//''
atha brāhmaṇāni ---
``trayo dharmaskandhāḥ ---yajño 'dhyayanaṃ dānam iti prathamas tapa eva dvitīyo brahmacāry ācāryakulavāsīti tṛtīyo 'tyantam ātmānam ācāryakule 'vasādayan sarve evaite puṇyalokā bhavanti brahmasaṃstho 'mṛtatvam eti/''
``etam eva pravrājino lokam icchantaḥ pravrajantīti''/
children.translated_text: And the <s>Ṛg</s> verses and <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> that speak of <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) are recited. The <s>Ṛg</s> verses and <s>Brāhmaṇas</s> speak of <s>apavarga</s>. First, the <s>Ṛg</s> verses: 'By rites the sages warded off death, desiring offspring and wealth. But other sages, the wise, attained immortality beyond rites.' 'Not by rites, not by offspring, not by wealth — by renunciation alone some attained immortality. Beyond heaven, hidden in the cave, it shines forth — that which the ascetics enter.' 'I know this great <s>Puruṣa</s> (person), sun-colored, beyond darkness. Only by knowing him does one cross beyond death; there is no other path for going.' And the <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>: 'There are three branches of <s>dharma</s>: sacrifice, study, and charity — these are the first; austerity alone is the second; the student dwelling in the teacher's house is the third. One who constantly establishes himself in the teacher's house — all these become meritorious worlds; the one established in <s>Brahman</s> attains immortality.' 'Desiring this very world, the renouncers renounce.'

children.text:
% p.1023
atho khalv āhuḥ kāmamaya evāyaṃ puruṣa iti sa yathākāmo bhavati tatkratur bhavati yatkratur bhavati tat karma kurute yat karma kurute tad abhisaṃpadyate/''
iti karmabhiḥ saṃsaraṇam uktvā prakṛtam anyad upadiśanti ``iti nu kāmayamāno 'thākāmayamāno yo 'kāmo niṣkāma ātmakāma āptakāmo bhavati na tasya prāṇā utkrāmanti ihaiva samavalīyante brahmaiva san brahmāpy etīti''/
tatra yad uktam ṛṇānubandhād apavargābhāva ity etad ayuktam iti/ ``ye catvāraḥ pathayo devayānā'' iti ca cāturāśramyaśruter aikāśramyān upapattiḥ//59//
children.translated_text: Now indeed they say: 'This person is made of desire. As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the action he performs; as is the action he performs, so he attains.' Having thus described transmigration through actions, they teach something else as the main point: 'Thus, the one who desires — and the one who is without desire, who is free from desire, whose desire is fulfilled, whose desire is the <s>ātman</s> (self) — his vital breaths do not depart; right here they dissolve. Being <s>Brahman</s>, he goes to <s>Brahman</s>.' Therefore, what was stated — that there is no <s>apavarga</s> because of the bondage of debts — is unreasonable. And from the Vedic teaching 'those four paths leading to the gods,' the system of four <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life) is [established], and from this, the restriction to a single <s>āśrama</s> is tenable. //59//

children.text: phalārthinaś cedaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ``jarāmaryaṃ vā etat satraṃ yad agnihotram. darśapūrṇam āsau ceti'' katham?
children.translated_text: If this <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> [text] is for those desiring results — 'The <s>Agnihotra</s> is indeed a <s>sattra</s> (sacrificial session) lasting until old age and death; the <s>Darśapūrṇamāsa</s> (new and full moon sacrifices) are that' — how [is renunciation justified]?
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.60: Because of the [ritual of] placing [the fires] in the self, there is no prohibition.

children.text:
% p.1024
``prājāpatyām iṣṭaṃ nirūpya tasyāṃ sarvavedasaṃ hutvā ātmany agnīn samāropya brāhmaṇaḥ pravrajed'' iti *śrūyate (corr.; śrūyate, ed.)/ tena vijānīmaḥ prajāvittalokaiṣaṇābhyo vyutthitasya nivṛtte phalārthitve samāropaṇaṃ vidhīyate iti/
evaṃ ca brāhmaṇāni ``so 'nyad vratam upākariṣyamāṇo yājñavalkyo maitreyīm iti hovāca pravrajiṣyan vā are aham asmāt sthānād asmi hanta te 'nayā kātyāyanyā sahāntaṃ karavāṇīti/ athāpy uktānuśāsanāsi maitreyi etāvad are khalv amṛtatvam iti hoktvā yājñavalkyaḥ pravavrājeti''
children.translated_text: It is heard: 'Having offered the <s>Prājāpatya</s> (sacrifice to <s>Prajāpati</s>) and having performed the rites, having offered all the <s>Vedas</s> into it, having placed the fires in the self, the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> should renounce.' From this we understand that for one who has risen above the desires for offspring, wealth, and worlds, when the desire for results has ceased, the [ritual of] placing [the fires in the self] is prescribed. And thus the <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> texts [state]: '<s>Yājñavalkya</s>, about to undertake another observance, said to <s>Maitreyī</s>: "I am about to depart from this place, come, let me make a settlement between you and <s>Kātyāyanī</s>." And having instructed her as taught, [he said]: "<s>Maitreyī</s>, this much indeed is immortality," and having spoken thus, <s>Yājñavalkya</s> renounced.'
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.61: And because [rituals] ending with the collection of vessels [would be] untenable, there is the absence of fruit [for such rituals after renunciation].

children.text: jarāmarye ca karmaṇy aviśeṣeṇa kalpyamāne sarvasya pātracayāntāni karmāṇīti prasajyate, tatraiṣaṇāvyutthānaṃ na śrūyeta/ ``etad dha sma vai tat pūrve brāhmaṇā anūcānā vidvāṃsaḥ prajāṃ na kāmayante kiṃ prajayā kariṣyāmo yeṣāṃ no 'yam ātmāyaṃ loka iti te ha sma putraiṣaṇāyāś ca vittaiṣaṇāyāś ca lokaiṣaṇāyāś ca vyutthāyātha bhikṣācaryaṃ carantīti''/ eṣaṇābhyaś ca vyutthitasya pātracayāntāni karmāṇi nopapadyante iti nāviśeṣeṇa karttuḥ prayojakaṃ phalaṃ bhavatīti/
children.translated_text: If the <s>karma</s> lasting until old age and death were to be conceived without distinction for everyone, it would follow that the rituals ending with the collection of vessels [apply to] all — and the rising above desires would not be heard [in scripture]. [The <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> states:] 'Indeed, the ancient <s>Brāhmaṇas</s>, learned and wise, did not desire offspring — "What shall we do with offspring, we for whom this <s>ātman</s> is this world?" They indeed, having risen above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, then lived the life of mendicants.' And for one who has risen above desires, rituals ending with the collection of vessels are untenable — thus, the fruit [of ritual] does not belong without distinction to every performer.

children.text:
% p.1026
cāturāśramyavidhānāc cetihāsapurāṇadharmaśāstreṣv aikāśramyānupapattiḥ/ tad apramāṇam iti ced na, pramāṇena prāmāṇyābhyanujñānāt --- pramāṇena khalu brāhmaṇenetihāsapurāṇasya prāmāṇyam abhyanujñāyate ``te vā khalv ete atharvāṅgirasa etad itihāsapurāṇam abhyavadann itihāsapurāṇaṃ pañcamaṃ vedānāṃ veda iti''/ tasmād ayuktam etadaprāmāṇyam iti/ aprāmāṇye ca dharmaśāstrasya prāṇabhṛtāṃ vyavahāralopāl lokocchedaprasaṅgaḥ/
children.translated_text: And from the prescription of the four <s>āśramas</s> (stages of life) in the <s>Itihāsa</s>, <s>Purāṇa</s>, and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>, the restriction to a single <s>āśrama</s> is untenable. If [one says] these are not authoritative — no, because their authority is accepted through [another] authoritative source. For the authority of the <s>Itihāsa</s> and <s>Purāṇa</s> is accepted through the authoritative <s>Brāhmaṇa</s> [text]: 'These <s>Atharvāṅgirasas</s> declared this <s>Itihāsa-Purāṇa</s> — the <s>Itihāsa-Purāṇa</s> is the fifth <s>Veda</s> among the <s>Vedas</s>.' Therefore, it is unreasonable to deny their authority. And if the <s>Dharmaśāstra</s> were without authority, from the loss of practical conduct for living beings, the consequence would be the destruction of the world.

children.text:
% p.1027
draṣṭṛpravaktṛsāmāṇyāc cāprāmānyānupapattiḥ/ ye eva mantrabrāhmaṇasya draṣṭāraḥ pravaktāraś ca, te khalv itihāsapurāṇasya dharmaśāstrasya ceti/
viṣayavyavasthānāc ca yathāviṣayaṃ prāmāṇyam/ anyo mantrabrāhmaṇasya viṣayo 'nyac cetihāsapurāṇadharmaśāstrāṇām iti/ yajño mantrabrāhmaṇasya, lokavṛttam itihāsapurāṇasya, lokavyavahāravyavasthānaṃ dharmaśāstrasya viṣayaḥ/ tatraikena na sarvaṃ vyavasthāpyate iti yathāviṣayam etāni pramāṇānīndriyādivad iti//61//
children.translated_text: And because of the commonality of the seers and promulgators, the denial of authority is untenable. The very same [sages] who are the seers and promulgators of the <s>Mantra-Brāhmaṇa</s> [texts] are also those of the <s>Itihāsa-Purāṇa</s> and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>. And because of the arrangement of subject matter, authority pertains to each in its own domain. The <s>Mantra-Brāhmaṇa</s> has one domain, and the <s>Itihāsa-Purāṇa</s> and <s>Dharmaśāstra</s> have another. Sacrifice is the domain of the <s>Mantra-Brāhmaṇa</s>; worldly affairs are the domain of the <s>Itihāsa-Purāṇa</s>; the establishment of worldly conduct is the domain of the <s>Dharmaśāstra</s>. In that regard, not everything can be established by one alone — hence these are authoritative each in its own domain, like the sense organs and the like. //61//

children.text:
% p.1028
yat punar etat kleśānubandhasyāvicchedād iti ---
children.translated_text: Now, regarding what was said — that because the connection with afflictions is unbroken —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.62: In deep sleep, when dreams are not seen, there is the absence of afflictions — hence <s>apavarga</s> (liberation) [is possible].

children.text: yathā suṣuptasya khalu svapnādarśane rāgānubandhaḥ sukhaduḥkhānubandhaś ca vicchidyate tathāpavarge 'pīti/ etac ca brahmavido muktasyātmano rūpam udāharantīti//62//
children.translated_text: Just as in deep sleep, when dreams are not seen, the connection with attachment and the connection with pleasure and pain are interrupted, so too in <s>apavarga</s>. And the knowers of <s>Brahman</s> cite this as the form of the liberated <s>ātman</s> (self). //62//
And regarding what was said about the connection with activity —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.63: There is no activity leading to re-connection for one whose afflictions are diminished.

children.text:
prakṣīṇeṣu rāgadveṣamoheṣu pravṛttir na pratisandhānāya/ pratisandhis tu pūrvajanmanivṛttau punarjanma, tac cādṛṣṭakāritam, tasyāṃ prahīṇāyāṃ pūrvajanmābhāve janmāntarābhāvo 'pratisandhānam apavargaḥ/
karmavaiphalyaprasaṅga iti ced na, karmavipākapratisaṃvedanasyāpratyākhyānāt/ pūrvajanmanivṛttau punarjanma na bhavatīty ucyate, na tu karmavipākapratisaṃvedanaṃ pratyākhyāyate, sarvāṇi pūrvakarmāṇi hy ante janmani pipacyanta iti//63//
children.translated_text: When <s>rāga</s> (attachment), <s>dveṣa</s> (aversion), and <s>moha</s> (delusion) have been exhausted, activity does not lead to re-connection. Re-connection is rebirth upon the cessation of the previous life; and that is caused by the unseen [force of <s>karma</s>]. When that [force] has been abandoned, in the absence of the previous birth, the absence of another birth — non-re-connection — is <s>apavarga</s> (liberation). If [one objects that] the consequence would be the fruitlessness of <s>karma</s> — no, because the experience of the ripening of <s>karma</s> is not denied. It is said that when the previous life ceases, there is no rebirth; but the experience of the ripening of <s>karma</s> is not denied, for all previous <s>karmas</s> ripen in the final birth. //63//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.64: Not so, because the continuum of afflictions is natural.

children.text: nopapadyate kleśānubandhavicchedaḥ, kasmāt? kleśasantateḥ svābhāvikatvāt/ anādir iyaṃ kleśasantatiḥ, na cānādiḥ śakya ucchetum iti//64//
children.translated_text: The interruption of the connection with afflictions is not tenable. Why? Because the continuum of afflictions is natural. This continuum of afflictions is beginningless, and what is beginningless cannot be cut off. //64//
Here someone offers a response —

children.text: NyS_4,1.65: prāg utpatter abhāvānityatvavat svābhāvike 'py anityatvam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.65: Just as the absence [of something] prior to origination is non-eternal, so too there can be non-eternality even in what is natural.

children.text: yathānādiḥ prāg utpatter abhāva utpannena bhāvena nivartyate, evaṃ svābhāvikī kleśasantatir anityeti//65//
children.translated_text: Just as the beginningless absence [of a thing] prior to origination is terminated by the originated existent, so too the natural continuum of afflictions is non-eternal. //65//
Another says —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 4,1.66: Or, like the non-eternality of the dark color of an atom.

children.text: yathānādir aṇuśyāmatā atha cāgnisaṃyogād anityā, tathā kleśasantatir apīti/ sataḥ khalu dharmo nityatvam anityatvaṃ ca, tattvaṃ bhāve abhāve bhāktam iti/ anādir aṇuśyāmateti hetvabhāvād ayuktam/ anutpattidharmakam anityam iti nātra hetur astīti//66//
children.translated_text: Just as the dark color of an atom is beginningless, yet is non-eternal due to contact with fire, so too the continuum of afflictions. Eternality and non-eternality are indeed properties of what exists; the real [sense applies] to existence, the figurative [sense] to non-existence. 'The dark color of an atom is beginningless' — this is unreasonable due to the absence of a reason.
