If the <s>ātman</s> possesses action like a <s>loṣṭa</s> (clod) because of possessing qualities that are causes of action, then it should also be tangible like a <s>loṣṭa</s>. If it is not tangible, then it should also not possess action like a <s>loṣṭa</s>; or else a distinguishing reason must be stated for the difference. The <s>apakarṣasama</s> consists in imputing the absence of a property in the <s>sādhya</s> from the example. The <s>loṣṭa</s> is seen to possess action and to be non-pervasive;

children.text:
% -vibhur dṛṣṭaḥ,] p.1110
kāmam ātmāpi kriyāvān avibhur astu, viparyaye vā viśeṣo vaktavya iti/
khyāpanīyo varṇyo viparyayād avarṇyaḥ/ tāv etau sādhyadṛṣṭāntadharmau viparyasyato varṇyāvarṇyasamau bhavataḥ/
sādhanadharmayukte dṛṣṭānte dharmāntaravikalpāt sādhyadharmavikalpaṃ prasañjayato vikalpasamaḥ/ kriyāhetuguṇayuktaṃ kiñcid guru yathā loṣṭaḥ, kiṃcil laghu yathā vāyuḥ, evaṃ kriyāhetuguṇayuktaṃ kiñcit kriyāvat syāt yathā loṣṭaḥ, kiñcid akriyaṃ yathātmā, viśeṣo vā vācya iti/
hetvādyavayavasāmarthyayogī dharmaḥ sādhyaḥ, taṃ dṛṣṭānte prasañjayataḥ sādhyasamaḥ/ yadi yathā loṣṭas tathātmā, prāptas tarhi yathātmā tathā loṣṭa iti/ sādhyaś cāyam ātmā kriyāvān iti kāmaṃ loṣṭo 'pi sādhyaḥ/ atha naivam, na tarhi yathā loṣṭaḥ tathātmā//4//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.1110] let the <s>ātman</s> too be active and non-pervasive; or else a distinguishing reason must be stated for the difference. That which is to be made known is <s>varṇya</s> (commendable); the opposite is <s>avarṇya</s> (non-commendable). These two, by reversing the properties of the <s>sādhya</s> and the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, constitute the <s>varṇyāvarṇyasama</s> (commendable/non-commendable equivalence). The <s>vikalpasama</s> (alternative-equivalence) consists in imputing an alternation of the property to be proved from the alternation of other properties in the example that possesses the proving property. Something possessing qualities that are causes of action is heavy, like a <s>loṣṭa</s>; something is light, like <s>vāyu</s> (wind). Likewise, something possessing qualities that are causes of action may possess action, like a <s>loṣṭa</s>; something may lack action, like the <s>ātman</s>; or else a distinguishing reason must be stated. The <s>sādhyasama</s> (probandum-equivalence): the property that is to be proved is that which is capable of being connected with the members of the syllogism such as the reason; imputing that to the example constitutes <s>sādhyasama</s>. If the <s>ātman</s> is like the <s>loṣṭa</s>, then it follows that the <s>loṣṭa</s> is like the <s>ātman</s>. And since the <s>ātman</s>'s possessing action is what is to be proved, let the <s>loṣṭa</s> too be something to be proved. If this is not so, then the <s>ātman</s> is not like the <s>loṣṭa</s>. // 4 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.5]
[Note: p.1113] The reply to these is —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.5: Since positive correlation is established through partial similarity, there is no refutation through dissimilarity.

children.text: alabhyaḥ siddhasya nihnavaḥ/ siddhaṃ ca kiñcitsādharmyād upamānaṃ yathā gaus tathā gavaya iti/
children.translated_text: The denial of what is established is unattainable. And what is established through partial similarity is the <s>upamāna</s> (analogy) — "as a cow, so a <s>gavaya</s> (wild ox)."

children.text:
% iti/] p.1114
tatra na labhyo gogavayayor dharmavikalpaś codayitum/ evaṃ sādhake dharme dṛṣṭāntādisāmarthyayukte na labhyaḥ sādhyadṛṣṭāntayor dharmavikalpād vaidharmyāt pratiṣedho vaktum iti//5//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.1114] There, one cannot raise the objection of alternation of properties between a cow and a <s>gavaya</s>. Likewise, when the proving property is capable of being connected with the example and the other members, the refutation through alternation of properties between the <s>sādhya</s> and the <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, or through dissimilarity, cannot be stated. // 5 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.6]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.6: And because the example is cogent through the attribution of the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum).

children.text: yatra laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ buddhisāmyaṃ tenāviparīto 'rtho 'tidiśyate prajñāpanārtham/ evaṃ sādhyātideśād dṛṣṭānte upapadyamāne sādhyatvam anupapannam iti//6//
children.translated_text: Where ordinary people and investigators share the same understanding, the meaning is extended without distortion for the purpose of making it known. Thus, when the example is cogent through the attribution of the <s>sādhya</s>, the charge of being unproved is itself untenable. // 6 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.7]

children.text: NyS_5,1.7: prāpya sādhyam aprāpya vā hetoḥ prāptyāviśiṣṭatvād aprāptyāsādhakatvāc ca prāptyaprāptisamau ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.7: Whether reaching the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) or not reaching it, since by reaching it the <s>hetu</s> (reason) is no different, and since by not reaching it the <s>hetu</s> is ineffective, these constitute <s>prāptisama</s> (attainment-equivalence) and <s>aprāptisama</s> (non-attainment-equivalence).

children.text:
hetuḥ prāpya vā sādhyaṃ sādhayed aprāpya vā? na tāvat prāpya prāptyām aviśiṣṭatvād asādhakaḥ/ dvayor vidyamānayoḥ prāptau satyāṃ kiṃ kasya sādhakaṃ sādhyaṃ vā?
aprāpya sādhakaṃ na bhavati, nāprāptaḥ pradīpaḥ prakāśayatīti/ prāptyā pratyavasthānaṃ prāptisamaḥ, aprāptyā pratyavasthānam aprāptisamaḥ//7//
children.translated_text: Does the <s>hetu</s> (reason) prove the <s>sādhya</s> (probandum) by reaching it or without reaching it? Not by reaching it, for when it reaches, being no different from it, it is non-probative — when both exist and there is contact between them, what proves what, and what is to be proved? Nor can it prove without reaching, for a lamp that has not reached does not illuminate. The objection through reaching is <s>prāptisama</s>; the objection through non-reaching is <s>aprāptisama</s>. // 7 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.8]
[Note: p.1117] The reply to these two is —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.8: Since the production of a pot and the like is observed, and since in the case of affliction there is sorcery, there is no refutation.

children.text: ubhayathā khalv ayuktaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ kartṛkaraṇādhikaraṇāni prāpya mṛdaṃ ghaṭādikāryaṃ niṣpādayanti, abhicārāc ca pīḍane sati dṛṣṭam aprāpya sādhakatvam iti//8//
children.translated_text: In both ways the refutation is untenable. The agent, instrument, and locus, by reaching the clay, produce the effect such as a pot; and from <s>abhicāra</s> (sorcery), when there is affliction, causation without contact is observed. // 8 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.9]

children.text: NyS_5,1.9: dṛṣṭāntasya kāraṇānapadeśāt pratyavasthānāc ca pratidṛṣṭāntena prasaṅgapratidṛṣṭāntasamau ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.9: Since no cause is stated for the example, and because of the objection through a counter-example, <s>prasaṅgasama</s> (implication-equivalence) and <s>pratidṛṣṭāntasama</s> (counter-example-equivalence) arise.

children.text: sādhanasyāpi sādhanaṃ vaktavyam iti prasaṅgena pratyavasthānaṃ prasaṅgasamaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/ kriyāhetuguṇayogī kriyāvān loṣṭa iti hetur nāpadiśyate, na ca hetum antereṇa siddhir astīti/
children.translated_text: The objection that one must state a proof for the proof itself — the objection through implication (<s>prasaṅga</s>) — constitutes the <s>prasaṅgasama</s> futile rejoinder. "The <s>loṣṭa</s> (clod) possesses action because it possesses qualities that are causes of action" — no reason is adduced for this, and without a reason there is no establishment.

children.text:
% p.1119
pratidṛṣṭāntena pratyavasthānaṃ pratidṛṣṭāntasamaḥ/ kriyāvān ātmā kriyāhetuguṇayogād loṣṭavad ity ukte pratidṛṣṭānta upādīyate --- kriyāhetuguṇayuktam ākāśaṃ niṣkriyaṃ dṛṣṭam iti/ kaḥ punar ākāśasya kriyāhetuguṇaḥ? vāyunā saṃyogaḥ saṃskārāpekṣaḥ, vāyuvanaspatisaṃyogavad iti//9//
children.translated_text: [Note: p.1119] The objection through a counter-example constitutes <s>pratidṛṣṭāntasama</s>. When it is said "the <s>ātman</s> possesses action because of possessing qualities that are causes of action, like a <s>loṣṭa</s>," a counter-example is adduced: <s>ākāśa</s> (space), though possessing qualities that are causes of action, is seen to be devoid of action. What then is the quality that is a cause of action in <s>ākāśa</s>? It is conjunction with <s>vāyu</s> (wind), which depends on <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impressions), like the conjunction of wind and trees. // 9 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.10]
[Note: p.1120] The reply to these two is —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5.1.10: Their removal is like the removal of the objection regarding the taking up of a lamp.

children.text: idaṃ tāvad ayaṃ pṛṣṭo vaktum arhati, atha ke pradīpam upādadate, kimarthaṃ veti? didṛkṣamāṇā dṛśyadarśanārtham iti/ atha pradīpaṃ didṛkṣamāṇāḥ pradīpāntaraṃ kasmān nopādadate? antareṇāpi pradīpāntaraṃ dṛśyate pradīpaḥ, tatra pradīpadarśanārthaṃ pradīpopādānaṃ nirarthakam/ atha dṛṣṭāntaḥ kimartham ucyata iti? aprajñātasya jñāpanārtham iti/ atha dṛṣṭānte kāraṇāpadeśaḥ kimarthaṃ deśyate? yadi prajñāpanārtham, prajñāto dṛṣṭāntaḥ/ sa khalu ``laukikaparīkṣakāṇāṃ yasminn arthe buddhisāmyaṃ sa dṛṣṭānta'' iti/ tatprajñāpanārthaḥ kāraṇāpadeśo nirarthaka iti prasaṅgasamasyottaram//10//
children.translated_text: First, this person who is asked should say: who takes up a lamp, and for what purpose? Those who wish to see [take up a lamp] for the purpose of seeing visible things. But why do those who wish to see a lamp not take up another lamp? A lamp is seen even without another lamp; therefore, taking up a lamp for the purpose of seeing a lamp is purposeless. Now, for what purpose is an example stated? For the purpose of making known what is not known. But why is a statement of the reason pointed out in the example? If for the purpose of making known — the example is [already] known. For indeed, 'an example is that regarding which ordinary people and investigators have the same understanding.' Therefore, the statement of the reason for the purpose of making that known is purposeless — this is the response to the objection through [undesirable] consequence. //10//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.11]

[Note: p.1121]
Now, the response to the objection through counter-example —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.11: And when the counter-example has the status of a reason, the example is not without a reason.

children.text: pratidṛṣṭāntaṃ bruvatā na viśeṣahetur apadiśyate, --- anena prakāreṇa pratidṛṣṭānataḥ sādhako na dṛṣṭānta iti/ evaṃ pratidṛṣṭāntahetutve nāhetur dṛṣṭānta ity upapadyate/ sa ca katham ahetur na syāt? yady apratiṣiddhaḥ sādhakaḥ syād iti//11//
children.translated_text: One who states a counter-example does not point out a reason for the distinguishing feature — [namely] that in this manner a counter-example is probative, not an example. Thus, when the counter-example has the status of a reason, it is proper [to say] the example is not without a reason. And how could it be without a reason? If, when unrefuted, it would be probative. //11//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.12]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.12: <s>Anutpattisama</s> (the rejoinder of non-origination) — because prior to origination there is absence of the reason.

children.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad ity ukte apara āha --- prāgutpatter anutpanne śabde prayatnānantarīyakatvam anityatvakāraṇaṃ nāsti, tadabhāvāt nityatvaṃ prāptam, nityasya cotpattir nāsti/ anutpattyā pratyavasthānam anutpattisamaḥ//12//
children.translated_text: When it is stated 'sound is impermanent because it arises from effort, like a pot,' another says: prior to its origination, when sound has not yet arisen, the property of arising from effort, which is the reason for impermanence, does not exist; from its absence, permanence is obtained; and what is permanent has no origination. Countering with non-origination is <s>anutpattisama</s>. //12//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.13]

[Note: p.1123]
The response to this —

children.text: NyS_5,1.13: tathābhāvād utpannasya kāraṇopapatter na kāraṇapratiṣedhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.13: Because the reason is applicable to what has arisen in that state, there is no negation of the reason.

children.text: tathābhāvād utpannasyeti/ utpannaḥ khalv ayaṃ śabda iti bhavati/ prāgutapatteḥ śabda eva nāsti, utpannasya śabdabhāvāc chabdasya sataḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvam anityatvakāraṇam upapadyate, kāraṇopapatter ayukto 'yaṃ doṣaḥ ``prāgutpatteḥ kāraṇābhāvād'' iti//13//
children.translated_text: 'Because the reason is applicable to what has arisen in that state' — for indeed this sound has arisen, such is the case. Prior to origination, there is simply no sound at all. Since the sound exists after having arisen, the property of arising from effort, the reason for impermanence, is applicable. Because the reason is applicable, this fault 'prior to origination there is absence of the reason' is untenable. //13//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.14]

children.text: NyS_5,1.14: sāmānyadṛṣṭāntayor aindriyakatve samāne nityānityasādharmyāt saṃśayasamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.14: <s>Saṃśayasama</s> (the rejoinder of doubt) — because of the common resemblance to the permanent and impermanent, when the perceptibility of the universal and the example is the same.

children.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad ity ukte hetau saṃśayena pratyavatiṣṭate --- sati prayatnānantarīyakatve asty evāsya nityena sāmānyena sādharmyam aindriyakatvam, asti ca ghaṭenānityena, ato nityānityasādharmyād anivṛttiḥ saṃśaya iti//14//
children.translated_text: When it is stated 'sound is impermanent because it arises from effort, like a pot,' one counters by [raising] doubt regarding the reason — given that it arises from effort, sound has a common property with the permanent universal, namely perceptibility, and also with the impermanent pot; therefore, because of the resemblance to both permanent and impermanent, the unresolved [state] is doubt. //14//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.15]

[Note: p.1126]
The response to this —

children.text: NyS_5,1.15: sādharmyāt saṃśaye na saṃśayo vaidharmyād ubhayathā vā saṃśaye 'tyantasaṃśayaprasaṅgo nityatvānabhyupagamāc ca sāmānysyāpratiṣedhaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.15: When there is doubt due to resemblance, there is no doubt because of dissimilarity; or if there is doubt in both ways, perpetual doubt would follow; and since permanence is not accepted, there is no refutation of the universal.

children.text: viśeṣād vaidharmyād avadhāryamāṇe 'rthe puruṣa iti, na sthāṇupuruṣasādharmyāt saṃśayo 'vakāśaṃ labhate/ evaṃ vaidharmyād viśeṣāt prayatnānantarīyakatvād avadhāryamāṇe śabdasyānityatve nityānityasādharmyāt saṃśayo 'vakāśaṃ na labhate/ yadi vai labhate, tataḥ sthāṇupuruṣasādharmyānucchedād atyantaṃ saṃśayaḥ syāt/ gṛhyamāṇe ca viśeṣe nityaṃ sādharmyaṃ saṃśayahetur iti nābhyupagamyate/ na hi gṛhyamāṇe puruṣasya viśeṣe sthāṇupuruṣasādharmyaṃ saṃśayahetur bhavati//15//
children.translated_text: When an object is being determined through a distinguishing feature, a dissimilarity — [as when one determines] 'it is a person' — the doubt arising from the resemblance between a post and a person does not find scope. Similarly, when the impermanence of sound is being determined through the distinguishing feature of arising from effort, the doubt arising from resemblance to permanent and impermanent does not find scope. For if it did find scope, then because the resemblance between post and person is never eliminated, there would be perpetual doubt. And when a distinguishing feature is being grasped, it is not accepted that resemblance is perpetually a cause of doubt. For when the distinguishing feature of a person is being grasped, the resemblance between post and person does not serve as a cause of doubt. //15//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.16]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.16: <s>Prakaraṇasama</s> (the rejoinder of thesis-equality) — because of the establishment of the procedure through resemblance to both.

children.text: ubhayena nityena cānityena ca sādharmyāt pakṣapratipakṣayoḥ pravṛttiḥ prakriyā/ anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad ity ekaḥ pakṣaṃ pravarttayati, dvitīyaś ca nityasādharmyāt pratipakṣaṃ pravarttayati --- nityaḥ śabdaḥ śrāvaṇatvāt śabdatvavad iti/ evaṃ ca sati prayatnānantarīyakatvād iti hetur anityasādharmyeṇa ucyamāno na prakaraṇam ativarttate, prakaraṇānativṛtter nirṇayānativartanam/ samānaṃ caitan nityasādharmyeṇocyamāṇe hetau/ tad idaṃ prakaraṇānativṛttyā pratyavasthānaṃ prakaraṇasamaḥ/ samānaṃ caitad vaidharmye 'pi, ubhayavaidharmyāt prakriyāsiddheḥ prakaraṇasama iti//16//
children.translated_text: Because of resemblance to both the permanent and the impermanent, the procedure — that is, the activity — of the thesis and counter-thesis [proceeds]. One person advances the thesis: 'sound is impermanent because it arises from effort, like a pot.' A second, because of resemblance to the permanent, advances the counter-thesis: 'sound is permanent because it is audible, like sound-hood [the universal].' This being so, the reason 'because it arises from effort,' being stated through resemblance to the impermanent, does not go beyond the topic of dispute; from the non-transcendence of the topic, there is no transcendence to a conclusion. The same applies when the reason is stated through resemblance to the permanent. This countering through non-transcendence of the topic of dispute is <s>prakaraṇasama</s>. The same applies to dissimilarity as well — because of the establishment of the procedure through dissimilarity from both, it is <s>prakaraṇasama</s>. //16//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.17]

[Note: p.1128]
The response to this —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.17: Because of the establishment of the topic from the counter-thesis, there is no possibility of refutation; because the counter-thesis is possible.

children.text: ubhayasādharmyāt prakriyāsiddhiṃ bruvatā pratipakṣāt prakriyāsiddhir uktā bhavati/ yady ubhayasādharmyam, tatra ekataraḥ pratipakṣa ity evaṃ saty upapannaḥ pratipakṣo bhavati/ pratipakṣopapatter anupapannaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ, yadi pratipakṣopapattiḥ pratiṣedho nopapadyate, atha pratiṣedhopapattiḥ pratipakṣo nopapadyate, pratipakṣopapattiḥ pratiṣedhopapattiś ceti vipratiṣiddham iti/ tattvānavadhāraṇāc ca prakriyāsiddhir viparyaye prakaraṇāvasānāt, tattvāvadhāraṇe hy avasitaṃ prakaraṇaṃ bhavatīti//17//
children.translated_text: One who says the procedure is established because of resemblance to both has thereby stated that the procedure is established from the counter-thesis. If there is resemblance to both, then one of the two is a counter-thesis — this being so, the counter-thesis is possible. Because the counter-thesis is possible, the refutation is untenable. If the counter-thesis is possible, the refutation is not possible; and if the refutation is possible, the counter-thesis is not possible — 'the counter-thesis is possible and the refutation is possible' is contradictory. And because the truth is not determined, the procedure is established — in the opposite case [where truth is determined], the topic would be concluded, for when truth is determined, the topic of dispute is concluded. //17//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.18]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.18: <s>Ahetusama</s> (the rejoinder of non-reason) — because of the impossibility of the reason regarding the three times.

children.text: hetuḥ sādhanam, tat sādhyāt pūrvaṃ paścāt saha vā bhavet/ yadi pūrvaṃ sādhanam, asati sādhye kasya sādhanam? atha paścād, asati sādhane kasyedaṃ sādhyam? atha yugapat sādhyasādane, dvayor vidyamānayoḥ kiṃ kasya sādhanaṃ kiṃ kasya sādhyam iti hetur ahetunā na viśiṣyate/ ahetunā sādharmyāt pratyavasthānam ahetusamaḥ//18//
children.translated_text: The reason is the means of proof. That [reason] may be prior to, subsequent to, or simultaneous with what is to be proved. If the means of proof is prior, in the absence of what is to be proved, what is it a means of proving? If subsequent, in the absence of the means of proof, of what is this the thing to be proved? If the means of proof and the thing to be proved are simultaneous, when both exist, what is the means of proving what, and what is to be proved by what? — thus the reason is not distinguished from a non-reason. Countering through resemblance to a non-reason is <s>ahetusama</s>. //18//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.19]

[Note: p.1130]
The response to this —
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.19: There is no impossibility regarding the three times, because the thing to be proved is established from the reason.

children.text: na traikālyāsiddhiḥ/ kasmāt? hetutaḥ sādhyasiddheḥ/ nirvartanīyasya nirvṛttir vijñeyasya vijñānam ubhayaṃ kāraṇato dṛśyate, so 'yaṃ mahān pratyakṣaviṣaya udāharaṇam iti/ yat tu khalūktam asati sādhye kasya sādhanam iti? yat tu nirvatyate yac ca vijñāpyate tasyeti//19//
children.translated_text: There is no impossibility regarding the three times. Why? Because the thing to be proved is established from the reason. The bringing about of what is to be brought about, the making known of what is to be made known — both are observed [to proceed] from a cause. This is a vast domain of perception, and [constitutes] an example. As for the question 'in the absence of what is to be proved, what is the means of proving?' — it is the means of proving that which is [about to be] brought about and that which is [about to be] made known. //19//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.20]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.20: And because refutation is untenable, the thing to be refuted is not refuted.

children.text: pūrvaṃ paścād yugapad vā pratiṣedha iti nopapadyate, pratiṣedhānupapatteḥ sthāpanāhetuḥ siddha iti//20//
children.translated_text: Refutation — whether prior, subsequent, or simultaneous — is untenable. Since refutation is untenable, the reason for establishment is proved. //20//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.21]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.21: <s>Arthāpattisama</s> (the rejoinder of presumption) — because of the establishment of the counter-thesis through presumption.

children.text: anityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād ghaṭavad iti sthāpite pakṣe arthāpattyā pratipakṣaṃ sādhayato 'rthāpattisamaḥ/ yadi prayatnānantarīyakatvād anityasādharmyād anityaḥ śabda iti, arthād āpadyate nityasādharmyān nitya iti, asti cāsya nityena sādharmyam asparśatvam iti//21//
children.translated_text: When the thesis 'sound is impermanent because it arises from effort, like a pot' has been established, one who establishes the counter-thesis through <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) [commits] <s>arthāpattisama</s>. 'If sound is impermanent because of resemblance to the impermanent through arising from effort, then it is presumed from the meaning that it is permanent because of resemblance to the permanent, and it does have a resemblance to the permanent — namely intangibility.' //21//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.22]

[Note: p.1132]
The response to this —

children.text: NyS_5,1.22: anuktasyārthāpatteḥ pakṣahāner upapattir anuktatvād anaikānatikatvāc cārthāpatteḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.22: Since the presumption is of what has not been stated, the abandonment of the thesis is tenable, because [the presumption] is unstated and because presumption is not conclusive.

children.text: anupapādya sāmarthyam anuktam arthād āpadyate iti bruvataḥ pakṣahāner upapattir anuktatvāt, anityapakṣasiddhāv arthād āpannaṃ nityapakṣasya hānir iti/ anaikānatikatvāc cārthāpatteḥ/
children.translated_text: One who says 'it is presumed from the meaning without establishing the capacity [of the reason]' — the abandonment of [that person's] thesis is tenable because of the unstated nature [of the counter-reason]. When the impermanence thesis is established, what is presumed from the meaning is the abandonment of the permanence thesis. And because presumption is not conclusive:

children.text:
% p.1133
ubhayapakṣasamā ceyam arthāpattiḥ/ yadi nityasādharmyād asparśatvād ākāśavac ca nityaḥ śabdaḥ arthād āpannam anityasādharmyāt prayatnānantarīyakatvād anitya iti/ na ceyaṃ viparyayamātrād ekāntenārthāpattiḥ/ na khalu vai ghaṇasya grāvṇaḥ patanam ity arthād āpadyate --- dravāṇām apāṃ patanābhāva iti//22//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1133]
this presumption is equal to both theses. If sound is permanent because of resemblance to the permanent through intangibility and like space, then it is presumed from the meaning that it is impermanent because of resemblance to the impermanent through arising from effort. And this presumption is not conclusive from mere reversal alone. For it is not the case that from the falling of a heavy stone it is presumed that liquids — waters — do not fall. //22//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.23]

children.text: NyS_5,1.23: ekadharmopapatter aviśeṣe sarvāviśeṣaprasaṅgāt sadbhāvaupapatter aviśeṣasamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.23: <s>Aviśeṣasama</s> (the rejoinder of non-distinction) — because when a single property is applicable, in the absence of distinction, total non-distinction would follow, since existence is applicable [to everything].

children.text: eko dharmaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvaṃ śabdaghaṭayor upapadyata ity aviśeṣe ubhayor anityatve,
children.translated_text: The single property 'arising from effort' is applicable to both sound and pot — and when there is no distinction, [concluding] that both are impermanent,

children.text:
% p.1134
sarvasyāviśeṣaḥ prasajyate/ katham? sadbhāvopapatteḥ/ eko dharmaḥ sadbhāvaḥ sarvasyopapadyate, sadbhāvopapatteḥ sarvāviśeṣaprasaṅgāt pratyavasthānam aviśeṣasamaḥ//23//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1134]
total non-distinction would follow. How? Because existence is applicable. The single property 'existence' is applicable to everything; because of the applicability of existence, total non-distinction would follow — countering [in this way] is <s>aviśeṣasama</s>. //23//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.24]
The response to this —

children.text: NyS_5,1.24: kvacit taddharmopapatteḥ kvacic cānupapatteḥ pratiṣedhābhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.24: Because that property is applicable in some cases and not applicable in others, there is no refutation.

children.text:
yathā sādhyadṛṣṭāntayor ekadharmasya prayatnānantarīyakatvasyopapatter anityatvaṃ dharmāntaram aviśeṣaḥ, naivaṃ sarvabhāvānāṃ sadbhāvopapattinimittaṃ dharmāntaram asti, yena aviśeṣaḥ syāt/
atha matam anityatvam eva dharmānataraṃ sadbhāvopapattinimittaṃ bhāvānāṃ sarvatra syād iti, evaṃ khalu vai kalpyamāne anityāḥ sarve bhāvāḥ sadbhāvopapatter iti pakṣaḥ prāpnoti/ tatra pratijñārthavyatiriktam anyad udāharaṇaṃ nāsti, anudāharaṇaś ca hetur nāstīti/ pratijñaiekadeśasya codāharaṇatvam anupapannam,
children.translated_text:
Just as from the applicability of the single property 'arising from effort' to the thesis and the example, impermanence is a further property [that follows] — a non-distinction — not so for all existents is there a further property occasioned by the applicability of existence, by which there would be non-distinction.
And if it is thought that impermanence itself is the further property occasioned by the applicability of existence to all things, and would apply everywhere — well then, when such a thing is conceived, the thesis follows that 'all things are impermanent because of the applicability of existence.' In that case, there is no other example apart from what is stated in the thesis; and a reason without an example is no reason. And for a part of the thesis to serve as an example is untenable,

children.text:
% -jñaikadeśasya ...] p.1135
na hi sādhyam udāharaṇaṃ bhavati/ sataś ca nityānityabhāvāt anityatvānupapattiḥ/ tasmāt sadbhāvopapatteḥ sarvāviśeṣaprasaṅga iti nirabhidheyam etad vākyam iti/ sarvabhāvānāṃ sadbhāvopapatter anityatvam iti bruvatā 'nujñātaṃ śabdasyānityatvam, tatrānupapannaḥ pratiṣedha iti//24//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1135 — -jñaikadeśasya ...]
for what is to be proved cannot be an example. And since what exists is of both permanent and impermanent nature, impermanence does not [universally] apply. Therefore, the statement 'total non-distinction would follow because of the applicability of existence' is a meaningless statement. And one who says 'all things are impermanent because of the applicability of existence' has [thereby] conceded the impermanence of sound — the refutation of that is untenable. //24//
[Section: NySBh_5,1.25]
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,1.25: <s>Upapattisama</s> (the rejoinder of equal applicability) — because of the applicability of reasons on both sides.

children.text: yady anityatvakāraṇam upapadyate śabdasyety anityaḥ śabdo nityatvakāraṇam apy upapadyate 'syāsparśatvam iti nityatvam apy upapadyate/ ubhayasyānityatvasya nityatvasya ca kāraṇopapattyā pratyavasthānam upapattisamaḥ//
children.translated_text: If the reason for non-eternality is applicable to sound, and hence sound is non-eternal, (then) the reason for eternality is also applicable — its intangibility — and thus eternality is also applicable. The objection based on the applicability of reasons for both non-eternality and eternality is (the futile rejoinder called) <s>upapattisamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the applicable).
The response to this is —
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.26: Because of the acknowledgment of the applicable reason, there is no refutation.

children.text: ubhayakāraṇopapatter iti bruvatā nānityatvakāraṇopapatter anityatvaṃ pratiṣidhyate, yadi pratiṣidhyate nobhayakāraṇopapattiḥ syāt/ ubhayakāraṇopapattivacanād anityatvakāraṇopapattir abhyanujñāyate, abhyanujñānād anupapannaḥ pratiṣedhaḥ/
children.translated_text: By one who says 'because of the applicability of both reasons,' the non-eternality is not refuted on account of the applicability of the reason for non-eternality. If it were refuted, there would not be the applicability of both reasons. From the statement of the applicability of both reasons, the applicability of the reason for non-eternality is acknowledged; and because of this acknowledgment, the refutation is unfounded.

children.text:
% p.1137
vyāghātāt pratiṣedha iti cet, samāno vyāghātaḥ/ ekasya nityatvānityatvaprasaṅgaṃ vyāhataṃ bruvatoktaṃ pratiṣedha iti cet? svapakṣaparapakṣayoḥ samāno vyāghātaḥ, sa ca naikatarasya sādhaka iti//26//
children.translated_text:
[p.1137]
If it is said that the refutation is due to contradiction — the contradiction is equal. If it is said that the attribution of both eternality and non-eternality to one and the same [thing] is contradictory and hence constitutes a refutation? The contradiction is equal in one's own position and the opponent's position, and that does not establish either one. //26//
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.27: Because of observation even in the absence of the stated reason, (the futile rejoinder is called) <s>upalabdhisamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the observed).

Even in the absence of the stated reason for non-eternality — namely, being consequent upon effort — the non-eternality of sound produced by the breaking of tree branches due to wind force is observed.

children.text:
% vṛkṣaśākhābhaṅgajasya ...] p.1138
nirdiṣṭasya sādhanasyābhāve 'pi sādhyadharmopalabdhyā pratyavasthānam upalabdhisamaḥ//27//
children.translated_text:
[Note: vṛkṣaśākhābhaṅgajasya ...] p.1138
The objection based on observing the property to be proved even in the absence of the stated means of proof is <s>upalabdhisamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the observed). //27//

[p.1139]
The response to this is —
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.28: Because the same property is applicable from another cause as well, there is no refutation.

children.text: prayatnānantarīyakatvād iti bruvatā kāraṇata utpattir abhidhīyate, na kāryasya kāraṇaniyamaḥ/ yadi ca kāraṇāntarād apy utpadyamānasya śabdasya tad anityatvam upapadyate, kim atra pratiṣidhyata iti//28//
children.translated_text: By one who says 'because of being consequent upon effort,' origination from a cause is being stated, not a restriction that the effect [can come] only from [that specific] cause. And if the non-eternality of sound is applicable even when it is produced from another cause, what is being refuted here? //28//

children.text:
% p.1140
na prāg uccāraṇād vidyamānasya śabdasyānupalabdhiḥ, kasmāt ? āvaraṇāadyanupalabdheḥ/ yathā vidyamānasyodakāder arthasyāvaraṇāder anupalabdhiḥ naivaṃ śabdasyāgrahaṇakāraṇenāvaraṇādinānupalabdhiḥ/ gṛhyeta caitad asyāgrahaṇakāraṇam udakādivat, na gṛhyate/ tasmād udakādiviparītaḥ śabdo 'nupalabhyamāna iti/
children.translated_text:
[p.1140]
It is not the case that sound, existing prior to utterance, is not perceived. Why? Because of the non-perception of an obstruction and the like. Just as a real object such as water is not perceived due to an obstruction and the like, so too the non-perception of sound is due to an obstruction and the like that cause its non-apprehension. And this cause of its non-apprehension should be perceived, just like water and the like; but it is not perceived. Therefore, sound, being unperceived, is the opposite of water and the like.

children.text: NyS_5,1.29: tadanupalabdher anupalambhād abhāvasiddhau tadviparītopapatter anupalabdhisamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5,1.29: Because of the establishment of non-existence through the non-perception of that non-perception, and because of the applicability of the opposite of that, (the futile rejoinder is called) <s>anupalabdhisamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the non-perceived).

children.text: teṣām āvaraṇādīnām anupalabdhir nopalabhyate/ anupalambhān nāstīty abhāvo 'syāḥ sidhyati/ abhāvasiddhau hetvabhāvāt tadviparītam astitvam āvaraṇādīnām avadhāryate/ tadviparītopapatter yatpratijñātaṃ ``na prāg uccāraṇād vidyamānasya śabdasyānupalabdhir ity'' etan na sidhyati/ so 'yaṃ hetur ``āvaraṇādyanupalabdher'' ity āvaraṇādiṣu cāvaraṇādyanupalabdhau ca samayānupalabdhyā pratyavasthito 'nupalabdhisamo bhavati//29//
children.translated_text: The non-perception of those obstructions and the like is not perceived. From this non-perception, the non-existence of that [non-perception] is established. Upon the establishment of non-existence, due to the absence of the reason, the opposite — namely the existence of obstructions and the like — is ascertained. Because of the applicability of the opposite, the claim that 'sound, existing prior to utterance, is not perceived due to the non-perception of obstructions and the like' is not established. This reason — 'because of the non-perception of obstructions and the like' — being countered with regard to the obstructions and the like and their non-perception through the non-perception of agreement, becomes <s>anupalabdhisamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the non-perceived). //29//

[p.1141]
The response to this is —
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.30: Because non-perception is of the nature of non-apprehension, the non-perception [of obstruction] is not a valid reason.

children.text: āvaraṇādyanupalabdhir nāsti, anupalambhād ity ahetuḥ/ kasmāt? anupalambhātmakatvād anupalabdheḥ/ upalambhābhāvamātratvād anupalabdheḥ/ yad asti tad upalabdher viṣayaḥ, upalabdhyā tad astīti pratijñāyate/ yan nāsti tad anupalabdher viṣayaḥ, anupalabhyamānaṃ nāstīti pratijñāyate/ so 'yam āvaraṇādyanupalabheḥ anupalambha upalabdhyabhāve 'nupalabdhau svaviṣaye pravarttamāno na svaviṣayaṃ pratiṣedhati/
children.translated_text: The non-perception of obstructions and the like does not exist — because of non-apprehension — this is not a valid reason. Why? Because non-perception is of the nature of non-apprehension. Non-perception is merely the absence of apprehension. What exists is the object of perception; by perception one asserts 'it exists.' What does not exist is the object of non-perception; what is not perceived is asserted as 'it does not exist.' This non-apprehension of the obstructions and the like — the non-perception operating in its own domain, namely the absence of perception — does not negate its own domain.

children.text:
% p.1142
apratiṣiddhā cāvaraṇādyanupalabdhir hetutvāya kalpate/ āvaraṇādīni tu vidyamānatvād upalabdher viṣayāḥ, teṣām upalabdhyā bhavitavyam/ yat tāni nopalabhyante, tad upalabdheḥ svaviṣayapratipādikāyā abhāvād anupalambhād anupalabdher viṣayo gamyate --- na santy āvaraṇādīni śabdasyāgrahaṇakāraṇānīti/ anupalambhāt tv anupalabhiḥ sidhyati, viṣayaḥ sa tasyeti//30//
children.translated_text:
[p.1142]
And the non-perception of obstructions and the like, being unrefuted, qualifies as a reason. But the obstructions and the like, since they exist, are objects of perception; their perception should occur. That they are not perceived — this, from the absence of perception which demonstrates its own domain, and from non-apprehension — is understood as the domain of non-perception: there are no obstructions and the like that are causes of the non-apprehension of sound. But non-perception is established through non-apprehension — that is its domain. //30//
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.31: And because of the awareness of the presence and absence of the varieties of cognition within oneself.

children.text: ahetur iti varttate/ śarīre śarīre jñānavikalpānāṃ bhāvābhāvau saṃvedanīyau/ asti me saṃśayajñānaṃ nāsti me saṃśayajñānam iti/ evaṃ pratyakṣānumānāgamasmṛtijñāneṣu/ seyam āvaraṇāadyanupalabdhir upalabdhyabhāvaḥ svasaṃvedyaḥ --- nāsti me śabdasyāvaraṇādyupalabdhir iti nopalabhyante śabdasyāgrahaṇakāraṇāny āvaraṇādīnīti/ tatra yad uktaṃ tad anupalabdher anupalambhād abhāvasiddhir iti, etan nopapadyate//31//
children.translated_text: 'Is not a valid reason' — this continues. In each body, the presence and absence of the varieties of cognition are to be ascertained: 'I have doubt-cognition,' 'I do not have doubt-cognition' — similarly for perception, inference, testimony, and memory cognitions. This non-perception of obstructions and the like — the absence of perception — is self-ascertainable: 'I do not have the perception of obstructions and the like of sound' — hence the obstructions and the like that are causes of the non-apprehension of sound are not perceived. In that regard, the statement 'because of the establishment of non-existence through the non-perception of that non-perception' is untenable. //31//

<s>NyS</s> 5,1.32: Because of the applicability of common properties from similarity, the consequence of universal non-eternality — (the futile rejoinder is called) <s>anityasamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the non-eternal).

children.text: anityena ghaṭena sādharmyād anityaḥ śabda iti bruvato 'sti ghaṭenānityena sarvabhāvānāṃ sādharmyam iti sarvasyānityatvam aniṣṭaṃ sampadyate/ so 'yam anityatvena pratyavasthānād anityasama iti//32//
children.translated_text: When one says 'sound is non-eternal because of its similarity to the non-eternal pot,' there is a similarity between the non-eternal pot and all entities — and thus the unwanted consequence of the non-eternality of everything would follow. This objection based on non-eternality is <s>anityasamaḥ</s>. //32//

[p.1145]
The response to this is —
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.33: Because of the non-establishment [of any position] from similarity, the non-establishment of the refutation too, due to its similarity with what is to be refuted.

children.text: pratijñādyavayavayuktaṃ vākyaṃ pakṣanivartakaṃ pratipakṣalakṣaṇaṃ pratiṣedhaḥ/ tasya pakṣeṇa pratiṣedhyena sādharmyaṃ pratijñādiyogaḥ/ tad yady anityasādharmyād anityatvasyāsiddhiḥ, sādharmyād asiddheḥ pratiṣedhasyāpy asiddhiḥ, pratiṣedhyena sādharmyād iti//33//
children.translated_text: A statement equipped with the components of thesis and so forth (<s>pratijñā</s>, etc.) that negates the [opponent's] position — having the character of a counter-thesis — is the refutation. Its similarity with the refuted position [consists in] the possession of thesis and other components. Therefore, if because of the similarity with the non-eternal, non-eternality is not established, then because of the non-establishment [of anything] from similarity, the refutation too is not established, since it has similarity with the refuted [position]. //33//

children.text: NyS_5,1.34: dṛṣṭānte ca sādhyasādhanabhāvena prajñātasya dharmasya hetutvāt tasya cobhayathābhāvān nāviśeṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5,1.34: And because in the example, a property recognized as standing in the relation of probandum and probans is the reason, and because that [property] exists in both ways, there is no absence of distinction.

children.text: dṛṣṭānte yaḥ khalu dharmaḥ sādhyasādhanabhāvena prajñāyate, sa hetutvenābhidhīyate/ sa cobhayathā bhavati,
children.translated_text: In the example, the property that is recognized as standing in the relation of probandum and probans is stated as the reason. And that exists in both ways —

children.text:
% cobhayathā bhavati,] p.1146
--- kenacit samānaḥ, kutaścid viśiṣṭaḥ/ sāmānyāt sādharmyaṃ viśeṣāc ca vaidharmyam/ evaṃ sādharmyaviśeṣo hetuḥ, nāviśeṣeṇa sādharmyamātraṃ vaidharmyamātraṃ vā/ sādharmyamātraṃ vaidharmyamātraṃ cāśritya bhavān āha --- ``sādharmyāt tulyadharmopapatteḥ sarvānityatvaprasaṅgād anityasam'' iti, etad ayuktam iti/ aviśeṣasamapratiṣedhe ca yad uktaṃ tad api veditavyam//34//
children.translated_text:
[Note: cobhayathā bhavati,] p.1146
— it is similar to something in some respect, and different from it in another respect. From the commonality there is similarity, and from the distinction there is dissimilarity. Thus the reason is similarity-cum-distinction, not mere undifferentiated similarity alone or dissimilarity alone. And you, relying on mere similarity or mere dissimilarity, say — 'because of the applicability of common properties from similarity, the consequence of universal non-eternality is <s>anityasamaḥ</s>' — this is improper. And what was stated regarding the refutation of <s>aviśeṣasamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the non-distinctive) should also be understood here. //34//

children.text: NyS_5,1.35: nityam anityabhāvād anitye nityatvopapatter nityasamaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5,1.35: [Sound is] eternal, because non-eternality exists in the non-eternal; and because the applicability of eternality for the non-eternal — (the futile rejoinder is called) <s>nityasamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the eternal).

children.text: anityaḥ śabda iti pratijñāyate/ tad anityatvaṃ kiṃ śabde nityam athānityam? yadi tāvat sarvadā bhavati? dharmasya sadā bhāvād dharmiṇo 'pi sadā bhāva iti nityaḥ śabda iti/ atha na sarvadā bhavati? anityatvasyābhāvān nityaḥ śabdaḥ/ evaṃ nityatvena pratyavasthānān nityasamaḥ//35//
children.translated_text: It is asserted that sound is non-eternal. Is that non-eternality eternal or non-eternal in sound? If it always exists — then because of the constant presence of the property, the possessor of the property also always exists; hence sound is eternal. If it does not always exist — then because of the absence of non-eternality, sound is eternal. Thus, the objection based on eternality is <s>nityasamaḥ</s>. //35//

[p.1148]
The response to this is —

children.text: NyS_5,1.36: pratiṣedhye nityam anityabhāvād anitye 'nityatvopapatteḥ pratiṣedhābhāvaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5,1.36: Because non-eternality constantly exists in what is to be refuted, and because non-eternality is applicable for the non-eternal, there is no refutation.

children.text: pratiṣedhye śabde nityam anityatvasya bhāvād ity ucyamāne 'nujñātaṃ śabdasyānityatvam, anityatvopapatteś ca ``nānityaḥ śabda'' iti pratiṣedho nopapadyate/ atha nābhyupagamyate, nityam anityatvasya bhāvād iti hetur na bhavatīti hetvabhāvāt pratiṣedhānupapattir iti/
children.translated_text: When it is said that non-eternality constantly exists in the thing to be refuted (sound), the non-eternality of sound is thereby acknowledged; and because of the applicability of non-eternality, the refutation 'sound is not non-eternal' is untenable. Alternatively, if it is not accepted [that non-eternality constantly exists], then the reason — 'because non-eternality constantly exists' — is invalid, and from the absence of the reason, the refutation is untenable.

children.text:
% p.1149
utapannasya nirodhād abhāvaḥ śabdasyānityatvam, tatra paripraśnānupapattiḥ/ yo 'yaṃ paripraśnaḥ --- tad anityatvaṃ kiṃ śabde sarvadā bhavati atha neti, ayam anupapannaḥ/ kasmāt? utpannasya yo nirodhād abhāvaḥ śabdasya tad anityatvam; evaṃ ca saty adhikaraṇādheyavibhāgo vyāghātān nāstīti/ nityānityatvavirodhāc ca/ nityatvam anityatvaṃ ca ekasya dharmiṇo dharmāv iti virudhyete, na sambhavataḥ/
children.translated_text:
[p.1149]
The non-eternality of sound is its cessation after having arisen; in that case, the cross-examination is inapplicable. The cross-examination — 'does that non-eternality always exist in sound or not?' — is inapplicable. Why? Because the non-eternality of sound is its destruction after having arisen; and this being so, the distinction between substratum and superimposed [property] does not exist, due to contradiction. And because eternality and non-eternality are mutually contradictory — eternality and non-eternality, being properties of one and the same possessor of properties, are contradictory and cannot coexist.

children.text:
% ekasya dharmiṇo ...] p.1150
tatra yad uktaṃ --- nityam anityatvasya bhāvān nitya eva, tad avartamānārtham uktam iti//36//
children.translated_text:
[Note: ekasya dharmiṇo ...] p.1150
Therefore, what was said — 'because non-eternality constantly exists, [sound] is indeed eternal' — that has been stated as having no applicable meaning. //36//
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.37: Because the effects of effort are many, (the futile rejoinder is called) <s>kāryasamaḥ</s> (the balancing of the effect).

children.text: prayatnānantarīyakatvād anityaḥ śabda iti/ yasya prayatnānantaram ātmalābhaḥ tat khalv abhūtvā bhavati, yathā ghaṭādikāryam; anityam iti ca bhūtvā na bhavatīty etad vijñāyate/
children.translated_text: Sound is non-eternal because it is consequent upon effort — so it is said. That whose existence follows effort, that indeed comes into being having not existed before, like the effect of a pot and the like; and 'non-eternal' means it ceases to exist after having existed.

children.text:
% p.1151
evam avasthite prayatnakāryānekatvād iti pratiṣedha ucyate/ prayatnānantaram ātmalābhaś ca dṛṣṭo ghaṭādīnām, vyavadhānāpohāc cābhivyaktir vyavahitānām/ tat kiṃ prayatnānantaram ātmalābhaḥ śabdasyāho 'bhivyaktir iti viśeṣo nāsti/ kāryāviśeṣeṇa pratyavasthānam kāryasamaḥ//37//
children.translated_text:
[p.1151]
Given this, the refutation through the multiplicity of effects of effort is stated. The coming into existence following effort is observed for pots and the like, and the manifestation of obstructed [things] is through the removal of the obstruction. So is there origination of sound following effort, or manifestation? — there is no distinction. The objection through the absence of distinction in effects is <s>kāryasamaḥ</s>. //37//

[p.1152]
The response to this is —
<s>NyS</s> 5,1.38: If the effect is different, then effort is not the cause, because the applicability of a cause of non-perception.

children.text: sati kāryānyatve anupalabdhikāraṇopapatteḥ prayatnasyāhetutvaṃ śabdasyābhivyaktau/ yatra prayatnānantaram abhivyaktis tatrānupalabdhikāraṇaṃ vyavadhānam upapadyate, vyavadhānāpohāc ca prayatnānantarabhāvino 'rthasyopalabdhilakṣaṇā 'bhivyaktir bhavatīti,
children.translated_text: If the effect is different, then because of the applicability of a cause of non-perception, effort is not the cause of the manifestation of sound. Where there is manifestation following effort, there the cause of non-perception — namely obstruction — is applicable; and through the removal of the obstruction, the manifestation (characterized as perception) of the object that follows effort occurs.

children.text:
% prayatnānantarabhāvino ...] p.1153
na tu śabdasyānupalabdhikāraṇaṃ kiñcid upapadyate, yasya prayatnānantaram apohāc chabdasyopalabhilakṣaṇā 'bhivyaktir bhavatīti, tasmād utpadyate śabdo nābhivyajyate iti//38//
children.translated_text:
[Note: prayatnānantarabhāvino ...] p.1153
But no cause of non-perception for sound is applicable, through whose removal by effort the manifestation (characterized as perception) of sound would occur. Therefore, sound is produced, not manifested. //38//

children.text:
% p.1154
hetoś ced anaikāntikatvam upapadyate anaikātikatvād asādhakaḥ syād iti/ yadi cānaikāntikatvād asādhakatvam ---
children.translated_text:
[p.1154]
If the non-conclusiveness of the reason is applicable — then due to non-conclusiveness it would be non-probative. And if because of non-conclusiveness it is non-probative —
<s>NyS</s> 5.1.39: The same fault applies to the counter-argument as well.

children.text: pratiṣedho 'py anaikāntikaḥ, kiñcit pratiṣedhati kiñcin neti anaikāntikatvād asādhaka iti/ atha vā śabdasyānityatvapakṣe prayatnānantaram utpādo nābhivyaktir iti viśeṣahetvabhāvaḥ, nityatvapakṣe 'pi prayatnānantaram abhivyaktir notpāda iti viśeṣahetvabhāvaḥ/ so 'yam ubhayapakṣasamo viśeṣahetvabhāva ity ubhayam apy anaikātikam iti//39//
children.translated_text: The counter-argument too is non-conclusive (<s>anaikāntika</s>) — it refutes some things but not others — and because of its non-conclusiveness, it is ineffective. Alternatively: on the position that sound is impermanent, its origination after effort, not its manifestation, (is maintained) — and the absence of a distinguishing reason (follows); on the position that sound is permanent too, its manifestation after effort, not its origination, (is maintained) — and the absence of a distinguishing reason (follows). This absence of a distinguishing reason is equal in both positions — therefore both are non-conclusive. // 39 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.40]
<s>NyS</s> 5.1.40: The same applies everywhere.

children.text: sarveṣu sādharmyaprabhṛtiṣu pratiṣedhahetuṣu yatra yatrāviśeṣo dṛśyate tatrobhayoḥ pakṣayoḥ samaḥ prasajyata iti//40//
children.translated_text: In all the counter-reasons beginning with <s>sādharmya</s> (similarity), wherever a lack of distinction is seen, the fault is equal in both positions. // 40 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.41]
<s>NyS</s> 5.1.41: In the counter-refutation of the refutation, the fault is like that of the refutation.

children.text: yo 'yaṃ pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣo 'naikāntikatvam āpadyate so 'yaṃ pratiṣedhasya vipratiṣedhe 'pi samānaḥ/
children.translated_text: This fault of non-conclusiveness that attaches to the counter-argument equally applies to the counter-refutation of the refutation.

children.text:
% vipratiṣedhe 'pi samānaḥ/] p.1156
tatrānityaḥ śabdaḥ prayatnānantarīyakatvād iti sādhanavādinaḥ sthāpanā prathamaḥ pakṣaḥ/ ``prayatnakāryānekatvāt kāryasama'' iti dūṣaṇavādinaḥ pratiṣedhahetunā dvitīyaḥ pakṣaḥ/ sa ca pratiṣedha ity ucyate/ tasyāsya pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa iti tṛtīyaḥ pakṣaḥ vipratiṣedha ucyate/ tasmin pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣo 'naikāntikatvaṃ caturthaḥ pakṣaḥ//41//
children.translated_text:
[Note: vipratiṣedhe 'pi samānaḥ/] p.1156
Therein: 'sound is impermanent because it arises immediately after effort' — this establishment by the proponent is the first position. 'Because the effects of effort are many, this is the <s>kāryasama</s> (objection of equal applicability to the effect)' — this, by the counter-reason of the objector, is the second position. And that is called the refutation. 'The same fault applies to the refutation as well' — this is the third position, called the counter-refutation. 'In the counter-refutation of the refutation too, the same fault of non-conclusiveness' — this is the fourth position. // 41 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.42]

children.text: NyS_5,1.42: pratiṣedhaṃ sadoṣam abhyupetya pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe samāno doṣaprasaṅgo matānujñā ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.1.42: Having accepted the refutation as faulty, if one adduces the same fault in the counter-refutation, the consequence is <s>matānujñā</s> (conceding the opponent's position).

children.text: pratiṣedhaṃ dvitīyaṃ pakṣaṃ sadoṣam abhyupetya taduddhāram akṛtvānujñāya pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe tṛtīyapakṣe samānam anaikāntikatvam iti samānaṃ dūṣaṇaṃ prasañjayato dūṣaṇavādino matānujñā prasajyata iti pañcamaḥ pakṣaḥ//42//
children.translated_text: Having accepted the refutation — the second position — as faulty, without removing that fault and (instead) granting it, if one adduces the same non-conclusiveness in the counter-refutation — the third position — then for the objector who adduces the same fault, the consequence of <s>matānujñā</s> (conceding the opponent's position) arises. This is the fifth position. // 42 //
[Section: NySBh_5,1.43]

children.text: NyS_5,1.43: svapakṣalakṣaṇāpekṣopapattyupasaṃhāre hetunirdeśe parapakṣadoṣābhyupagamāt samāno doṣaḥ ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.1.43: When in the statement of a reason, in the application and conclusion that depend on the defining characteristic of one's own position, there is acceptance of the fault in the opponent's position — then the fault is equal.

children.text: sthāpanāpakṣe prayatnakāryānekatvād iti doṣaḥ sthāpanāhetuvādinaḥ svapakṣalakṣaṇo bhavati/ kasmāt? svapakṣasamutthatvāt/ so 'yaṃ svapakṣalakṣaṇaṃ doṣam apekṣamāṇo 'nuddhṛtyānujñāya pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa ity upapadyamānaṃ doṣaṃ parapakṣe upasaṃharati/ itthaṃ cānaikāntikaḥ pratiṣedha iti hetuṃ nirdiśati/ tatra svapakṣalakṣaṇāpekṣayopapadyamānadoṣopasaṃhāre hetunirdeśe ca saty anena parapakṣadoṣo 'bhyupagato bhavati/ kathaṃ kṛtvā? yaḥ pareṇa prayatnakāryānekatvād ityādinānaikāntikadoṣa uktaḥ, tam anuddhṛtya pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa ity āha/ evaṃ sthāpanāṃ sadoṣām abhyupetya pratiṣedhe 'pi samānaṃ doṣaṃ prasañjayataḥ parapakṣābhyupagamāt samāno doṣo bhavati/
children.translated_text: In the establishment-position, the fault 'because the effects of effort are many' pertains to the defining characteristic of the proponent's own position. Why? Because it arises from his own position. Now, this proponent, depending on the fault that pertains to the defining characteristic of his own position, without removing it and (instead) granting it, applies the inferred fault to the opponent's position (in the argument) 'the same fault applies to the refutation as well.' Thus he states a reason: 'the refutation is non-conclusive.' When, in that context, there is an application of the inferred fault and a statement of a reason that depend on the defining characteristic of one's own position, this person has (thereby) accepted the fault in the opponent's position. How so? The fault of non-conclusiveness stated by the opponent through 'because the effects of effort are many' and so on — without removing that, he says 'the same fault applies to the refutation as well.' Thus, having accepted the establishment as faulty, for one who adduces the same fault in the refutation, because of accepting the opponent's position, the fault is equal.

children.text:
% prasañjayataḥ parapakṣābhyupagamāt...] p.1158
yathā parasya pratiṣedhaṃ sadoṣam abhyupetya pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣaprasaṅgo matānujñā prasajyata iti, tathāsyāpi sthāpanāṃ sadoṣām abhyupetya pratiṣedhe 'pi samānaṃ doṣaṃ prasañjayato matānujñā prasajyata iti/ sa khalv ayaṃ ṣaṣṭhaḥ pakṣaḥ/
tatra khalu sthāpanāhetuvādinaḥ prathamatṛtīyapañcamapakṣāḥ, pratiṣedhahetuvādinaḥ dvitīyacaturthaṣaṣṭhapakṣāḥ/ teṣāṃ sādhvasādhutāyāṃ mīmāṃsyamānāyāṃ caturthaṣaṣṭhayor arthāviśeṣāt punaruktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ/ caturthapakṣe samānadoṣatvaṃ parasyocyate --``pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe pratiṣedhadoṣavad doṣa'' iti/ ṣaṣṭhe 'pi ``parapakṣadoṣābhyupagamāt samāno doṣa'' iti samānadoṣatvam evocyate, nārthaviśeṣaḥ kaścid asti/ samānas tṛṭīyapañcamayoḥ punaruktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ, tṛṭīyapakṣe 'pi ``pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa'' iti samānatvam abhyupagamyate/ pañcamapakṣe 'pi ``pratiṣedhavipratiṣedhe samāno doṣaprasaṅgo'' 'bhyupagamyate, nārthaviśeṣaḥ kaścid ucyata iti/ tatra pañcamaṣaṣṭhapakṣayor arthāviśeṣāt punaruktadoṣaprasaṅgaḥ, tṛtīyacaturthayor matānujñā, prathamadvitīyayor viśeṣahetvabhāva iti ṣaṭpakṣyām ubhayor asiddhiḥ/
kadā ṣaṭpakṣī? yadā ``pratiṣedhe 'pi samāno doṣa'' ity evaṃ pravarttate/ tadobhayoḥ pakṣayor asiddhiḥ/ yadā tu ``kāryānyatve prayatnāhetutvam anupalabdhikāraṇopapatter'' ity anena tṛṭīyapakṣo yujyate,
children.translated_text:
[Note: prasañjayataḥ parapakṣābhyupagamāt...] p.1158
Just as, for the opponent, having accepted the refutation as faulty, the consequence of <s>matānujñā</s> (conceding the opponent's position) arises in the counter-refutation because of adducing the same fault — so too for this (proponent), having accepted the establishment as faulty, because of adducing the same fault in the refutation, the consequence of <s>matānujñā</s> arises. This is the sixth position.
Therein, the proponent of the establishment-reason has the first, third, and fifth positions; the proponent of the refutation-reason has the second, fourth, and sixth positions. When their validity or invalidity is being examined: between the fourth and sixth, because there is no difference in meaning, the fault of redundancy arises. In the fourth position, it is stated that the fault is equal for the opponent — 'in the counter-refutation of the refutation, the fault is like that of the refutation.' In the sixth too, 'because of accepting the fault in the opponent's position, the fault is equal' — equality of fault is stated, and there is no difference in meaning. The same fault of redundancy (applies) between the third and fifth — in the third position too, equality is accepted in 'the same fault applies to the refutation as well'; in the fifth position too, 'the consequence of the same fault in the counter-refutation' is accepted — and no difference in meaning is stated. Between the fifth and sixth positions, because there is no difference in meaning, the fault of redundancy arises; between the third and fourth, <s>matānujñā</s> (conceding the opponent's position follows); between the first and second, the absence of a distinguishing reason — thus in the six-position (analysis), neither side's (thesis) is established.
When does the six-position (analysis) arise? When it proceeds as 'the same fault applies to the refutation as well.' Then neither position is established. But when the third position is properly (formulated) as 'because, when the effect is different, effort would not be a cause, since the cause of non-apprehension is accounted for,'

children.text:
% tṛtīyapakṣo yujyate,] p.1159
tadā viśeṣahetuvacanāt ``prayatnānantaram ātmalābhaḥ śabdasya, nābhivyaktir'' iti siddhaḥ prathamapakṣo na ṣaṭpakṣī pravartata iti//43//
children.translated_text:
[Note: tṛtīyapakṣo yujyate,] p.1159
then, because a distinguishing reason is stated — 'after effort, there is the origination of sound, not its manifestation' — the first position is established, and the six-position (analysis) does not arise. // 43 //
Thus ends the first section of the fifth chapter in the revered <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> of <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.

children.text:
% p.1160
nyāyadarśanam
pañcamādhyāyasya dvitīyam āhnikam
vipratipattyapratipattyor vikalpān nigrahasthānabahutvam iti saṅkṣepeṇoktam, tad idānīṃ vibhajanīyam/ nigrahasthānāni khalu parājayavastūny aparādhādhikaraṇāni prāyeṇa pratijñādyavayavāśrayāṇi tattvavādinam atattvavādinaṃ cābhisaṃplavante/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1160]
<s>Nyāyadarśana</s> (The Nyāya System)
Second section of the fifth chapter.
It was stated in summary that the multiplicity of <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat) consists in the alternatives of misapprehension and non-apprehension. That is now to be analyzed. The <s>nigrahasthānas</s> are indeed grounds for defeat, occasions of error, and are generally based on the members (of the syllogism) such as the thesis and the rest; they befall both the speaker of truth and the speaker of untruth.
[Note: prāyeṇa ... cābhisaṃplavante/] p.1162
[Section: NySBh_5,2.1]
Their classification —

children.text: NyS_5,2.1: pratijñāhāniḥ pratijñāntaraṃ pratijñāvirodhaḥ pratijñāsannyāso hetvantaram arthāntaraṃ nirarthakam avijñātārtham apārthakam aprāptakālaṃ nyūnam adhikaṃ punaruktam ananubhāṣaṇam ajñānam apratibhā vikṣepo matānujñā paryanuyojyopekṣaṇaṃ niranuyojyānuyogo 'pasiddhānto hetvābhāsāś ca nigrahasthānāni ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.2.1: The <s>nigrahasthānas</s> (points of defeat) are: abandoning the thesis (<s>pratijñāhāni</s>), shifting to another thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>), contradicting the thesis (<s>pratijñāvirodha</s>), renouncing the thesis (<s>pratijñāsannyāsa</s>), shifting the reason (<s>hetvantara</s>), shifting the meaning (<s>arthāntara</s>), meaninglessness (<s>nirarthaka</s>), unintelligibility (<s>avijñātārtha</s>), incoherence (<s>apārthaka</s>), untimeliness (<s>aprāptakāla</s>), deficiency (<s>nyūna</s>), redundancy (<s>adhika</s>), repetition (<s>punarukta</s>), failure to respond (<s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s>), ignorance (<s>ajñāna</s>), lack of ready wit (<s>apratibhā</s>), evasion (<s>vikṣepa</s>), conceding the opponent's position (<s>matānujñā</s>), overlooking the censurable (<s>paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s>), censuring the uncensurable (<s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s>), deviation from one's own doctrine (<s>apasiddhānta</s>), and fallacious reasons (<s>hetvābhāsa</s>).

[Note: p.1163]
These are classified into twenty-two and defined —
[Section: NySBh_5,2.2]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.2: Accepting the property of the counter-example in one's own example is abandoning the thesis (<s>pratijñāhāni</s>).

children.text: sādhyadharmapratyanīkena dharmeṇa pratyavasthite pratidraṣṭāntadharmaṃ svadṛṣṭānte 'bhyanujānan pratijñāṃ jahātīti pratjñāhāniḥ/ nidarśanam --- ``aindriyakatvād anityaḥ śabdo ghaṭavad'' ity kṛte apara āha -- dṛṣṭam aindriyakatvaṃ sāmānye nitye, kasmān na tathā śabda iti pratyavasthite idam āha ---
children.translated_text: When an objector opposes with a counter-example having a property contrary to the property to be proven, one who accepts the property of the counter-example in one's own example abandons the thesis — this is <s>pratijñāhāni</s>. Illustration: When one says 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses, like a pot,' another says — 'perceptibility to the senses is observed in the universal (<s>sāmānya</s>), which is permanent; why should sound not be likewise?' — and to this objection, one replies:

children.text:
% pratyavasthite idam āha ---] p.1164
yady aindriyakaṃ sāmānyaṃ nityaṃ kāmaṃ ghaṭo nityo 'stv iti/
children.translated_text:
[Note: pratyavasthite idam āha ---] p.1164
'If the universal, being perceptible to the senses, is permanent, then let the pot too be permanent!'

children.text:
% p.1165
sa khalv ayaṃ sādhakasya dṛṣṭāntasya nityatvaṃ prasañjayan nigamanāntam eva pakṣaṃ jahāti, pakṣaṃ jahatpratijñāṃ jahātīty ucyate, pratijñāśrayatvāt pakṣasyeti//2//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1165]
This (proponent), by entailing the permanence of his own probative example, abandons the position up to and including the conclusion; one who abandons the position is said to abandon the thesis, because the position is the basis of the thesis. // 2 //
[Section: NySBh_5,2.3]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.3: When the thesis is refuted, the statement of another meaning due to differentiation of properties is shifting to another thesis (<s>pratijñāntara</s>).

children.text: pratijñātārtho ``anityaḥ śabda aindriyakatvād ghaṭavad'' ity ukte yo 'sya pratiṣedhaḥ pratidṛṣṭāntena hetuvyabhicāraḥ --- sāmānyam aindriyakaṃ nityam iti, tasmiṃś ca pratijñātārthapratiṣedhe, ``dharmavikalpād'' iti dṛṣṭāntapratidṛṣṭāntayoḥ sādharmyayoge dharmabhedāt sāmānyam aindriyakaṃ sarvagatam aindriyakas tv asarvagato ghaṭa iti dharmavikalpāt, ``tadarthanirdeśa'' iti sādhyasiddhyartham/ katham? yathā ghaṭo 'sarvagata evaṃ śabdo 'py asarvagato ghaṭavad evānitya iti/
children.translated_text: The thesis is: 'Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses, like a pot.' The refutation of this through a counter-example is the deviation of the reason — 'the universal is perceptible to the senses but is not impermanent.' When this refutation of the thesis (occurs), 'due to differentiation of properties' means: because of the difference in properties between the example and counter-example when (one attempts) their agreement in similarity — 'the universal is perceptible to the senses and all-pervading, but the pot, being perceptible to the senses, is not all-pervading' — due to this differentiation of properties, the 'statement of another meaning' is for the purpose of establishing the thesis. How? 'Just as the pot is not all-pervading, so too sound, being not all-pervading and like the pot, is impermanent.'

children.text:
% p.1168
tatrānityaḥ śabda iti pūrvā pratijñā, asarvagata iti dvitīyā pratijñā pratijñāntaram/ tat kathaṃ nigrahasthām iti? na pratijñāyāḥ sādhanaṃ pratijñāntaram, kiṃ tu hetudṛṣṭāntau sādhanaṃ pratijñāyāḥ, tad etad asādhanopādānam anarthakam iti/ ānarthakyān nigrahasthānam iti//3//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1168]
Therein, 'sound is impermanent' is the first thesis; 'sound is not all-pervading' is a second thesis — a shifting to another thesis. How is that a point of defeat? Another thesis is not a proof of the thesis; rather, the reason and the example are the proof of the thesis. This adoption of a non-proof is meaningless. Because of its meaninglessness, it is a point of defeat. // 3 //
[Section: NySBh_5,2.4]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.4: The contradiction between the thesis and the reason is <s>pratijñāvirodha</s> (thesis-contradiction).

children.text: guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyam iti pratijñā, ``rūpādito 'rthāntarasyānupalabdher'' iti hetuḥ/
children.translated_text: The thesis is: 'substance is distinct from qualities.' The reason is: 'because nothing other than color and the like is perceived.'

children.text:
% p.1170
so 'yaṃ pratijñāhetvor virodhaḥ/ katham? yadi guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyam, rūpādibhyo 'rthāntarasyānupalabdhir nopapadyate/ atha rūpādibhyo 'rthāntarasyānupalabdhiḥ, guṇavyatiriktaṃ dravyam iti nopapadyate/
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1170]
This is a contradiction between the thesis and the reason. How? If substance is distinct from qualities, then the non-perception of something other than color and the like is not tenable. And if nothing other than color and the like is perceived, then (the claim that) substance is distinct from qualities is not tenable.

children.text:
% nopapadyate/] p.1171
guṇavyatiriktaṃ ca dravyaṃ rūpādibhyaś cārthāntarasyānupalabdhir iti virudhyate --- vyāhanyate na sambhavatīti//4//
children.translated_text:
[Note: nopapadyate/] p.1171
'Substance is distinct from qualities' and 'nothing other than color and the like is perceived' — these are contradictory, mutually incompatible, impossible together. // 4 //
[Section: NySBh_5,2.5]
<s>NyS</s> 5.2.5: The denial of the thesis-meaning when the position is refuted is <s>pratijñāsannyāsa</s> (renouncing the thesis).

children.text: anityaḥ śabda aindriyakatvād ity ukte paro brūyāt sāmānyam aindriyakaṃ na cānityam,
children.translated_text: When it is stated 'sound is impermanent because it is perceptible to the senses,' the opponent says: 'the universal is perceptible to the senses but is not impermanent;

children.text:
% p.1173
evaṃ śabdo 'py aindriyako na cānitya iti/ evaṃ pratiṣiddhe pakṣe yadi brūyāt --- ``ka punar āhānityaḥ śabda'' iti, so 'yaṃ pratijñātārthanihnavaḥ pratijñāsannyāsa iti//5//
children.translated_text:
[Note: p.1173]
likewise sound too is perceptible to the senses but is not impermanent.' When the position has been thus refuted, if one says 'but who ever said sound is impermanent?' — this denial of the thesis-meaning is <s>pratijñāsannyāsa</s> (renouncing the thesis). // 5 //
[Section: NySBh_5,2.6]

children.text: NyS_5,2.6: aviśeṣokte hetau pratiṣiddhe viśeṣam icchato hetvantaram ||
children.translated_text: <s>NyS</s> 5.2.6: When a reason stated without specificity is refuted, seeking specificity is shifting the reason (<s>hetvantara</s>).

children.text: nidarśanam --- ekaprakṛtīdaṃ vyaktam iti pratijñā/ kasmād dhetoḥ? ekaprakṛtīnāṃ vikārāṇāṃ parimāṇāt/ mṛtpūrvakāṇāṃ śarāvādīnāṃ dṛṣṭaṃ parimāṇam, yāvān prakṛter vyūho bhavati tāvān vikāra iti/ dṛṣṭaṃ ca prativikāraṃ parimāṇam/ asti cedaṃ parimāṇam prativyaktaṃ tadekaprakṛtīnāṃ vikārāṇāṃ parimāṇāt paśyāmo vyaktam idam ekaprakṛtīti/
children.translated_text: Illustration: The thesis is 'this manifest (world) has a single material cause.' For what reason? 'Because the products of a single material cause have a (definite) measure.' The (definite) measure of saucers and the like, which are preceded by clay, is observed — the product has the same extent as the arrangement of the material cause. And the (definite) measure is observed for each product. And this (definite) measure exists for each manifest (thing); therefore, from the (definite) measure of products of a single material cause, we see that this manifest (world) has a single material cause.

children.text:
% p.1174
asya vyabhicāreṇa pratyavasthānaṃ --- nānāprakṛtīnām ekaprakṛtīnāṃ ca vikārāṇāṃ dṛṣṭaṃ parimāṇam iti/ evaṃ pratyavasthite āha --- ekaprakṛtisamanvaye sati śarāvādivikārāṇāṃ parimāṇadarśanāt/ sukhaduḥkhamohasamanvitaṃ hīdaṃ vyaktaṃ parimitaṃ gṛhyate, --- tatra prakṛtyantararūpasamanvayābhāve saty ekaprakṛtitvam iti/ tad idam aviśeṣokte hetau pratiṣiddhe viśeṣaṃ bruvato hetvantaraṃ bhavati/ sati ca hetvantarabhāve pūrvasya hetor asādhakatvān nigrahasthānam/ hetvantaravacane sati yadi hetvarthanidarśano dṛṣṭānta upādīyate,
children.translated_text: The rejoinder to this, through its deviation, [is as follows]: the [fixed] magnitude of products is observed both for those having diverse material causes and for those having a single material cause. When this rejoinder is made, he says: because of the observation of the magnitude of products like plates and the like, when there is the continuity of a single material cause. For this manifest [world] is perceived as finite, being accompanied by pleasure, pain, and delusion — and in the absence of the continuity of the form of another material cause, it has a single material cause. Now, when the [original] reason, stated without specification, has been refuted, the stating of a specification becomes a different reason. And when there is a different reason, the previous reason fails to establish [the thesis] — this is a point of defeat. If, when stating a different reason, an example illustrating the meaning of the reason is adduced —

children.text:
% dṛṣṭānta upādīyate,] p.1175
nedaṃ vyaktam ekaprakṛti bhavati, prakṛtyantaropādānāt/ atha nopādīyate, dṛṣṭānte hetvarthasyānidarśitasya sādhakabhāvānupapatter ānarthakyād dhetor anivṛttaṃ nigrahasthānam iti//6//
children.translated_text: [then one should say:] 'This manifest [world] does not have a single material cause, because of the presence of another material cause.' But if [such an example] is not adduced, then since the meaning of the reason that is not illustrated in the example cannot function as a proof, the reason is futile — and the point of defeat remains unresolved. //6//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.7: <s>Arthāntara</s> (irrelevance) is a meaning unconnected with the subject at hand.

children.text: yathoktalakṣaṇe pakṣapratipakṣaparigrahe (corr.; pakṣapatipakṣa-, ed.) hetutaḥ sādhyasiddhau prakṛtāyāṃ brūyāt --- nityaḥ śabdo 'sparśatvād iti hetuḥ/ hetur nāma hinoter dhātos tuni pratyaye kṛdantaṃ padam/ padaṃ ca nāmākhyātopasarganipātāḥ/ abhidheyasya kriyāntarayogād viśiṣyamāṇarūpaḥ śabdo ``nāma''/ kriyākārakasamudāyaḥ kārakasaṅkhyāviśiṣṭakriyākālayogābhidhāyākhyātam, dhātvarthamātraṃ ca kālābhidhānaviśiṣṭam/ prayogeṣv arthād abhidyamānārūpā nipātāḥ/
children.translated_text: In the adoption of thesis and counter-thesis as described, when the establishment of what is to be proved through a reason is the subject at hand, one might say: 'Sound is eternal because of intangibility' — that is the <s>hetu</s> (reason). The word '<s>hetu</s>' is a nominal form derived from the root <s>hi</s> with the suffix <s>tun</s>. And a word is either a noun, a verb, a prefix, or an indeclinable. A sound whose form is distinguished by the connection of the thing to be expressed with another action is called a 'noun.' A verb expresses the combination of action and case-relation, the connection of action distinguished by case-number with time, and the mere meaning of the root distinguished by the expression of time. Indeclinables are those whose form is expressed from the context in [actual] usage.

children.text:
% -rūpā nipātāḥ/] p.1177
upasṛjyamānāḥ kriyāvadyotakā upasargā ity evamādi/ tadarthāntaraṃ veditavyam iti//7//
children.translated_text: Prefixes are those that are attached [to verbs] and illuminate the action — and so forth. That [digression] should be understood as <s>arthāntara</s> (irrelevance). //7//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.8: [A statement that is] meaningless, like the recitation of phonemes in order.

children.text: yathā 'nityaḥ śabdaḥ --- kacaṭatapāḥ, javagaḍadaśatvāt, jhabhañ ghaḍhadhaṣavad iti ----
children.translated_text: For example: 'Sound is eternal — <s>ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa</s>, because of <s>ja-va-ga-ḍa-da-śa-tva</s>, like <s>jha-bha-ña-gha-ḍha-dha-ṣa-va</s>' —

children.text:
% p.1178
evamprakāraṃ nirarthakam/ abhidhānābhidheyabhāvānupapattau arthagater abhāvād varṇā eva krameṇa nirdiśyanta iti//8//
children.translated_text: such is meaningless. Since the relationship between signifier and signified is untenable, there is no conveyance of meaning — only phonemes are recited in order. //8//

children.text: NyS_5,2.9: pariṣatprativādibhyāṃ trir abhihitam apy avijñātam avijñātārtham ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.9: What is not understood even when stated three times by the assembly and the opponent is <s>avijñātārtha</s> (unintelligible).

children.text: yad vākyaṃ pariṣadā prativādinā ca trir abhihitam api na vijñāyate śliṣṭaśabdam apratītaprayogam atidrutoccaritam ity evamādinā kāraṇena,
children.translated_text: A statement which, even when stated three times by the assembly and the opponent, is not understood — due to compressed wording, unfamiliar usage, excessively rapid utterance, and other such reasons —

children.text:
% -pratītaprayogam ... kāraṇena,] p.1179
tadavijñātam avijñātārtham asāmarthyasaṃvaraṇāya prayuktam iti nigrahasthānam iti//9//
children.translated_text: that unintelligible, unintelligible-in-meaning [statement], employed to conceal one's incapacity, is a point of defeat. //9//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.10: What is meaningless due to the impossibility of sequential connection is <s>apārthaka</s> (incoherent).

children.text: yatrānekasya padasya vākyasya vā paurvāparyeṇānvayayogo nāstīty asambaddhārthatvagṛhyate, tat samudāyārthasyāpāyād apārthakam/ yathā --- daśa dāḍimāni, ṣaḍ apūpāḥ;
children.translated_text: Where there is no connection through sequence of multiple words or sentences, such that their disconnected meaning is grasped, that — because the collective meaning is lost — is incoherent. For example: 'Ten pomegranates, six cakes;

children.text:
% p.1180
kuṇḍam, ajājinam, palalapiṇḍaḥ, atha raurukam etad, kumāryāḥ pāyaṃ tasyāḥ pitā 'pratiśīna iti//10//
children.translated_text: a pot, an antelope skin, a lump of rice-husks, now this is a rauruka deer, a girl's drink, her father is unshaven.' //10//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.11: A statement with the members [of the syllogism] transposed is <s>aprāptakāla</s> (untimely).

children.text: pratijñādīnām avayavānāṃ yathālakṣaṇam arthavaśāt kramaḥ, tatrāvayavaviparyāsena vacanam aprāaptakālam asambaddhārthaṃ nigrahasthānam iti//11//
children.translated_text: The members — proposition and the rest — have an order determined by the nature of their meaning according to their definitions. A statement with the transposition of these members is untimely, with disconnected meaning — a point of defeat. //11//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.12: What is deficient by even one of the members [of the syllogism] is <s>nyūna</s> (deficient).

children.text: pratijñādīnām avayavānām anyatamenāpy avayavena hīnaṃ nyūnaṃ nigrahasthānam, sādhanābhāve sādhyāsiddhir iti//12//
children.translated_text: What is deficient by even one of the members — proposition and the rest — is <s>nyūna</s> (deficient), a point of defeat, since in the absence of the means of proof, what is to be proved is not established. //12//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.13: What has more than the reason and example is <s>adhika</s> (redundant).

children.text: ekena kṛtatvād anyatarasyānarthakyam iti, tad etan niyamābhupagame veditavyam iti//13//
children.translated_text: Since the task is accomplished by one, the other is futile — and this should be understood when a restriction is accepted. //13//

children.text: NyS_5,2.14: śabdārthayoḥ punar vacanaṃ punaruktam anyatrānuvādāt ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.14: The repetition of a word or meaning is <s>punarukta</s> (tautology), except in the case of restatement.

children.text:
anyatrānuvādāt śabdapunaruktam arthapunaruktaṃ vā, nityaḥ śabdo nityaḥ śabda iti śabdapunaruktam/ arthapunaruktam --- anityaḥ śabdo nirodhadharmako dhvanir iti/
anuvāde tv apunaruktaṃ śabdābhyāsād arthaviśeṣopapatteḥ/ yathā hetvapadeśāt pratijñāyāḥ punar vacanaṃ nigamanam iti//14//
children.translated_text: Except in the case of restatement, there is verbal repetition or repetition of meaning. 'Sound is eternal, sound is eternal' — this is verbal repetition. Repetition of meaning: 'Sound is non-eternal, subject to destruction, a noise.' But in a restatement, it is not repetition, since from the reiteration of words, a specification of meaning is warranted. For example, the restatement of the proposition after the statement of the reason is the conclusion (<s>nigamana</s>). //14//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.15: The restatement in one's own words of what is already obtained from the meaning [is also tautology].

children.text: punaruktam iti prakṛtam/ nidarśanam --- utpattidharmakatvād anityam ity uktvā arthād āpannasya yo 'bhidhāyakaḥ śabdas tena svaśabdena brūyād anutpattidharmakaṃ nityam iti,
children.translated_text: <s>Punarukta</s> (tautology) is the subject at hand. An illustration: having said 'because of being subject to origination, it is non-eternal,' if one restates in one's own words what is already obtained from the meaning — 'what is not subject to origination is eternal' —

children.text:
% -pannasya yo ... nityam iti,] p.1188
tac ca punarukataṃ veditavyam/ arthasampratyayārthe śabdaprayoge pratītaḥ so 'rtho 'rthāpttyeti//15//
children.translated_text: that should be understood as tautology. When a word is used for the purpose of conveying a meaning, that meaning, being obtained [already], is obtained from the meaning. //15//

children.text: NyS_5,2.16: vijñātasya pariṣadā, trir abhihitasyāpy apratyuccāraṇam ananubhāṣaṇam ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.16: <s>Ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (non-response) is the failure to repeat what has been understood by the assembly, even when stated three times.

children.text: vijñātasya vākyārthasya pariṣadā, prativādinā trir abhihitasya yad apratyauccāraṇaṃ tad ananubhāṣaṇaṃ nāma nigrahasthānam iti/ apratyuccārayan kimāśrayaṃ parapakṣapratiṣedhaṃ brūyāt//16//
children.translated_text: When a statement whose meaning has been understood by the assembly, stated three times by the opponent, is not repeated — that non-repetition is the point of defeat called <s>ananubhāṣaṇa</s> (non-response). For without responding, on what basis would one state the refutation of the opponent's thesis? //16//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.17: And what is not understood is <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance).

children.text: vijñātārthasya pariṣadā, prativādinā trir abhihitasya yad avijñātaṃ tad ajñānaṃ nāma nigrahasthānam iti/ ayaṃ khalv avijñāya kasya pratiṣedhaṃ brūyād iti//17//
children.translated_text: When a statement whose meaning has been understood by the assembly, stated three times by the opponent, is not understood — that is the point of defeat called <s>ajñāna</s> (ignorance). For this person, not having understood, whose [thesis] would he refute? //17//
