<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.18: The inability to formulate a reply is <s>apratibhā</s> (lack of ready wit).

children.text: parapakṣapratiṣedha uttaram, tad yadā na pratipadyate tadā nigṛhīto bhavati//18//
children.translated_text: A reply is the refutation of the opponent's thesis. When one is unable to formulate it, one is defeated. //18//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.19: <s>Vikṣepa</s> (evasion) is the interruption of the debate due to being occupied with another task.

children.text: yatra kartavyaṃ vyāsajya kathāṃ vyavacchinatti --- idaṃ me karaṇīyaṃ vidyate, tasmin avasite paścāt kathayāmīti, vikṣepo nāma nigrahasthānam/ ekanigrahāvasānāyāṃ kathāyāṃ svayam eva kathāntaraṃ pratipadyata iti//19//
children.translated_text: Where one interrupts the debate by interposing a task [to be done] — 'I have something that needs to be done; when that is completed, I shall debate afterwards' — that is the point of defeat called <s>vikṣepa</s> (evasion). When the debate is to end with the defeat of one [party], he himself takes up another debate. //19//

children.text: NyS_5,2.20: svapakṣe doṣābhyupagamāt parapakṣe doṣaprasaṅgo matānujñā ||
children.translated_text: <s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.20: <s>Matānujñā</s> (concession to the opponent) is the consequence of a fault in the opponent's thesis [arising] from having accepted a fault in one's own thesis.

children.text: yaḥ pareṇa coditaṃ doṣaṃ svapakṣe 'bhyupagamyānuddhṛtya vadati --- bhavatpakṣe 'pi samāno doṣa iti,
children.translated_text: One who, having accepted without removing a fault pointed out by the opponent in one's own thesis, says: 'The same fault exists in your thesis as well' —

children.text:
% doṣa iti,] p.1194
sa svapakṣe doṣābhyupagamāt parapakṣe doṣaṃ prasañjayan paramatam anujānātīti matānujñāṃ nāma nigrahasthānam āpadyata iti//20//
children.translated_text: such a person, by accepting a fault in his own thesis while imputing a fault to the opponent's thesis, concedes the opponent's view — and thus incurs the point of defeat called <s>matānujñā</s> (concession to the opponent). //20//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.21: <s>Paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa</s> (overlooking what is censurable) is the failure to censure one who has incurred a point of defeat.

children.text: paryanuyojyo nāma nigrahopapattyā codanīyaḥ, tasyopekṣaṇaṃ nigrahasthānaṃ prāpto 'sīty ananuyogaḥ/ etac ca kasya parājaya ity anuyuktayā pariṣadā vacanīyam, na khalu nigrahaṃ prāptaḥ svakaupīnaṃ vivṛṇuyād iti//21//
children.translated_text: One who is censurable is one who should be challenged because defeat is warranted against him. Overlooking such a person — not challenging [him by saying] 'you have incurred a point of defeat' — [is itself a point of defeat]. And this — whose defeat it is — should be declared by the assembly when asked. For indeed, one who has incurred defeat would not [willingly] expose his own disgrace. //21//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.22: <s>Niranuyojyānuyoga</s> (censuring what is not censurable) is the charge of a point of defeat where none exists.

children.text: nigrahasthālakṣaṇasya mithyādhyavasāyād anigrahasthāne nigṛhīto 'sīti paraṃ bruvan niranuyojyānuyojgān nigṛhīto veditavya iti//22//
children.translated_text: Due to a false determination of what constitutes a point of defeat, one who says to another 'you are defeated' where no point of defeat exists should be understood as defeated himself through <s>niranuyojyānuyoga</s> (censuring what is not censurable). //22//

<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.23: <s>Apasiddhānta</s> (contradicting one's own doctrine) is the engagement in a debate that, due to a lack of consistency resulting from contradicting one's own stated position, [leads to defeat].

children.text: kasyacid arthasya tathābhāvaṃ pratijñāya pratijñātārthaviparyayād aniyamāt kathāṃ prasañjayato 'pasiddhānto veditavyaḥ/ yathā na sad ātmānaṃ jahāti, na sato vināśo, nāsad ātmānaṃ labhate, nāsad utpadyata iti siddhāntam abhyupetya svapakṣaṃ vyavasthāpayati --- ekaprakṛtīdaṃ vyaktaṃ vikārāṇām anvayadarśanāt/ mṛdanvitānāṃ śarāvādīnāṃ dṛṣṭam ekaprakṛtitvam, tathā cāyaṃ vyaktabhedaḥ sukhaduḥkhamohānvito dṛśyate/ tasmāt samanvayadarśanāt sukhādibhir ekaprakṛtīdaṃ viśvam iti/ evam uktavān anuyujyate --- atha pratṛtir vikāra iti kathaṃ lakṣitavyam iti/ yasyāvasthitasya dharmāntaranivṛttau dharmāntaraṃ pravartate, sā prakṛtiḥ/ yad dharmāntaraṃ pravartate nivartate vā sa vikāra iti/ so 'yaṃ pratijñātārthaviparyāsād aniyamāt kathāṃ prasañjayati/ pratijñātaṃ khalv anena --- nāsad āvirbhavati,
children.translated_text: Having asserted the being-so of some object, one who engages in a debate due to a lack of consistency arising from the contradiction of the asserted meaning should be understood as [guilty of] <s>apasiddhānta</s>. For example, having accepted the established doctrine that 'an existent does not lose its self, there is no destruction of the existent; a non-existent does not gain self, a non-existent does not originate,' one establishes one's own thesis: 'This manifest [world] has a single material cause, because of the observation of continuity of products.' The single-material-cause nature of plates and the like, accompanied by clay, is observed; and likewise this differentiated manifest [world] is seen to be accompanied by pleasure, pain, and delusion. Therefore, from the observation of continuity, this entire [world] has a single material cause, namely pleasure and the rest. Having stated this, he is challenged: 'Now, how is the distinction between material cause and product to be characterized?' That which, while remaining established, undergoes the cessation of one property and the arising of another — that is the material cause. The property that arises or ceases — that is the product. Now, this person engages in a debate due to the lack of consistency arising from contradicting his stated position. For he had asserted: 'A non-existent does not come into being,

children.text:
% p.1198
na sat tirobhavatīti/ sadasatoś ca tirobhāvāvirbhāvam antareṇa na kasyacit pravṛttiḥ pravṛttyuparamaś ca bhavati/ mṛdi khalv avasthitāyāṃ bhaviṣyati śarāvādilakṣaṇaṃ dharmāntaram iti pravṛttir bhavati, abhūd iti ca pravṛttyuparamaḥ/ tad etad mṛddharmāṇām api na syāt/ evaṃ pratyavasthito yadi sataś cātmahānam asataś cātmalābham abhyupaiti, tad asyāpasiddhānato nigrahasthānaṃ bhavati/ atha nābhyupaiti, pakṣo 'sya na sidhyati//23//
children.translated_text: an existent does not disappear.' But without the disappearance and appearance of existent and non-existent, there is neither the arising nor the cessation of anything. When clay remains established, the arising of the property of a plate and the like — 'it will be' — occurs; and 'it was' — the cessation of arising [occurs]. But this should not [happen] to the properties of clay either. When thus confronted, if he accepts the loss of self of the existent and the gain of self of the non-existent, then his <s>apasiddhānta</s> (contradicting his own doctrine) becomes a point of defeat. But if he does not accept it, his thesis is not established. //23//
<s>Nyāyasūtra</s> 5,2.24: And the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons) are as previously stated.

children.text: hetvābhāsāś ca nigrahasthānāni/ kiṃ punar lakṣaṇāntarayogād hetvābhāsā nigrahasthānatvam āpannāḥ yathā pramāṇāni prameyatvam ity ata āha --- yathoktā iti/ hetvābhāsalakṣaṇenaiva nigrahasthānabhāva iti/
children.translated_text: The <s>hetvābhāsas</s> (fallacious reasons) are also points of defeat. But have the <s>hetvābhāsas</s> become points of defeat through the application of a different definition, just as <s>pramāṇas</s> (means of valid knowledge) [can become] objects of valid knowledge? To this he says: 'as previously stated.' They are points of defeat by virtue of the very definition of <s>hetvābhāsa</s>.

children.text:
% p.1200
ta ime pramāṇādayaḥ padārthā uddiṣṭā lakṣitāḥ parīkṣitāś ceti//24//
children.translated_text: These categories beginning with <s>pramāṇa</s> have been enumerated, defined, and examined. //24//

children.text:
yo 'kṣapādam ṛṣiṃ nyāyaḥ pratyabhād vadatāṃ varam/
tasya vātsyāyana idaṃ bhāṣyajātam avartayat//
children.translated_text:
The <s>Nyāya</s> (system of logic) that appeared to the sage <s>Akṣapāda</s>, the foremost among speakers —
this commentary (<s>bhāṣyajāta</s>) on it was composed by <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
Thus ends the fifth chapter of the revered <s>Nyāyabhāṣya</s> by <s>Vātsyāyana</s>.
